requirements.statement: Car-years (exposure) are the number of vehicles multiplied by the policy term in years, so a 24-month policy on one vehicle represents 2 car-years of written exposure.

places.quote: A $12$-month policy contributes **one** earned car-year in total, spread pro rata over its term: written the day it is issued, earned $1/12$ per month, in force from effective date to expiry.

requirements.statement: Earned exposure is the portion of a policy's exposure for which coverage has already been provided as of a date, accruing evenly over the policy term.

places.quote: **Earned Exposure** is the portion of written exposure for which coverage has actually been provided during the period — the exposure analogue of [[Earned Premium|earned premium]], and the correct denominator for a pure premium.

requirements.statement: Calendar year earned exposure counts only the exposure earned during that calendar year, regardless of when the policy was written.

places.quote: With policies written **uniformly** through the year, a calendar year earns roughly half of that year's written exposure plus half of the prior year's.

**Calendar Year** (CY) is a data aggregation method that groups every transaction by the calendar year in which it is *booked* — premium as it is earned, losses as they are paid or as case reserves change — without regard to the policy's effective date or the claim's accident date.

requirements.statement: Policy year groups all policies by the year they were written/effective, and its earned exposure at a given evaluation date is the exposure earned to date on those policies, including earnings in later calendar years.

places.quote: **Policy Year** (PY), also called underwriting year or year of account, is a data aggregation method that groups every premium and loss transaction belonging to policies *incepting* in a given calendar year, and follows that cohort until the last claim closes.
**Policy year** earned premium comes from one cohort only, and is fully earned $24$ months after the policy year begins (for annual policies).

requirements.statement: Calendar year written exposure is recorded in the year the policy is written and is not affected by later cancellations in the original year's value; the calendar year of the transaction records any adjustment.

places.quote: **Calendar Year** (CY) is a data aggregation method that groups every transaction by the calendar year in which it is *booked* — premium as it is earned, losses as they are paid or as case reserves change — without regard to the policy's effective date or the claim's accident date.

Written premium may still change after issuance — endorsements, cancellations and [[Premium Audit|audits]] all book additional or return premium into a later period, so "written premium" for a policy year keeps moving until the audits close.

requirements.statement: When a policy is cancelled mid-term, the unearned exposure is returned as a negative written exposure (cancellation) in the period of cancellation: in calendar year it is negative in the cancellation year, and in policy year it reduces the original policy year's written exposure at later evaluations.

places.quote: In the ratemaking data both the return premium and the shortened exposure must flow through, or the average premium per [[Earned Exposure|earned exposure]] will be misstated.

Written premium may still change after issuance — endorsements, cancellations and [[Premium Audit|audits]] all book additional or return premium into a later period, so "written premium" for a policy year keeps moving until the audits close.

requirements.statement: Policy year written exposure evaluated before a cancellation occurs equals the full original written exposure, and only after the cancellation date does it reflect the reduction.

places.quote: Written premium may still change after issuance — endorsements, cancellations and [[Premium Audit|audits]] all book additional or return premium into a later period, so "written premium" for a policy year keeps moving until the audits close.

requirements.statement: Customer lifetime value (lifetime profit) analysis sums the expected profit from a policyholder over all expected future policy years, rather than only a single policy period.

places.quote: **Lifetime Value** (LTV) is the present value of the expected profit from a customer relationship over its whole life, rather than over a single policy period.

requirements.statement: Compute expected profit for each policy year as premium minus expected losses minus expenses per policy in force, using new business expense and loss assumptions in year 1 and renewal assumptions (with any given loss trend or change) in later years.

places.quote: $$\text{LTV} = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{\left(P_t - L_t - E_t\right) \times {}_{t}p}{(1 + r)^{t}}$$

requirements.statement: Persistency (retention) is the probability that a policyholder renews; cumulative persistency for a given year is the product of the renewal probabilities up to that year.

places.quote: $$\text{Retention Ratio} = \frac{\text{Policies renewed}}{\text{Policies eligible to renew}}$$

requirements.statement: Weight each year's expected profit and premium by cumulative persistency, and discount each to present value by dividing by (1+i)^(t-1), with year 1 undiscounted.

places.quote: $$\text{LTV} = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{\left(P_t - L_t - E_t\right) \times {}_{t}p}{(1 + r)^{t}}$$
$$\text{EPV of premiums} = \sum_{t=0}^{n-1} P\,{}_tp_x\,(1+r)^{-t}$$

requirements.statement: Lifetime profit as a percentage of premium equals the sum of persistency-weighted discounted profits divided by the sum of persistency-weighted discounted premiums.

places.quote: $$\text{Profit margin} = \frac{\text{NPV}}{\text{EPV of premiums}}$$

requirements.statement: Lifetime value analysis differs from standard ratemaking in that it uses a multi-year horizon, models persistency, discounts cash flows to present value, and distinguishes new from renewal business expenses, whereas standard ratemaking considers only the single period rates will be in effect.

places.quote: The professional boundary matters: the **indication** is an actuarial estimate of expected cost; LTV is a **business decision layer** applied to it.
and some model it directly with [[Lifetime Value|lifetime value]] analysis and retention and conversion models.

requirements.statement: Using credit score as a rating variable raises concerns that it lacks a demonstrable causal link to loss, may act as a proxy for socioeconomic status, and may invade insureds' privacy.

places.quote: **Social** — privacy, causality, controllability and affordability; these are where public and regulatory objections arise.

places.quote: **Social** — privacy, causality, controllability and affordability; these are where public and regulatory objections arise.

places.quote: **Operational** — objective, inexpensive to obtain and verify, not manipulable by the insured.

requirements.statement: Good rating variables show meaningful loss cost differentiation, have objective and well-defined levels, and are inexpensive to administer; social concerns alone do not preclude a variable if it is legal and meets the actuarial criteria.

places.quote: **Operational** — objective, inexpensive to obtain and verify, not manipulable by the insured.

requirements.statement: The indicated relativity of a class equals its pure premium divided by the base (or total) pure premium; the competitor relativities must be made revenue-neutral on the same base before being combined.

Under the [[Pure Premium Method|pure premium method]], it is the class pure premium divided by the base class pure premium.

requirements.statement: Under the square root rule, partial credibility is Z = sqrt(n / full credibility standard), where n is the expected claim count (exposures times frequency), and the standard is a claim count, not an exposure count.

places.quote: Partial credibility uses the **square root rule**, $Z = \sqrt{n / n_{\text{full}}}$, capped at $1$ — a class with a quarter of the required claims gets $Z = 0.50$.
It is the smallest expected claim count $n_F$ for which the observed value stays within $100k\%$ of its expected value with probability $p$.

places.quote: $$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$
$$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$

requirements.statement: After credibility weighting, re-base the relativities by dividing each by the base class's credibility-weighted relativity so the base class equals 1.000.

places.quote: $$\text{Relativity}_i = \frac{\text{Pure Premium}_i}{\text{Pure Premium}_{\text{base}}}$$

requirements.statement: If the confidence interval (about ±2 standard errors) of a GLM relativity includes the base level's value of 1.00, the level is not statistically significantly different from the base level, so the indicated factor is not supported.

places.quote: **Loss Elimination Ratio** (LER) is the proportion of ground-up losses removed by a deductible — the share of expected loss that the insured retains rather than transfers.
