$$L = \min\left(\max(A,\ r_H E),\ r_G E\right)$$

requirements.statement: Retrospective premium is adjusted periodically as reported losses are re-evaluated; when premium is at the maximum it can only stay flat or decrease (through downward loss development or claims closing below reserve), and further adverse development does not raise it.

places.quote: Outside it, nothing. So the insured is buying:
Later PDLDs fall well **below 1** as more of each new dollar of loss lands above a cap.

requirements.statement: An age-to-age (link ratio) factor is the ratio of cumulative claim counts at one development age to the cumulative count at the previous age for the same accident period.

places.quote: **Age-to-Age Factor** (link ratio) is the ratio of a cohort's cumulative amount at one maturity to its amount at the previous maturity — the observed development between two ages.

requirements.statement: Project ultimate claims by multiplying the latest cumulative value by the cumulative development factor, which is the product of the selected age-to-age factors from the current age to ultimate.

places.quote: **Chain Ladder Method** (development or link-ratio method) projects each cohort to ultimate by multiplying its latest cumulative amount by a [[Cumulative Development Factor|cumulative development factor]] derived from the historical pattern.

**Cumulative Development Factor** (CDF, or age-to-ultimate factor) is the product of all selected [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] from a given maturity through to ultimate, including the [[Tail Factor|tail]].

requirements.statement: Select age-to-age factors by averaging the observed factors in a column (e.g., a simple average of available factors).

places.quote: **Simple average** — equal weight to each year, so a small, volatile year counts as much as a large one.

requirements.statement: When age-to-age factors show seasonality across accident periods, such as systematically different factors for first-half versus second-half accident half-years, separate factors should be selected and applied for each season, not blended across seasons.
Claim counts assumed to have no development after the last age use a tail factor of 1.000, so the cumulative factor includes only the remaining age-to-age factors.

places.quote: A tail of exactly $1.000$ is itself an assumption — that development is complete — and it is the wrong one for any casualty line.

requirements.statement: An accident year's ultimate is obtained by estimating ultimate for each of its accident half-years from its own latest diagonal value and summing them.
Using shorter accident periods (half-years) rather than full accident years captures seasonality in development patterns, which annual data would average together and obscure.

places.quote: Finer periods are more responsive and show seasonality; they also thin the data and multiply the factors to select.

Short-tail reserves are also sensitive to seasonality: the December diagonal of a property triangle behaves differently from the June one, which is why quarterly rather than annual cohorts are common.

requirements.statement: With rapidly growing exposures, the average accident date within a full accident year shifts away from the midpoint; shorter accident periods keep the average accident date closer to the midpoint, making development more comparable across periods.

The case outstanding development technique estimates total unpaid claims (case outstanding plus IBNR) for an accident year by multiplying current case outstanding by a case outstanding development factor derived from benchmark reported and paid CDFs.

places.quote: **Case Outstanding Development Method** projects future payments from the **case outstanding** balance rather than from paid or reported losses — developing the reserve the claims department has already set, instead of the losses that have emerged.

requirements.statement: The case outstanding development factor equals (RCDF − 1) × PCDF / (PCDF − RCDF) + 1, equivalently RCDF × (PCDF − 1)/(PCDF − RCDF), where RCDF and PCDF are the reported and paid CDFs to ultimate; unpaid = case outstanding × this factor.
Reported claims equal ultimate divided by the reported CDF, paid claims equal ultimate divided by the paid CDF, case outstanding equals reported minus paid, and unpaid equals ultimate minus paid.

places.quote: $$\text{Unpaid} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Paid to date}$$
The reciprocal is the **percentage reported** (or paid): $p_n = 1/\text{CDF}_n$, and $1 - p_n$ is the percentage unreported.
$$\text{Reported Losses} = \text{Paid Losses} + \text{Case Reserves}$$

requirements.statement: A limitation of the case outstanding development technique is that industry benchmark CDFs may not reflect the entity's own claims mix, settlement patterns, or reserving practices.

places.quote: Two books with the same nominal line code can have very different development if one is written at higher limits.
**Industry benchmarks** — published patterns (ISO, NCCI, Schedule P aggregates) for the same line, adjusted for differences in limits, mix and case reserving.

requirements.statement: A limitation of the case outstanding development technique is that a large unusual open claim in case outstanding is scaled by the same factor and can distort the unpaid estimate.

places.quote: A [[Large Loss|shock loss]] reported early is multiplied by the full CDF.
Leaving a $\$2$M claim in an immature diagonal and multiplying it by a CDF of $4$ produces an $\$8$M estimate from one claim.

requirements.statement: A limitation of the case outstanding development technique is that the factor is highly leveraged, so small errors in the selected CDFs (especially for immature years) cause large errors in the unpaid estimate.

places.quote: Because the [[Cumulative Development Factor|CDF]] at early maturities is large, estimates are highly **leveraged**: a small proportional change in a factor moves ultimate by a large dollar amount.

requirements.statement: The case outstanding development technique is particularly useful when case outstanding is the only claims data available, such as when an entity has no paid or reported loss history.

The Bornhuetter-Ferguson method assumes that claims reported (or paid) to date carry no information about future development, so the unreported (or unpaid) portion is best estimated from the a priori expected ultimate claims rather than from emerging experience.

places.quote: **Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method** (BF) estimates ultimate losses by adding to what has actually been reported an estimate of what has *not* — computed from an a priori expectation and the percentage still unreported.

requirements.statement: The BF ultimate equals claims to date plus (1 - percent reported or paid) times the a priori expected ultimate claims (ELR x premium).

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$

requirements.statement: The BF ultimate can be written as a credibility-weighted average of the development method ultimate and the expected claims ultimate, with credibility Z equal to the percent reported (or paid), i.e. 1/CDF.

places.quote: BF is a **credibility weighting** in disguise: it equals $Z \, U_{\text{CL}} + (1-Z)\,U_0$ with $Z = 1/\text{CDF}$.

In reserving, credibility appears explicitly in the [[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method|BF method]], where $Z = 1/\text{CDF}$: the reported portion of an accident year is its own experience and the unreported portion is priced from the a priori.

In reserving, the [[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method|BF]] method is a credibility weighting of the development method (credibility $Z = 1/\text{CDF}$) with the expected claims method, which receives the complement $(1-Z)$

requirements.statement: The credibility interpretation of BF breaks down when cumulative percent reported or paid exceeds 100% (e.g. due to salvage and subrogation recoveries), since Z cannot exceed 1.

Percent reported is generally greater than percent paid at a given maturity, so the reported BF gives more weight to the development method (and less to the a priori) than the paid BF, making it more responsive to changes in claim ratios.

places.quote: **Reported (incurred) development** is normally faster than **paid development**, because claims are reported sooner than they are paid, so cumulative reported CDFs are usually smaller than paid ones at the same age.
Paid losses lag reported losses, so paid development factors are larger at every maturity

requirements.statement: The Cape Cod method estimates the expected loss ratio from the data as total reported (or paid) losses divided by total used-up premium (premium times percent reported or paid), then applies it like the BF method to the unreported portion.

places.quote: The ELR is estimated as total reported losses over total *used-up* (on-level, developed) premium across all years.

requirements.statement: Cape Cod and BF are similar in estimating unreported claims from an expected loss ratio times percent unreported, but differ in that BF uses an externally selected a priori loss ratio while Cape Cod derives it from the experience, making Cape Cod more responsive to emerging experience.

places.quote: Where no reliable external ELR exists, the [[Cape Cod Method|Cape Cod]] technique derives one from the data instead.
The whole difference between the two methods is **where the a priori comes from**: BF imports it, Cape Cod estimates it.

requirements.statement: Ultimate claim counts (or ultimate severities) equal reported counts (or severities) divided by the percentage reported at that maturity; the percent-reported factor is the inverse of the age-to-ultimate factor.

places.quote: $$\text{Ultimate Counts} = N_n \times \text{CDF}^{\text{count}}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$1 - 1/\text{CDF}$ the percentage unreported from the [[Development Triangle|development pattern]]

requirements.statement: Trend historical ultimate frequency and severity (and exposure such as payroll) to the projected accident year's level by applying the annual trend factor compounded for the number of years between each accident year and the target year.

places.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.
$$\text{Trended Exposure} = \text{Historical Exposure} \times (1 + t_E)^{n}$$
The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: Pure premium equals frequency times severity, where frequency is ultimate claim counts per unit of exposure (e.g. payroll); ultimate loss for the target year equals selected pure premium times that year's exposure.

places.quote: $$U = \text{Exposures} \times \text{Frequency}_{\text{ult}} \times S_{\text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Frequency} = \frac{\text{Number of Claims}}{\text{Earned Exposures}}$$
$$\text{Pure Premium} = \text{Frequency} \times \text{Severity}$$

requirements.statement: Accident year data affected by an unusual event (such as a temporary slowdown in claim opening) is unreliable for selecting frequency and should be excluded from the selection, while severity, being a per-claim average, may be unaffected and justified separately.

resolution.quote: judgmental selection, documented — the honest answer when the column contains a known one-off
resolution.note: Syllabus page: a period distorted by a known one-off is excluded or handled by documented judgment in the selection.

requirements.statement: Select the frequency/pure premium by averaging the trended, developed indications from the reliable accident years, with the averaging choice justified by stability.

places.quote: whether to weight the three years by premium volume (as here — summing losses and premium across years, which weights each year's loss ratio by its premium) or to select weights that give more to the most recent years

requirements.statement: IBNR equals estimated ultimate losses minus reported losses, where reported losses equal reported claim counts times reported average severity.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Reported}$$
$$\text{Severity} = \frac{\text{Total Losses}}{\text{Number of Claims}}$$

requirements.statement: Premium trend measures the change in average premium per exposure over time (due to shifts in mix of business such as coverages, deductibles, or insured characteristics), computed from written premium at current rate level divided by exposures.

places.quote: **Premium Trend** is the change over time in the average premium per exposure at a *constant rate level* — the drift caused by distributional shifts in the policies written (amounts of insurance, limits, deductibles, [[Mix of Business|mix of business]]), as distinct from deliberate [[Rate Change|rate changes]]

requirements.statement: Select a premium trend by computing average written premium per exposure for successive overlapping 12-month periods, finding the change between periods, and annualizing the per-period change to an annual trend factor.

places.quote: The trend is measured on the **average premium per exposure at current rate level**, usually from written data — a leading indicator, reflecting distributional shifts sooner than earned premium — often quarterly.

requirements.statement: In one-step trending, project the historical earned premium at current rate level by applying the trend factor raised to the period from the average written date of the historical earned premium to the average written date of the future policy period.

places.quote: The trend period $n$ runs from the average written date of the policies earning premium in the experience period to the **average written date of the policies in effect while the new rates are**

requirements.statement: For annual policies written uniformly, the average written date of a calendar year's earned premium is the start of that year (January 1), and the average written date of a one-year future rate period is its midpoint (July 1 for a Jan 1 start with one-year rates).

places.quote: for calendar-year 2011 earned premium and annual policies written in 2013, $1/1/2011$ to $6/30/2013$, or $2.5$ years.

requirements.statement: Premium trend should be based on written premium at current rate level, not at historical rate levels, because historical-rate-level premium includes the effect of rate changes, which would double-count the rate change already reflected in on-leveling.

places.quote: Written premium is the right measure for production, market share, commission (paid on writings) and for the **average written premium** series used in [[Premium Trend|premium trend]] analysis — trend is a written-level phenomenon, since it is driven by what is being sold today.

requirements.statement: Moving insureds to a higher deductible shifts more loss to the insured, lowering expected losses and the premium charged, so average premium per exposure falls relative to a projection that ignores the shift.

places.quote: a move of insureds to higher deductibles

requirements.statement: Average paid claim (severity) at a given age equals cumulative paid claims divided by cumulative closed claim counts; average reported claim equals cumulative reported claims divided by cumulative reported counts.

places.quote: \text{Avg closed claim} &= \frac{\$3{,}500{,}000}{700} \\

requirements.statement: Average case outstanding equals case outstanding claims divided by outstanding claim counts, and the closed-to-reported claim count ratio equals cumulative closed counts divided by cumulative reported counts.

places.quote: $$\text{Avg Case Outstanding} = \frac{\text{Case Reserves}}{\text{Open Claim Counts}}$$
The [[Settlement Rate|disposal rate]] is closed counts over ultimate (or reported) counts.

requirements.statement: Compare diagnostics down the columns of the triangle (same age, successive accident years), compute year-to-year changes, and compare them to the known severity trend to judge whether they are stable.

places.quote: Reading **down a column** compares years at the same age, which shows trends and mix.
Read down each column, year over year:
It should grow at roughly the severity trend.

requirements.statement: A rising closed-to-reported count ratio at a given age indicates that claims are being settled faster (a change in settlement rate).

places.quote: **Faster [[Settlement Rate|settlement]]:** closure rates and paid-to-reported rise together.
Closure at $24$ months has risen from $45\%$ to $63\%$ — claims are settling substantially faster, and the trend is steady rather than a one-off.
a jump in closure rates points to settlement speed.

requirements.statement: The paid development method is distorted by a change in settlement rate because historical paid CDFs are applied to paid amounts that are further along than in the past, overstating the ultimate when faster settlement occurs.

places.quote: - **Faster settlement** pushes losses from open to paid, so the recent paid diagonal is high relative to history. Historical paid factors — built when claims closed more slowly — then **over-develop** it and overstate ultimate.
Speeding up claim closure inflates the paid diagonal and makes historical paid factors too high;

requirements.statement: A change in settlement rate alters the mix of open claims, so an apparent change in average case outstanding may not indicate a change in case reserve adequacy; case outstanding alone is inconclusive.

If average reported claims move in line with the underlying severity trend, case adequacy is stable and the unadjusted reported development method is appropriate, so no Berquist-Sherman adjustment is needed.

places.quote: It should grow at roughly the severity trend.
Applying the case adequacy adjustment here would correct a distortion that is not present.

requirements.statement: Expected paid (or reported) claims emerging in a calendar period for an accident year equal its ultimate claims times the difference between the cumulative % paid (or reported) at the end of the period and at the start of the period.

places.quote: $$\text{Expected emergence} = U_{\text{prior}} \times \left(\frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n+1}} - \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n}}\right)$$

resolution.quote: The expected figure comes from the prior ultimate and the emergence pattern: the share of ultimate the pattern says should report (or be paid) between the two valuations.
resolution.note: Re-quote after today's edit: expected emergence = ultimate times the change in percent reported (paid).

requirements.statement: Each accident year ages by 12 months over a calendar year, so the starting and ending ages for the expected emergence are read from the cumulative development pattern at the current age and the next 12-month age.

places.quote: At $12/31/2023$, AY 2022 was estimated at ultimate $\$10{,}000{,}000$ with $60\%$ reported at $24$ months and $75\%$ at $36$ months.

requirements.statement: Compare actual emergence in the period (current cumulative less prior cumulative reported or paid claims) with expected emergence to identify whether paid and reported development are running faster, slower, or as expected.

places.quote: - A/E is run **by accident year and by maturity**, on paid and reported separately. Where the deviation sits is as informative as its size: concentrated in recent years points at the current diagonal; spread across all years points at a calendar-year effect; concentrated at old maturities points at the [[Tail Factor|tail]].

- Paid and reported A/E together diagnose the cause. Reported running high with paid on track suggests [[Case Adequacy|case strengthening]]; paid running high with reported on track suggests faster [[Settlement Rate|settlement]].

requirements.statement: A speed-up in claim settlement (shorter settlement lag) makes paid claims exceed expectations while reported claims (paid plus case reserves) stay near expected, because case reserves fall as payments rise.

places.quote: - **Faster settlement** pushes losses from open to paid, so the recent paid diagonal is high relative to history. Historical paid factors — built when claims closed more slowly — then **over-develop** it and overstate ultimate.

- Faster closing inflates the recent paid diagonal, so historical paid factors **over-develop** it. Slower closing does the reverse. The intuitive answer is usually the wrong sign, which is why the disposal-rate table is computed rather than reasoned about.

requirements.statement: The paid development technique is distorted by changes in settlement rates because historical paid patterns no longer apply, while the reported development technique is less sensitive to settlement timing changes and is preferred in that case.

places.quote: - **Reported data is largely immune**, because reported losses include the case reserve whether or not the claim has closed. So a paid-versus-reported divergence, together with a moving disposal rate, is the diagnostic pair.

- Faster closing inflates the recent paid diagonal, so historical paid factors **over-develop** it. Slower closing does the reverse. The intuitive answer is usually the wrong sign, which is why the disposal-rate table is computed rather than reasoned about.

requirements.statement: A change in the per-occurrence retention or limit changes the layer of loss in the data, so historical claim data and development triangles must be restated to a consistent retention basis before development factors are selected, since mixing bases distorts age-to-age factors.

places.quote: the development technique assumes stable retention limits over the experience period — so factors must be built on data capped at the *same* retention
restate history to current retentions or benefit levels.

requirements.statement: Increased limits factors or loss limitation factors are applied to restate losses from one retention or limit level to another.

places.quote: $$\text{ILF}(L) = \frac{E[X \wedge L]}{E[X \wedge B]}$$

requirements.statement: A change in the risk profile of the insured (such as a shift in workforce mix to lower-hazard jobs) changes claim frequency and severity, so historical data must be adjusted to the current risk profile or only the relevant period's data used for development patterns and projections.

places.quote: rising frequency at flat severity points at underwriting, mix or the claim environment
**Mix and dilution** — late-reported small claims pulling averages down, or a shift in the [[Mix of Business|mix]] of coverages and limits.

requirements.statement: In the expected claims method, put historical exposures and claims on current levels by adjusting for retention changes, risk profile changes, exposure trend (e.g. trending payroll to current wage level) and loss/benefit level trend.

places.quote: adjust a priori ratios for rate level and trend; segment for mix; restate history to current retentions or benefit levels.
from mature years' ultimate loss ratios adjusted for [[Rate Level Change|rate level]] and [[Loss Trend|trend]]

requirements.statement: A self-insured entity has no premium for its retained layer, so exposure bases such as payroll are used rather than premium, and premium on-leveling (rate level adjustments) does not apply.

places.quote: Self-insurers collect no premium in the insurer's sense, so exposure bases such as payroll, vehicles or property values stand in for it.

requirements.statement: Before using the frequency-severity method, examine a triangle of average severity (e.g. paid loss divided by closed claim counts) by accident year and age for trends and level shifts that reflect known changes such as retention or risk changes.

places.quote: Reading **down a column** compares years at the same age, which shows trends and mix.
Severity triangles are read down the **column**, not across the row: comparing accident years at the *same* maturity isolates the change in cost level, while movement along a row is development.

requirements.statement: Before using the frequency-severity method, examine claim frequency (claim counts per unit of exposure such as payroll) by accident year for trends and structural breaks, and use only representative periods if a break is found.

places.quote: rising frequency at flat severity points at underwriting, mix or the claim environment

requirements.statement: Average case outstanding is the case outstanding reserve divided by the number of open claim counts at the same evaluation.

places.quote: $$\text{Avg Case Outstanding} = \frac{\text{Case Reserves}}{\text{Open Claim Counts}}$$
Open counts — the inventory. Divided into case reserves it gives **average case outstanding**, the sharpest [[Case Adequacy|case adequacy]] diagnostic.

requirements.statement: In the Berquist-Sherman case outstanding adjustment, take the latest diagonal average case outstanding at each age as the base and restate earlier accident years at that age by de-trending it at the selected severity trend, dividing by one trend factor per year of lag.

places.quote: $$\text{Adjusted Case}_{\text{AY},n} = \text{Case}_{\text{latest},n} \times \left(1 + t\right)^{-(\text{years before latest})}$$

resolution.quote: Trend the latest diagonal's average case outstanding backwards at…to restate each historical cell at today's adequacy level.
resolution.note: Re-quote after today's edit: the case adequacy adjustment de-trends the latest diagonal's average case outstanding.

requirements.statement: Adjusted case outstanding equals the adjusted average case outstanding multiplied by the actual open claim counts for each cell.

places.quote: Multiply the restated averages by the open claim counts to get adjusted case reserves, add paid, and rebuild the reported triangle.

requirements.statement: Adjusted cumulative reported claims equal cumulative paid claims plus adjusted case outstanding.

places.quote: $$\text{Adjusted Reported}_{\text{AY},n} = \text{Paid}_{\text{AY},n} + \text{Adjusted Case}_{\text{AY},n}$$

resolution.quote: Multiply the restated averages by the open claim counts to get adjusted case reserves, add paid, and rebuild the reported triangle.
resolution.note: Re-quote after today's edit: adjusted reported = paid + adjusted case outstanding.

requirements.statement: The Berquist-Sherman case outstanding adjustment is used when case reserve adequacy has changed over time, restating historical case reserves to the current reserving level so that development factors are not distorted.

places.quote: restates a historical [[Development Triangle|triangle]] so that every year reflects **current** claims practice, removing the distortion caused by a change in [[Case Adequacy|case reserve adequacy]] or in [[Settlement Rate|claim settlement rates]].

The remedy is the [[Berquist-Sherman Method|Berquist-Sherman]] case adjustment: restate historical average case outstanding to the current adequacy level using a selected severity trend, rebuild the reported triangle, and select factors from the restated history.

requirements.statement: Higher historical reported values in the adjusted triangle (with the latest diagonal unchanged) lower the age-to-age development factors, which lowers projected ultimate claims and IBNR relative to the unadjusted reported development method.

places.quote: in the original triangle, the $12$-month column was artificially *low* in the old years relative to their subsequent (post-strengthening) development, inflating the $12$–$24$ factors.

requirements.statement: A volume-weighted (all-year weighted) average age-to-age factor for a development age is the sum of the later-age values divided by the sum of the corresponding earlier-age values over the accident years that have both.

places.quote: $$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{vol-wtd}} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$
$$f_{k \to k+1} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k}}$$

requirements.statement: In the development method, the cumulative development factor to ultimate is the product of the selected age-to-age factors from the current age through ultimate (including any tail factor), and ultimate is the latest value times that CDF.

places.quote: $$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$

**Cumulative Development Factor** (CDF, or age-to-ultimate factor) is the product of all selected [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] from a given maturity through to ultimate, including the [[Tail Factor|tail]].
$$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: Salvage and subrogation development approach: develop the paid salvage and subrogation triangle by itself with age-to-age factors to project ultimate S&S.

places.quote: S&S must be **projected on its own triangle**, not scaled from losses.

**Salvage and subrogation** (Friedland Ch. 14) are projected either by the development technique on reported or received S&S, or by the **ratio approach**: develop the ratio of received S&S to paid claims to an ultimate ratio, and multiply by selected ultimate claims gross of S&S.

requirements.statement: Salvage and subrogation ratio approach: compute the ratio of paid S&S to paid claims (gross of S&S) at each age, select an ultimate ratio from the ratios of mature accident years, and multiply it by the accident year's estimated ultimate claims.

places.quote: **Salvage and subrogation** (Friedland Ch. 14) are projected either by the development technique on reported or received S&S, or by the **ratio approach**: develop the ratio of received S&S to paid claims to an ultimate ratio, and multiply by selected ultimate claims gross of S&S.

requirements.statement: With no development after the last triangle age, the tail factor is 1.000, so the ratio or S&S at the last observed age is ultimate.

places.quote: A tail of exactly $1.000$ is itself an assumption — that development is complete — and it is the wrong one for any casualty line.

Consequently development is compact, [[Tail Factor|tail factors]] are near $1.000$, and the [[Chain Ladder Method|chain ladder]] on **paid** data is reliable at maturities where a long-tail line would still be guessing.

requirements.statement: The ratio approach is generally preferred for immature accident years because it is more stable and less leveraged than applying large development factors to small early S&S amounts, which are volatile.

places.quote: The ratio's development factors are less leveraged than those of S&S dollars, and the ultimate ratio is easier to select for immature years.

requirements.statement: Reported (incurred) claims for a calendar year equal paid claims plus the change in case reserves plus the change in IBNR over the year.

places.quote: \text{CY Incurred Losses (finance)} = \text{Paid} + \Delta\text{Case Reserves} + \Delta\text{IBNR}

requirements.statement: The Kittel ULAE ratio for a calendar year is paid ULAE divided by the average of paid claims and reported (incurred) claims.

places.quote: R_{\text{Kittel}} = \frac{\text{Paid ULAE}}{0.5(\text{Paid Loss}) + 0.5(\text{Incurred Loss})}

requirements.statement: Compute the ULAE ratio separately for each calendar year, examine the trend for stability, and select a ratio rather than pooling all years into a single weighted average.

places.quote: Compute the ratio $R$ of calendar-year paid ULAE to calendar-year paid loss, review it for trend, and apply it to unpaid claims.

requirements.statement: The classical ULAE reserve is the selected ratio times [50% of case reserves plus 100% of pure IBNR], since half of a claim's ULAE is spent at opening and half at closing, and no ULAE has yet been spent on unreported claims.

places.quote: \text{ULAE Reserve} = R \times \left(0.5 \times \text{Case} + 1.0 \times \text{IBNR}\right)

requirements.statement: On a claims-made policy, all covered claims are reported by the end of the policy period, so there is no pure IBNR; IBNR consists of development on known claims (IBNER), which are already opened, so the 50% factor applies to IBNR as well as case reserves.

places.quote: **A claims-made book has no pure IBNR** by construction — every claim in a [[Report Year|report year]] is already reported — so its IBNR is entirely IBNER.

Because the trigger is the report date, a claims-made policy has **no pure IBNR** — only IBNER on claims already reported — so the risk of reserve inadequacy is greatly reduced relative to the [[Occurrence Coverage|occurrence]] form.

requirements.statement: The purpose of the Kittel adjustment is to improve the classical paid-to-paid method for growing lines of business, where paid claims understate the claim activity (open reported claims) generating ULAE expense.

places.quote: The classical ratio is distorted in a growing book, because paid ULAE reflects today's claim *activity* (much of it on newly reported claims) while paid loss reflects older claims.

requirements.statement: The classical method assumes ULAE is split 50/50 between opening and closing a claim; this assumption is inflexible and is not addressed by the Kittel adjustment, which retains it.

places.quote: If ULAE is assumed to be spent half at reporting and half at settlement, only $50\%$ remains on reported-but-unpaid claims while $100\%$ remains on [[IBNR]] — the formula above.

requirements.statement: If case reserves are strengthened (case adequacy increases), the reported claims triangle shows artificially high development, so applying historical reported LDFs to the inflated reported amounts overstates ultimate claims, while paid methods are unaffected by case reserve changes.

places.quote: Applying historical factors — built under weaker reserving — to a strengthened diagonal **over-states** ultimate, because the strengthening is developed a second time.

The cost is exposure to adjuster judgment. Reported development mixes genuine emergence with **IBNER** — re-estimation of known claims — so any systematic change in [[Case Adequacy|case adequacy]] corrupts the historical factors.

Paid data is **objective**. It carries no adjuster judgment, so a paid triangle is immune to changes in [[Case Adequacy|case reserve adequacy]] — the single most common distortion in reported triangles.

requirements.statement: If claim settlement slows down, paid amounts at the evaluation date are lower than historical patterns imply, so applying historical paid CDFs to the lower paid base understates ultimate claims, while reported methods are less affected.

places.quote: **Slower settlement** does the reverse and understates ultimate from paid data.

requirements.statement: Large differences between paid-based and reported-based ultimate estimates for an accident year signal a change in case reserve adequacy or settlement speed that violates the stable-pattern assumption of the development methods.

places.quote: **Paid data is immune**, so a divergence between paid and reported chain ladder estimates is the corroborating evidence.
Running paid and reported methods **side by side** is standard practice. Agreement is reassuring; divergence is a diagnostic.

requirements.statement: To test for case reserve strengthening, compare average case outstanding per open claim across accident years at the same maturity, looking for a step-change larger than the trend in average paid severity.

places.quote: **The diagnostic is average case outstanding per open claim**, compared *down each column* of the triangle. It should grow at roughly the severity trend.
**[[Case Adequacy|Case strengthening]]:** average case outstanding rises faster than trend on the latest diagonals, and paid-to-reported falls.

requirements.statement: To test for a settlement slowdown, compare paid-to-reported claim ratios or closed-to-reported count ratios across accident years at the same maturity; lower ratios for the recent year indicate slower settlement.

places.quote: a rising ratio is consistent with faster settlement or weaker case reserves, a falling one with slower settlement or stronger case reserves
**Faster [[Settlement Rate|settlement]]:** closure rates and paid-to-reported rise together.

requirements.statement: To choose a projection method, consult the claims department about changes in case reserving or settlement practices, confirm the cause with diagnostics, then select or weight the methods not distorted by the identified anomaly.

places.quote: Meet claims, underwriting and operations to identify changes in coding, processing, case reserving, underwriting, policy provisions, marketing and reinsurance.
the restated result should be compared against methods that are insensitive to the distortion in question (paid methods for a case-adequacy change; reported methods for a settlement-rate change).

requirements.statement: The Berquist-Sherman technique adjusts the reported (case outstanding) triangle to restore consistent case reserve adequacy levels before applying development, and can be used when case strengthening is confirmed.

places.quote: The remedy is the [[Berquist-Sherman Method|Berquist-Sherman]] case adjustment: restate historical average case outstanding to the current adequacy level using a selected severity trend, rebuild the reported triangle, and select factors from the restated history.

restates a historical [[Development Triangle|triangle]] so that every year reflects **current** claims practice, removing the distortion caused by a change in [[Case Adequacy|case reserve adequacy]] or in [[Settlement Rate|claim settlement rates]].

requirements.statement: On-level historical earned premium to current rate level (e.g., with the parallel-grid/extension-of-exposures method) so that loss ratios across years reflect premium at the same rate level and are comparable.

places.quote: **On-Level Premium** is historical earned premium restated as though every policy had been written at the rate level currently in effect.
**On-Leveling** is the procedure that restates historical earned premium to the current rate level, producing [[On Level Premium|on-level premium]].

requirements.statement: Apply loss trend (frequency and severity changes) to historical losses to project them to the cost level of the future period during which the new rates will be in effect.

places.quote: **Loss Trend** is the annual rate of change in loss cost over time — driven by inflation, the legal environment, technology, safety and mix — applied to bring historical losses from the cost level of the experience period to the cost level of the **future policy period**.

requirements.statement: Apply loss development factors to reported losses to develop them to ultimate, capturing IBNR and further development so that loss ratios are not understated.

places.quote: Development has two drivers: **pure IBNR** (claims that occurred but have not yet been reported) and **IBNER** (incurred but not enough reported — development on claims already known, as [[Case Reserves|case reserves]] are re-estimated toward settlement).

An AY cohort is **not final** at year end: losses still develop as claims are reported and case reserves are re-estimated, so an AY must be brought to ultimate with a [[Cumulative Development Factor|CDF]] before it can be compared with a mature year.

requirements.statement: A rate indication should include unallocated loss adjustment expense (ULAE) in addition to allocated loss adjustment expense, because ULAE is part of the insurer's total loss-related claims cost.

places.quote: In **ratemaking**, ULAE may be handled as a load on losses or as a [[Fixed Expenses|fixed expense]] provision. Either is acceptable; doing both double-counts, and doing neither leaves a real cost unfunded.
$$\text{Loss \& LAE} = \text{Loss} + \text{ALAE} + \text{ULAE}$$

requirements.statement: Combining years' loss ratios should use a premium-weighted (volume-weighted) average rather than a simple average, so that years with more exposure carry more influence.

places.quote: Weighting across years in the experience period is a judgment: many companies sum projected losses and premium across all years, which weights each year's loss ratio by its premium; others select weights, often giving more to the most recent years.

requirements.statement: In the loss ratio method, fixed expenses should be treated separately from variable expenses (added to the loss ratio / handled via a fixed expense provision) instead of being embedded in the permissible loss ratio, to avoid distortion for risks with premium above or below average.

places.quote: The first form is Werner's: [[Fixed Expenses|fixed expenses]] as a ratio in the **numerator**, [[Variable Expenses|variable expenses]] $V$ and profit $Q_T$ in the denominator.

The loss ratio indication compares the projected loss & LAE ratio plus the fixed expense ratio to the VPLR — **fixed expenses sit in the numerator with the losses**, because they are assumed to be the same for each risk rather than a percentage of premium, and so do not scale with the rate being solved for.

requirements.statement: Rate indication data should be on a consistent basis: accident-year losses should be matched with premium on a consistent (e.g., accident-year/earned) basis rather than mixing calendar-year premium with accident-year losses.

places.quote: CY incurred losses **mix accident years**: a CY 2024 figure contains payments and reserve changes on claims from $2024$ and from every prior year.
AY matches premium and losses better than [[Calendar Year]], and its claims occur over a shorter time frame than a [[Policy Year]]'s, so its ultimate can be reliably estimated sooner.

requirements.statement: The profit provision in a rate indication can reflect investment income, accounting for the time value of money between premium receipt and loss payment.

places.quote: Total return also includes investment income on policyholder-supplied funds (the loss and unearned premium reserves) and on capital (whether to include the latter is disputed), so the actuary typically determines the underwriting profit needed to achieve the target total return after consideration of investment income.

In ratemaking, the actuary typically determines the **target** underwriting profit provision $Q_T$ needed to achieve the target total rate of return after consideration of investment income — see [[Profit and Contingency Provision]].

requirements.statement: The reported Bornhuetter-Ferguson ultimate loss equals reported losses to date plus expected losses (premium times expected loss ratio) times the percentage unreported (1 minus percent reported, i.e., 1 − 1/reported CDF).

places.quote: $C$ is reported (or paid) losses to date, $U_0 = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}$ the a priori expectation, and $1 - 1/\text{CDF}$ the percentage unreported from the [[Development Triangle|development pattern]].
$$U = \text{ELR} \times \text{Earned Premium}$$

requirements.statement: To use historical selected loss ratios as the expected loss ratio for a new accident year, adjust each to the new year's level by trending losses from its accident year to the new year and putting premium on current rate level, then average the adjusted ratios.

places.quote: $$\text{Adjusted ELR}_i = \text{ELR}_{\text{base}} \times \frac{\text{Rate level}_{\text{base}}}{\text{Rate level}_i} \times \frac{\text{Loss trend}_i}{\text{Loss trend}_{\text{base}}}$$

The **ELR** is the whole method, and it must be derived, not assumed: from the pricing indication for that year, from mature years' ultimate loss ratios adjusted for [[Rate Level Change|rate level]] and [[Loss Trend|trend]], or from [[External Information in Reserving|industry benchmarks]].

requirements.statement: The parallelogram method computes on-level factors for calendar year earned premium with annual policies by finding the fraction of each year's earned premium written at each rate level, based on the effective dates of rate changes, and dividing the current rate level by the weighted average rate level.

places.quote: For **annual** policies written uniformly, a rate change effective at time $p$ through year $Y$ earns over a triangle of area $\tfrac{1}{2}(1-p)^2$ in year $Y$ — so a $7/1$ change affects only $0.125$ of that year's earned premium, and a $1/1$ change affects $0.500$.

**Werner's six steps:** date the changes and form rate level groups; find each group's area in each year; build cumulative indices; take the area-weighted average index; divide it into the current index; apply the factor to the year's earned premium.

requirements.statement: With annual policies, a rate change takes a full year after its effective date to be fully earned, so calendar year earned premium reflects a mix of old and new rate levels, and premium earned after all rate changes have fully earned needs no on-level adjustment.

places.quote: Calendar year $2025$ would be fully at the new level, with an on-level factor of $1.000$. Notice how a single mid-year change takes two full years to work through earned premium — the reason rate changes feel slow to show up in results.
Even $2024$ needs a factor: policies written before $10/1/2023$, at the old level, still earn $28\%$ of its premium.

requirements.statement: Putting premium on current rate level raises premium, so the on-level factor divides (lowers) the historical loss ratio, while loss trend compounds at the annual rate over the number of years between accident years and multiplies the loss ratio.

places.quote: $$\text{On-Level Factor} = \frac{\text{Current cumulative index}}{\text{Index in force during the period}}$$
$$\text{Trend Factor} = (1 + t)^{n}$$

requirements.statement: The percentage of loss reported at a given maturity is the reciprocal of the reported loss development factor, and the unreported share (1 minus percent reported) is the portion of expected loss that the BF method adds.

places.quote: BF is a **credibility weighting** in disguise: it equals $Z \, U_{\text{CL}} + (1-Z)\,U_0$ with $Z = 1/\text{CDF}$.
The share emerged is $1/14.4466 = 0.06922$.

requirements.statement: Age-to-age development factors are ratios of reported losses at successive evaluation ages for each accident year, and a selected factor (e.g., an average) is chosen for each age interval.

resolution.quote: Selecting a factor from the column of observations is the central judgment of the
resolution.note: Syllabus page defines age-to-age factors and their selection.

requirements.statement: The cumulative development factor to ultimate at a given age is the product of the selected age-to-age factors from that age through the tail; ultimate losses equal reported losses times this factor.

places.quote: $$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \left(\prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1}\right) \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: If rates have not changed during the historical experience period, the on-level factor is 1.00 and no premium adjustment for rate changes is needed.

places.quote: Calendar year $2025$ would be fully at the new level, with an on-level factor of $1.000$.

requirements.statement: Trend periods run from the average date of the historical period (average accident date for losses, average written date for premium) to the average date of the future period: for losses, the average accident date under the new rates (average written date plus half the policy term); for premium, the average written date of the new rates.

places.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.
The trend period $n$ runs from the average written date of the policies earning premium in the experience period to the **average written date of the policies in effect while the new rates are**

requirements.statement: Trended values are computed by compounding the annual trend rate over the trend period: historical amount × (1 + trend)^t, applied to losses (loss trend) and premium (premium trend).

places.quote: $$\text{Trend Factor} = (1 + t)^{n}$$
$$\text{Premium Trend Factor} = (1 + t_P)^{n}$$

requirements.statement: Loss adjustment expense provided as a percentage of loss is included by multiplying losses by (1 + LAE provision).
The permissible loss ratio equals 1 minus the variable expense ratio minus the underwriting profit and contingencies provision; fixed expenses are handled separately.

places.quote: $$\text{VPLR} = 1 - V - Q_T \quad \text{(variable permissible loss ratio)}$$
The first form is Werner's: [[Fixed Expenses|fixed expenses]] as a ratio in the **numerator**, [[Variable Expenses|variable expenses]] $V$ and profit $Q_T$ in the denominator.

requirements.statement: When variable expenses change during the future rate period (e.g., a commission cut), compute the permissible loss ratio for each sub-period and weight them by the portion of the rate period (time) each covers.

resolution.quote: must be reflected prospectively rather than from historical ratios
resolution.note: Page teaches that a commission change is reflected prospectively in V; weighting the two sub-periods by time is this solution's own step.

requirements.statement: With fixed expenses as a ratio to premium, the indicated rate change = (projected loss & LAE ratio + fixed expense ratio) / permissible loss ratio − 1, where the loss ratio is the average across years.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{\text{VPLR}} - 1$$

requirements.statement: Pure IBNR is the portion of IBNR for claims that have occurred but have not yet been reported, whereas IBNER (incurred but not enough reported) is expected development on claims already reported.

places.quote: **Pure IBNR** (narrow IBNR) covers claims that have occurred but are unknown to the insurer.

Development has two drivers: **pure IBNR** (claims that occurred but have not yet been reported) and **IBNER** (incurred but not enough reported — development on claims already known, as [[Case Reserves|case reserves]] are re-estimated toward settlement).

requirements.statement: A mature claims-made policy has no pure IBNR at the end of the report year because all claims reported during the period are known, so its IBNR consists only of IBNER, while an occurrence policy has both pure IBNR and IBNER.

places.quote: **A claims-made book has no pure IBNR** by construction — every claim in a [[Report Year|report year]] is already reported — so its IBNR is entirely IBNER.
Because the trigger is the report date, a claims-made policy has **no pure IBNR** — only IBNER on claims already reported

The insurer bears the mirror image of that promise. It must reserve for **pure [[IBNR]]** — claims it has no knowledge of — for as long as claims from expired policies can still emerge, which for a product like medical malpractice can be many years.

requirements.statement: A claims-made policy covers claims reported during the policy period regardless of when the loss occurred, while an occurrence policy covers losses that occur during the policy period regardless of when they are reported.

places.quote: **Claims-Made Coverage** is a policy trigger under which the policy responds to claims *reported* during the policy period, provided the underlying loss occurred on or after the policy's **retroactive date**.
**Occurrence Coverage** is a policy trigger under which the policy responds to losses that *occur* during the policy period, however long afterwards the claim is reported.

requirements.statement: When claim costs are increasing, a claims-made policy costs less than an occurrence policy because its claims are reported at near-current cost levels with a short report lag, while occurrence claims are reported and paid at higher future cost levels with added pricing risk from the long report lag.

places.quote: A claims-made policy should always cost less than an occurrence policy **as long as claim costs are increasing**.
And as long as claim costs are increasing, the occurrence policy costs more than the claims-made one (Principle 1 of claims-made policies).

requirements.statement: Because the trend period for an occurrence policy runs from the date of loss to a distant report date, a change in trend compounds over a longer horizon and affects its premium more than that of a claims-made policy, whose trend period is only to the near-term report date.

places.quote: because the occurrence policy's claims are reported further into the future, where trend has pushed costs higher.

requirements.statement: A retroactive date on a claims-made policy restricts coverage to claims from losses occurring on or after that date.

places.quote: **Claims-Made Coverage** is a policy trigger under which the policy responds to claims *reported* during the policy period, provided the underlying loss occurred on or after the policy's **retroactive date**.
The retroactive date applies to the date of the injury or damage, not to the date of the act that caused it, and it stops an insured from buying coverage for injury that has already happened.

requirements.statement: When an insured switches from an occurrence policy to claims-made without a retroactive date, a loss that occurred during the occurrence policy and is reported during the claims-made period is covered by both, creating an overlap; setting the retroactive date to the first claims-made policy's inception eliminates it.

places.quote: Switching the other way, from occurrence to claims-made, the retroactive date should be coordinated with the expiration of the last occurrence policy to give complete coverage without overlap.

requirements.statement: When an insured switches from claims-made to occurrence coverage, there is a gap for losses that occurred during the claims-made period but are reported after it ended, since neither policy covers them; the insurer can close it by offering an extended reporting endorsement (tail coverage).

places.quote: An **extended reporting endorsement** (ERP, or "tail coverage") covers claims that occurred during the claims-made coverage period but are reported after the last policy expires — what a retiring physician, or an insured switching to an occurrence policy, needs to avoid a gap.
If a claims-made CGL is cancelled or not renewed, replaced with an occurrence policy, or renewed with a later retroactive date, a basic extended reporting period applies automatically at no charge.

requirements.statement: To project historical losses to a future rate period, trend each accident year's losses from its average accident date to the average accident date of the future period, compounding the annual trend over the number of years between those dates.

places.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.

$t_E$ is the annual exposure trend and $n$ the trend period in years, measured from the average date of the historical period to the average date of the forecast period — the same period used for [[Loss Trend|loss trend]].

requirements.statement: For annual policies written uniformly over a period the rates are in effect, the average accident date of the future period is the average written date (midpoint of the effective period) plus half the policy term (six months for annual policies).

places.quote: The first policy is exposed $7/1/2025$–$6/30/2026$ and the last $7/1/2026$–$6/30/2027$, so the exposure period runs $7/1/2025$ to $6/30/2027$ and its midpoint — the average loss date — is $7/1/2026$.

requirements.statement: A benefit change that applies to losses by accident date affects losses from accidents after the change date, while a benefit change that applies by policy effective date affects only policies written after the change date; this distinction determines which losses are affected.

places.quote: Changes attach to the **policy**, so they phase in over the policy term.
On an accident year basis, AY 2024 is a blend: losses occurring in $2024$ arise both from $2024$-written policies (new deductible) and from $2023$-written policies still running off (old deductible).

requirements.statement: To bring historical losses stated at an old benefit level to the benefit level in effect for the future rate period, multiply by a benefit level adjustment factor equal to the product of (1 + impact) of each benefit change applicable to future losses; the full factor is applied to every accident year when losses are stated at the pre-change level.

places.quote: **Benefit-level changes** in statutory lines (workers compensation reform, auto no-fault changes) are the same problem at industry scale, and are handled by a law-level adjustment factor applied to historical losses before trend

requirements.statement: In workers compensation indemnity loss projection, wage inflation acts as an annual trend on indemnity benefits and is applied as a separate multiplicative factor from benefit level changes.

places.quote: **Loss Trend** is the annual rate of change in loss cost over time — driven by inflation, the legal environment, technology, safety and mix — applied to bring historical losses from the cost level of the experience period to the cost level of the **future policy period**.

**Benefit-level changes** in statutory lines (workers compensation reform, auto no-fault changes) are the same problem at industry scale, and are handled by a law-level adjustment factor applied to historical losses before trend — deliberately kept separate from trend so the two are not confused.

requirements.statement: Ultimate loss equals reported (or paid) loss to date multiplied by the age-to-ultimate loss development factor at the loss's current maturity.

places.quote: $$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: Age-to-ultimate factors are cumulative factors applied directly at the current age; they should not be multiplied or compounded again as if they were age-to-age factors.

places.quote: $$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: Determine an accident year's maturity in months at the evaluation date (months from the start of the accident year to the valuation date) to select the correct development factor.

resolution.quote: maturities as columns (age in months since the start of the cohort)
resolution.note: Syllabus page: maturity is the age in months since the start of the accident year.

requirements.statement: The trend factor equals (1 + frequency trend) × (1 + severity trend), or equivalently (1 + pure premium trend), raised to the trend period in years.

places.quote: $$1 + t_{PP} = (1 + t_{\text{freq}})(1 + t_{\text{sev}})$$
The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: Estimate trend rates by fitting an exponential curve to historical frequency, severity or pure premium data; the choice of number of points (shorter vs longer window) is judged by stability and relevance of the data.

places.quote: Linear and exponential regressions are the most common measures; exponential models may be fit to the whole of the data and to more recent periods, supplemented with multi-state, countrywide or industry data and non-insurance indices, and the trend selected with judgment.
Werner's example fits windows of 20, 16, 12, 8, 6 and 4 points, and $R^2$ is the usual diagnostic; the recent windows show whether the trend has shifted.

requirements.statement: When a past change (such as underwriting guideline revisions) altered the book's composition, historical trends mixing pre- and post-change data are not representative of the future; use a two-step trend with separate historical and projected trend rates, with the projected rate based on post-change data.

places.quote: A **two-step** trend is used when the trend in the historical period differs from the trend expected in the forecast period (legislative changes are one example)
**Two-step trending** is used when the recent history contains a shift the historical fit would understate or overstate.

requirements.statement: The historical trend period runs from the average accident date of the experience period to the latest data point (end of the experience data); the projected trend period runs from there to the average accident date of the future policy period.

places.quote: losses are first trended at a *current* trend from the experience period's average accident date to that of the latest data point in the trend data, then projected at a separately selected trend to the forecast period's average accident date.
The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: For annual policies written on a single date each year, the average accident date of a policy period is the midpoint of the policy term's year (e.g., July 1 for January 1 policies), and the future period's average accident date is based on when rates take effect, counted for a one-year policy term.

places.quote: The first policy is exposed $7/1/2025$–$6/30/2026$ and the last $7/1/2026$–$6/30/2027$, so the exposure period runs $7/1/2025$ to $6/30/2027$ and its midpoint — the average loss date — is $7/1/2026$.

requirements.statement: The permissible loss ratio when all expenses are variable equals 1 minus the variable expense ratio minus the profit and contingency provision.

places.quote: The **variable permissible loss ratio** is what is left after the variable expense and profit provisions, $\text{VPLR} = 1 - V - Q_T$, and pays for loss, LAE and fixed expenses
$$\text{VPLR} = 1 - V - Q_T \quad \text{(variable permissible loss ratio)}$$

requirements.statement: The loss ratio indicated rate change equals experience loss ratio divided by permissible loss ratio, minus 1.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio}}{\text{PLR}} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss Ratio}}{\text{PLR}} - 1 \quad \text{(all-variable form)}$$

requirements.statement: When fixed expenses are separated, the indicated rate change equals (experience loss ratio + fixed expense ratio) divided by (1 - variable expense ratio - profit provision), minus 1.
requirements.concept: Fixed and Variable Expenses in Ratemaking

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$

requirements.statement: Fixed expenses do not scale with premium, so they are added to the experience loss ratio in the numerator, while only variable expenses reduce the permissible loss ratio; treating some expenses as fixed raises the permissible loss ratio and lowers the indicated change relative to treating all as variable.
requirements.concept: Fixed and Variable Expenses in Ratemaking

places.quote: $F$ enters the **numerator** of the rate; [[Variable Expenses|variable expenses]] $V$ and the profit provision $Q_T$ enter the **denominator**.
**fixed expenses sit in the numerator with the losses**, because they are assumed to be the same for each risk rather than a percentage of premium, and so do not scale with the rate being solved for.

requirements.statement: Treating all expenses as variable overcharges large-premium risks and undercharges small-premium risks, so separating fixed expenses improves equity across risk sizes.
requirements.concept: Fixed and Variable Expenses in Ratemaking

places.quote: Treating a fixed cost as variable over-charges large policies and under-charges small ones.

Loading fixed expenses as a percentage of premium instead — the **all-variable expense method** — undercharges risks with below-average premium and overcharges those above it, so large policies subsidize small ones.

requirements.statement: Fixed and variable expenses behave and trend differently over time, so separating them allows separate trending and monitoring of each expense component.
requirements.concept: Fixed and Variable Expenses in Ratemaking

places.quote: Expense **trend**: a variable expense ratio needs none, since it changes with premium automatically.
Because $F$ is a dollar amount, it is expected to rise with inflation.

requirements.statement: A good exposure base is proportional to expected losses, meaning twice the exposure implies twice the expected loss.

places.quote: All else equal, a policy with two exposures should have twice the expected loss of a similar policy with one.

requirements.statement: A good exposure base is practical: objective, easy to obtain, and inexpensive to verify and administer, and not easily manipulated by the insured.

places.quote: Objective, and relatively easy and inexpensive to obtain and verify — which also keeps policyholders and producers from manipulating it (declared annual mileage invites more dishonesty than car-years).
**Operational** — objective, inexpensive to obtain and verify, not manipulable by the insured.

requirements.statement: A good exposure base should take historical precedence into account, since changing the base can cause large premium swings, costly system changes, and require adjustments to future ratemaking analyses.

places.quote: A change of base can cause large premium swings for individual insureds, requires a change in the rating algorithm and systems, and may force significant adjustments to the several years of data a ratemaking analysis uses.

requirements.statement: Claim frequency equals claim counts divided by exposures, so changing to an exposure base with larger numerical values lowers frequency (and a smaller base raises it).

places.quote: $$\text{Frequency} = \frac{\text{Number of Claims}}{\text{Earned Exposures}}$$
Frequency is only meaningful **relative to its exposure base** and its claim definition.

requirements.statement: Claim severity equals loss dollars divided by claim counts, so it does not depend on the exposure base and is unaffected by a change in exposure base.

places.quote: $$\text{Severity} = \frac{\text{Total Losses}}{\text{Number of Claims}}$$

requirements.statement: An exposure base change shifts premiums among insureds; those with premium increases may leave for other insurers, producing adverse or favorable selection that changes the company's loss ratio, and insureds may also manipulate the new base to understate exposure.

places.quote: Objective, and relatively easy and inexpensive to obtain and verify — which also keeps policyholders and producers from manipulating it (declared annual mileage invites more dishonesty than car-years).
Price at the population average; low risks find the price poor value and leave; the remaining pool is worse, so the price rises

requirements.statement: To evaluate a rating variable's predictive value in a GLM, examine the indicated relativities by level: a consistent, monotonic pattern without reversals suggests the variable is statistically significant and predictive.
requirements.concept: GLM Model Diagnostics and Variable Selection

places.quote: Output is judged on more than significance: consistency of the pattern across levels, standard errors, the effect of removing the variable (analysis of deviance), and validation on a holdout period.

requirements.statement: Consistency test: compare a variable's indicated relativities across individual years; if the yearly curves follow similar patterns and direction, the variable's results are stable and pass the consistency test.
requirements.concept: GLM Model Diagnostics and Variable Selection

requirements.statement: Levels with few exposures have volatile, less credible results, so disparities at those levels do not invalidate the stable results at well-populated levels.
CART (classification and regression trees) is a data mining technique that builds a tree-structured series of if-then splits to identify relationships among variables.

places.quote: A **regression tree** is a [[Decision Tree|decision tree]] for a quantitative [[Response Variable|response]]: recursive binary splitting divides the predictor space into regions $R_1, \ldots, R_J$, and every observation that falls in region $R_j$ is predicted by the mean response $\hat{y}_{R_j}$ of the training observations in that region.

requirements.statement: CART can enhance a GLM by identifying interactions between variables that can then be included as interaction terms in the GLM.

places.quote: The tree has built an interaction between vehicle age and garaging, which a linear model would include only if an interaction term were specified.

requirements.statement: A neural network is a data mining technique that is trained on data and automatically learns the structure of the data, essentially an iterative GLM-like process.

places.quote: A **Neural Network** (also called an **artificial neural network** or **multilayer perceptron**) is a [[Statistical Learning]] model composed of layers of interconnected **neurons** (units) that learn complex, non-linear mappings from inputs to outputs.

requirements.statement: A neural network can enhance a GLM analysis by identifying missing predictive variables not yet included in the GLM.
In the pure premium method, the indicated pure premium for each class is its ultimate losses (including loaded ALAE) divided by its earned exposures.
requirements.concept: Pure Premium Method for Territory Ratemaking

places.quote: **Pure Premium Method** derives the indicated **rate** directly: project loss and LAE per exposure, add the fixed expense per exposure, and gross up for variable expenses and profit.
$$\text{Pure Premium} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Exposures}}$$

requirements.statement: Loss and ALAE are combined by multiplying ultimate losses by (1 + ratio of ALAE to loss).

requirements.statement: Calendar year earned premium is the premium earned on all policies during the calendar year, equal to the portion of each policy's term falling in that year (plus any audit premium recognized in that year).

requirements.statement: Calendar year written premium is the premium on policies written (effective) during the calendar year, plus premium changes such as audits that are booked during that year.

places.quote: - **Policy year** earned premium comes from one cohort only, and is fully earned $24$ months after the policy year begins (for annual policies).

**Policy Year** (PY), also called underwriting year or year of account, is a data aggregation method that groups every premium and loss transaction belonging to policies *incepting* in a given calendar year, and follows that cohort until the last claim closes.

requirements.statement: Premium audit adjustments are treated as written and earned in full at the time the audit occurs (booked in the calendar year of the audit), not spread over the policy term.

requirements.statement: For a policy year, audit premium is attributed back to the policy's original policy year, so it is included in policy year written premium once the audit occurs before the evaluation date (a later evaluation includes the audit).

places.quote: An audit on a policy written in $2023$ books premium in $2025$, so **[[Policy Year]] premium keeps changing** for two or three years and [[Calendar Year|calendar year]] premium contains audit adjustments belonging to prior years.

A quota share reinsurance treaty cedes a fixed percentage of every claim (and premium) to the reinsurer, so the net-to-gross claim ratio is constant across all development ages within an accident year.

places.quote: **Quota share** — a flat percentage of every policy. Ceded losses are a scalar multiple of gross, so the ceded triangle has the same shape as the gross one.
Under **quota share**, ceded is a fixed share $c$ of gross, so the ceded triangle is a scalar multiple of the gross one and develops identically.

requirements.statement: To identify the reinsurance structure, compute the net-to-gross ratio of cumulative reported claims for each cell of the triangle; a constant ratio within each accident year indicates quota share (the percentage may differ between accident years), whereas a ratio that varies with age or claim size would suggest excess of loss.

places.quote: Under **quota share**, ceded is a fixed share $c$ of gross, so the ceded triangle is a scalar multiple of the gross one and develops identically. … Under **excess of loss**, ceded responds only to claims piercing retention $R$, and the pattern is entirely different — later, steeper, and far more volatile.

requirements.statement: Age-to-age (link ratio) reported development factors are computed as the ratio of cumulative reported claims at consecutive ages for each accident year.

places.quote: **Age-to-Age Factor** (link ratio) is the ratio of a cohort's cumulative amount at one maturity to its amount at the previous maturity — the observed development between two ages.

requirements.statement: Select an age-to-age factor for each development period by averaging the observed factors (e.g., a volume-weighted or simple average), and set the factor to 1.0 beyond the last age when no further development is assumed.

places.quote: - **Volume-weighted (all-year)** — the ratio of column sums.

requirements.statement: Age-to-ultimate factors are obtained by multiplying the selected age-to-age factors from a given age through the last age, and ultimate claims equal latest cumulative reported claims times the age-to-ultimate factor.

places.quote: $$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$

**The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.

requirements.statement: IBNR (reported-claim basis) equals ultimate claims minus cumulative reported claims to date.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = U_{\text{AY}} - C_{\text{AY},\,n}$$
$$\text{IBNR} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Reported}$$

requirements.statement: Ceded claims equal gross claims minus net claims, and under a quota share the ceded IBNR can be found by applying the ceded percentage (1 minus net/gross ratio) to gross IBNR, or equivalently by developing the ceded or the gross and net triangles separately, with the same factors, and differencing; the ceded percentage must be applied to gross, not net, amounts.

places.quote: $$\text{Ceded} = \text{Gross} - \text{Net}$$
**[[Quota Share|Quota share]]** cedes a fixed percentage of ultimate, paid, case and IBNR alike.
For reserving, ceded losses are a scalar multiple of gross and develop on the gross pattern, unlike [[Excess of Loss]] cessions.

requirements.statement: The expected percent reported at a given maturity equals the reciprocal of the selected cumulative claim development factor to ultimate at that maturity (% reported = 1 / CDF).

places.quote: The reciprocal is the **percentage reported** (or paid): $p_n = 1/\text{CDF}_n$, and $1 - p_n$ is the percentage unreported.
$$\text{Reported \%} = \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}}$$

requirements.statement: Linear interpolation estimates a value at an intermediate maturity by assuming the change between two known maturities occurs uniformly (a straight line) over the interval, so the fraction of the interval elapsed times the total change is added to the starting value.

Expected emergence in a future period under the Expected Claims (Bornhuetter-Ferguson style) method equals the unreported (IBNR) amount, ultimate minus reported, divided by the percent unreported at the current maturity (1 minus % reported), times the change in expected % reported over the period.
requirements.concept: Expected Claims Emergence / Reported Claims Projection

places.quote: $$\text{Expected emergence} = U_{\text{prior}} \times \left(\frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n+1}} - \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n}}\right)$$

resolution.quote: $$\text{Expected emergence} = \frac{U_{\text{prior}} - \text{Reported}_{n}}{1 - 1/\text{CDF}_{n}} \times \left(\frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n+1}} - \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n}}\right)$$
resolution.note: Re-quote after today's edit: the page's formula is the unreported amount divided by percent unreported times percent emerging (Friedland p.351).

requirements.statement: Projected reported claims at a future date equal claims reported to date plus the expected emergence between the evaluation date and that future date.
requirements.concept: Expected Claims Emergence / Reported Claims Projection

places.quote: The **expected** figure comes from the prior ultimate and the emergence pattern: the share of ultimate the pattern says should report (or be paid) between the two valuations.

requirements.statement: Months of development for an accident year at an evaluation date are measured from the start of the accident year to the evaluation date (e.g., a date at the end of a month counts that full month), so the maturity is determined by the evaluation date.

places.quote: **maturities as columns** (age in months since the start of the cohort), and **valuation dates as diagonals**.

requirements.statement: Linear interpolation of claim development may be inappropriate for an immature accident year because claims do not emerge uniformly; the development pattern is a curve (e.g., seasonality, faster early reporting, highly leveraged development factors), so a straight line can misestimate expected claims.
The paid Bornhuetter-Ferguson ultimate equals paid claims to date plus the expected claims times (1 − 1/CDF), where the CDF is the paid cumulative development factor to ultimate.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$

requirements.statement: The cumulative development factor to ultimate at a given age is the product of the age-to-age factors from that age onward, with each age-to-age factor selected as an average (e.g., simple average) of the observed link ratios.

places.quote: **Development Factor** (link ratio or age-to-age factor) is the ratio used to project cumulative losses from one maturity age to the next, forming the building blocks of the [[Chain Ladder Method]]; chaining them together produces the [[Cumulative Development Factor]] to ultimate.
$$\text{CDF}_{12 \to \text{ult}} = 2.40 \times 1.45 \times 1.60 = 5.568$$
**Simple average** — equal weight to each year, so a small, volatile year counts as much as a large one.

requirements.statement: IBNR is the ultimate claims minus reported (paid plus case outstanding) claims, so it is not the same as total unpaid claims, which are ultimate minus paid.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Reported}$$
$$\text{Unpaid} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Paid to date}$$
