places.quote: A "defence and settle" strategy shift moves both components, in opposite directions, and shows up in the triangles as a change in the ALAE ratio.

requirements.statement: The frequency-severity technique can be applied to ALAE by projecting ultimate claim counts and ultimate average ALAE per claim and multiplying them to get ultimate ALAE.

places.quote: **Frequency-Severity Method** projects [[Claim Count Triangle|claim counts]] and average [[Severity|severity]] separately and multiplies them, instead of developing loss dollars directly.
$$\text{Ultimate Counts} = N_n \times \text{CDF}^{\text{count}}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: The frequency-severity technique works best when claim settlement practices, business mix, and claim definitions are stable; operational changes require adjusting the data and monitoring frequency and severity.

places.quote: The method needs **consistent count definitions** across the whole triangle, and it is sensitive to [[Large Loss|large losses]] in the severity series, so severities are usually capped and the excess layer added back separately.

Counts must be **defined consistently**: per claim or per claimant, counting claims closed without payment or not, treating reopened claims as new or as continuing. A definition change mid-triangle looks exactly like a frequency trend.

requirements.statement: The cumulative percent reported (or paid) at an age equals the reciprocal of the cumulative development factor to ultimate at that age (1/CDF).

places.quote: The reciprocal is the **percentage reported** (or paid): $p_n = 1/\text{CDF}_n$, and $1 - p_n$ is the percentage unreported.

requirements.statement: To find the percent reported or paid at an age between evaluation points, linearly interpolate between the cumulative percentages at the adjacent ages, using the accident-period age in months at the evaluation date.

Expected claims emerging over a period equal the prior unreported (or unpaid) amount, ultimate minus actual to date, times the percent emerging in the period divided by the percent still unreported (or unpaid) at the start; adding this to the actual to date gives the cumulative expected.

resolution.quote: $$\text{Expected emergence} = \frac{U_{\text{prior}} - \text{Reported}_{n}}{1 - 1/\text{CDF}_{n}} \times \left(\frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n+1}} - \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n}}\right)$$
resolution.note: Tagged page's formula: prior unreported amount over percent unreported, times percent emerging in the period.

requirements.statement: Expected emergence in a period can alternatively be computed as selected ultimate times the difference in the percent reported (or paid) at the period's end and start (e.g., difference in 1/CDF, prorated for a partial period).

places.quote: $$\text{Expected emergence} = U_{\text{prior}} \times \left(\frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n+1}} - \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n}}\right)$$

resolution.quote: The expected figure comes from the prior ultimate and the emergence pattern: the share of ultimate the pattern says should report (or be paid) between the two valuations.
resolution.note: Re-quote after today's edit: expected emergence = ultimate times the change in percent reported (paid).

requirements.statement: Reported claims that emerge higher than expected, with paid in line with expected, suggest the ultimate should be revised upward if driven by a real change in underlying losses (deteriorating loss ratio, a claim influx or catastrophe, an unanticipated large loss, or a law change raising losses).

places.quote: The distinction matters: the first three are process failures to be corrected in the method, the fourth is a real-world change to be quantified and reflected in *both* reserves and pricing.

requirements.statement: Changes in operations, such as case reserve strengthening or faster claim reporting or processing, shift the timing of reported or paid claims without changing ultimate claims, so the actuary would not revise the ultimate estimate for them.

places.quote: The wider consequence: paid A/E at $1.0$ means the ultimate cost of these claims may not have changed at all.

requirements.statement: Comparing reported and paid actual-vs-expected results together diagnoses the cause of a deviation: reported deviating while paid matches expectation points to case reserve or reporting changes, whereas both deviating points to a real change in ultimate losses.

places.quote: Paid and reported A/E together diagnose the cause. Reported running high with paid on track suggests [[Case Adequacy|case strengthening]]; paid running high with reported on track suggests faster [[Settlement Rate|settlement]].

requirements.statement: IBNR under the expected claims / IBNR-to-case approach is the selected ultimate claims minus reported (case-incurred) claims.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Reported}$$
$$\text{IBNR} = U - \text{Reported}$$

requirements.statement: Expected emergence of reported claims over a period equals current IBNR times the proportion of remaining unreported claims that emerges, (percent reported at end of period minus percent reported at start) divided by (1 minus percent reported at start).

places.quote: $$\text{Expected emergence} = U_{\text{prior}} \times \left(\frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n+1}} - \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n}}\right)$$

resolution.quote: $$\text{Expected emergence} = \frac{U_{\text{prior}} - \text{Reported}_{n}}{1 - 1/\text{CDF}_{n}} \times \left(\frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n+1}} - \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n}}\right)$$
resolution.note: Re-quote after today's edit: current IBNR over percent unreported times percent emerging (syllabus page).

requirements.statement: Update reported and paid claims at the new evaluation date by adding the period's expected (or actual) emergence to the prior cumulative reported and paid claims.

resolution.note: Adding the period's emergence to the prior cumulative amount is the definition of a cumulative figure (arithmetic), not separate course content.

requirements.statement: Case outstanding claims equal cumulative reported (case-incurred) claims minus cumulative paid claims.

places.quote: $$= \text{Paid Losses} + \text{Case Reserves}$$

requirements.statement: In the case outstanding development technique, unpaid claims = case outstanding × (1 + IBNR/case ratio), where IBNR/case = (1 − percent reported)/(percent reported − percent paid) at the current age; equivalently, using CDFs, Case × [(Reported CDF − 1)(Paid CDF)/(Paid CDF − Reported CDF) + 1].

places.quote: $$U = \text{Paid to date} + \text{Case Outstanding} \times f_{\text{case}}$$

requirements.statement: The case outstanding development technique uses the selected percentages reported and paid at the current evaluation age (after the period's development), not the earlier age.

places.quote: $f_{\text{case}}$ converts the current case balance into *all* remaining payments

requirements.statement: Written exposures for a calendar year are the exposures of policies written (effective) in that year; a mid-term cancellation produces negative written exposure in the cancellation year equal to the unexpired portion.

places.quote: A $12$-month policy contributes **one** earned car-year in total, spread pro rata over its term: written the day it is issued, earned $1/12$ per month, in force from effective date to expiry.

written premium $\text{WP}_r$ (and, the same way, written exposure) is recorded once at issue and again, positive or negative, for every cancellation or mid-term change, so the policy's figure is the sum of its records.

requirements.statement: Earned exposure is the portion of a policy's exposure whose coverage period has already elapsed as of a date, and unearned exposure is the portion remaining after that date; earned plus unearned equals the policy's total exposure (1 for a single policy).

places.quote: **Earned Exposure** is the portion of written exposure for which coverage has actually been provided during the period — the exposure analogue of [[Earned Premium|earned premium]], and the correct denominator for a pure premium.

requirements.statement: In-force exposure as of a date counts policies that are in effect (effective on or before the date and not yet expired or cancelled) on that date.

places.quote: **In-Force** describes the policies, exposures or premium that are actively providing coverage at a single point in time — a *stock* measured at a date, as opposed to the *flows* of written and earned business measured over a period.

requirements.statement: With exposure earned uniformly over an annual policy term, the fraction earned at a date equals the elapsed time since the effective date divided by the term, so earned exceeds unearned only once more than half the term (six months) has elapsed.

places.quote: A $12$-month policy contributes **one** earned car-year in total, spread pro rata over its term: written the day it is issued, earned $1/12$ per month, in force from effective date to expiry.
$$\text{EP for one policy} = \text{Full premium} \times \frac{\text{days elapsed}}{\text{policy term}}$$
$$\text{UEP for one policy} = \text{Full premium} \times \frac{\text{days remaining}}{\text{policy term}}$$

requirements.statement: A cancelled policy's exposure ends at its cancellation date; a policy that is in force on a date must have been cancelled after that date, and a negative calendar-year written total requires the policy to have been written in an earlier year and cancelled in that year.

places.quote: Written premium may still change after issuance — endorsements, cancellations and [[Premium Audit|audits]] all book additional or return premium into a later period, so "written premium" for a policy year keeps moving until the audits close.
Policy X ran 9 of its 12 months, so the cancellation record reverses the last quarter of the term.

requirements.statement: Historical losses must be developed to ultimate and trended to the future period in which the rates will be in effect; using unadjusted historical losses gives a distorted (typically understated) prospective loss estimate.

places.quote: Trend and [[Loss Development|development]] answer different questions and must both be applied: development brings immature losses to *their own* ultimate level; trend restates past losses to the level expected for similar losses in the *future* period.

The pure premium used in a rate is always **projected**: historical losses developed to ultimate, trended to the forecast period, adjusted for [[Large Loss|large losses]] and [[Catastrophe Loss|catastrophes]], and divided by exposures that are themselves trended if the base inflates ([[Exposure Trend]]).

requirements.statement: The pure premium method computes the indicated rate from projected ultimate losses (and LAE) per exposure, so it uses exposures rather than premium and needs no on-level adjustment for past rate changes.

places.quote: **Pure Premium Method** derives the indicated **rate** directly: project loss and LAE per exposure, add the fixed expense per exposure, and gross up for variable expenses and profit. It never divides by premium, so it requires no [[On-Leveling|on-levelling]].
Pure premium is the **premium-free** view of cost: because it never divides by premium, it needs no [[On-Leveling|on-levelling]] and is unaffected by rate history.

requirements.statement: Exposures should be trended to the projected period when the exposure base is inflation sensitive.

places.quote: Inputs: losses developed to ultimate and trended, [[Earned Exposure|earned exposures]] (trended if the base inflates — see [[Exposure Trend]]), the fixed expense per exposure $F$, the variable expense ratio $V$, and the target profit provision $Q_T$.
Exposure trend applies **only** to inflation-sensitive bases. Car-years and house-years do not inflate; payroll, receipts and amount of insurance do.

requirements.statement: When underwriting changes such as a higher minimum deductible will alter future covered losses, restate historical losses and LAE to the new deductible level using deductible factors (or confirm the trend already reflects the change); otherwise the loss provision is overstated.

places.quote: The adjustment is a **pro-forma restatement**: take each historical claim and recompute what the insurer would have paid under the new terms, then develop the restated history. This is exactly the [[Loss Elimination Ratio|loss elimination ratio]] calculation applied retrospectively.

requirements.statement: Experience from a small number of exposures or a single year has low credibility and should be supplemented by lengthening the experience period or by a complement of credibility such as industry/benchmark data, a larger related class, or external data.

places.quote: When $Z$ is low — a small class, a new territory, an excess layer — the complement, not the data, determines the answer.
Partial credibility uses the **square root rule**, $Z = \sqrt{n / n_{\text{full}}}$, capped at $1$ — a class with a quarter of the required claims gets $Z = 0.50$.

requirements.statement: Excluding losses above a cap from the indication understates losses and makes rates inadequate; losses above the cap must be included via a large loss (excess) provision or by using uncapped or a higher-capped loss data.
requirements.concept: Capped Losses and Large Loss Provision

places.quote: The standard treatment has three steps: **cap** each claim at a threshold $M$ for the experience analysis, **compute** an excess load from a longer-term view of how often such losses occur, and **add it back**.

requirements.statement: The capping level should be chosen to include as much loss data as possible while limiting the volatility introduced by large losses, and premium must be kept at a consistent limit with the losses.

places.quote: Ideally the threshold is the point at which losses become extraordinary and their inclusion makes rates volatile. It may be the basic limit — and then the premium in a loss ratio indication must be put on a basic-limits basis too. Otherwise Werner sets it to balance including as many losses as possible against minimizing volatility: for example at the $99$th percentile of claim sizes, or at a percentage of losses;

requirements.statement: Use the parallelogram method to bring historical earned premium to current rate level, weighting each rate change by the portion of the period's earned premium written at the old and new rate levels (annual policies make earning span two years).

places.quote: - **Werner's six steps:** date the changes and form rate level groups; find each group's area in each year; build cumulative indices; take the area-weighted average index; divide it into the current index; apply the factor to the year's earned premium.
The *average* index for a year is the earned-premium-weighted blend of the levels in force during that year.

requirements.statement: Select a one-step premium trend from historical average premiums at current rate level, and apply it over the period from the average written/earned date of the experience period to the average date the new rates will be in effect.

places.quote: **One-step trending** applies a single selected annual trend across the whole period. It is adequate when the drift has been steady.

requirements.statement: Determine the trend period for premium and loss trend: from the average date of the experience period (average written or accident date) to the average date of the future period when the filed rates will be in effect (for annual policies, policy-year effective date plus half of the policy term).

places.quote: The trend period $n$ runs from the average written date of the policies earning premium in the experience period to the **average written date of the policies in effect while the new rates are** — for calendar-year 2011 earned premium and annual policies written in 2013, $1/1/2011$ to $6/30/2013$, or $2.5$ years.
$t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.

requirements.statement: Develop reported loss and ALAE to ultimate by multiplying by the cumulative development factor, built from selected age-to-age factors (chain-ladder) for the remaining development ages and a tail factor.

places.quote: **Development Factor** (link ratio or age-to-age factor) is the ratio used to project cumulative losses from one maturity age to the next, forming the building blocks of the [[Chain Ladder Method]]; chaining them together produces the [[Cumulative Development Factor]] to ultimate.
$$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: When selecting age-to-age factors, choose an averaging method that reflects a change in the claims process (such as new claims software): use only recent diagonals/years when the development pattern has shifted, and the full or excluding high/low average when the pattern appears stable.

places.quote: **Latest-$k$-year average**: uses only the most recent $k$ accident years — reduces the influence of older, potentially unrepresentative data

requirements.statement: Apply one-step loss trend to developed ultimate losses over the period from the accident period's average date to the average date the new rates will be in effect, and load for ULAE by multiplying loss and ALAE by (1 + ULAE ratio).

places.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.

It cannot be traced to a claim, so it is estimated in aggregate — classically as the ratio of calendar-year paid ULAE to calendar-year paid loss plus ALAE, applied to loss plus ALAE that has been adjusted for extraordinary events, development and trend.

requirements.statement: Select the fixed expense provision by averaging historical fixed expense ratios while excluding anomalous years caused by extraordinary events, and justify the exclusion.
Indicated rate change = (projected loss & LAE ratio + fixed expense ratio) / (1 − variable expense ratio − profit and contingencies provision) − 1.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{\text{VPLR}} - 1$$

requirements.statement: Desirable qualities of a credibility complement include being independent of (uncorrelated with) the base statistic, unbiased, easy to compute, available, and logically related to the base data.

places.quote: (3) **statistically independent** from the base statistic, or any error in the base statistic can be compounded; (4) **available** — the data needed to compute it readily obtainable; … (6) **logically related** to the base statistic, so that its use is easy to support.

requirements.statement: Countrywide loss costs as a complement are readily available and easy to compute, but they include the state's own data, so they are not fully independent of the state's experience, and they may be biased if the state differs systematically from the countrywide experience.

places.quote: **Loss costs of a larger group that includes the group being rated** — e.g. all states in the region for the state under review. It can be built to include or exclude the subject experience; if included, the subject must not dominate the group.

requirements.statement: Criteria for evaluating a rating variable in a risk classification system fall into four categories: statistical (e.g., significance, credibility, homogeneity), operational (e.g., objective, inexpensive to administer, verifiable), social (e.g., privacy, causality, controllability, affordability), and legal.

places.quote: Werner's criteria for evaluating a rating variable (after Finger's *Risk Classification*) are **statistical** (statistical significance, homogeneity, credibility), **operational** (objective, inexpensive to administer, verifiable), **social** (affordability, causality, controllability, privacy concerns) and **legal**

requirements.statement: An operational criterion requires a rating variable to be objective, well defined, and practical to obtain and verify, so that policyholders cannot easily misreport it or manipulate it (moral hazard) to lower their premium.

places.quote: **Operational** — objective, inexpensive to obtain and verify, not manipulable by the insured.
It should be objective and hard to manipulate, practical to collect and verify, and legal

requirements.statement: Privacy is a social consideration: rating variables requiring personal or intrusive information may be viewed by the public as an invasion of privacy and be unacceptable.

places.quote: **Social** — privacy, causality, controllability and affordability; these are where public and regulatory objections arise.

requirements.statement: Causality is a social consideration: a variable with a plausible causal relationship to losses is more readily accepted by the public, but causality is not required for a variable to be used and cannot be proven by the insurer.

places.quote: It must be statistically related to expected losses; a causal story strengthens the case, but ASOP No. 12 does not require one.

requirements.statement: Controllability is a social consideration: a rating variable is more acceptable when the insured can influence their own classification by changing the underlying characteristic.

places.quote: - **Social:** it passes. The variable is controllable by the insured, causally intuitive and not a proxy for a protected class.

requirements.statement: A rating variable must be permitted by law, so the insurer must check state regulations on whether a variable may be used for rating.

places.quote: **Legal** — some variables are prohibited outright in some jurisdictions.
and legal ([[Risk Classification Restrictions]], [[Unfair Discrimination]]) and socially acceptable.

requirements.statement: Under the increased limits (ILF) approach for a layer's complement of credibility, scale the capped (basic-limit) losses by the ratio of the ILF difference across the layer's limits to the ILF at the capping limit to estimate losses in the layer.
requirements.concept: Complements of Credibility for Excess Loss Ratemaking (Increased Limits Method)

places.quote: $$\text{Layer } (M, L] \text{ cost} = \text{Basic LC} \times \left[\text{ILF}(L) - \text{ILF}(M)\right]$$

requirements.statement: In the limits analysis approach, the complement for a layer equals the expected total limits loss ratio times the sum, over each policy limit above the layer's attachment point, of premium at that limit times (ILF at layer top minus ILF at layer bottom) divided by the ILF at that limit.

places.quote: For casualty, use a severity curve or ILFs: $\big[E[X \wedge \min(PL, R+L)] - E[X \wedge \min(PL, R)]\big] / E[X \wedge PL]$ by policy limit $PL$. In both cases the factor multiplies subject premium times the expected loss ratio.

resolution.quote: The complement is the total limits expected loss ratio times the sum, over the policy limits, of the total premium at each limit times that limit's share.…For a limit inside the layer the share is the ILF at the limit minus the ILF at the attachment point, divided by the ILF at the limit. For a limit above the top of the layer the share is the ILF at the top of the layer minus the ILF at the attachment point, divided by the ILF at the limit.
resolution.note: Limits analysis complement formula; W&M Ch.12 p.234 and Table 12.7 (PDF 246)

requirements.statement: Policies with limits at or below a layer's attachment point contribute nothing to losses in that layer, while policies with limits at or above the layer's top contribute using the layer's ILF difference (the layer's full width).

places.quote: The layer tops out at $\$1$M, so for both limits the numerator is $\text{ILF}(1\text{M}) - \text{ILF}(300\text{K}) = 0.40$.

resolution.quote: A limit at or below the attachment point contributes nothing to the layer.…For a limit above the top of the layer the share is the ILF at the top of the layer minus the ILF at the attachment point, divided by the ILF at the limit.
resolution.note: Which limits contribute in limits analysis; W&M Ch.12 Table 12.7 col (8) (PDF 246)

requirements.statement: The ratio of a limit's ILF to another's applies to premium and losses alike, so the ILF ratio multiplied by premium and the expected loss ratio gives expected losses in a layer from policies at that limit (premium at a limit × ILF share of layer ÷ ILF at limit = layer premium).

places.quote: In both cases the factor multiplies subject premium times the expected loss ratio.

resolution.quote: Premium at a limit times the expected loss ratio estimates the expected losses of the policies at that limit, and an ILF ratio takes the share of those losses that falls in the layer.
resolution.note: Premium x ELR x ILF share in limits analysis; W&M Ch.12 p.234 (PDF 246)

requirements.statement: Criticisms of the limits analysis approach: it assumes the same expected loss ratio for all limits, and it relies on ILFs and industry data that may be inaccurate (e.g., thin, volatile data at upper layers) or not apply to the company, with no actual layer losses used.

places.quote: Data at high limits is sparse and volatile, which is why ILFs are calculated from a broader body of experience (class group, state group or countrywide) and applied to class-, state- and territory-specific basic limit loss costs.

requirements.statement: Under the adjusted pure premium method, adjust each territory's exposures for the other rating variable by weighting exposures by that variable's current relativities (e.g., male at 1.0, female at 0.8), so that the territory indication is not distorted by the mix of the other variable.

places.quote: When other rating variables also apply, each class's exposures are first multiplied by their average relativity for those other variables, so that the factor measures only this variable's effect on the average premium.

requirements.statement: Adjusted pure premium for a class = loss and LAE divided by the exposures adjusted (weighted) by the other variable's current relativities.

places.quote: When other rating variables also apply, each class's exposures are first multiplied by their average relativity for those other variables, so that the factor measures only this variable's effect on the average premium.

requirements.statement: Indicated relativity for a class equals its pure premium divided by the overall (total) average pure premium; relativity to base equals the class's indicated relativity divided by the base class's indicated relativity.

places.quote: $$\text{Territory Relativity}_i = \frac{\text{Pure Premium}_i}{\text{Pure Premium}_{\text{base}}}$$
$$\text{Relativity}_i = \frac{\text{Pure Premium}_i}{\text{Pure Premium}_{\text{base}}}$$

requirements.statement: Indicated relativity change equals indicated relativity (relative to base) divided by current relativity, minus 1.

places.quote: A class's rate change is $(1 + \Delta)\,\text{OBF}\,r_i^{\text{new}}/r_i^{\text{old}} - 1$.

requirements.statement: Keeping the base territory's relativity at 1.0 means indicated relativities are rebased to the base class, and the overall change is revenue neutral through the base rate offset.
requirements.concept: Base Rate Offset and Revenue Neutrality

places.quote: Relativity changes almost always change the average rate. The base rate must be adjusted so that the combined effect equals the intended [[Overall Rate Level Indication|overall indication]] — see [[Rate Change]].
Raising the relativities of large or high-rated classes raises that sum, and the base rate must fall in the same proportion if the overall change is to stay at $\Delta$.

requirements.statement: Interpret GLM output for a rating variable by comparing each level's indicated relativity with its standard error: non-overlapping standard error ranges (or small standard errors relative to the relativity) indicate the variable is statistically significant and levels differ significantly.

places.quote: The 95% [[Confidence Interval|confidence interval]] is $\hat{\beta} \pm 1.96\,\mathrm{SE}$, and exponentiating it gives an interval for the class's relativity, and so for its [[Loss Cost|loss cost]].
The usual one is the normal interval, the estimate plus or minus a normal percentile times a standard error taken from the [[Fisher Information|Fisher information]].

requirements.statement: Levels with low exposure or volume have low credibility, so their GLM-indicated relativities are less reliable and should be adjusted when selecting relativities.

places.quote: Partial credibility uses the **square root rule**, $Z = \sqrt{n / n_{\text{full}}}$, capped at $1$ — a class with a quarter of the required claims gets $Z = 0.50$.
A class can be significant yet not [[Credibility|credible]] enough to use at face value.
a territory should be granular enough to capture differences in expected loss cost yet large enough to be [[Credibility|credible]] (CIA §1.1).

requirements.statement: A model built on only one year of data may be distorted by anomalies, shock losses, or random fluctuation, so its results may not be reliable enough to support implementation.

places.quote: A small class with one unusually large loss can look very risky with the loss in the data and very safe without it, with the same confidence both times.

A prediction is only as good as its out-of-sample performance: in-sample fit always improves as terms are added, so a model is judged on hold-out data or by [[Cross-Validation]] (see [[Bias-Variance Tradeoff]])

requirements.statement: Operational criteria for a good rating variable: objective, clearly defined, easy to administer and verify, and not manipulable by the insured.

places.quote: **Operational** — objective, inexpensive to obtain and verify, not manipulable by the insured.
It should be objective and hard to manipulate, practical to collect and verify, and legal ([[Risk Classification Restrictions]], [[Unfair Discrimination]]) and socially acceptable.
*For:* strong, validated predictive power; cheap, objective and hard to manipulate; its use lowers premiums for most insureds.

requirements.statement: Social criteria for a rating variable include affordability, causality (a logical relationship to expected loss), controllability by the insured, and privacy and public acceptability.

places.quote: **Social** — privacy, causality, controllability and affordability; these are where public and regulatory objections arise.
**Social:** it passes. The variable is controllable by the insured, causally intuitive and not a proxy for a protected class.

requirements.statement: Failing to charge a rate that reflects a high-risk group's true expected loss (underpricing) can lead to adverse selection against the insurer.

places.quote: In a competitive market an insurer that charges one average rate to a heterogeneous group loses the better risks to competitors that price them properly, and retains the worse ones — the **adverse selection spiral**.

**Adverse Selection** is the tendency for those who know they are worse-than-average risks to buy more insurance, and better-than-average risks to buy less, when the insurer cannot distinguish between them.

risks with different expected costs pay the same rate, so the low-cost risks subsidise the high-cost ones, and a company doing this while competitors differentiate faces [[Adverse Selection|adverse selection]] (Ch.9).

requirements.statement: Credit score is a commonly used insurance rating variable whose use is debated: it is predictive of loss and easy to verify, but it may lack a clear causal link to the peril and may be poorly perceived by the public.
requirements.concept: Credit Score as a Rating Variable

places.quote: It is one of the most predictive [[Rating Variable|rating variables]] U.S. insurers use and one of the most contested, because its predictive power is well documented while its causal link to loss and its effect on protected groups are disputed.

requirements.statement: Written exposures for a calendar year are the exposures of policies written (effective) during that year; earned exposures are the portion of policy exposure whose coverage period falls within that year.

places.quote: **Earned Exposure** is the portion of written exposure for which coverage has actually been provided during the period — the exposure analogue of [[Earned Premium|earned premium]], and the correct denominator for a pure premium.

requirements.statement: With a car-year exposure base, a policy with a term shorter than one year contributes only the fraction of a car-year equal to its term (e.g., a six-month policy contributes 0.5 car-year).

places.quote: A $12$-month policy contributes **one** earned car-year in total, spread pro rata over its term: written the day it is issued, earned $1/12$ per month, in force from effective date to expiry.

requirements.statement: Earned exposure in a calendar year for a policy is its exposure multiplied by the fraction of its term falling in that year, assuming exposure is earned evenly over the term.

places.quote: With policies written **uniformly** through the year, a calendar year earns roughly half of that year's written exposure plus half of the prior year's.

requirements.statement: Parallelogram method: draw the policy-year/calendar-year square, find the area earned at the new rate level in the calendar year, compute the average rate level as an area-weighted average of old and new levels, and the on-level factor is the current rate level divided by the average rate level.

places.quote: $$\text{On-Level Factor} = \frac{\text{Current cumulative rate level index}}{\text{Average rate level index for the period}}$$

**Werner's six steps:** date the changes and form rate level groups; find each group's area in each year; build cumulative indices; take the area-weighted average index; divide it into the current index; apply the factor to the year's earned premium.

Picture a unit square whose horizontal axis is calendar time and whose vertical axis is the fraction of the policy term elapsed. A rate change effective on date $d$ enters as a diagonal line; each region's **area** is the share of the year's earned premium written at that rate level.

requirements.statement: The parallelogram method assumes policies are written uniformly throughout the period; it is inappropriate when writings are concentrated on specific dates or the volume is trending.

places.quote: It assumes uniform writing — false for seasonal business such as boat owners, whose policies are bought ahead of the season; refining to quarters or months, or weighting by the actual distribution of writings, helps.
The method's assumptions are its weaknesses: premium written **uniformly** through the year, a **single** policy term, and rate changes applied uniformly to all risks.

requirements.statement: Extension of exposures: re-rate each earned exposure at current rates, so earned premium at current rate level equals earned exposures times current rate (annualized premium per exposure).

places.quote: **Extension of Exposures** is the [[On-Leveling|on-leveling]] method that re-rates every historical policy under the rates in effect today, using each policy's own rating characteristics, so that historical premium is restated at the current rate level policy by policy rather than by an average factor.
**Extension of exposures** has none of those assumptions — it simply re-rates each historical policy at today's rates — and it automatically captures distributional shifts.
[[Extension of Exposures|Extension of exposures]] re-rates every policy at today's rates, which is the most accurate approach but needs policy-level data.

requirements.statement: Premium per policy for a term shorter than a year must be annualized (e.g., multiplied by 12/term in months) when applied to car-year exposures to get premium per car year.

places.quote: Each policy in force contributes its full-term premium — D its six-month $\$500$, not an annualized $\$1{,}000$:

requirements.statement: A good rating variable produces clear differentiation between its levels, i.e. distinct indicated relativities for each level.
requirements.concept: Criteria for a Good Rating Variable

places.quote: A categorical one uses the levels of a [[Categorical Predictor|categorical predictor]], possibly with [[Interaction|interactions]].

requirements.statement: A good rating variable has stable, consistent indicated relativities from year to year (stability over time).
requirements.concept: Criteria for a Good Rating Variable

places.quote: Models lose accuracy as the world changes, so they are also rebuilt periodically.

requirements.statement: Assess statistical significance of a GLM relativity by checking whether its +/-2 standard error band (approximate 95% confidence interval) contains the base relativity of 1.0; if it does, the level is not significantly different from the base.
requirements.concept: GLM Standard Errors and Confidence Intervals

places.quote: Urban risks are estimated to have $12\%$ to $80\%$ higher frequency. The interval excludes $1.00$, so the effect is significant at $5\%$ — but it is wide enough that the indicated relativity is far from precisely known.

requirements.statement: When the one-way loss ratio relativity differs materially from the GLM relativity, the variable is probably correlated with other rating variables, since the GLM adjusts for correlations and the loss ratio method does not.

places.quote: A **univariate** (one-way) pure premium or loss ratio analysis attributes to a variable the effect of everything correlated with it. If young drivers also drive older cars, a one-way age relativity contains part of the vehicle-age effect, and rating both double-counts.

requirements.statement: Levels with very few exposures yield less credible, more volatile estimates (wider standard errors), so such a level may be combined with an adjacent level.
requirements.concept: Credibility and Exposure Volume in GLM

places.quote: Very high correlation makes the model unstable, with erratic coefficients, large standard errors and estimates that swing with small changes in the data.

requirements.statement: Operational and practical criteria for a good rating variable include objectivity/controllability, ease and cost of verification, resistance to manipulation, social acceptability (privacy), regulatory acceptability, relationship to expected loss, and historical precedent.
requirements.concept: Criteria for a Good Rating Variable

places.quote: **Operational** — objective, inexpensive to obtain and verify, not manipulable by the insured.
It should be objective and hard to manipulate, practical to collect and verify, and legal ([[Risk Classification Restrictions]], [[Unfair Discrimination]]) and socially acceptable.

requirements.statement: A recommendation on adding a rating variable weighs statistical evidence (differentiation, stability, significance) against operational criteria (verifiability, manipulation, acceptability), and should be consistent with earlier findings.
requirements.concept: Criteria for a Good Rating Variable

places.quote: Model relativities are still [[Credibility|credibility]]-weighted and are still subject to the operational, social and legal criteria for a rating variable — statistical significance alone does not make a variable usable.
**Operational** — objective, inexpensive to obtain and verify, not manipulable by the insured.

Adopt it only in a verifiable form — odometer readings at renewal or telematics — or with a moderated factor and audit rights. A strong model coefficient does not by itself make a usable rating variable.

requirements.statement: Using the extension of exposures method, compute current premium by multiplying each cell's exposures by the base rate and the current relativities of each rating variable, and sum across cells (dividing by total exposures gives average premium).

places.quote: $$\text{Rate}_i = \text{Base Rate} \times \prod_k R_{i,k}$$

**Extension of Exposures** is the [[On-Leveling|on-leveling]] method that re-rates every historical policy under the rates in effect today, using each policy's own rating characteristics, so that historical premium is restated at the current rate level policy by policy rather than by an average factor.
Each exposure in class $i$ pays $B\,r_i$, so the book's premium is $B \sum_i w_i r_i$.

requirements.statement: The target premium after a rate change equals current premium times one plus the indicated overall average rate change.

places.quote: Taking $+8.0\%$ on the base rate *and* implementing the new relativities would deliver $1.08 \times 1.03 = +11.2\%$ — three points more than intended
$$\sum_i w_i\, B_{\text{new}}\, r_i^{\text{new}} = (1 + \Delta) \sum_i w_i\, B_{\text{old}}\, r_i^{\text{old}}$$

requirements.statement: When the base class is kept, rebase the indicated relativities by dividing each level's indicated relativity by the indicated relativity of the base class so the base class equals 1.000.
requirements.concept: Rebalancing Relativities to the Base Class

places.quote: $$\text{Relativity}_i = \frac{\text{Pure Premium}_i}{\text{Pure Premium}_{\text{base}}}$$
Relative to class A, the new relativities are $1.25(0.660/0.600) = 1.375$ for B and $1.60(0.750/0.600) = 2.000$ for C.

requirements.statement: To find the new base rate, set the proposed premium (exposures times new base rate times proposed relativities, summed) equal to the target premium and solve for the base rate, which offsets the effect of relativity changes.
requirements.concept: Base Rate Offset for Relativity Changes

places.quote: **Off-balance.** Relativity changes almost always change the average rate. The base rate must be adjusted so that the combined effect equals the intended [[Overall Rate Level Indication|overall indication]]
any simultaneous change to classification relativities must be **off-balanced** so the two together produce the intended overall effect, not the sum of both.
$$B_{\text{new}} = B_{\text{old}} \times (1 + \Delta) \times \text{OBF}$$

requirements.statement: A minimum premium requirement means any policy whose calculated premium falls below the minimum is charged the minimum premium instead.

places.quote: $$\text{Premium} = \max\!\left(\text{Rate} \times \text{Exposure},\; \text{Minimum Premium}\right)$$

requirements.statement: Identify which classes fall below the minimum premium using the new base rate and relativities, then compute the extra premium raised by charging the minimum in those classes.

places.quote: Since $\$600 < \$750$, the minimum applies and the charge is $\$750$.

requirements.statement: Offset the extra premium from the minimum premium by lowering the base rate: divide the base rate by an off-balance factor of one plus the extra premium over target premium (or equivalently, solve for a base rate so the other cells produce the target premium less the minimum-premium cells' premium).

places.quote: **Off-balance.** Relativity changes almost always change the average rate. The base rate must be adjusted so that the combined effect equals the intended [[Overall Rate Level Indication|overall indication]]
The relativity revision already delivers part of the increase, so the base rate must supply only the remainder — multiplicatively, not by subtraction:
$$\text{OBF} = \frac{\sum_i w_i\, r_i^{\text{old}}}{\sum_i w_i\, r_i^{\text{new}}}$$

requirements.statement: The coinsurance requirement means the insured must carry insurance at least equal to the coinsurance percentage times the property value; the required amount of insurance is c × V.

places.quote: The insured must carry insurance of at least $cV$, e.g. $80\%$ of the property's value $V$, or the payment on a covered loss is reduced in proportion to the underinsurance.

requirements.statement: With a coinsurance penalty, the indemnity is I = min(L × F/(cV), L, F), where L is the loss, F the amount of insurance, c the coinsurance requirement and V the property value; the penalty is L − I.

places.quote: $$I = L \times \frac{F}{cV}, \quad \text{where } I \le F \text{ and } I \le L$$

requirements.statement: The coinsurance penalty as a function of loss rises linearly from the origin to its maximum at L = F (where the indemnity reaches the face amount), then falls linearly to zero at L = cV, and is zero for larger losses.

resolution.quote: It arises only when $L > 0$, $F < cV$ and $L < cV$, rises linearly to its largest at $L = F$, falls back to zero at $L = cV$
resolution.note: The penalty-versus-loss shape (rises to its maximum at L = F, falls to zero at cV) is stated on the tagged page.

requirements.statement: For a loss distribution mixing a point mass at total loss with a uniform distribution on the remaining losses, the probability of each segment is found by scaling the uniform portion by (1 − point mass probability) and the interval's share of the range, with the remaining probability going to the segment above the cap.

resolution.note: The point mass and uniform distribution are given by the question; finding each segment probability is probability arithmetic (Exam P), not Exam 5 course content.

requirements.statement: The limited average severity at the amount of insurance is the probability-weighted average of losses capped at the amount of insurance: uniform losses below the cap average the midpoint, and losses at or above the cap contribute the cap amount.

places.quote: The **Limited Expected Value** (LEV) of a random variable $X$ at limit $u$ is the expected value of the payment under a policy that pays $X$ up to a maximum of $u$.
$E[X \wedge u]$ is the [[Limited Expected Value|limited expected value]], the expected loss capped at $u$.

requirements.statement: Pure premium equals loss frequency times limited average severity.

places.quote: $$\text{Pure Premium} = \text{Frequency} \times \text{Severity}$$
$$\text{Pure Premium} = \text{Frequency} \times \text{Severity}$$

requirements.statement: The rate per $1000 of insurance equals the pure premium divided by the amount of insurance in thousands.

resolution.quote: the rate per amount of insurance is set by the face amount chosen, as expected indemnity divided by face value
resolution.note: Rate per amount of insurance = expected indemnity / face value; per $1000 is the unit.

requirements.statement: Retrospective premium = (basic premium + loss conversion factor × limited reported losses) × tax multiplier, subject to the minimum and maximum retrospective premium.

places.quote: $$R = \left(\text{BP} + L \times \text{LCF}\right) \times \text{TM}$$

requirements.statement: The minimum and maximum retrospective premiums equal the minimum and maximum retro premium ratios multiplied by the standard premium.

resolution.quote: is the standard premium on which the basic premium factor, the minimum and the maximum are all computed
resolution.note: Syllabus page: the retro minimum and maximum are computed on standard premium.

requirements.statement: If the calculated retrospective premium falls below the minimum, the minimum premium is charged; if it exceeds the maximum, the maximum is charged; otherwise the calculated premium applies.

places.quote: $$\text{Retro Premium} = \min\!\left(\max(R,\, R_{\min}),\, R_{\max}\right)$$
This is above the maximum, so the premium is capped at $\$200{,}000$ and the insurer **charges** $200{,}000 - 111{,}280 = \$88{,}720$.

requirements.statement: A retrospectively rated policy's premium is recomputed at each successive evaluation age using the limited reported losses at that age, with the same parameters.

places.quote: Incurred loss retro plans are typically first evaluated 6 months after policy expiration (18 months of development) and annually thereafter.
Losses valued six months after expiration are $\$70{,}000$. A year later they have developed to $\$150{,}000$.

requirements.statement: Combining segments (e.g., states) in an unpaid claims analysis gives more data volume and greater credibility/stability, which favors combining when a segment is small and its development patterns are similar to the other segment's.
requirements.concept: Segmentation of Data in Loss Reserving

places.quote: fine enough that each group's risks share similar expected costs and emergence patterns ([[Homogeneity|homogeneity]]), yet large and stable enough that each group's own experience can be relied on ([[Credibility|credibility]]).
Splitting a book finer makes each group more alike but leaves each with less data; combining groups buys volume at the price of averaging together risks that genuinely differ.

requirements.statement: Combined data should be homogeneous with a stable mix of business; differing policy limits or a shifting mix of volume between segments makes development and severity patterns distort, which argues against combining.
requirements.concept: Segmentation of Data in Loss Reserving

places.quote: In **reserving**, a mix shift breaks the [[Homogeneity|homogeneity]] assumption behind the [[Development Triangle|triangle]]. If the segments have different emergence patterns, the blended development factors drift as the weights drift — and the triangle gives no signal that this is what is happening.
Do not combine segments whose relative volume is changing — see [[Mix of Business]] and [[Reserving Data Organization]].
Two books with the same nominal line code can have very different development if one is written at higher limits.

requirements.statement: Reported CDFs (loss development patterns) that are similar across segments support combining those segments, since combining will not materially distort development.

places.quote: group claims that share coverage (the same laws, policy terms and claims handling), with enough claim counts, and similar reporting patterns, ability to set case reserves, settlement patterns, reopening likelihood and severity;
Two coverages may have similar loss ratios and completely different reporting and settlement speeds; combining them into one triangle produces development factors that describe neither.

requirements.statement: Higher policy limits allow larger claims, so a segment with higher limits has higher expected severity, and a shift in the mix of business toward the higher-limit segment increases the combined average severity.

places.quote: For that reason severity is usually studied on **capped** or **basic limits** data, with the excess layer priced separately through [[Increased Limits|increased limits factors]]. Trending unlimited severity mixes a genuine cost trend with the leveraged growth of the excess layer.

requirements.statement: A large claim threshold should reflect the number of claims exceeding it, so that enough large claims exist to assess them credibly and the remaining basic-limit data is stable.

places.quote: Otherwise Werner sets it to balance including as many losses as possible against minimizing volatility

requirements.statement: A large claim threshold should consider the size of claims relative to policy limits and reinsurance retention or limits, since these cap or transfer the exposure to large claims.

places.quote: where the size-of-loss distribution varies a lot by policy (property), as a percentage of the amount of insurance rather than a fixed amount.
because reinsurance caps exactly the large losses that drive volatility

requirements.statement: A large claim threshold may vary by line of business and by the size of the book, and can be informed by loss distribution percentiles, industry benchmarks, external data, and discussion with the claims department.

places.quote: for example at the $99$th percentile of claim sizes, or at a percentage of losses

requirements.statement: Large claims distort the development technique because LDFs derived from data without large claims (or leveraged by large claims) are applied to the reported or paid claims of immature years that contain large claims, overstating unpaid claims.

places.quote: Leaving a $\$2$M claim in an immature diagonal and multiplying it by a CDF of $4$ produces an $\$8$M estimate from one claim.
A [[Large Loss|shock loss]] reported early is multiplied by the full CDF.

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson technique is less affected by large claims than the development technique because its unpaid claims are based on an a priori expected claims estimate, weighted with the development method by credibility.

places.quote: The key structural property: **actual emergence is taken at face value and only the unemerged portion is estimated**. The chain ladder instead scales the whole diagonal, so a distorted diagonal is multiplied by the full CDF.

requirements.statement: Report year aggregation groups claims by the year in which they were reported, whereas accident year aggregation groups claims by the year in which the accident occurred.
requirements.concept: Data Aggregation Methods (Accident, Report, Policy Year)

places.quote: **Accident Year** (AY) is a data aggregation method that groups losses by the calendar year in which the loss event *occurred*, and matches them against the [[Earned Premium|premium earned]] in that same year — regardless of when the policy was written, when the claim was reported, or when it was paid.
**Report Year** (RY) is a data aggregation method that groups claims by the calendar year in which the claim was first *reported* to the insurer, regardless of when the loss occurred.

requirements.statement: Reported (incurred) claims at an evaluation date equal cumulative paid claims plus case outstanding reserves, net of any recoveries such as deductible recoveries.

places.quote: $$\text{Reported (Incurred)} = \text{Paid} + \text{Case Reserves}$$

requirements.statement: To build a cumulative development triangle, assign each claim to its aggregation period, evaluate its cumulative amount at each annual valuation date (12, 24, 36 months), and sum across claims, with later evaluations only for periods old enough to have reached them.

places.quote: Cell $C_{\text{AY},k}$ holds the cumulative amount for that accident year at age $k$. The triangle is triangular because a $2024$ accident year cannot yet have a $36$-month valuation.

requirements.statement: Paid claims count only actual payments net of recoveries; case outstanding is excluded, and a claim closed without payment contributes zero paid.

places.quote: $$\text{Net Loss} = \text{Gross Paid} - \text{Collected Recoveries}$$

requirements.statement: Report year aggregation has fixed claim counts at year end, suits claims-made policies and shifts in legal climate tied to report date, and has only settlement lag with no report lag, but it contains no pure IBNR and so cannot be used to estimate IBNR (IBNYR) and has less benchmark data.

places.quote: A report year **closes to new claims** at year end — pure [[IBNR]] is zero by construction, since every claim in the cohort is already known.

**[[Report Year]]** is the basis actuaries often prefer for [[Claims Made Coverage|claims-made]] business: a report year contains no pure [[IBNR]], and its claim count is fixed at the close of the year.

requirements.statement: Accident year aggregation is common with abundant industry benchmarks, easy to understand, and useful for changes in legal or economic environment and for catastrophe events, but it imperfectly matches losses to premium or exposure, mixes policies at different rate levels, and can mask changes in policy limits or deductibles or business mix.

places.quote: Premium and losses are only *approximately* matched. AY $n$ earned premium comes partly from policies written in year $n-1$, whose rates and terms differ — which is why the premium must still be brought to current level ([[On-Leveling]]).
On an accident year basis, AY 2024 is a blend: losses occurring in $2024$ arise both from $2024$-written policies (new deductible) and from $2023$-written policies still running off (old deductible).

requirements.statement: An age-to-age (link ratio) factor is the reported claims at a later age divided by the reported claims at the prior age for the same accident year.

places.quote: $$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{AY}} = \frac{C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$

requirements.statement: Select an age-to-age factor for each development period from the observed factors using an average (volume-weighted, simple, geometric, or latest-years), choosing based on trends in the factors.

places.quote: Look at the column **before** averaging it. A steady column supports a volume-weighted all-year selection; a column trending over time is a signal, not noise, and calls for the latest years or an investigation.

requirements.statement: Compute the age-to-ultimate factor (CDF) by multiplying the selected age-to-age factors from the given age through the last development age, with a tail factor of 1.000 if no development is assumed beyond the last age.

places.quote: CDFs are built **backwards from the tail**: start with the tail factor, multiply in each successive age-to-age factor moving toward younger ages.
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: The reported development technique estimates ultimate claims as reported claims to date times the age-to-ultimate factor for that age.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: In the expected claims technique, estimate each prior year's ultimate claims by developing it to ultimate, trend it to the cost level of the projected year, and divide by on-level earned premium to get an expected claim ratio for that year.

places.quote: The **ELR** is the whole method, and it must be derived, not assumed: from the pricing indication for that year, from mature years' ultimate loss ratios adjusted for [[Rate Level Change|rate level]] and [[Loss Trend|trend]], or from [[External Information in Reserving|industry benchmarks]].
estimates a separate a priori [[Expected Loss Method|expected claim ratio]] for each accident year as a weighted average of the trended, on-level loss ratios of all the years

requirements.statement: Select the expected claim ratio from prior years' ratios (excluding the year being projected), justified by the pattern in the data such as an increasing trend favoring recent years for responsiveness versus more years for stability, and apply it to the projected year's on-level earned premium to get ultimate claims.

places.quote: Select $70\%$ as the base-year (AY 2020) expectation, from the three mature years.
Choosing $D$ is a judgment about how far the true loss ratio drifts from year to year.

requirements.statement: Annual claims trend compounds, so trending a year's claims to a later cost level multiplies by (1 + trend) raised to the number of years between the accident years.

places.quote: $$\text{Trend Factor} = (1 + t)^{n}$$
The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: The age-to-age (link ratio) factor for a development interval is the cumulative reported claims at the later age divided by cumulative reported claims at the earlier age for the same accident year.

places.quote: $$f_{n \to n{+}1} = \frac{\text{Losses at age }n{+}1}{\text{Losses at age }n}$$
**Age-to-Age Factor** (link ratio) is the ratio of a cohort's cumulative amount at one maturity to its amount at the previous maturity — the observed development between two ages.

requirements.statement: Select an age-to-age factor for each development interval from the observed factors (e.g., simple average, excluding anomalous outliers), and justify the selection based on the pattern in the data and the number of observations available.

places.quote: **Volume-weighted average**: $\Sigma(\text{col }n{+}1) / \Sigma(\text{col }n)$ — gives more credibility to larger accident years; the standard default selection

Look at the column **before** averaging it. A steady column supports a volume-weighted all-year selection; a column trending over time is a signal, not noise, and calls for the latest years or an investigation.

requirements.statement: The cumulative development factor (CDF) to ultimate at a given age is the product of the selected age-to-age factors from that age through the last development age (with a tail factor of 1.00 if no development after the final age).

places.quote: $$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$
CDFs are built **backwards from the tail**: start with the tail factor, multiply in each successive age-to-age factor moving toward younger ages.

requirements.statement: Bornhuetter-Ferguson ultimate claims = reported claims to date + (a priori expected claim ratio × earned premium) × (1 − 1/CDF), where the second term is the expected unreported (IBNR) claims.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$
$$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$

requirements.statement: The BF method can be interpreted as a credibility weighting of the development (chain-ladder) method and the expected claims method, with credibility Z = 1/CDF assigned to the development method.

places.quote: BF is a **credibility weighting** in disguise: it equals $Z \, U_{\text{CL}} + (1-Z)\,U_0$ with $Z = 1/\text{CDF}$.

It is one end of the spectrum the reserving methods occupy: **expected claims** puts $100\%$ weight on the a priori, the [[Chain Ladder Method|chain ladder]] puts $100\%$ on actual emergence, and the [[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method|BF]] method blends them by the percentage reported.

requirements.statement: When CDFs are less than 1.00, the implied credibility Z = 1/CDF exceeds 1, which is not a valid credibility weight; the BF method may still be used with adjustments such as capping CDFs at 1.00, or an alternative technique may be used.
The development (chain-ladder) method estimates ultimate claims as current reported or paid claims multiplied by the cumulative development factor (CDF) to ultimate.

places.quote: **Chain Ladder Method** (development or link-ratio method) projects each cohort to ultimate by multiplying its latest cumulative amount by a [[Cumulative Development Factor|cumulative development factor]] derived from the historical pattern.
$$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate} = C_n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson ultimate equals actual reported (or paid) claims to date plus expected claims (earned premium × expected claims ratio) times the percent unreported (or unpaid), 1 − 1/CDF.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$
$$\text{IBNR}_j = \text{ELR}_j \times P_j \times \left(1 - \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_j}\right)$$

requirements.statement: A tail factor beyond the last observed age can be selected from the ratio of reported claims to paid claims at the latest maturity, and the paid CDFs are multiplied by this tail factor to update the paid development and paid B-F methods.

places.quote: **Paid-to-reported convergence** — reported losses must eventually equal paid, so the ratio of the two at the oldest maturities implies how much paid development remains.
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \left(\prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1}\right) \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: The expected claims ratio in B-F should be selected by reviewing the ultimate claims ratios from historical years and methods, and lowered if the selected ratio exceeds what history supports.

places.quote: The ultimate loss ratio ($U / \text{EP}$) is the number that links reserving to pricing: it is the retrospective test of whether the year was priced adequately, and it is the input to the a priori for future years ([[Rate Level Change]]).

requirements.statement: A drop in the paid-to-reported claims ratio at a given maturity, together with a jump in reported claims but stable paid claims, indicates a possible increase in case reserve adequacy rather than a settlement slowdown.
requirements.concept: Case Reserve Adequacy and Settlement Rate Changes

places.quote: a rising ratio is consistent with faster settlement or weaker case reserves, a falling one with slower settlement or stronger case reserves
**Strengthening** raises reported losses immediately, so recent age-to-age factors fall (more of the ultimate is already booked).

requirements.statement: To adjust for a change in case reserve adequacy, restate reported claims (or the reported CDF) by the adequacy change factor, e.g. dividing the reported CDF or reported claims by the ratio of the current to prior case reserve level, before applying reported development or B-F.
requirements.concept: Case Reserve Adequacy and Settlement Rate Changes

places.quote: The remedy is the [[Berquist-Sherman Method|Berquist-Sherman]] case adjustment: restate historical average case outstanding to the current adequacy level using a selected severity trend, rebuild the reported triangle, and select factors from the restated history.
3. **Trend the latest diagonal's** average case outstanding backwards at $t$ to restate each historical cell at today's adequacy level.

requirements.statement: If case reserve adequacy has increased, reported-claims-based methods (reported development, and to a lesser degree reported B-F) overstate ultimate claims, while paid methods are more reliable; B-F is less affected than development because it gives weight to the expected claims.

places.quote: BF's answer moves dollar-for-dollar with a reporting anomaly; the chain ladder's moves by CDF-times.
Applying historical factors — built under weaker reserving — to a strengthened diagonal **over-states** ultimate, because the strengthening is developed a second time.

requirements.statement: Assess a selected ultimate by comparing it to the revised method estimates (range, average) and explaining why it lies outside them, considering which methods are distorted and which are stable.

places.quote: No method is right; the **selection** is the deliverable. Methods disagree in informative ways, and the disagreement between paid and reported estimates is a diagnostic about the diagonal, not a menu.

Standard practice is to run several methods on both paid and reported data, lay the results side by side by accident year, and select — leaning on a priori methods at immature ages and development methods at mature ones, with reasons recorded.

requirements.statement: An exposure base is a measure of the size of the risk or unit of exposure (e.g., sales, payroll, number of patients) to which a rate is applied to compute premium.

places.quote: **Exposure Base** is the basic unit of risk that underlies the premium — the quantity the rate is charged *per*. It measures a policy's exposure to loss, which is why it is the basis of the premium: base rates are expressed per exposure, and it is the denominator of the pure premium.

requirements.statement: A good exposure base is proportional to expected losses, meaning it is correlated with and responsive to changes in the underlying exposure to loss.

places.quote: **Proportional to expected loss.** All else equal, a policy with two exposures should have twice the expected loss of a similar policy with one.

Payroll is the workers compensation base because it is responsive to changes in exposure: as the number of workers or the hours they work rise or fall, both payroll and the risk of loss move with them.

requirements.statement: A good exposure base is practical: it is easy and inexpensive to obtain and verify, and hard for the insured to manipulate or misreport (limiting moral hazard).

places.quote: **Practical.** Objective, and relatively easy and inexpensive to obtain and verify — which also keeps policyholders and producers from manipulating it (declared annual mileage invites more dishonesty than car-years).

requirements.statement: A good exposure base has historical precedence: using the established industry-standard base avoids large premium swings and system change costs.

places.quote: **Consistent with historical precedence.** A change of base can cause large premium swings for individual insureds, requires a change in the rating algorithm and systems, and may force significant adjustments to the several years of data a ratemaking analysis uses.

requirements.statement: Common exposure bases by line: sales/revenue for general liability, and number of patients, physicians/nurses, or occupied beds for hospital professional liability.
requirements.concept: Common Exposure Bases by Line of Business

places.quote: Common bases: earned car-years (personal auto), earned house-years (homeowners), payroll — in hundreds of dollars in the U.S. — (workers compensation), sales revenue, payroll, square footage or number of units (commercial general liability), amount of insurance (commercial business property).

requirements.statement: The frequency-severity technique is applicable to all lines but is most often used for long-tailed lines, where ultimate severities are not known for a long time and separate frequency and severity trends/projections give better estimates than development of reported or paid claims alone.

places.quote: Projecting each with the tool it suits — development for counts, trend for severity — is often better than developing either alone.

No single method dominates. Practice is to run [[Chain Ladder Method|chain ladder]], [[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method|BF]], [[Expected Loss Method|expected claims]] and [[Frequency-Severity Method|frequency-severity]] on both paid and reported data, and to weight toward the a priori methods at immature ages.

requirements.statement: General liability is a long-tailed, low-frequency, high-severity line, so analyzing frequency and severity separately is sensible.

places.quote: Typical long-tail lines: medical malpractice, workers compensation (especially permanent total disability), general and products liability, excess casualty, environmental and asbestos exposures.
In **liability**, nothing below the limit caps the loss: tails are heavy, reporting is slow, and whether ALAE sits inside or outside the limit matters.

requirements.statement: The frequency-severity technique assumes that claim definitions, policy terms and the mix of claims (e.g., deductible levels) are consistent over time; changes in these violate its key assumptions unless historical data are adjusted to the current basis.

places.quote: The method needs **consistent count definitions** across the whole triangle, and it is sensitive to [[Large Loss|large losses]] in the severity series, so severities are usually capped and the excess layer added back separately.
The adjustment is a **pro-forma restatement**: take each historical claim and recompute what the insurer would have paid under the new terms, then develop the restated history.

requirements.statement: Lowering the deductible increases claim frequency (more losses exceed the deductible and are reported as claims) and changes average severity because many small claims are added (decreasing average severity per claim, while the loss amount per claim rises since less is eliminated by the deductible).

places.quote: A higher deductible eliminates small, fast-closing claims, so the surviving claims are larger and slower
an insured with a higher deductible may not report a claim whose small net payment is not worth a claim surcharge

requirements.statement: Data on losses below a large deductible are censored/unavailable, so historical data cannot be restated to a smaller deductible basis without information on those small losses.

places.quote: When the data hold only losses net of the deductible, policies with a deductible *higher* than the one being priced cannot be used.
Data are [[Truncation|truncated]] below deductibles and [[Censoring|censored]] at policy limits.

requirements.statement: When policy terms change, use policy-year rather than accident-year grouping to separate policies with different deductibles, and adjust prior policy years to the new deductible level.
requirements.concept: Policy Year vs Accident Year Data

places.quote: On a [[Policy Year]] basis the change is clean; on an [[Accident Year]] basis it phases in over roughly two years, which is one of the few situations where policy year is the better reserving basis.
and it is the required basis where a policy's terms (limits, deductibles, rate level) matter more than the calendar.

requirements.statement: The expected claims method or Bornhuetter-Ferguson method, using an expected claim ratio selected from judgment or industry data, is preferable when little experience exists under changed conditions because it does not rely solely on historical development patterns.

places.quote: The responses here are to weight recent years more heavily, to segment the data so the changing mix is visible, or to lean on a priori methods whose ELR can be set for the new book.
It is therefore the method of choice at **immature maturities** and for [[Long Tail Lines|long-tail lines]], converging to the chain ladder as the cohort matures.

requirements.statement: A disposal rate is the cumulative closed claim count at a given age divided by the ultimate reported claim count for that accident year.

places.quote: $$\text{Disposal Rate}_n = \frac{\text{Closed claims at age } n}{\text{Ultimate claim counts}}$$
(in Friedland, cumulative closed claim counts divided by the selected ultimate claim count for the accident year; other authors define it differently)

requirements.statement: Ultimate reported claim counts are estimated by developing the reported count triangle with age-to-age factors, selecting an average for each age, and multiplying by the age-to-ultimate factor (the product of the selected factors; 1.000 if no development after the last age).

places.quote: $$\text{Ultimate Counts} = N_n \times \text{CDF}^{\text{count}}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{vol-wtd}} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$

**The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.

requirements.statement: A Berquist-Sherman paid claim adjustment is appropriate when disposal rates show a change in the rate of settlement (e.g., a shift along the latest diagonal), since this distorts a paid development pattern built from historical data.

places.quote: Which adjustment applies is decided by the **diagnostic**, not by preference: a jump in average case outstanding across all years points to adequacy; a jump in closure rates points to settlement speed.

A moving **disposal rate** is a [[Settlement Rate|settlement speed]] change and distorts **paid** development; a jump in **average case outstanding** is a [[Case Adequacy|case adequacy]] change and distorts **reported** development. Both call for the corresponding [[Berquist-Sherman Method|Berquist-Sherman]] adjustment.

requirements.statement: The Berquist-Sherman paid adjustment assumes that a higher proportion of closed claim counts corresponds to a higher proportion of claims paid, with the same mix of claim sizes being closed.

places.quote: For each historical cell, interpolate the paid losses that *would* have been paid had that year closed claims at the current rate — reading along the row's paid-versus-disposal-rate relationship.
The trade-off is severe selection bias: within any recent accident year the claims that close first are the small, simple ones.

requirements.statement: Falling paid severity on closed claims together with rising disposal rates suggests a change in claim handling, such as closing small claims faster, which violates the method's assumption and distorts the adjusted development pattern, whereas ordinary severity trends can be accommodated by the method.

places.quote: Closed-claim severity therefore **understates** ultimate severity, and the bias is worst in the [[Long Tail Lines|long-tail lines]] where the expensive claims litigate for years.
Faster closing inflates the recent paid diagonal, so historical paid factors **over-develop** it.

requirements.statement: At early maturities the development (chain-ladder) technique is highly leveraged: small fluctuations in the few reported or paid losses are multiplied by a large CDF, giving volatile, unreliable ultimate estimates when the development pattern is long.

places.quote: **Long-tail lines** ([[Long Tail Lines|liability, workers compensation]]) have large CDFs at early maturities and need a [[Tail Factor]] beyond the observed triangle;
In a triangle, PY rows develop more slowly than AY rows and the earliest maturities are thin, so [[Chain Ladder Method|chain ladder]] factors at $12$ months are highly leveraged.

The chain ladder is at its best on **mature cohorts with stable patterns and ample volume** — and at its worst at immature ages in [[Long Tail Lines|long-tail lines]], where the CDF is large and the diagonal is thin.

requirements.statement: When the development technique is too leveraged at early maturities, respond by using the Bornhuetter-Ferguson or Expected Claims method, which relies on an a priori expected ultimate and so reduces the leverage of the actual emerged losses.

places.quote: There, [[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method|BF]] or the [[Expected Loss Method|expected claims]] technique is preferred.
It is therefore the method of choice at **immature maturities** and for [[Long Tail Lines|long-tail lines]], converging to the chain ladder as the cohort matures.

requirements.statement: If a change such as tort reform or faster claim processing shortens development or lowers severity, historical development factors are too high, so the development technique overstates ultimate claims.

places.quote: *Faster settlement*: paid development overstates; reported methods are largely unaffected.
Faster closing inflates the recent paid diagonal, so historical paid factors **over-develop** it.

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson method is inappropriate when severity changes, because the change also alters the percent unreported implied by the historical pattern.

To handle a shift in severity or settlement speed, use the Frequency-Severity technique with modified severity, or use report-year data, rather than relying on unadjusted historical development factors.

places.quote: Develop counts, but estimate severity by **trending** a mature year's severity forward rather than developing an immature one — useful where severity development is unstable but severity trend is well understood.

That makes RY triangles develop faster and more smoothly than [[Accident Year]] triangles, and it makes RY the natural basis for **severity** studies: the claim count denominator is fixed, so an average-severity triangle is not distorted by late-emerging claims.
