requirements.statement: When claim settlement speeds up (e.g., a new claims system), use the Berquist-Sherman method to adjust the historical data (paid and reported triangles) so that development factors reflect the current settlement rate.

places.quote: **Berquist-Sherman Method** restates a historical [[Development Triangle|triangle]] so that every year reflects **current** claims practice, removing the distortion caused by a change in [[Case Adequacy|case reserve adequacy]] or in [[Settlement Rate|claim settlement rates]].

A moving **disposal rate** is a [[Settlement Rate|settlement speed]] change and distorts **paid** development; a jump in **average case outstanding** is a [[Case Adequacy|case adequacy]] change and distorts **reported** development. Both call for the corresponding [[Berquist-Sherman Method|Berquist-Sherman]] adjustment.

requirements.statement: Higher policy deductibles slow development, since losses take longer to reach the deductible and a larger share of loss comes from large claims that settle later, and they also shift the business mix and lower average loss paid, so historical development factors misstate ultimates.

places.quote: Other common causes: a new distribution channel, entering or exiting a territory, a change in the [[Deductible Rating|deductible]] or limit profile, a growth push in one segment, and [[Underwriting Changes|underwriting]] tightening.
On an accident year basis, AY 2024 is a blend: losses occurring in $2024$ arise both from $2024$-written policies (new deductible) and from $2023$-written policies still running off (old deductible).

requirements.statement: To address a change in deductibles, restate historical claims at the current deductible level or use policy-year data, which isolates the change in coverage to policies written under the new terms.
requirements.concept: Policy Year vs Accident Year Data

places.quote: restate history to current retentions or benefit levels.
The deductible change attaches to the *policy*, so PY 2024 contains only $\$1{,}000$-deductible business while PY 2023 contains only $\$500$-deductible business — a clean before/after comparison.

requirements.statement: IBNR (including IBNER) for a policy year equals the ultimate claims estimate minus reported (case-incurred) claims.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Reported}$$
$$\text{Ultimate} = \text{Reported} + \text{IBNR}$$

requirements.statement: Unpaid claims for a policy year equal the ultimate claims estimate minus claims paid to date.

places.quote: $$\text{Unpaid} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Paid to date}$$

requirements.statement: To get claims net of all reinsurance when a policy has both excess of loss and stop loss cover, first apply the excess of loss cover to get net-of-XOL amounts, then apply the stop loss limit to those net amounts (the net amount is the lesser of the net-of-XOL amount and the stop loss limit).

places.quote: Order matters too: a surplus share may *inure* to the benefit of a per-risk or catastrophe cover, which then applies to what the cedant has left after it.

**Order matters.** Covers inure in a stated sequence. Typically per-occurrence excess comes off first, then the quota share applies to what remains, and the stop-loss applies last to protect the final net result.

requirements.statement: A stop loss limit caps the insurer's retained claims, so it must be applied consistently to the ultimate, reported, and paid amounts, since otherwise IBNR can come out negative when reported exceeds the limit.

places.quote: the insurer keeps $S \wedge d$, so the retention caps the insurer's total cost for the period.
**Stop-loss:** the ceded ultimate is $3{,}220 - 3{,}000 = 220$, and nothing is ceded on paid because $2{,}100 < 3{,}000$.

requirements.statement: Unpaid claims net of reinsurance must use the net ultimate after the stop loss cap, not the net-of-XOL ultimate estimate.

places.quote: It must also reflect [[Salvage and Subrogation|salvage and subrogation]] and [[Reinsurance Recovery|reinsurance recoveries]] on whatever basis is being reported.
**Stop-loss:** the ceded ultimate is $3{,}220 - 3{,}000 = 220$, and nothing is ceded on paid because $2{,}100 < 3{,}000$.

requirements.statement: To project ultimate ALAE with a ratio technique, form a triangle of paid ALAE-to-paid claims ratios at each evaluation age and develop that ratio, rather than developing paid ALAE dollars directly.

places.quote: Friedland gives three approaches: develop a **combined** loss-and-ALAE triangle, develop **ALAE separately** in its own triangle, or develop a **ratio of ALAE to loss** and apply it to projected losses.

requirements.statement: Multiplicative age-to-age factors are the ratio of the value at the later age to the value at the earlier age, and age-to-ultimate factors are the cumulative product of the age-to-age factors from that age through the last age (with a tail of 1.0 if no development occurs after the last age).

places.quote: \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}

**Cumulative Development Factor** (CDF, or age-to-ultimate factor) is the product of all selected [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] from a given maturity through to ultimate, including the [[Tail Factor|tail]].
**Age-to-Age Factor** (link ratio) is the ratio of a cohort's cumulative amount at one maturity to its amount at the previous maturity — the observed development between two ages.

requirements.statement: Select age-to-age factors from the historical triangle by averaging the observed factors across accident years at each maturity, using all available years including the oldest.

places.quote: f_{k \to k+1} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k}}
**Simple average** — equal weight to each year, so a small, volatile year counts as much as a large one.

requirements.statement: Ultimate ALAE-to-loss ratio by accident year equals the latest diagonal ratio times the age-to-ultimate factor (multiplicative) or plus the additive age-to-ultimate difference (additive).

places.quote: U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}

requirements.statement: Convert the ultimate ALAE-to-claims ratio to ultimate ALAE dollars by multiplying it by the selected ultimate claims (not paid claims to date).

places.quote: \text{Ultimate ALAE} &= 0.19 \times \$12{,}000{,}000

requirements.statement: The additive development technique computes age-to-age differences in the ratio (later minus earlier), sums them from a given age to the last age to get the additive age-to-ultimate amount, and adds that to the current ratio.

Multiplicative development is highly leveraged and sensitive to an unusually high early-maturity observation, while additive development is more stable at early maturities; the multiplicative method is more responsive if the change in the ratio is genuine, and an outlier early ratio may justify using the stable historical ultimate ratio instead.

places.quote: At a CDF of $4$, a dollar of distortion on the diagonal becomes four dollars of ultimate
A [[Large Loss|shock loss]] reported early is multiplied by the full CDF.

requirements.statement: The age-to-ultimate (cumulative) development factor is the ratio of ultimate claims to claims to date at a given maturity, and its reciprocal is the percent reported (or paid) at that maturity.

places.quote: The reciprocal is the **percentage reported** (or paid): $p_n = 1/\text{CDF}_n$, and $1 - p_n$ is the percentage unreported.
$$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: At a valuation date, an accident year is at a maturity equal to 12 months times the number of years since the start of that accident year (e.g., the latest accident year is at 12 months and the prior one at 24 months), so the age-to-ultimate factors for each maturity can be taken from the corresponding accident years' ultimate-to-date ratios.

places.quote: **maturities as columns** (age in months since the start of the cohort), and **valuation dates as diagonals**.

requirements.statement: Expected incremental reported (or paid) claims in the next calendar year for the latest accident year equal (ultimate − claims to date) times (% at next age − % at current age) divided by (1 − % at current age), which equals the ultimate times the % at next age minus claims to date.

places.quote: $$\text{Expected emergence} = U_{\text{prior}} \times \left(\frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n+1}} - \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n}}\right)$$
$$\text{Expected emergence} = \text{IBNR} \times \frac{p_{t+\Delta} - p_t}{1 - p_t}$$

requirements.statement: To get expected emergence consistent with the actuary's selection, apply the same percent reported/paid pattern but use the selected ultimate claims in place of the development-technique ultimate.

places.quote: The **expected** figure comes from the prior ultimate and the emergence pattern: the share of ultimate the pattern says should report (or be paid) between the two valuations.
It holds for both chain ladder and BF IBNR: chain ladder IBNR is its ultimate times $1 - p_t$, and BF IBNR is the expected claims times $1 - p_t$.

requirements.statement: Compare actual to expected reported and paid claims in the period; if actual emergence is consistent with expected (especially reported, which is more mature and less leveraged), the ultimate selection need not change.
requirements.concept: Actual vs Expected Claim Emergence Monitoring

places.quote: **One period's deviation is noise; a run of them is a signal.** Emergence is volatile, so a single A/E of $1.15$ means little.
A well-estimated ultimate should move randomly around its final value, not drift consistently in one direction.

requirements.statement: Paid claims at early maturities are highly leveraged and volatile, and a shortfall in paid versus expected can reflect changes in settlement rates or claim mix (small vs large claims) rather than a change in ultimate, so it warrants investigation rather than automatic revision of the estimate.
requirements.concept: Actual vs Expected Claim Emergence Monitoring

places.quote: **Faster settlement** pushes losses from open to paid, so the recent paid diagonal is high relative to history.
Reported running high with paid on track suggests [[Case Adequacy|case strengthening]]; paid running high with reported on track suggests faster [[Settlement Rate|settlement]].
The CDF measures **leverage**. At a CDF of $4$, a dollar of distortion on the diagonal becomes four dollars of ultimate

requirements.statement: Credibility is the weight given to an insurer's own observed data (versus a complement) in an indication, reflecting how much predictive value the data has based on its volume and stability.

places.quote: **Credibility** $Z$ is the weight given to a body of observed experience when it is blended with a broader estimate — the [[Complement of Credibility|complement]] — to produce an estimate more accurate than either alone.
**Partial credibility** is the weight $Z < 1$ that [[Limited Fluctuation Credibility|classical credibility]] gives to experience that falls short of the [[Full Credibility Standard]].

requirements.statement: The role of credibility in ratemaking is to ensure rate changes reflect true signal rather than noise from sparse or erratic data, by blending the data with a complement so that rates are not excessive or inadequate.

places.quote: Credibility rises with size. A small risk's mod stays near $1.0$ however good or bad its recent record, because a few claims say little; a large risk approaches $Z = 1$ and effectively self-rates.

**Credibility Theory** provides the framework for weighting observed experience data against prior or external expectations, balancing the statistical reliability of an individual group's data with the stability of broader pooled data.

requirements.statement: The complement of credibility is the estimate (alternative information) that receives the remaining weight (1 - Z) when the observed data is not fully credible.

places.quote: **Complement of Credibility** is the estimate that receives the weight $(1-Z)$ when observed experience receives [[Credibility|credibility]] $Z$.
$Z \in [0, 1]$ is the **credibility factor**, $\bar{X}$ is the observed experience, and $\mu_0$ is the **complement of credibility** (a class mean, industry data, or manual rate)

requirements.statement: Desirable qualities of a credibility complement are that it is unbiased (accurately estimates the expected value), uncorrelated/independent of the data being weighted, and logically related to the data (e.g., available, relevant, easy to compute).

places.quote: (2) **unbiased** — not routinely higher or lower than the observed experience; (3) **statistically independent** from the base statistic, or any error in the base statistic can be compounded; … and (6) **logically related** to the base statistic, so that its use is easy to support.

requirements.statement: Evaluate a proposed complement by assessing it against each desirable quality, e.g., a complement from a larger related group's experience (such as the acquirer's own indication) is independent if it excludes the data being weighted, logically related, but may be biased if the groups have different underwriting guidelines or rates.

places.quote: **Loss costs of a larger related group** — a *separate* but similar group, e.g. owners-form contents experience for the condo form. It is generally biased, but because it does not contain the subject experience it may be a better choice than method 1 on independence.

requirements.statement: Trended present rates are an appropriate complement mainly when no larger group data is available; when larger related group data exists, it is preferred because trended present rates are biased and correlated with the company's own experience.

places.quote: Note the complement here is the *current* relativity, which embeds whatever was believed last year. Where the current relativity is itself stale, a better complement is the statewide or countrywide relativity for the same class — see [[Complement of Credibility]].

requirements.statement: When the frequency or severity trend changes significantly over time, use a two-step trend: apply one selected trend from the historical period's average accident date to the latest data's date, and a different selected (projected) trend from there to the future period.

places.quote: losses are first trended at a *current* trend from the experience period's average accident date to that of the latest data point in the trend data, then projected at a separately selected trend to the forecast period's average accident date.
**Two-step trending** is used when the recent history contains a shift the historical fit would understate or overstate.

requirements.statement: Select a trend from the exponential fits by judging stability across the different numbers of points: use a longer period when fits are stable, and use shorter-period fits when recent data show a shift in the trend.

places.quote: exponential models may be fit to the whole of the data and to more recent periods, supplemented with multi-state, countrywide or industry data and non-insurance indices, and the trend selected with judgment.
Werner's example fits windows of 20, 16, 12, 8, 6 and 4 points, and $R^2$ is the usual diagnostic; the recent windows show whether the trend has shifted.

requirements.statement: The trend period runs from the average accident date of the historical experience period to the average accident date of the future period in which the rates will apply.

places.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.
The trend period runs from the average date of historical losses (midpoint of the accident year) to the average date of future losses (midpoint of the prospective rating period)

requirements.statement: The average accident date of the future period equals the rate effective date plus half of the period rates are in effect (to the average written date) plus half of the policy term (to the average accident date within policies).

places.quote: The first policy is exposed $7/1/2025$–$6/30/2026$ and the last $7/1/2026$–$6/30/2027$, so the exposure period runs $7/1/2025$ to $6/30/2027$ and its midpoint — the average loss date — is $7/1/2026$.

requirements.statement: Pure premium trend factor equals (1 + frequency trend)^t multiplied by (1 + severity trend)^t, compounded over each trend period and multiplied across steps.

places.quote: $$1 + t_{PP} = (1 + t_{\text{freq}})(1 + t_{\text{sev}})$$
Separately selected frequency and severity trends combine multiplicatively: $1 + T_{PP} = (1 + T_F)(1 + T_S)$.

requirements.statement: The average accident date of a calendar-accident-year-based period such as an accident year is its midpoint (e.g., July 1 for a calendar year), and the latest 12-month data period ending a given date has its average accident date six months before that date.

places.quote: The trend period runs from the average date of historical losses (midpoint of the accident year) to the average date of future losses (midpoint of the prospective rating period)
Accident year $2023$ runs $1/1$–$12/31/2023$; with losses occurring uniformly, its average loss date is $7/1/2023$.

requirements.statement: To adjust losses for direct benefit changes, compute the average benefit level for the period as the area-weighted average of benefit levels in each region of the exposure diagram, then divide the current benefit level by it to get the adjustment factor.

places.quote: each region's **area** is the share of the year's earned premium written at that rate level.
$$\text{OLF}_Y = \frac{I_{\text{current}}}{\sum_k A_{Y,k}\, I_k}$$

requirements.statement: When a benefit change applies only to policies written on or after its effective date, the change phases in gradually over a policy term, so its boundary on an accident-time diagram is diagonal and the calendar accident period contains a mix of benefit levels.

places.quote: For **annual** policies written uniformly, a rate change effective at time $p$ through year $Y$ earns over a triangle of area $\tfrac{1}{2}(1-p)^2$ in year $Y$ — so a $7/1$ change affects only $0.125$ of that year's earned premium, and a $1/1$ change affects $0.500$.
A rate change for policies written on or after a date is a **diagonal** line whose slope is set by the term (steeper for six-month policies).

requirements.statement: When a benefit change applies to all claims occurring on or after its effective date, the boundary is a vertical line in accident time, and for a policy-period analysis the policies written in that quarter are followed through their full terms, so the regions take different shapes.

places.quote: it takes effect immediately across the whole book and is drawn as a **vertical** line rather than a diagonal one.
A change forced by law onto policies already in force is a **vertical** line.

requirements.statement: The current benefit level is the cumulative product of all benefit change factors (1 plus each direct impact), and successive changes compound multiplicatively.

places.quote: Rate level indices **compound**: successive changes of $+8\%$ and $+5\%$ give a cumulative index of $1.08 \times 1.05 = 1.134$, not $1.13$.
$I_k$ is the cumulative rate level index of rate level group $k$ (each index is the previous one times $1 +$ that change)

requirements.statement: Loss trend should be selected from pure premium or loss data that has first been adjusted for direct benefit changes; using unadjusted data distorts the trend (overstating it when benefits increased) and double-counts the benefit change when the adjustment is applied separately.

places.quote: **Benefit-level changes** in statutory lines (workers compensation reform, auto no-fault changes) are the same problem at industry scale, and are handled by a law-level adjustment factor applied to historical losses before trend — deliberately kept separate from trend so the two are not confused.
A benefit-level change is restated in the data, or allowed for in the selection, so that it is not double counted.

requirements.statement: The operating expense ratio is the sum of the underwriting expense ratios (commissions, taxes/licenses/fees, general expenses) and the LAE ratio, each expressed relative to the appropriate premium base.

places.quote: The **operating expense ratio** adds all loss adjustment expense — allocated and [[Unallocated Loss Adjustment Expenses ULAE|unallocated]] — to the underwriting expense ratio, as a ratio to earned premium: it is the share of each premium dollar spent on loss adjustment and underwriting expenses.

The **operating expense ratio** is $\text{OER} = \text{UW expense ratio} + \text{LAE}/\text{EP}$, and $\text{Combined Ratio} = \text{LR} + \text{OER}$ with the loss ratio *excluding* LAE — otherwise LAE is counted twice.

requirements.statement: Commissions and taxes, licenses and fees are incurred when a policy is written, so their ratios are measured against written premium, while general expenses are measured against earned premium.

places.quote: those incurred at the onset of the policy (commissions, other acquisition, taxes, licenses and fees) are measured against written premium, those incurred throughout the policy (general expenses) against [[Earned Premium|earned premium]]

Expenses incurred at the onset of the policy — commissions, other acquisition, and taxes, licenses and fees — are calculated on [[Written Premium]]; general expenses, incurred throughout the policy, on [[Earned Premium]].
the expense ratio is conventionally on [[Written Premium|written premium]] (commissions and taxes are incurred when the policy is written)

requirements.statement: Combined ratio = loss ratio + LAE ratio + underwriting expense ratio, so the loss-and-LAE ratio equals loss ratio × (1 + LAE ratio to loss).

places.quote: $\text{LAE ratio} = \text{LAE}/\text{Losses}$ (allocated and unallocated). So the loss and LAE ratio is $\text{LR} \times (1 + \text{LAE ratio})$ — **not** the sum of the two.
**Combined Ratio** is the sum of the [[Loss Ratio|loss and LAE ratio]] and the underwriting expense ratio

requirements.statement: To find the LAE ratio to premium when the LAE-to-loss ratio is given, derive the loss ratio from the combined ratio less the expense ratio, then multiply the loss ratio by the LAE-to-loss ratio.

places.quote: **The LAE ratio is to losses, not premium:** $\text{LAE ratio} = \text{LAE}/\text{Losses}$ (allocated and unallocated). So the loss and LAE ratio is $\text{LR} \times (1 + \text{LAE ratio})$ — **not** the sum of the two.
whichever is done, LAE must be counted once, so a loss ratio combined with the OER must exclude it.

requirements.statement: In a frequency-severity projection, select an ultimate frequency and severity (e.g., a recent-years average when there is a clear shift, an all-year average when there is no pattern) and justify the choice based on the pattern in the trended data.

resolution.note: Choosing which years to average is a selection from the question's own data, judged from its pattern.

requirements.statement: To restate trended-to-latest-year frequency and severity selections to an earlier accident year, de-trend them by dividing by one plus the annual trend rate raised to the number of years between the years.

resolution.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the trend period, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period
resolution.note: Trend factor (1+t)^n over the trend period; de-trending divides by it.

requirements.statement: Ultimate loss and ALAE for an accident year equals selected frequency times selected severity times that year's earned exposures (not amount of insurance years).

places.quote: $$U = \text{Exposures} \times \text{Frequency}_{\text{ult}} \times S_{\text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: Trend each accident year's pure premium from its accident year to the average accident date of the future policy period; for annual policies written over a one-year period starting at the effective date, the average accident date is one year after the effective date, so the trend period runs from the accident year midpoint to that date.

places.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.

requirements.statement: The non-modeled catastrophe provision per exposure is the long-term average ratio of non-modeled cat loss and ALAE to AIY times the AIY per exposure trended to the future period, and then loaded for loss-based adjustments such as ULAE.

places.quote: express historical catastrophe losses as a ratio to a stable base (non-catastrophe losses, or amount of insurance years) over $10$–$30$ years, and apply that ratio to the current book.
$$\text{Trended Exposure} = \text{Historical Exposure} \times (1 + t_E)^{n}$$

requirements.statement: Pure premium method indicated rate = (pure premium loss and ALAE with ULAE load + cat provisions + fixed expense per exposure) / (1 − variable expense ratio − profit provision).

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Rate} = \frac{\text{Pure Premium} + F}{1 - V - Q_T}$$
$$\text{Rate} = \frac{\text{Pure Premium} + F}{1 - V - Q_T}$$

requirements.statement: The indicated rate change equals the indicated rate divided by the current (projected average) rate, minus one.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Indicated Rate}}{\text{Current Rate}} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Indicated Rate}}{\text{Current Rate}} - 1$$

requirements.statement: ULAE is loaded as a percentage of loss and ALAE, so it is applied by multiplying the non-catastrophe loss and ALAE pure premium by one plus the ULAE percentage.

places.quote: In **ratemaking**, ULAE may be handled as a load on losses or as a [[Fixed Expenses|fixed expense]] provision.
classically as the ratio of calendar-year paid ULAE to calendar-year paid loss plus ALAE, applied to loss plus ALAE that has been adjusted for extraordinary events, development and trend.

requirements.statement: The combined ratio is the loss ratio (including loss adjustment expenses) plus the expense ratio, and a value above 100% indicates an underwriting loss before investment income.

places.quote: **Combined Ratio** is the sum of the [[Loss Ratio|loss and LAE ratio]] and the underwriting expense ratio — the share of premium consumed by claims and the cost of doing business. A combined ratio below $100\%$ means the book is profitable **before** investment income; above $100\%$ means underwriting is losing money.

requirements.statement: Investment income on policyholder-supplied funds and surplus can offset an underwriting loss, so a company with a combined ratio above 100% can still earn an overall profit.

places.quote: Because it excludes investment income, a combined ratio above $100\%$ is not automatically unprofitable.

In long-tailed lines (personal auto bodily injury, workers compensation) years may pass between the premium and the settlement of all claims, and the investment income can be large enough to accept an underwriting loss and still achieve the target total return;
Investment income on the [[Unearned Premium|unearned premium]] and loss reserves lets a line accept a lower underwriting profit and still earn its target return.

requirements.statement: New business typically has higher expenses (e.g., higher commissions, marketing, startup costs) than renewal business, so the expense ratio falls as the book matures.

places.quote: LTV justifies **first-year pricing below full cost** where acquisition costs are large and renewal margins are reliable — but only if the retention and loss-improvement assumptions hold.

requirements.statement: New business tends to have higher loss ratios than renewal business, because riskier insureds who shop frequently leave while better risks persist, so loss ratios improve as policies renew.

places.quote: The "seasoning" effect (a policy's loss ratio improving with tenure) is real in personal lines and is one of the strongest arguments for the approach.

requirements.statement: Asset share pricing evaluates the long-term profitability of a policy over its expected life by accounting for persistency, allowing a first-year loss to be recouped through later renewals.

places.quote: **Lifetime Value** (LTV) is the present value of the expected profit from a customer relationship over its whole life, rather than over a single policy period.
LTV justifies **first-year pricing below full cost** where acquisition costs are large and renewal margins are reliable — but only if the retention and loss-improvement assumptions hold.

requirements.statement: Redundant (over-stated) reserves produce favorable (downward) loss development in later periods, which improves later-period results without rate increases.

places.quote: Lines dominated by salvage/subrogation recoveries or by conservative initial case reserving produce age-to-age factors below $1.000$

requirements.statement: A small new book has volatile results, and as premium volume grows, the loss experience becomes more credible and less volatile; the insurer also gains underwriting and claims-handling experience that can improve the loss ratio.

places.quote: It is the formal reason risk pooling works: the average loss per policy becomes predictable as an insurer writes more independent policies.

resolution.note: One of ten alternative acceptable answers (two needed for credit); not a fact the question requires.

requirements.statement: Current on-level premium for a class or territory equals exposures times the base rate times the territory relativity times the other rating-variable relativities, summed over the cells.

places.quote: \text{Premium} = \text{Rate} \times \text{Exposure}
Each exposure in class $i$ pays $B\,r_i$, so the book's premium is $B \sum_i w_i r_i$.

requirements.statement: In the loss ratio method for territorial relativities, compute each territory's loss ratio (losses divided by premium at current rates), divide it by the total loss ratio for all territories to get the indicated relativity change, and multiply the current relativity by that change to get the indicated relativity.
requirements.concept: Loss Ratio Method for Territorial Relativities

places.quote: Under the [[Loss Ratio Method|loss ratio method]], a class's indicated relativity is its current relativity times its loss ratio divided by the base class's loss ratio, with premiums at current rates.

requirements.statement: When full credibility is assumed, the indicated relativity is used without any credibility weighting against the current relativity.

places.quote: Partial credibility uses the **square root rule**, $Z = \sqrt{n / n_{\text{full}}}$, capped at $1$ — a class with a quarter of the required claims gets $Z = 0.50$.

requirements.statement: To apply a cap on the maximum-to-minimum relativity ratio, set the capped territory's relativity at the cap multiple of the lowest territory's relativity, rebasing the lowest territory to 1.000.

resolution.note: The max-to-min cap is the question's own constraint; applying it is arithmetic on the given relativities.

requirements.statement: To keep a revenue-neutral change after adjusting relativities, compute an off-balance factor equal to premium at current relativities divided by premium at the adjusted relativities (same exposures and base rate), and multiply the adjusted relativities by it. Equivalently, solve for a new base rate that preserves total premium.

places.quote: \text{Off-balance factor} &= \frac{1.080}{1.030}
OBF, the off-balance factor, is the average relativity before the change divided by the average relativity after it.

requirements.statement: Raising rates for a lower-risk territory and lowering them for a higher-risk territory (because of a cap) causes adverse selection: in the short term, lower-risk insureds leave and higher-risk insureds are attracted, and in the long term the book concentrates in the underpriced territory and rates must move toward its level.

places.quote: Every classification restriction reintroduces adverse selection by forcing a single price across risks the insurer knows differ

A rate change also changes the **mix**: price-sensitive risks shop, so a large increase can worsen the remaining experience through adverse selection — an effect the indication itself does not capture.

risks with different expected costs pay the same rate, so the low-cost risks subsidise the high-cost ones, and a company doing this while competitors differentiate faces [[Adverse Selection|adverse selection]] (Ch.9).

requirements.statement: In the ISO Personal Auto classification plan, a driver's combined class factor is the sum of the primary classification factor and the secondary classification factor (added, not multiplied).

places.quote: The manual adds the secondary factor to the primary factor to give each vehicle's combined rating factor, rather than multiplying by it (for example Rule 53 of the CAR Commercial Automobile Insurance Manual).

resolution.note: ISO Personal Automobile Manual classification plan (primary + secondary factors added): that manual is no longer an Exam 5 reading; Werner & Modlin do not teach it.

requirements.statement: When a vehicle has multiple operators, the principal operator (the driver with the highest primary classification factor) determines the classification applied to the vehicle's rating.

places.quote: When a household has more than one driver and car, the insurer's principal operator rule decides which driver rates each car: some insurers use the driver who uses the car most, and others the highest-risk driver, usually the youngest.

resolution.note: ISO Personal Automobile Manual principal-operator rule: that manual is no longer an Exam 5 reading.

requirements.statement: The primary classification is based on auto usage (e.g., work commute distance, pleasure, farm, business), and the secondary classification is based on the driver's age, SDIP driving record points and licensing experience.

resolution.note: ISO Personal Automobile Manual primary/secondary classification definitions: that manual is no longer an Exam 5 reading; the question also gives the factor tables.

requirements.statement: Remove the per-policy expense fee from the total premium to get the premium subject to class factors, then the premium for a new classification equals the premium without the fee times the ratio of the new combined factor to the old combined factor, and the fee is added back.
requirements.concept: Expense Fee in Personal Auto Rating

places.quote: Without the credit factor the 0.90 drops out, and the premium is $1{,}091.48 / 0.90 = 1{,}212.75$.

requirements.statement: A mid-term policy change's additional premium is the annual premium difference prorated by the fraction of the policy term remaining (pro rata on time).
requirements.concept: Mid-Term Policy Changes and Pro Rata Premium

places.quote: $$R_{\text{pro rata}} = P \times \frac{T - t}{T}$$
$$\text{UPR}_{\text{policy}} = \text{WP} \times \frac{\text{Days unexpired}}{\text{Days in term}}$$

resolution.quote: recognized pro rata as the policy term elapses
resolution.note: Pro rata on time for the remaining term.

requirements.statement: With all expenses variable, the permissible loss ratio equals 1 minus the variable expense ratio (V) minus the profit and contingencies provision (Q): PLR = 1 – V – Q.

places.quote: $$\text{VPLR} = 1 - V - Q_T \quad \text{(variable permissible loss ratio)}$$
If *all* expenses are treated as variable, the VPLR and the PLR are the same, and the indication is simply:

requirements.statement: Under the loss ratio method, the indicated rate change for a class or territory equals its expected (ultimate) loss ratio divided by the permissible loss ratio, minus 1.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio}}{\text{PLR}} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss Ratio}}{\text{PLR}} - 1 \quad \text{(all-variable form)}$$

requirements.statement: When a cap on rate changes limits an indicated increase in one territory, the premium falls short of what is needed to reach the permissible loss ratio overall, so the shortfall must be offset by raising rates in other territories (less decrease) to keep the total loss ratio at the permissible level.

places.quote: The base rate has to be adjusted to make up the capped premium
a cap on the change for any level of a rating variable is made up by adjusting the base rate and the other relativities

requirements.statement: To offset a capping shortfall, compute the premium lost in the capped territory (premium × (indicated change – capped change)) and spread it over the uncapped territories by adjusting their rate changes multiplicatively so that total expected losses divided by total capped premium equals the permissible loss ratio.

places.quote: a cap on the change for any level of a rating variable is made up by adjusting the base rate and the other relativities
The relativity revision already delivers part of the increase, so the base rate must supply only the remainder — multiplicatively, not by subtraction:

requirements.statement: The fundamental insurance equation balances premium against expected losses, expenses, and profit; if pricing cannot be changed enough, balance can be restored with non-pricing actions such as reducing expected losses (loss control, reduced coverage, changing business mix), reducing expenses, or lowering the profit provision (e.g., via asset share pricing).

places.quote: **Non-Pricing Solutions** are actions that bring the fundamental insurance equation back into balance by **reducing costs** — expenses or expected losses — rather than by raising rates.
Where a full increase is unavailable, the same gap can be closed by:

requirements.statement: Select loss development factors at each age by averaging the historical age-to-age factors (e.g., all-year or fewer-year averages), justifying the choice from the pattern of variation, and compound the selected factors to get age-to-ultimate factors.

places.quote: **Medial average**: drops the highest and lowest individual factors before averaging — reduces the impact of outliers without discarding recent years
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: Develop the ratio of subrogation/salvage to paid loss to ultimate with its own development factors, then subtract ultimate salvage/subrogation (gross loss times the ratio) from gross loss to get net loss, using one minus the ratio rather than the ratio itself.

places.quote: S&S must be **projected on its own triangle**, not scaled from losses.

**Salvage and subrogation** (Friedland Ch. 14) are projected either by the development technique on reported or received S&S, or by the **ratio approach**: develop the ratio of received S&S to paid claims to an ultimate ratio, and multiply by selected ultimate claims gross of S&S.

requirements.statement: Trend historical losses and premiums from each year's average accident (or earned) date to the average accident date of the future period, which is the midpoint of the period the new rates are in effect plus the policy term; with semi-annual policies the future average accident date lies half a policy term past the end of the rate period's midpoint.

places.quote: The trend period $n$ runs from the average written date of the policies earning premium in the experience period to the **average written date of the policies in effect while the new rates are**
$t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.
It is applied over the period from the midpoint of the experience period to the midpoint of the rating period, as in [[Trend|property-casualty trending]] and [[Loss Trend|loss trend]].

requirements.statement: Trend on-level earned premium using the premium trend rate over the same period lengths, using earned rather than written dates, to get trended on-level premium for the loss ratio.

places.quote: Measuring between average *earned* dates gives the same $2.5$ years, because both dates shift by the same amount

requirements.statement: LAE is included by loading losses by the LAE provision percentage; the trended loss and LAE ratio equals trended net loss plus LAE divided by trended on-level premium.

places.quote: and including [[Allocated Loss Adjustment Expense|ALAE]] and [[Unallocated Loss Adjustment Expenses ULAE|ULAE]].

The numerator's loss ratio must be **projected**: ultimate losses (developed), trended to the future policy period, over earned premium brought to **current rate level** ([[On-Leveling]]) and trended ([[Premium Trend]]).
Werner & Modlin define two permissible loss ratios, both with LAE included in losses:

requirements.statement: Loss ratio method indicated rate change = (loss ratio + fixed expense ratio) / (1 − variable expense ratio − profit and contingencies provision) − 1.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + \text{Fixed Expense Ratio}}{1 - V - Q} - 1$$

requirements.statement: With the square root rule, partial credibility Z = sqrt(actual exposures / full credibility standard), capped at 1.

places.quote: Partial credibility uses the **square root rule**, $Z = \sqrt{n / n_{\text{full}}}$, capped at $1$
$$Z = \min\!\left(1,\, \sqrt{\frac{n}{n_{\text{full}}}}\right)$$
$$Z = \min\left(\sqrt{\frac{n}{n_F}},\; 1\right)$$

requirements.statement: Credibility-weight the indicated rate changes (not the loss ratios): Z times the company indication plus (1 − Z) times the complement of credibility.

places.quote: **Credibility** — weight the indication against a [[Complement of Credibility|complement]] where the data is thin.
$$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$

requirements.statement: Trended present rates complement = (prior indicated change / prior implemented change) × (premium-trend-adjusted loss trend ratio, (1+loss trend)/(1+premium trend)) raised to the years between the prior target effective date and the current target effective date.
requirements.concept: Complement of Credibility: Trended Present Rates

places.quote: **Trended present rates** — the current rate adjusted to what was last *indicated* rather than implemented, and trended from the original target effective date of the current rates to that of the new rates.

requirements.statement: One primary purpose of risk classification is to enhance fairness: premiums reflect differences in expected future losses, so low-risk insureds do not subsidize high-risk insureds and similar risks are charged similar rates.

places.quote: **Classification Ratemaking** is the segmentation of a book into rating classes and the derivation of **relativities** — the factors by which each class's rate differs from the base class — so that each risk pays according to its own expected cost.
Note what follows: a rate differential that reflects a genuine cost difference is **not** unfair discrimination, and charging the same rate for materially different risks fails Principle 3.

requirements.statement: One primary purpose of risk classification is to protect the financial stability of the insurance system: without classification, adverse selection occurs as low-risk insureds leave for insurers that price accurately, leaving an underpriced, high-risk book that can become insolvent.

places.quote: In a competitive market an insurer that charges one average rate to a heterogeneous group loses the better risks to competitors that price them properly, and retains the worse ones — the **adverse selection spiral**.
**The death spiral.** Price at the population average; low risks find the price poor value and leave; the remaining pool is worse, so the price rises; more of the remaining low risks leave; repeat.

requirements.statement: One primary purpose of risk classification is to permit economic incentives to operate and promote widespread availability of coverage: when insurers can charge adequate, fair rates to every class, they are willing to offer coverage to all classes, including high-risk ones.

places.quote: ASOP 12 states that risk classification is generally used for three purposes: to treat participants with similar risk characteristics in a consistent manner, to permit economic incentives to operate and thereby encourage widespread availability of coverage, and to protect the soundness of the system.

requirements.statement: Criteria for evaluating a rating variable include statistical criteria (homogeneity, credibility, statistical significance), operational criteria (objective, inexpensive to administer, verifiable, measurable), social criteria (causality, controllability, privacy, public acceptability) and legal criteria (permitted by law).
requirements.concept: Risk Classification Considerations for Rating Variables

places.quote: **Statistical** — statistical significance, [[Homogeneity|homogeneity]] within levels, and [[Credibility|credibility]].

Werner's criteria for evaluating a rating variable (after Finger's *Risk Classification*) are **statistical** (statistical significance, homogeneity, credibility), **operational** (objective, inexpensive to administer, verifiable), **social** (affordability, causality, controllability, privacy concerns) and **legal**
It should be objective and hard to manipulate, practical to collect and verify, and legal ([[Risk Classification Restrictions]], [[Unfair Discrimination]]) and socially acceptable.

requirements.statement: When exposures are unevenly distributed across another rating variable (e.g., vehicle symbol) within each class of the variable being analyzed, the one-way pure premium approach is distorted by distributional bias.

places.quote: A **univariate** (one-way) pure premium or loss ratio analysis attributes to a variable the effect of everything correlated with it. If young drivers also drive older cars, a one-way age relativity contains part of the vehicle-age effect, and rating both double-counts.

They must be [[Credibility|credibility-weighted]] against the overall average, and — because a univariate pure premium picks up the effect of every correlated variable — checked against a multivariate ([[Generalized Linear Model|GLM]]) result before use.

requirements.statement: The adjusted pure premium approach corrects for distributional bias, so it is preferred over the simple pure premium approach when exposures are correlated across rating variables and the other variable's current relativities are available.

places.quote: A **univariate** (one-way) pure premium or loss ratio analysis attributes to a variable the effect of everything correlated with it.

When other rating variables also apply, each class's exposures are first multiplied by their average relativity for those other variables, so that the factor measures only this variable's effect on the average premium.

requirements.statement: Adjusted pure premium approach: compute each class's adjusted exposures by weighting exposures at each level of the other variable by its current relativity (equivalently, exposures times the average current relativity of the other variable), then divide losses by adjusted exposures to get the adjusted pure premium.

places.quote: When other rating variables also apply, each class's exposures are first multiplied by their average relativity for those other variables, so that the factor measures only this variable's effect on the average premium.

requirements.statement: The indicated relativity for a class equals its pure premium divided by the base class's pure premium (or divided by the total pure premium and then rebased to the base class).

places.quote: $$\text{Relativity}_i = \frac{\text{Pure Premium}_i}{\text{Pure Premium}_{\text{base}}}$$
$$\text{Relativity}_i = \frac{\text{Pure Premium}_i}{\text{Pure Premium}_{\text{base}}}$$

requirements.statement: Revenue-neutral base rate change: compute the exposure-weighted average relativity under current and under indicated factors; the off-balance factor is current average divided by proposed average (the inverse of the average change in relativities), and the new base rate equals the current base rate times this factor.

places.quote: $$\text{Base Rate}_{\text{new}} = \text{Base Rate}_{\text{current}} \times \frac{1 + \text{overall change}}{1 + \text{change in average rate differential}}$$
$$B_{\text{new}} = B_{\text{old}} \times \frac{\bar{R}_{\text{old}}}{\bar{R}_{\text{new}}}$$
$$\text{OBF} = \frac{\sum_i w_i\, r_i^{\text{old}}}{\sum_i w_i\, r_i^{\text{new}}}$$

requirements.statement: The limited average severity (LAS) at limit L is the average claim size with each loss capped at L, i.e. total losses limited to L divided by total claim count.

places.quote: $E[X \wedge L]$ is the **limited expected value**, the expected loss capped at $L$.
Exam 5 (Werner & Modlin) writes the limit as $H$ and calls $E[X \wedge H]$ the **limited average severity** $\text{LAS}(H)$.

requirements.statement: The increased limits factor for limit L equals LAS at L divided by LAS at the basic limit.

places.quote: \text{ILF}(L) = \frac{E[X \wedge L]}{E[X \wedge B]}
Under its simplifying assumptions, the increased limit factor for limit $H$ over basic limit $B$ is $\text{ILF}(H) = \text{LAS}(H)/\text{LAS}(B)$ (see [[Increased Limits]])

requirements.statement: To compute limited losses from binned data, losses in size bins entirely below the limit are kept as reported, and each claim above the limit is replaced by the limit; individual claim amounts are used when a limit falls inside a bin.

places.quote: For a discrete loss with probability function $p(x)$, the payment sums over the loss amounts above $d$, and the retained part takes each amount below $d$ at its value and every other at $d$.
The $400$ claims under $\$500$ contribute their **full** amount, $\$100{,}000$.

requirements.statement: The loss elimination ratio is the proportion of total ground-up losses eliminated by a deductible (or limit), i.e. losses eliminated divided by total ground-up losses.

places.quote: The rate credit is derived from the [[Loss Elimination Ratio|loss elimination ratio]] — the share of expected losses the deductible removes.
**Loss Elimination Ratio** (LER) is the proportion of ground-up losses removed by a deductible — the share of expected loss that the insured retains rather than transfers.

requirements.statement: For a policy with both a deductible and a policy limit, the limit applies to the loss payment after the deductible, so the insurer's maximum payment is the limit and the combined LER is eliminated losses (the deductible amount on each claim plus the portion above deductible plus limit) over total ground-up losses; the policy limit is not stacked on top of the deductible.

places.quote: With a deductible $d$ and coinsurance $\alpha$, the payment is $\alpha\big[(X \wedge u) - (X \wedge d)\big]$ and the policy limit is $\alpha(u - d)$, so a limit $L$ stated with a deductible and no coinsurance means $u = d + L$.

requirements.statement: Historical data from policies with deductibles is truncated (losses below the deductible are missing or only excess amounts are reported) and data from policies with limits is censored at the limit, which biases deductible factor estimates; remedies include fitting a theoretical severity distribution, using a loss ratio approach, using industry data, or using a GLM.

places.quote: The fit must allow for [[Truncation|truncation]] by deductibles and [[Censoring|censoring]] at policy limits.

Few claims reach the upper layers, so pricing leans on fitted curves and industry data, and the tail fit drives the answer. Data are [[Truncation|truncated]] below deductibles and [[Censoring|censored]] at policy limits.

resolution.quote: When the data hold only losses net of the deductible, policies with a deductible
resolution.note: Truncation of deductible data and the fitted-distribution remedy are on the tagged page (with Increased Limits on censoring).

requirements.statement: Insureds self-select deductibles and limits and claim reporting behavior varies by deductible, and data is thin at higher layers; these issues can be addressed with a GLM or by smoothing/curve fitting the data.

places.quote: an insured with a higher deductible may not report a claim whose small net payment is not worth a claim surcharge, and where insureds choose freely, lower-risk insureds tend to choose higher deductibles
Data at high limits is sparse and volatile

**Selection.** Insureds choose their limits and deductibles knowing their own risk. The GLM monograph therefore estimates coverage-option factors outside the model, by loss elimination and ILF methods, and enters them as an [[Offset Variable|offset]].

requirements.statement: Cumulative reported claims at an evaluation date equal cumulative paid claims plus the case reserve outstanding at that date.

places.quote: **Incurred Losses** — more precisely **reported losses** — are cumulative [[Paid Losses|payments]] plus [[Case Reserves|case outstanding]] on known claims at a valuation date.
$$\text{Reported Losses} = \text{Paid Losses} + \text{Case Reserves}$$

requirements.statement: On an accident year basis, each claim is assigned to the calendar year in which its accident occurred, regardless of when it is reported or paid.

places.quote: **Accident Year** (AY) is a data aggregation method that groups losses by the calendar year in which the loss event *occurred*, … regardless of when the policy was written, when the claim was reported, or when it was paid.

requirements.statement: On a report year basis, each claim is assigned to the calendar year in which it was reported to the insurer, so a claim has no reported amount before its report year.

places.quote: **Report Year** (RY) is a data aggregation method that groups claims by the calendar year in which the claim was first *reported* to the insurer, regardless of when the loss occurred.

requirements.statement: To build a loss development triangle from transactional data, evaluate each cohort (accident or report year) at each year-end, accumulating all payments to date and taking the latest case reserve at that date, with ages 12, 24, 36, ... months.

places.quote: **Development Triangle** is the fundamental data structure of reserving: cumulative amounts arranged with **cohorts as rows** (usually [[Accident Year|accident years]]), **maturities as columns** (age in months since the start of the cohort), and **valuation dates as diagonals**.

resolution.quote: maturities as columns (age in months since the start of the cohort), and valuation dates as diagonals
resolution.note: Re-quoted after the page was edited today: cohorts by row, ages by column, valuations by diagonal.

requirements.statement: A triangle includes only the development ages observed as of the latest evaluation date, so the most recent cohort has only a 12-month value and each older cohort one more age, with no later cells filled.

places.quote: The triangle is triangular because a $2024$ accident year cannot yet have a $36$-month valuation.

requirements.statement: Case reserves are a point-in-time balance, not incremental, so the case reserve at an evaluation date is the most recent ending reserve and must not be summed across transactions, while incremental payments are summed.

places.quote: $\Delta$ terms are ending balance minus beginning balance.

requirements.statement: The ratio of cumulative paid claims to cumulative reported (case-incurred) claims by accident year and maturity is a diagnostic; a ratio that rises down a column at the same maturity indicates claims are being paid/settled faster.

places.quote: **Faster [[Settlement Rate|settlement]]:** closure rates and paid-to-reported rise together.
a rising ratio is consistent with faster settlement or weaker case reserves, a falling one with slower settlement or stronger case reserves

requirements.statement: The ratio of closed claim counts to reported claim counts by accident year and maturity measures the claim closure (disposal) rate; a ratio that rises down a column at the same maturity indicates a speedup in claim settlement.

places.quote: $$\text{Disposal Rate}_n = \frac{\text{Closed claims at age } n}{\text{Ultimate claim counts}}$$
**Closed counts** — how fast claims settle. The [[Settlement Rate|disposal rate]] is closed counts over ultimate (or reported) counts.

requirements.statement: Average case outstanding is (reported claims minus paid claims) divided by open claim counts (reported counts minus closed counts); an increase down a column at the same maturity indicates case reserve strengthening (increasing case adequacy).

places.quote: The first block is the **average case outstanding** for accident year $w$ at age $d$: reported less paid losses, per open claim.
**The diagnostic is average case outstanding per open claim**, compared *down each column* of the triangle. It should grow at roughly the severity trend.

requirements.statement: Paid severity (paid claims per closed count) and reported severity (reported claims per reported count) are diagnostics; rising values down a column may reflect larger claims closing faster or increasing case adequacy.

places.quote: **Counts closed with payment** (vs. closed without) — a shift in the CWP proportion changes average paid severity without any change in claim cost.
Reported losses over reported counts, paid over closed, ultimate over ultimate — mixing them (reported losses over closed counts is the classic) produces a series that measures nothing.

requirements.statement: The Berquist-Sherman paid method adjusts historical paid claims to a common (latest diagonal) settlement rate, and the Berquist-Sherman reported method adjusts reported claims to the current case reserve adequacy, so they suit environments with changing settlement rates or case adequacy.

places.quote: The remedy is the [[Berquist-Sherman Method|Berquist-Sherman]] paid adjustment: restate each historical year's paid losses to what they would have been at the *current* disposal pattern

**Berquist-Sherman Method** restates a historical [[Development Triangle|triangle]] so that every year reflects **current** claims practice, removing the distortion caused by a change in [[Case Adequacy|case reserve adequacy]] or in [[Settlement Rate|claim settlement rates]].

The remedy is the [[Berquist-Sherman Method|Berquist-Sherman]] case adjustment: restate historical average case outstanding to the current adequacy level using a selected severity trend, rebuild the reported triangle, and select factors from the restated history.

requirements.statement: The expected claims method relies on an a priori estimate of ultimate claims and is unaffected by changes in claim development patterns, settlement rates or case reserve adequacy, so it suits a changing environment.

places.quote: Lean on methods that do not depend on the triangle's recent diagonal at all: the [[Expected Loss Method|expected claims]] technique and [[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method|BF]] with an externally derived ELR.

**Expected Loss Method** (expected claims technique) estimates ultimate losses entirely from an a priori expectation — usually an expected loss ratio applied to earned premium — giving **no weight** to what has actually been reported.

requirements.statement: The reported development (chain ladder) technique is not distorted by speedups in claim settlement, because it uses reported claims rather than paid claims, provided case reserve practices stay consistent; paid development is distorted by changing settlement rates.

places.quote: A moving **disposal rate** is a [[Settlement Rate|settlement speed]] change and distorts **paid** development; a jump in **average case outstanding** is a [[Case Adequacy|case adequacy]] change and distorts **reported** development.
**Reported data is largely immune**, because reported losses include the case reserve whether or not the claim has closed.

requirements.statement: Cape Cod method: the expected loss ratio (or pure premium) is the sum of trended reported losses divided by the sum of used-up (on-level) premium or exposure, where used-up premium equals on-level premium divided by the CDF.

places.quote: The ELR is estimated as total reported losses over total *used-up* (on-level, developed) premium across all years.

requirements.statement: Cape Cod IBNR for a year equals the ELR times the premium (or exposure) times (1 - 1/CDF), i.e. the percent unreported.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$
$$\text{IBNR}_j = \text{ELR}_j \times P_j \times \left(1 - \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_j}\right)$$

requirements.statement: To select a claims trend, develop reported claims to ultimate with the CDFs, divide by exposures to get pure premiums, and compute year-over-year changes in pure premium.

places.quote: - Inputs: losses developed to ultimate and trended, [[Earned Exposure|earned exposures]] (trended if the base inflates — see [[Exposure Trend]]), the fixed expense per exposure $F$, the variable expense ratio $V$, and the target profit provision $Q_T$.
for long-tailed lines, accident-year losses developed to ultimate.

requirements.statement: Pure premium changes from the most immature accident year are highly leveraged and unreliable, so they may be excluded when selecting a trend; select a trend consistent with the more stable mature-year changes.

resolution.quote: At a CDF of $4$, a dollar of distortion on the diagonal becomes four dollars of ultimate
resolution.note: Leverage of immature years is taught on a linked page; excluding the leveraged point is the selection judgment.

requirements.statement: Trend each year's reported claims to the target accident year's cost level by applying the selected annual trend factor compounded over the number of years between the year and the target year.

places.quote: $$\text{Trend Factor} = (1 + r)^n$$
$t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.

requirements.statement: Extension of exposures on-leveling: restate each year's premium at the current rate level by multiplying exposures by the current average rate per exposure; this requires on-level premium to be on a consistent rate level across years.

places.quote: [[Extension of Exposures|Extension of exposures]] re-rates every policy at today's rates, which is the most accurate approach but needs policy-level data.
$$\text{Premium at CRL} = \sum_{j} P_{\text{current}}(\mathbf{x}_j,\ e_j)$$

requirements.statement: Cape Cod can be done on an exposure basis instead of on-level premium, because premium cancels in the IBNR calculation and gives the same IBNR.

resolution.note: Algebra of the Cape Cod formula on the tagged page: premium appears in both the ELR and the IBNR, so any proportional exposure base gives the same IBNR.

requirements.statement: In the expected claims technique, ultimate claims for the projected year equal the selected expected pure premium (expected claims per exposure unit) multiplied by the projected year's exposure base.

places.quote: $$U = \text{ELR} \times \text{Earned Premium}$$

requirements.statement: Estimate the expected pure premium for each historical year by developing its reported claims to ultimate with cumulative development factors, dividing by that year's exposure, and trending to the projected year's cost level.

places.quote: The pure premium used in a rate is always **projected**: historical losses developed to ultimate, trended to the forecast period, adjusted for [[Large Loss|large losses]] and [[Catastrophe Loss|catastrophes]], and divided by exposures that are themselves trended if the base inflates ([[Exposure Trend]]).
$$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: A cumulative development factor to ultimate for a given age is the product of the age-to-age factors from that age through to ultimate, including the tail factor.

places.quote: $$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \left(\prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1}\right) \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: An age-to-age (link ratio) factor is the ratio of cumulative reported claims at a later age to that at the earlier age for the same accident year, and a selected factor can be a straight or weighted (volume-weighted) average of the observed ratios.

places.quote: $$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{AY}} = \frac{C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$
$$f_{k \to k+1} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k}}$$

requirements.statement: Trend a historical pure premium to the projected year by multiplying by (1 + annual trend) raised to the number of years between the historical accident year and the projected accident year.

places.quote: $$\text{Trend Factor} = (1 + t)^{n}$$
The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: Selecting the expected pure premium requires judgment and justification: for example, weigh whether a recent spike reflects lasting change or noise, and prefer years with stable results and less leveraged (highly uncertain) development factors, or average all years to retain information.

places.quote: Look at the column **before** averaging it. A steady column supports a volume-weighted all-year selection; a column trending over time is a signal, not noise, and calls for the latest years or an investigation.

The CDF measures **leverage**. At a CDF of $4$, a dollar of distortion on the diagonal becomes four dollars of ultimate — which is why the chain ladder is unreliable at immature ages in [[Long Tail Lines|long-tail lines]] and why methods that develop only the *unreported* portion are preferred there.

requirements.statement: The paid development technique's ultimate equals paid claims to date times the paid cumulative development factor to ultimate, so the paid CDF to ultimate equals ultimate divided by paid claims to date.

places.quote: $$\text{Ultimate} = C_n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: Bornhuetter-Ferguson ultimate = claims to date (paid or reported) + a priori expected ultimate claims × percent unpaid (or unreported), where percent unpaid/unreported = 1 − 1/CDF to ultimate.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$
$$\text{IBNR}_j = \text{ELR}_j \times P_j \times \left(1 - \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_j}\right)$$

requirements.statement: Back out the a priori expected claims from a given paid BF estimate by using the paid claims to date and the paid CDF-based percent unpaid, then apply it with the reported CDF to compute the reported BF estimate.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$

requirements.statement: The Benktander ultimate = reported claims to date + (prior BF ultimate estimate × percent unreported), i.e. it reuses the BF ultimate in place of the a priori estimate.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{GB}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) U_{\text{BF}}$$
Iterating $U \to C_{i,n-i+1} + q_i U$ from the burning cost $V_i\sum_k m_k$ gives first the collective reserve, then the Benktander reserve, and converges to the individual reserve.

requirements.statement: The Benktander method is a credibility-weighted average of the development technique and the BF technique, and each successive iteration gives more weight to the development technique, so the estimate converges to the development technique result (moving monotonically from the BF estimate toward it).

places.quote: Repeating $R = qU$ then $U = C + R$ from $U_0$ gives $U^{(m)} = (1 - q^m)\,U_{\text{CL}} + q^m U_0$. BF is $m = 1$, Benktander is $m = 2$, and the limit is the chain ladder.
Benktander credibility-weights the development and BF ultimates for the same year, giving the development method weight equal to the year's percent reported.

requirements.statement: Development techniques are more responsive but leveraged and volatile at immature ages, while BF is more stable and preferred for immature years; diverging paid and reported estimates can indicate changes in case reserve adequacy (strengthening/weakening) or claim settlement speed, which distorts reported or paid development methods respectively.

places.quote: a change in the paid-to-reported ratio signals a change in settlement patterns or in case adequacy — a rising ratio is consistent with faster settlement or weaker case reserves, a falling one with slower settlement or stronger case reserves

The chain ladder is at its best on **mature cohorts with stable patterns and ample volume** — and at its worst at immature ages in [[Long Tail Lines|long-tail lines]], where the CDF is large and the diagonal is thin. There, [[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method|BF]] or the [[Expected Loss Method|expected claims]] technique is preferred.
*Case strengthening*: reported development overstates, reported BF and Cape Cod overstate less; paid methods and expected claims are unaffected.

requirements.statement: When there is no development after the final maturity, the CDF to ultimate at that age is 1.0, and the percent unreported/unpaid is zero for fully developed claims.

places.quote: $C$ is reported (or paid) losses to date, $U_0 = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}$ the a priori expectation, and $1 - 1/\text{CDF}$ the percentage unreported from the [[Development Triangle|development pattern]].
The reciprocal is the **percentage reported** (or paid): $p_n = 1/\text{CDF}_n$, and $1 - p_n$ is the percentage unreported.
$$\text{Reported \%} = \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}}$$

requirements.statement: An exposure base is a measure of the size of a risk (e.g. car-years, miles driven, payroll) that is used to scale expected losses and premium, and a good one is evaluated against several criteria.

places.quote: **Exposure Base** is the basic unit of risk that underlies the premium — the quantity the rate is charged *per*.

requirements.statement: A good exposure base should be proportional to expected losses, so that expected loss per unit of exposure stays roughly constant as exposure changes.

places.quote: **Proportional to expected loss.** All else equal, a policy with two exposures should have twice the expected loss of a similar policy with one.

requirements.statement: A good exposure base should be practical: it should be objective, easy and inexpensive to obtain and verify, and resistant to manipulation or misreporting by the insured.

places.quote: **Practical.** Objective, and relatively easy and inexpensive to obtain and verify — which also keeps policyholders and producers from manipulating it (declared annual mileage invites more dishonesty than car-years).

requirements.statement: A good exposure base should be consistent with historical precedent and industry practice, because changing it causes premium swings, IT and implementation costs, and data adjustments for future ratemaking.

places.quote: **Consistent with historical precedence.** A change of base can cause large premium swings for individual insureds, requires a change in the rating algorithm and systems, and may force significant adjustments to the several years of data a ratemaking analysis uses.

requirements.statement: The criteria for evaluating an exposure base (proportionality, practicality, historical precedent) differ from the criteria for evaluating rating variables (e.g. statistical, operational, social, legal considerations).

places.quote: **Statistical** — statistical significance, [[Homogeneity|homogeneity]] within levels, and [[Credibility|credibility]].
It should be objective and hard to manipulate, practical to collect and verify, and legal ([[Risk Classification Restrictions]], [[Unfair Discrimination]]) and socially acceptable.

requirements.statement: To select an exposure base, assess each candidate against each criterion and recommend the one whose overall evaluation is best, giving a clear rationale (which may be to keep the current base).

places.quote: On the criterion that the exposure base should be the factor most directly proportional to expected loss, **house-years remain the exposure base**, and amount of insurance is used as a **rating variable**

requirements.statement: Frequency-severity technique: ultimate claims = exposure units × ultimate (trended) frequency per exposure unit × ultimate (trended) severity.

places.quote: $$U = \text{Exposures} \times \text{Frequency}_{\text{ult}} \times S_{\text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: Trend a selected ultimate severity from its base accident year to the target accident year by compounding the annual severity trend rate over the number of years between them.

places.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.
The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: A selected ultimate frequency is already at ultimate, so the claim count development factor is not applied to it; the count development factor applies only to reported claim counts.

places.quote: Frequency computed on reported counts at an immature age is biased low, since claims are still being reported — the counts must be developed to ultimate with their own [[Claim Count Triangle|count triangle]].

requirements.statement: Claims development technique: ultimate claims = reported (or paid) claims to date × selected age-to-ultimate claims development factor.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: Reported Bornhuetter-Ferguson ultimate = reported claims + expected claims (exposure base × expected loss ratio, or premium × ELR) × (1 − 1/reported age-to-ultimate development factor).

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$

requirements.statement: Premium (the a priori exposure base for B-F) can be computed as exposure units times the rate per unit of exposure, with the rate quoted per 1,000 exposure units requiring a scaling adjustment.

places.quote: $$\text{Premium} = \text{Rate} \times \text{Exposures}$$

requirements.statement: A rise in reported claims not matched in paid claims indicates case reserve strengthening (or a shock loss), so the reported development technique overstates ultimate claims.

places.quote: A [[Large Loss|shock loss]] reported early is multiplied by the full CDF.
Applying historical factors — built under weaker reserving — to a strengthened diagonal **over-states** ultimate, because the strengthening is developed a second time.

requirements.statement: The paid development technique at early maturities is highly leveraged (large age-to-ultimate factor) and may be unreliable, while B-F is more stable at early maturities because it weights actual claims with an expected-claims IBNR.

places.quote: at its worst at immature ages in [[Long Tail Lines|long-tail lines]], where the CDF is large and the diagonal is thin.
It is therefore the method of choice at **immature maturities** and for [[Long Tail Lines|long-tail lines]], converging to the chain ladder as the cohort matures.
A CDF of $2.27$ means more than half the ultimate estimate is unreported.

requirements.statement: The frequency-severity technique's appropriateness depends on the currency of its selected severity and frequency, and it can be distorted by outdated selections or by changes not reflected in them.

places.quote: if severity trend has genuinely stepped up, the **pricing** severity trend selection is stale too, and the reserving finding is also a rate-adequacy finding.

requirements.statement: The disposal rate is the cumulative closed claim count at a development age divided by the ultimate claim count for the accident year.

places.quote: $$\text{Disposal Rate}_n = \frac{\text{Closed claims at age } n}{\text{Ultimate claim counts}}$$
$$\text{Disposal Rate}_n = \frac{\text{Closed claims at age } n}{\text{Ultimate claim counts}}$$

requirements.statement: Incremental average severity at a development age is the incremental paid claims divided by the incremental closed claim counts for that interval.

Project ultimate claims for an accident year as paid to date plus, for each remaining development interval, ultimate counts times the increase in selected disposal rate times the selected incremental severity trended to the accident year's level.

places.quote: Project the number of claims closing in each future period from historical **disposal rates**, value them at a trended severity for that maturity, and sum the future payments.

requirements.statement: Select disposal rates and incremental severities from the latest diagonal when it is representative of current claim adjusting practices, rather than averaging all years.

places.quote: Select the current disposal rate pattern as the target.
That applies a one-time level shift as though it were an ongoing pattern, and over-states every future year's development.

requirements.statement: Trend selected severities from the latest diagonal's year to the year in which each future payment occurs, using the annual severity trend compounded for the number of years between.

places.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.
- The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: If one accident year has a one-time severity shock, adjust that year's incremental severity (e.g. restate the affected severity) or exclude it from the averages used to select severities for other years, so the anomaly is not projected onto other years.

places.quote: That is a calendar-year signal, and averaging it into the selections applies a one-time shift as though it were an ongoing pattern.
That applies a one-time level shift as though it were an ongoing pattern, and over-states every future year's development.
