Counts must be **defined consistently**: per claim or per claimant, counting claims closed without payment or not, treating reopened claims as new or as continuing. A definition change mid-triangle looks exactly like a frequency trend.

requirements.statement: The frequency-severity technique assumes claims are paid in full at closure with no partial payments; partial payments on open claims violate this assumption.

The Berquist-Sherman method restates historical data for changes in claim settlement rates (adjusting closed counts/disposal rates to the current settlement speed) so that techniques like disposal-rate frequency-severity can be applied; the case-reserve-adequacy adjustment is a different one.

places.quote: For each historical cell, interpolate the paid losses that *would* have been paid had that year closed claims at the current rate — reading along the row's paid-versus-disposal-rate relationship.

The remedy is the [[Berquist-Sherman Method|Berquist-Sherman]] paid adjustment: restate each historical year's paid losses to what they would have been at the *current* disposal pattern, by interpolating along each year's paid-versus-disposal-rate relationship, then select factors from the restated triangle.

requirements.statement: Adjustments for violated assumptions include excluding partial payments from severity and reapplying them in the period the claim closes, selecting disposal rates using judgment or external information, and complementing severity trend selection with credibility-weighted industry data.

places.quote: The adjustments are **large and judgment-laden** — the severity trend and the target disposal pattern are both selections

requirements.statement: Bornhuetter-Ferguson IBNR = expected claims (expected claims ratio × on-level earned premium) × percent unreported, where the percent unreported is 1 minus the percent reported.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}$$
$$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$
It holds for both chain ladder and BF IBNR: chain ladder IBNR is its ultimate times $1 - p_t$, and BF IBNR is the expected claims times $1 - p_t$.

requirements.statement: The percent reported (or its complement, percent unreported) implied by the reported development technique equals reported claims divided by the development-technique ultimate, i.e. the inverse of the cumulative development factor.

places.quote: $p_t = 1/\text{CDF}_t$ is the expected percentage reported (or paid) at age $t$.
The reciprocal is the **percentage reported** (or paid): $p_n = 1/\text{CDF}_n$, and $1 - p_n$ is the percentage unreported.

requirements.statement: To assess an expected claims ratio assumption, compute the claims ratio (ultimate claims divided by on-level earned premium) for each accident year and compare it to the assumed ratio, looking for trends or systematic deviation.

places.quote: Then test the *selected* ultimates by the ratios they imply: ultimate claim ratios, severities, frequencies and pure premiums by year, and the implied average case outstanding and unreported claim on open and unreported claims.
**Ultimate loss ratios** by accident year, on-level. They should move with rate adequacy and trend, not jump.

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson technique assumes a constant expected claims ratio and relies on an a priori estimate that does not respond to emerging experience, so a trending claims ratio makes it inappropriate.

places.quote: BF does not respond to bad news. If emergence runs far ahead of the a priori, BF holds most of its estimate anchored — which is exactly right when the emergence is noise and exactly wrong when it is signal.
[[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method|Bornhuetter-Ferguson]] assumes unreported claims follow an independent a priori ratio.

requirements.statement: The Cape Cod technique derives the expected claims ratio from the data's own experience, so it responds to changing claims ratios across years, as does the reported development technique, which uses actual reported claims.

places.quote: **Cape Cod Method** (Stanard-Bühlmann) is the [[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method|Bornhuetter-Ferguson]] technique with the a priori loss ratio **derived from the data itself** rather than supplied externally.
$$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: To test whether claims are closing faster, compare the ratio of closed (or paid) claim counts to reported claim counts at the same maturity across accident years; a rising ratio at the same age indicates a speed-up in settlement.

places.quote: **Faster [[Settlement Rate|settlement]]:** closure rates and paid-to-reported rise together.
Closure at $24$ months has risen from $45\%$ to $63\%$ — claims are settling substantially faster, and the trend is steady rather than a one-off.

requirements.statement: When claim settlement rates are changing, closed claim counts and paid severity (and disposal-rate methods) are distorted, so the frequency-severity method should use reported claim counts and reported severity, which are not affected by closure timing.

places.quote: **Reported data is largely immune**, because reported losses include the case reserve whether or not the claim has closed.
*Faster settlement*: paid development overstates; reported methods are largely unaffected.

requirements.statement: Reported (or paid) severity at each maturity equals the cumulative reported (or paid) claim dollars divided by the corresponding cumulative claim count.

places.quote: **Severity** is the average cost per claim — total losses divided by claim count — as distinct from [[Frequency|how often claims occur]].
\text{Average Severity} = \frac{\text{Losses}}{\text{Claim Counts}}

requirements.statement: Develop claim counts and severity on separate triangles: compute age-to-age factors, select factors (e.g., all-year average when stable), apply a tail factor, and multiply to get cumulative development factors to ultimate.

places.quote: Develop the count triangle to ultimate counts; develop an average severity triangle (dollars ÷ counts at each age) to ultimate severity; multiply.
\text{Ultimate Counts} = N_n \times \text{CDF}^{\text{count}}_{n \to \text{ult}}

requirements.statement: Ultimate claims for an accident year equal ultimate claim count (latest count times count CDF) times ultimate severity (latest severity times severity CDF).

places.quote: U = N_{\text{ult}} \times S_{\text{ult}}
\text{Ultimate losses} &= 650 \times \$8{,}400 = \$5{,}460{,}000

requirements.statement: The Berquist-Sherman case reserve adequacy adjustment is needed when case reserve adequacy has changed, since an unadjusted reported triangle would give a distorted development pattern.

places.quote: **Berquist-Sherman Method** restates a historical [[Development Triangle|triangle]] so that every year reflects **current** claims practice, removing the distortion caused by a change in [[Case Adequacy|case reserve adequacy]] or in [[Settlement Rate|claim settlement rates]].
A *change* in adequacy over calendar time is one of the two distortions ([[Settlement Rate|settlement rate]] is the other) that make historical development factors misleading.

requirements.statement: To adjust for case reserve adequacy, compute average case outstanding (case outstanding divided by open claim counts), keep the latest diagonal, and detrend it backward at the severity trend rate to fill earlier ages in the triangle.

places.quote: 3. **Trend the latest diagonal's** average case outstanding backwards at $t$ to restate each historical cell at today's adequacy level.

The remedy is the [[Berquist-Sherman Method|Berquist-Sherman]] case adjustment: restate historical average case outstanding to the current adequacy level using a selected severity trend, rebuild the reported triangle, and select factors from the restated history.

requirements.statement: Adjusted reported claims = adjusted average case outstanding × open claim counts + paid claims.

places.quote: $$\text{Adjusted Reported}_{\text{AY},n} = \text{Paid}_{\text{AY},n} + \text{Adjusted Case}_{\text{AY},n}$$

resolution.quote: Multiply the restated averages by the open claim counts to get adjusted case reserves, add paid, and rebuild the reported triangle.
resolution.note: Re-quoted after the page was edited today: adjusted reported = adjusted average case x open counts + paid.

requirements.statement: Age-to-age factors are computed from the adjusted triangle, selected (e.g. by straight average), combined with a tail factor, and cumulated into CDFs to ultimate.

places.quote: **The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.
**Simple average** — equal weight to each year, so a small, volatile year counts as much as a large one.

requirements.statement: Calendar year earned premium equals written premium minus the change in unearned premium reserve (ending UEPR minus beginning UEPR); with annual policies written uniformly, the UEPR at each year-end is half of that year's written premium.
requirements.concept: Earned Premium and Unearned Premium Reserve

places.quote: For a book of annual policies written uniformly, the year-end UEP is about **half** of that year's written premium — the average policy is half expired.
$$\text{Earned Premium} = \text{Written Premium} - \Delta\text{UEP}$$

requirements.statement: Bornhuetter-Ferguson ultimate = developed ultimate × (1/CDF) + expected ultimate × (1 − 1/CDF), where expected ultimate = expected claim ratio × earned premium and the developed ultimate is reported claims × CDF.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$
$$U = \text{ELR} \times \text{Earned Premium}$$

requirements.statement: Unpaid claims = ultimate claims − paid claims to date (case outstanding plus IBNR).

places.quote: $$\text{Unpaid} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Paid to date}$$

requirements.statement: To develop a loss-type triangle (e.g., received salvage and subrogation), compute age-to-age factors as ratios of successive cumulative values for each accident year.

places.quote: $$f_{n \to n{+}1} = \frac{\text{Losses at age }n{+}1}{\text{Losses at age }n}$$
$$f_{k \to k+1} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k}}$$

requirements.statement: Select age-to-age development factors using a simple all-year average of the factors in each column, then multiply the selected factors to get cumulative age-to-ultimate factors (with no tail beyond the last age).

places.quote: **Simple average**: unweighted mean of all individual year factors — treats each accident year equally regardless of size
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$
CDFs are built **backwards from the tail**: start with the tail factor, multiply in each successive age-to-age factor moving toward younger ages.

requirements.statement: The development technique estimates ultimate by multiplying the latest cumulative amount by the age-to-ultimate factor.

places.quote: $$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate} = C_n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: In the ratio approach for salvage and subrogation, form the ratio of received S&S to paid claims at each age, develop those ratios with age-to-age factors, apply the age-to-ultimate factor to the current ratio, and multiply the resulting ultimate ratio by ultimate claims.

places.quote: **Salvage and subrogation** (Friedland Ch. 14) are projected either by the development technique on reported or received S&S, or by the **ratio approach**: develop the ratio of received S&S to paid claims to an ultimate ratio, and multiply by selected ultimate claims gross of S&S.

requirements.statement: Developing small S&S amounts directly gives volatile, highly leveraged factors for immature years, whereas the ratio approach is more stable because it is tied to paid claims and the ratios are consistent across accident years, so it is preferred.

places.quote: The ratio's development factors are less leveraged than those of S&S dollars, and the ultimate ratio is easier to select for immature years.

requirements.statement: For a new accident year, estimate ultimate S&S by applying the selected ultimate S&S-to-claims ratio (current ratio times age-to-ultimate factor, or the mature ratio) to that year's ultimate claims.

places.quote: Absent a reason, a selection near the historical level is typical — at $0.107$, ultimate S&S is $\$1{,}337{,}500$ and the recoverable $\$1{,}025{,}500$, against $\$858{,}000$ from the mechanical projection.

requirements.statement: An age-to-age (link ratio) factor is the ratio of cumulative reported claims at one maturity to the cumulative reported claims at the prior maturity for the same accident year.

places.quote: **Development Factor** (link ratio or age-to-age factor) is the ratio used to project cumulative losses from one maturity age to the next
**Age-to-Age Factor** (link ratio) is the ratio of a cohort's cumulative amount at one maturity to its amount at the previous maturity — the observed development between two ages.

requirements.statement: Select an age-to-age factor for each development period from the observed factors in the triangle (e.g., average of the accident-year factors).

places.quote: - **Simple average**: unweighted mean of all individual year factors — treats each accident year equally regardless of size

**The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.
- **Volume-weighted (all-year)** — the ratio of column sums. Weights each year by its size, so it is stable and dominated by the large years. The default choice.

requirements.statement: Compute age-to-ultimate factors by multiplying the selected age-to-age factors from a given maturity through the tail factor, working backward from the tail.

places.quote: CDFs are built **backwards from the tail**: start with the tail factor, multiply in each successive age-to-age factor moving toward younger ages.
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: Under the development technique, ultimate claims equal the latest diagonal value of reported claims for each accident year multiplied by the age-to-ultimate factor for its current maturity.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate} = C_n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: Claims and ALAE may be combined for development if their development patterns and ALAE-to-claim ratios are consistent over time; if patterns differ or ratios shift, they should be projected separately. Small ALAE amounts may argue for combining to gain credibility and stability.

places.quote: - Combining is simplest and is the usual choice, but it assumes ALAE develops like indemnity. It often does not: defence costs accrue steadily through litigation while indemnity lands at settlement, so an ALAE-only triangle can have a different shape and a different tail.
Because it attaches to a claim, it can be carried inside the loss triangle and developed with the losses.

requirements.statement: The development technique is less reliable when age-to-age factors are volatile or leveraged (e.g., small early-maturity amounts) or when claims-department practices change the emergence pattern, since factor selection becomes difficult and results erratic.

places.quote: The chain ladder is at its best on **mature cohorts with stable patterns and ample volume** — and at its worst at immature ages in [[Long Tail Lines|long-tail lines]], where the CDF is large and the diagonal is thin.

The CDF measures **leverage**. At a CDF of $4$, a dollar of distortion on the diagonal becomes four dollars of ultimate — which is why the chain ladder is unreliable at immature ages in [[Long Tail Lines|long-tail lines]] and why methods that develop only the *unreported* portion are preferred there.

- A factor that moves along the **diagonal** rather than down the column is a calendar-year effect ([[Development Triangle]]) and should be addressed by restating the triangle, not by averaging it away.

requirements.statement: In the classical paid-to-paid technique, the ULAE ratio for each calendar year is calendar-year paid ULAE divided by calendar-year paid claims.

places.quote: $$\text{Classical ratio} = \frac{\text{CY Paid ULAE}}{\text{CY Paid Loss}}$$

requirements.statement: Select a ULAE ratio from the calendar-year ratios by examining their pattern (e.g. choose the latest ratio when it trends steadily) rather than blindly averaging.

places.quote: Compute the ratio $R$ of calendar-year paid ULAE to calendar-year paid loss, review it for trend, and apply it to unpaid claims.

requirements.statement: Classical technique unpaid ULAE = selected ratio × (IBNR + 50% × case outstanding reserves), reflecting that half of ULAE is spent opening a claim and half closing it, so case reserves carry only the closing half while IBNR carries the full amount.

places.quote: If ULAE is assumed to be spent half at reporting and half at settlement, only $50\%$ remains on reported-but-unpaid claims while $100\%$ remains on [[IBNR]] — the formula above.
$$\text{ULAE Reserve} = R \times \left(0.5 \times \text{Case} + 1.0 \times \text{IBNR}\right)$$

requirements.statement: Key assumptions of the classical technique are that ULAE is spent 50% when a claim is opened and 50% when closed, and that ULAE and claim costs inflate at the same rate so the paid ULAE-to-paid claims ratio is stable over time.

places.quote: If ULAE is assumed to be spent half at reporting and half at settlement, only $50\%$ remains on reported-but-unpaid claims while $100\%$ remains on [[IBNR]] — the formula above.

requirements.statement: Test the same-inflation assumption by comparing trends in loss cost per exposure (ultimate claims ÷ exposures) with trends in paid ULAE; differing trends mean the assumption is violated and the ratio will misstate future ULAE.
The Kittel refinement adjusts the classical technique for a changing book size by using the average of paid and reported (incurred) claims as the denominator of the ratio instead of paid claims.

places.quote: Kittel divides by the **average of paid and incurred** loss instead:
$$R_{\text{Kittel}} = \frac{\text{Paid ULAE}}{0.5(\text{Paid Loss}) + 0.5(\text{Incurred Loss})}$$

requirements.statement: The Kittel refinement still assumes ULAE and claims inflate at the same rate, so it cannot correct for different ULAE and claim cost inflation rates; it only addresses changes in volume of business.

places.quote: Kittel divides by the **average of paid and incurred** loss instead:

requirements.statement: Actual versus expected claim count emergence compares the claim counts actually reported (or closed) during a calendar period with the counts expected to emerge in that period based on prior selected ultimates and the development pattern.

places.quote: **Actual vs. Expected Analysis** (A/E) compares the emergence that actually occurred in a period against what the previous valuation's assumptions implied should occur.

requirements.statement: Expected emergence over a period for an accident year equals (selected ultimate claim count minus reported claims to date) times (percent reported at end of period minus percent reported at start) divided by (1 minus percent reported at start).

places.quote: $$\text{Expected emergence} = U_{\text{prior}} \times \left(\frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n+1}} - \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n}}\right)$$

resolution.quote: \text{Expected emergence} = \frac{U_{\text{prior}} - \text{Reported}_{n}}{1 - 1/\text{CDF}_{n}}
resolution.note: Re-quoted after the page was edited today: expected emergence = unreported x (change in % reported)/(1 - % reported at start).

requirements.statement: Actual emergence in a calendar period for an accident year equals the cumulative reported claim counts at the end of the period minus those at the start of the period.

places.quote: $\Delta$ terms are ending balance minus beginning balance.

requirements.statement: Compare actual to expected emergence by accident year and in total (by difference or ratio); actual exceeding expected indicates ultimate claim counts were underestimated or reporting is faster than the pattern assumes.

places.quote: $$\text{A/E} = \frac{\text{Actual emergence}}{\text{Expected emergence}}$$

requirements.statement: A limitation of the actual vs. expected approach is that it relies on a historical development pattern and annual intervals, so it may not reflect changes in reporting speed, claim mix, settlement operations, or the techniques used to select ultimates, nor intra-year reporting timing.
requirements.concept: Limitations of Actual vs. Expected Claim Emergence

places.quote: Assumptions being made implicitly by using one at all: each cohort develops in a similar pattern, the pattern is stable over time, and the mix inside each cohort is comparable.
If the segments have different emergence patterns, the blended development factors drift as the weights drift — and the triangle gives no signal that this is what is happening.

**Faster settlement** pushes losses from open to paid, so the recent paid diagonal is high relative to history. Historical paid factors — built when claims closed more slowly — then **over-develop** it and overstate ultimate.

requirements.statement: Alternatives that address the limitations include using shorter time intervals, comparing expected closed (paid) claim counts using a closed claim count pattern or disposal rate triangles, and making Berquist-Sherman adjustments to restate the pattern for changes in operations.

places.quote: Triangles may be annual, semi-annual or quarterly. Finer periods are more responsive and show seasonality; they also thin the data and multiply the factors to select.
**Closed counts** — how fast claims settle. The [[Settlement Rate|disposal rate]] is closed counts over ultimate (or reported) counts.
Compute **disposal rates** — closed claims ÷ ultimate (or reported) claims — at each accident year and maturity.

requirements.statement: An occurrence policy covers losses that occur during the policy period, regardless of when they are reported, so the losses for a policy year are the diagonal of a report-lag triangle (all report lags for that accident/occurrence year, as reported by the evaluation date).

places.quote: **Occurrence Coverage** is a policy trigger under which the policy responds to losses that *occur* during the policy period, however long afterwards the claim is reported.
Claims-made business is organized on a [[Report Year]] basis: in Werner's report-year-by-lag table a claims-made policy is a row, where an occurrence policy is a diagonal.

requirements.statement: A claims-made policy covers claims reported during the policy period that arise from incidents occurring on or after the retroactive date, so only claims first reported in the policy year (lag 0 on that policy's report year) with occurrence dates after the retroactive date are included.

places.quote: **Claims-Made Coverage** is a policy trigger under which the policy responds to claims *reported* during the policy period, provided the underlying loss occurred on or after the policy's **retroactive date**.

RY is the correct basis for [[Claims Made Coverage|claims-made]] coverage, because a claims-made policy's trigger *is* the report date: every claim reported during the policy period is covered by that policy, so the report year cohort and the coverage cohort coincide.

requirements.statement: To find losses for a claims-made policy year from a report-year by lag triangle, sum the cells for that report year across the report lags that fall on or after the retroactive date (occurrence years covered), up to the evaluation date; for an occurrence policy year, sum the cells along the diagonal for that occurrence year.

places.quote: Claims-made business is organized on a [[Report Year]] basis: in Werner's report-year-by-lag table a claims-made policy is a row, where an occurrence policy is a diagonal.
Occurrence business is aggregated on an [[Accident Year]] basis, because the accident date is the trigger: in Werner's report-year-by-lag table an occurrence policy is a diagonal.

requirements.statement: Moving from occurrence to claims-made coverage reduces loss reserve risk because claims-made has little or no IBNR (pure IBNR/late-reported claims) beyond the policy period and a shorter tail, removing report-lag risk and leaving mostly development risk.
requirements.concept: Loss Reserve Risk for Claims-Made Policies

places.quote: Because the trigger is the report date, a claims-made policy has **no pure IBNR** — only IBNER on claims already reported — so the risk of reserve inadequacy is greatly reduced relative to the [[Occurrence Coverage|occurrence]] form.
A report year **closes to new claims** at year end — pure [[IBNR]] is zero by construction, since every claim in the cohort is already known.
It must reserve for **pure [[IBNR]]** — claims it has no knowledge of — for as long as claims from expired policies can still emerge, which for a product like medical malpractice can be many years.

requirements.statement: Moving from occurrence to claims-made coverage shortens the time between premium receipt and loss payment, reducing investment income, so the target underwriting profit provision must increase; alternatively, lower pricing/reserve risk could justify a lower target underwriting profit provision.

places.quote: The investment income earned from claims-made policies is substantially less than under occurrence policies — which the target underwriting profit provision must reflect, along with the reduced pricing risk.
Investment income on the [[Unearned Premium|unearned premium]] and loss reserves lets a line accept a lower underwriting profit and still earn its target return.

requirements.statement: The annual trend in frequency or severity between consecutive years is the ratio of the later year's value to the prior year's value, minus 1.

places.quote: \text{Frequency change} &= \frac{0.0720}{0.0600} - 1 = +20.0\%

requirements.statement: Select frequency and severity trends from the observed period changes, using all years when changes are stable and only recent years when there is a clear change in pattern; justify the choice from the data.

places.quote: exponential models may be fit to the whole of the data and to more recent periods, supplemented with multi-state, countrywide or industry data and non-insurance indices, and the trend selected with judgment.
Werner's example fits windows of 20, 16, 12, 8, 6 and 4 points, and $R^2$ is the usual diagnostic; the recent windows show whether the trend has shifted.

requirements.statement: The overall loss (pure premium) trend factor is the product of one plus the frequency trend and one plus the severity trend, compounded over the trending period.

places.quote: 1 + t_{PP} = (1 + t_{\text{freq}})(1 + t_{\text{sev}})
Separately selected frequency and severity trends combine multiplicatively: $1 + T_{PP} = (1 + T_F)(1 + T_S)$.

requirements.statement: Trend ultimate losses from the average accident date of each historical accident year to the average accident date of the future period, which is the rate effective date plus half the policy term plus half the accident-year length (for policies in effect one year with written term considered).

places.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.
The trend period runs from the average date of historical losses (midpoint of the accident year) to the average date of future losses (midpoint of the prospective rating period)

requirements.statement: For annual rates in effect for a year with semi-annual policies, the average accident date of the future period is determined by the effective date plus the rate-in-effect period and policy term, so that the future average accident date falls 1.5 years... after the effective date's midpoint of the exposure period.

places.quote: with six-month policies the trend-from date moves to $4/1/2011$ and the period is $2.25$ years.

requirements.statement: After trending each accident year's ultimate losses to the future period, average the trended ultimate losses across the selected years to get the projected losses (exposures constant).

resolution.note: Averaging the trended ultimates across the selected years is a step of this solution's plan.

requirements.statement: A one-time underwriting change that lowered claim counts distorts the frequency in earlier years, so the frequency trend may be selected using only post-change years or adjusted toward a less negative trend, which raises trended ultimate losses; if only post-change data was already used, the estimate is unchanged.
requirements.concept: Adjusting Trends for Changes in Underwriting

places.quote: rising frequency at flat severity points at underwriting, mix or the claim environment
The responses here are to weight recent years more heavily, to segment the data so the changing mix is visible, or to lean on a priori methods whose ELR can be set for the new book.

requirements.statement: Writing fewer high-deductible policies increases frequency (fewer claims fall below deductibles) and decreases severity (fewer large-average claims without nuisance claims), so frequency trend rises, severity trend falls, and the net effect on projected losses depends on the pure premium trend.
requirements.concept: Effect of Deductible Mix Shifts on Frequency and Severity

places.quote: Werner & Modlin's example is a heavily marketed higher deductible, which lowers frequency but is likely to increase severity, a shift that is hard to see in pure premium.
The deductible shift genuinely reduces the premium the insurer will collect per exposure going forward — and, importantly, it reduces expected losses too

requirements.statement: Frequency is claim counts divided by earned exposures, and severity is ultimate losses divided by claim counts; the frequency and severity trends are measured from the year-over-year changes in these values.

places.quote: The identity holds because $\dfrac{\text{Losses}}{\text{Exposures}} = \dfrac{\text{Claims}}{\text{Exposures}} \times \dfrac{\text{Losses}}{\text{Claims}}$ — and it is what allows the two components to be trended, developed and diagnosed separately ([[Frequency]], [[Severity]]).

requirements.statement: Select a trend rate from the observed annual changes in the historical series (e.g., by judgment based on the fitted or year-over-year rates), using gross direct losses (not losses net of reinsurance) to determine the severity trend.

places.quote: A change in attachment point makes prior net years non-comparable, while gross years remain usable.
Annual trends over different windows, from end point to end point (an exponential regression through every point gives $6.9\%$, $8.5\%$ and $8.7\%$):

requirements.statement: The trend period runs from the average accident date of each historical year to the average accident date of the future period in which the rates will be in effect.

places.quote: The trend period runs from the average date of historical losses (midpoint of the accident year) to the average date of future losses (midpoint of the prospective rating period)
$t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.

requirements.statement: For annual policies written uniformly, the average accident date of the future period is the rate effective date plus the policy term (one year for the rate-in-effect period and one year for policy term) at the midpoint, i.e., rate effective date plus one year for a one-year rate period; historical accident-year average accident date is the middle of the year (July 1).

places.quote: The trend period runs from the average date of historical losses (midpoint of the accident year) to the average date of future losses (midpoint of the prospective rating period)
The first policy is exposed $7/1/2025$–$6/30/2026$ and the last $7/1/2026$–$6/30/2027$, so the exposure period runs $7/1/2025$ to $6/30/2027$ and its midpoint — the average loss date — is $7/1/2026$.

requirements.statement: Trended value equals the historical value multiplied by (1 + trend) raised to the trend period in years.

places.quote: $$\text{Trend Factor} = (1 + r)^n$$
$$\text{Trended Exposure} = \text{Historical Exposure} \times (1 + t_E)^{n}$$

requirements.statement: To estimate losses net of reinsurance at the current retention, trend each large claim individually to the future level and then subtract the portion exceeding the current retention from the trended direct losses, rather than netting excess before trending.

places.quote: Trend each historical loss individually *before* applying the layer. Excess losses grow faster than trend because a loss just below $R$ trends into the layer.

requirements.statement: Pure premium equals losses divided by earned exposures; the all-year average is total trended net losses divided by total earned exposures.

places.quote: $$\text{Pure Premium} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Exposures}}$$
$$\text{Pure Premium} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Exposures}} = \text{Frequency} \times \text{Severity}$$

requirements.statement: The all variable expense method projects the expense provision as total historical expenses divided by total premium, treating every expense as proportional to premium.

places.quote: The **all-variable expense method** loads every expense as a percentage of premium.

Loading fixed expenses as a percentage of premium instead — the **all-variable expense method** — undercharges risks with below-average premium and overcharges those above it, so large policies subsidize small ones.

requirements.statement: Fixed expenses do not vary with premium, so treating them as variable overcharges when average premium is above average and undercharges when it is low; fixed and variable expenses should be separated, especially when premium is changing or shrinking.

places.quote: Treating a fixed cost as variable over-charges large policies and under-charges small ones.

Loading fixed expenses as a percentage of premium instead — the **all-variable expense method** — undercharges risks with below-average premium and overcharges those above it, so large policies subsidize small ones.

requirements.statement: Commissions/brokerage and other acquisition expenses are incurred at policy inception and so relate to written premium, while general expenses are incurred over the policy term and relate to earned premium.

places.quote: Expenses incurred at the onset of the policy — commissions, other acquisition, and taxes, licenses and fees — are calculated on [[Written Premium]]; general expenses, incurred throughout the policy, on [[Earned Premium]].

those incurred at the onset of the policy (commissions, other acquisition, taxes, licenses and fees) are measured against written premium, those incurred throughout the policy (general expenses) against [[Earned Premium|earned premium]]

requirements.statement: Compute expense ratios by year for each expense category using the appropriate premium base (written or earned) to identify trends before selecting a future ratio for each category.

places.quote: Expenses incurred at the onset of the policy — commissions, other acquisition, and taxes, licenses and fees — are calculated on [[Written Premium]]; general expenses, incurred throughout the policy, on [[Earned Premium]].

those incurred at the onset of the policy (commissions, other acquisition, taxes, licenses and fees) are measured against written premium, those incurred throughout the policy (general expenses) against [[Earned Premium|earned premium]]
Acquisition costs are incurred as policies are written, so they are related to written premium; general expenses are incurred through the policy term, so they are related to earned premium.

requirements.statement: In the exposure-based (policy-based) method, divide fixed expense dollars by exposures to get a per-exposure cost, trend it to the future period, and use percent-of-premium for variable expenses.

places.quote: The fixed dollars are then put per exposure either by multiplying the fixed expense ratio by the projected average premium, or by dividing fixed expenses directly by exposures or policy count.
a fixed expense *per exposure* on a base that does not inflate (car-years, house-years) or per policy is expected to change and is trended (see [[Loss Trend]], [[Premium Trend]]).

requirements.statement: Giving equal weight to multiple years of data in a shrinking book weights older years too heavily, and recent years are more representative; expense trend can differ from premium trend.

places.quote: In the premium-based method no trend is needed if average fixed expense and average premium change at the same rate; with a per-exposure figure on a base that does not inflate (car-years, house-years) or per policy, trending is appropriate.
many companies sum projected losses and premium across all years, which weights each year's loss ratio by its premium; others select weights, often giving more to the most recent years.

requirements.statement: The overall indicated rate per exposure with fixed expenses is (projected loss and LAE + fixed expenses per exposure total) / exposures divided by (1 - variable expense ratio - underwriting profit provision), i.e., indicated rate = [(L + F)/E] / (1 - V - Q).
requirements.concept: Loss Ratio and Pure Premium Ratemaking Methods

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Rate} = \frac{\text{Pure Premium} + F}{1 - V - Q_T}$$
$$\text{Rate} = \frac{\text{Pure Premium} + F}{1 - V - Q_T}$$

requirements.statement: Under the loss ratio method with fixed expenses, the indicated rate change equals [(projected loss and LAE + fixed expenses) / premium at current rates] / (1 - V - Q) minus 1.
requirements.concept: Loss Ratio and Pure Premium Ratemaking Methods

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$

requirements.statement: The underwriting profit provision (Q) is the target profit as a percentage of premium, included as a variable component in the permissible loss ratio (1 - V - Q); it is a provision rather than total projected profit dollars.

places.quote: $V$ is the [[Variable Expenses|variable expense]] ratio, $Q_T$ the target [[Underwriting Profit|underwriting profit]] provision, and $F\%$ the [[Fixed Expenses|fixed expense]] ratio.
$Q_T$ is a **target underwriting** profit provision, not a target total profit.

requirements.statement: A company may target a lower underwriting profit provision when it expects greater investment income (e.g., longer-tail lines with long loss payout), since total return includes investment income on float.

places.quote: [[Long Tail Lines|Long-tail lines]] hold reserves for years and earn substantial investment income on them, so they can support a low or even negative underwriting provision and still return the target on equity
Investment income on the [[Unearned Premium|unearned premium]] and loss reserves lets a line accept a lower underwriting profit and still earn its target return.

requirements.statement: Underwriting profit provisions can differ between companies due to business strategy (reducing the provision to grow or gain market share), risk level of insureds written (higher risk justifies higher provision), or differing regulatory restrictions on allowable profit.

places.quote: a charge for **random** variation from expected costs belongs in the total return consistent with the cost of capital, and so in the underwriting profit provision

requirements.statement: The loss ratio method with fixed expenses gives the indicated rate change as (projected ultimate loss & LAE ratio + fixed expense ratio) / (1 − variable expense ratio − target underwriting profit ratio) − 1.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$

requirements.statement: Split each expense category into fixed and variable portions by multiplying its expense ratio by its variable percentage (variable) and the remainder (fixed), then sum the portions across categories.

places.quote: Expense studies rarely split cleanly. Ideally detailed expense data or activity-based cost studies make the split; otherwise it is generally made judgmentally, with other professionals in the company, as a **fixed percentage** of each category (Werner's example: general expenses $75\%$ fixed).

requirements.statement: When expenses are incurred/paid at policy inception, expense ratios for those items (e.g., general expenses) are computed against written premium rather than earned premium.

places.quote: Because commissions and taxes attach when a policy is **written**, these ratios are computed against [[Written Premium|written premium]]; expenses incurred as coverage is provided use [[Earned Premium|earned premium]].

**Premium-based ratios use different denominators.** Expenses incurred at the onset of the policy — commissions, other acquisition, and taxes, licenses and fees — are calculated on [[Written Premium]]; general expenses, incurred throughout the policy, on [[Earned Premium]].

requirements.statement: A negative indicated rate change means the rate should decrease; the sign of the result (ratio minus 1) must be retained.

places.quote: an indicated change of $-6.8\%$.
When the projected loss ratio exceeds the target, rates are inadequate; when it falls below, rates are excessive; the ratio of projected to target drives the indicated change

requirements.statement: On-level factor is the ratio of the current rate (or benefit) level to the average rate (or benefit) level in effect over the period, used to restate premium (or losses) to current levels.

places.quote: $$\text{On-Level Factor} = \frac{\text{Current cumulative rate level index}}{\text{Average rate level index for the period}}$$
$$\text{On-Level Factor} = \frac{\text{Current cumulative index}}{\text{Average index for the year}}$$
$$\text{On-Level Factor} = \frac{\text{Current cumulative index}}{\text{Index in force during the period}}$$

requirements.statement: Compute the average rate level for an accident year by weighting each rate level by the share of the year's earned premium written at that level, using the parallelogram method when policies are written uniformly with one-year terms.

places.quote: The *average* index for a year is the earned-premium-weighted blend of the levels in force during that year.
$$\text{OLF}_Y = \frac{I_{\text{current}}}{\sum_k A_{Y,k}\, I_k}$$

requirements.statement: For a rate change effective mid-year with one-year policies, the portion of the accident year's earned premium at the new rate equals the area of the small triangle cut off in the unit square, and the remainder is at the old rate.

places.quote: The second formula is the area earned in the same calendar year at a new level effective a fraction $p$ of the way through it, for annual policies.

For **annual** policies written uniformly, a rate change effective at time $p$ through year $Y$ earns over a triangle of area $\tfrac{1}{2}(1-p)^2$ in year $Y$ — so a $7/1$ change affects only $0.125$ of that year's earned premium, and a $1/1$ change affects $0.500$.

requirements.statement: Benefit level changes affect losses by accident date for accident-year losses, but for policies written after a date they apply to policies, so the affected loss share is found with a parallelogram-type weighting; changes in rates do not affect losses.

places.quote: Changes attach to the **policy**, so they phase in over the policy term.
the effect of a coverage or benefit-level change on losses is a separate adjustment on the loss side.

requirements.statement: Successive benefit or rate changes compound multiplicatively to give the current level (e.g., a +10% change followed by a -5% change gives 1.10 × 0.95).

places.quote: Rate level indices **compound**: successive changes of $+8\%$ and $+5\%$ give a cumulative index of $1.08 \times 1.05 = 1.134$, not $1.13$.
$I_k$ is the cumulative rate level index of rate level group $k$ (each index is the previous one times $1 +$ that change)

requirements.statement: Trend on-level losses from the average accident date of the experience period to the average accident date of the period in which the new rates will be in effect, using (1 + annual trend) raised to the number of years.

places.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.
The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: When rates are filed once per year and policies have one-year terms, the average accident date of the period the new rates apply is six months after the effective date (the midpoint of a one-year policy period).

places.quote: Policies are written between $7/1/2025$ and $6/30/2026$; each provides coverage for a year after it is written. … so the exposure period runs $7/1/2025$ to $6/30/2027$ and its midpoint — the average loss date — is $7/1/2026$.

requirements.statement: On-level loss ratio = (losses × loss on-level factor × loss trend factor) / (earned premium × rate on-level factor).

places.quote: **Premium** — historical earned premium, brought to [[On Level Premium|current rate level]], developed to ultimate where it is still changing, and [[Premium Trend|trended]].

The numerator's loss ratio must be **projected**: ultimate losses (developed), trended to the future policy period, over earned premium brought to **current rate level** ([[On-Leveling]]) and trended ([[Premium Trend]]).

requirements.statement: Square root rule for partial credibility: Z = sqrt(n / full credibility standard), capped at 1.0 when the claim count meets or exceeds the standard.

places.quote: $$Z = \sqrt{\frac{n}{n_{\text{full}}}} \qquad \text{(limited fluctuation)}$$
$$Z = \min\!\left(1,\, \sqrt{\frac{n}{n_{\text{full}}}}\right)$$
$$Z = \min\left(\sqrt{\frac{n}{n_F}},\; 1\right)$$

requirements.statement: Compute a class's loss ratio relativity as its loss ratio divided by the overall (all-class) loss ratio, and multiply by the class's current relativity to get the indicated relativity.

places.quote: Under the [[Loss Ratio Method|loss ratio method]], a class's indicated relativity is its current relativity times its loss ratio divided by the base class's loss ratio, with premiums at current rates.

requirements.statement: Credibility-weight the indicated relativity with the current relativity, using the current relativity (no change) as the complement of credibility: Z × indicated + (1 − Z) × current.

places.quote: $$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$
$$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$
$Z$ multiplies the observed experience; $1 - Z$ goes to the [[Complement of Credibility]]

requirements.statement: Rebase credibility-weighted relativities to the base class by dividing each by the base class's relativity, then compare to the current relativity to get the change in each class's relativity.

places.quote: $$\text{Relativity}_i = \frac{\text{Pure Premium}_i}{\text{Pure Premium}_{\text{base}}}$$

requirements.statement: To make class rate changes revenue-neutral, compute the off-balance as the premium-weighted average change from rebasing and apply an offset factor of 1/(1 + average change) to every class's relativity change.

places.quote: The base rate must be adjusted so that the combined effect equals the intended [[Overall Rate Level Indication|overall indication]] — see [[Rate Change]].
OBF, the off-balance factor, is the average relativity before the change divided by the average relativity after it.

requirements.statement: Multivariate classification methods consider all rating variables simultaneously and so account for exposure and response correlations among variables, unlike one-way analysis.

places.quote: modern practice uses a [[Generalized Linear Model|GLM]], which estimates all variables simultaneously and reports each net of the others.
because it estimates every rating variable *simultaneously* and so reports each one net of the others — solving the correlation problem that makes univariate relativities double-count.

requirements.statement: Multivariate methods isolate the signal from the noise in each variable, provide diagnostic statistics for evaluating the model and variables, and allow investigation of interactions between rating variables.

places.quote: Model fit is assessed via [[Deviance]], [[AIC]], [[BIC]], and [[Residual Plot]]s

requirements.statement: The limited average severity (LAS) at a limit is the expected claim size with each loss capped at that limit; the increased limits factor is the ratio of LAS at the higher limit to LAS at the basic limit.

places.quote: $$\text{ILF}(L) = \frac{E[X \wedge L]}{E[X \wedge B]}$$

Exam 5 (Werner & Modlin) writes the limit as $H$ and calls $E[X \wedge H]$ the **limited average severity** $\text{LAS}(H)$. Under its simplifying assumptions, the increased limit factor for limit $H$ over basic limit $B$ is $\text{ILF}(H) = \text{LAS}(H)/\text{LAS}(B)$ (see [[Increased Limits]])

requirements.statement: With policy-limit-censored data, estimate LAS at the basic limit using all claims from all policy limits, with losses capped at the basic limit divided by total claim count.

resolution.quote: The limited average severity at the basic limit uses the claims from all policies, whatever their limits, each capped at the basic limit, and divides the total by the total number of claims.
resolution.note: LAS at the basic limit from censored data; W&M Ch.11 pp.194-195 (PDF 206-207)

requirements.statement: To extend LAS to a higher limit, add to LAS at the lower limit the average layer severity per claim (losses in the layer, with claims exceeding the layer capped at layer width, divided by claims exceeding the lower limit), using only policies whose limits reach the top of the layer, multiplied by the probability of exceeding the lower limit (the layer's claims per all claims in the data).

resolution.quote: The average severity of a layer is its losses divided by the number of claims reaching the layer (those exceeding its bottom), using only the policies whose limits reach the top of the layer. Before it is added to the limited average severity below it, it is multiplied by the probability that a claim exceeds the bottom of the layer, estimated from the same policies.
resolution.note: Extending LAS by a layer from censored data; W&M Ch.11 pp.195-197 (PDF 207-209)

requirements.statement: Severity trend has a leveraged effect on excess layers: excess layer losses trend faster than ground-up losses, which trend faster than basic-limit losses, so the ILF increases over time with trend.

places.quote: ILFs are **leveraged by inflation**. As losses grow, more of them pierce the basic limit and the excess layers grow faster than the ground-up trend — so ILF tables must be reviewed, not left in place, through inflationary periods.
Limits **leverage** severity trend: for a positive trend, basic-limits losses trend more slowly than total-limits losses and the excess layer faster

requirements.statement: The complement of credibility for an excess layer via the lower limits analysis is experience losses capped at a lower limit (using all policy limits) times the industry ILF difference between the layer's top and bottom limits divided by the industry ILF at the capping limit.
requirements.concept: Complement of Credibility for Excess Layers

resolution.quote: The same calculation with losses capped at a limit below the attachment point, often the basic limit: the losses capped at the lower limit are multiplied by the ILF at the top of the layer minus the ILF at the attachment point, divided by the ILF at the lower limit.
resolution.note: Lower limits analysis formula; W&M Ch.12 p.233 (PDF 245)

requirements.statement: Increased limits analysis (capping at the attachment point) requires data not truncated below the attachment point, so only policies with limits at or above it are used; lower limits analysis uses all policy limits and is more stable but less logically related to the excess layer.
requirements.concept: Complement of Credibility for Excess Layers

resolution.quote: It needs ground-up losses that have not been capped anywhere below the attachment point, so a policy whose limit is below the attachment point cannot supply them.…Losses capped at the basic limit can be taken from policies at every limit at or above it, and insurers usually code them for statistical reporting. Capping lower may make the estimate more stable, but differences in size-of-loss distributions are exacerbated, so it is likely more biased, and it is related to the lower-limit losses rather than to the losses in the layer.
resolution.note: Increased limits vs lower limits analysis: data needs, stability, bias, relation to the layer; W&M Ch.12 pp.232-234 (PDF 244-246)

requirements.statement: Estimate the average premium under a multiplicative rating plan by computing the exposure-weighted average of each rating variable's factor (and of each discount factor, i.e. 1 minus the discount) and multiplying these averages by the base premium.
Premium = base rate × product of rating factors × product of (1 − discount) factors, plus any additive (fixed) expense fee applied after the factors and discounts.

places.quote: $$\text{Rate}_i = \text{Base Rate} \times \prod_k R_{i,k}$$
$$\text{Premium} = \left[\text{Base Rate} \times \prod_i R_i + \sum_j A_j\right] \times (1 - D) + \text{Fees}$$

requirements.statement: The change in average premium equals proposed average premium divided by current average premium, minus 1.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Indicated Rate}}{\text{Current Rate}} - 1$$

requirements.statement: Using separate exposure-weighted average factors for each variable assumes the variables are independent and ignores correlation/interaction between them; re-rating each individual exposure (extension of exposures) and comparing total premium is more accurate.

places.quote: A **univariate** (one-way) pure premium or loss ratio analysis attributes to a variable the effect of everything correlated with it.
because each policy is re-rated, changes that differed by class, territory or fee are reflected exactly, and so is the mix of business in the historical period.

requirements.statement: Calculating premium change from the current exposure distribution ignores that the insured mix may shift after a rate change, so the future distribution may differ from the current one.

places.quote: One further check belongs here: the off-balance is computed on the **current** in-force distribution, which assumes the rate change will not alter the portfolio.

A rate change also changes the **mix**: price-sensitive risks shop, so a large increase can worsen the remaining experience through adverse selection — an effect the indication itself does not capture.

requirements.statement: Inadequate rates can be addressed with non-pricing actions that improve profitability, such as reducing expenses, tightening underwriting guidelines, targeting better-performing risks, requiring loss-control practices, restricting coverage (higher deductibles), or increasing investment income.

places.quote: Werner's central point is that rate adequacy is not only achieved through rate. Where a full increase is unavailable, the same gap can be closed by:
**Reduce expenses** — underwriting or LAE: a smaller marketing budget, lower staffing, lower acquisition cost.

requirements.statement: Develop losses to ultimate by multiplying each loss type's reported loss and ALAE by its own loss development factor, treating indemnity and medical separately because their development and trend differ.

places.quote: Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}

requirements.statement: Determine the trend period as the time from the average accident date of the experience period to the average accident date of the future period in which the rates will be effective.

places.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.

requirements.statement: Trended losses equal losses times (1 + annual trend) raised to the trend period, using the trend rate specific to each loss type.

places.quote: $$\text{Trend Factor} = (1 + t)^{n}$$
The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: Pure premium is trended ultimate loss and ALAE (summed across loss types) divided by exposures.

places.quote: $$\text{Pure Premium} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Exposures}} = \text{Frequency} \times \text{Severity}$$
$$\text{Pure Premium} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Exposures}}$$

requirements.statement: The indicated territorial relativity is the territory's pure premium divided by the base territory's pure premium (rebasing so the base territory equals 1.000).

places.quote: $$\text{Territory Relativity}_i = \frac{\text{Pure Premium}_i}{\text{Pure Premium}_{\text{base}}}$$
$$\text{Relativity}_i = \frac{\text{Pure Premium}_i}{\text{Pure Premium}_{\text{base}}}$$

requirements.statement: For no overall premium change when relativities change, compute an off-balance factor as the exposure-weighted average current relativity divided by the exposure-weighted average indicated relativity, and apply it (to the base rate) to the indicated relativities.

places.quote: $$\text{OBF} = \frac{\sum_i w_i\, r_i^{\text{old}}}{\sum_i w_i\, r_i^{\text{new}}}$$
OBF, the off-balance factor, is the average relativity before the change divided by the average relativity after it.

requirements.statement: Percent rate change by territory equals (indicated relativity / current relativity) times the off-balance factor minus 1, when the base territory is unchanged.

places.quote: A class's rate change is $(1 + \Delta)\,\text{OBF}\,r_i^{\text{new}}/r_i^{\text{old}} - 1$.

requirements.statement: An age-to-age (link ratio) factor is the ratio of cumulative claims at one maturity to cumulative claims at the previous maturity for the same accident year.

places.quote: **Development Factor** (link ratio or age-to-age factor) is the ratio used to project cumulative losses from one maturity age to the next
**Age-to-Age Factor** (link ratio) is the ratio of a cohort's cumulative amount at one maturity to its amount at the previous maturity — the observed development between two ages.

requirements.statement: Select age-to-age factors from the triangle by averaging observed factors (simple, volume-weighted, latest-n-year, or latest diagonal), choosing the average based on the stability and trend of the factors.

places.quote: **Latest-$k$-year average**: uses only the most recent $k$ accident years — reduces the influence of older, potentially unrepresentative data
A steady column supports a volume-weighted all-year selection; a column trending over time is a signal, not noise, and calls for the latest years or an investigation.

requirements.statement: A volume-weighted average age-to-age factor equals the sum of claims at the later maturity divided by the sum of claims at the earlier maturity for the same accident years.

places.quote: **Volume-weighted average**: $\Sigma(\text{col }n{+}1) / \Sigma(\text{col }n)$ — gives more credibility to larger accident years; the standard default selection
$$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{vol-wtd}} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$

requirements.statement: Under the paid claim development technique, ultimate claims equal current cumulative paid claims times the cumulative development factor, which is the product of selected age-to-age factors from the current maturity to ultimate (with a tail factor of 1.0 if no development after the last age).

places.quote: $$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \left(\prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1}\right) \times \text{Tail}$$
$$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: Industry development factors can be used in place of company factors for the development technique when company factors are volatile or sparse, by selecting industry age-to-age factors and applying them to the company's current claims.
requirements.concept: Use of Industry Benchmark Development Factors

places.quote: a small or newly segmented book whose triangle is too volatile to be [[Credibility|credible]]
**Industry benchmarks** — published patterns (ISO, NCCI, Schedule P aggregates) for the same line, adjusted for differences in limits, mix and case reserving.

requirements.statement: Development technique estimates at early maturities are highly leveraged and volatile because small changes in early factors, often driven by large losses, are multiplied by a large cumulative development factor; stable, credible industry patterns may then be preferred, while a large company's own experience reflects its own mix and practices.

places.quote: The chain ladder is at its best on **mature cohorts with stable patterns and ample volume** — and at its worst at immature ages in [[Long Tail Lines|long-tail lines]], where the CDF is large and the diagonal is thin.
The CDF measures **leverage**. At a CDF of $4$, a dollar of distortion on the diagonal becomes four dollars of ultimate
Because the [[Cumulative Development Factor|CDF]] at early maturities is large, estimates are highly **leveraged**: a small proportional change in a factor moves ultimate by a large dollar amount.

requirements.statement: Calendar year aggregation groups claims by the year in which they are reported or paid, so a calendar year's amount combines activity from several accident years and is fixed once the year ends.
requirements.concept: Calendar Year Aggregation of Claim Data

places.quote: **Calendar Year** (CY) is a data aggregation method that groups every transaction by the calendar year in which it is *booked* — premium as it is earned, losses as they are paid or as case reserves change — without regard to the policy's effective date or the claim's accident date.

requirements.statement: Calendar year reported claims are obtained from a cumulative triangle by summing the latest diagonal's incremental amounts, i.e., each cell minus the prior-age cell of the same accident year (the first-age value is taken in full).
requirements.concept: Calendar Year Aggregation of Claim Data

places.quote: $$\text{CY Reported Losses} = \text{Paid} + \Delta\text{Case Reserves}$$
Its diagonal *is* the data — a calendar year is one diagonal of every triangle

requirements.statement: Calendar year aggregation is generally inappropriate for estimating unpaid claims because calendar year totals do not develop, so there is no basis for projecting future development or IBNR, and few techniques use it.
requirements.concept: Calendar Year Aggregation of Claim Data

places.quote: A calendar year **never develops** — it is closed and fixed the moment the books close. Friedland counts that as an advantage and also as a disadvantage: calendar-year data cannot address development.
**[[Calendar Year]]** is never a reserving cohort.

requirements.statement: Accident year aggregation is appropriate for estimating unpaid claims because claims from an accident year continue to develop after year end, it matches losses to the corresponding earned premium, it permits isolating years with large claims, and it is the industry standard supported by many techniques and benchmarks.
requirements.concept: Accident Year Aggregation of Claim Data

places.quote: Friedland calls it the accepted norm for P&C insurers in the U.S. and Canada, and by far the most common grouping for the analysis of unpaid claims.

**[[Accident Year]]** is the default reserving basis for direct business: claims grouped by occurrence date produce a [[Development Triangle]] whose rows share an exposure period and whose columns share a maturity.

requirements.statement: Lines of business should be combined for unpaid claim estimation only if the data are homogeneous, with similar development patterns, growth rates and business mix; differing patterns would distort the combined development factors.
requirements.concept: Homogeneity and Credibility of Claims Data

places.quote: If the segments have different emergence patterns, the blended development factors drift as the weights drift — and the triangle gives no signal that this is what is happening.
Combining them would average a multi-year liability pattern with an essentially immediate property pattern, producing development factors that fit neither.
Segmentation *across* lines is rarely optional: combining auto physical damage with general liability is indefensible on either criterion.

requirements.statement: Combining lines can be motivated by a lack of credibility in a line's own data, so the tradeoff between homogeneity and credibility must be weighed; if each line has enough credible data, separate analysis is preferred.
requirements.concept: Homogeneity and Credibility of Claims Data

places.quote: Split into groups that balance [[Homogeneity]] against [[Credibility]] — by [[Line of Business|line]], coverage, [[Long Tail Lines|tail length]], and by claim type where settlement patterns genuinely differ.
Where a level is too thin, combine similar levels or find more data.

requirements.statement: An age-to-age (link ratio) development factor is the cumulative claims at a later age divided by cumulative claims at the earlier age for the same accident year, and comparing these across lines shows differences in development patterns.

places.quote: $$f_{k \to k+1} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k}}$$
**Age-to-Age Factor** (link ratio) is the ratio of a cohort's cumulative amount at one maturity to its amount at the previous maturity — the observed development between two ages.

requirements.statement: Case outstanding reserve equals reported (incurred) claims minus paid claims.

places.quote: AY 2023 at $24$ months: paid to date $\$800{,}000$, case outstanding $\$500{,}000$, so reported is $\$1{,}300{,}000$.

requirements.statement: IBNR equals ultimate claims minus reported claims, and total unpaid claims equal ultimate claims minus paid claims (equivalently case outstanding plus IBNR).

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = U - \text{Reported}$$
$$\text{Unpaid} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Paid to date}$$
$$\text{IBNR} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Reported}$$

requirements.statement: Under the expected claims technique, ultimate claims equal earned premium times the expected claim ratio.

places.quote: $$U = \text{ELR} \times \text{Earned Premium}$$

requirements.statement: An age-to-ultimate factor for a maturity is the ultimate claims divided by cumulative claims at that age, and successive age-to-age factors are obtained as the ratio of consecutive age-to-ultimate factors.

places.quote: $$\text{Ultimate} = C_n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: Cumulative development factors are computed by multiplying age-to-age factors from a given age through the final age (times any tail factor); replacing one age-to-age factor changes the CDFs at all earlier ages.

places.quote: CDFs are built **backwards from the tail**: start with the tail factor, multiply in each successive age-to-age factor moving toward younger ages.
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: Paid development technique ultimate claims equal cumulative paid claims times the paid age-to-ultimate factor.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: Paid Bornhuetter-Ferguson ultimate equals paid claims plus expected ultimate claims (premium times expected claim ratio) times (1 − 1/paid CDF).

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$
$$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$

requirements.statement: In the case outstanding development technique, current case outstanding is estimated as reported claims minus paid claims.

places.quote: $$\text{Reported Losses} = \text{Paid Losses} + \text{Case Reserves}$$

requirements.statement: Project future case outstanding at each later age by multiplying the prior age's case outstanding by the selected ratio of case outstanding to previous case outstanding.

places.quote: Friedland's fuller version works period by period, using two ratios estimated from history: **paid in the next period ÷ case outstanding at the start**, and **case outstanding at the end ÷ case outstanding at the start**.

requirements.statement: Project future incremental paid claims in each period by multiplying the prior age's case outstanding by the selected ratio of incremental paid claims to previous case outstanding.

places.quote: Friedland's fuller version works period by period, using two ratios estimated from history: **paid in the next period ÷ case outstanding at the start**, and **case outstanding at the end ÷ case outstanding at the start**.

requirements.statement: Unpaid claims under the case outstanding development technique equal the sum of projected future incremental paid claims only; amounts already paid at the evaluation date are excluded.

places.quote: $f_{\text{case}}$ converts the current case balance into *all* remaining payments — including payments on claims not yet reported.
$$\text{Unpaid} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Paid to date}$$

requirements.statement: The case outstanding development technique projects development only on reported claims, so it is appropriate only when most or all claims are reported in the first period; it is not appropriate when significant pure IBNR (unreported claims) exists.

resolution.quote: That holds only where most claims are reported within the accident period
resolution.note: Tagged page: the technique suits books where most claims are reported early (claims-made, report year).

requirements.statement: A reported claim count development factor to ultimate well above 1.0 (highly leveraged) indicates significant unreported claims (pure IBNR) remaining.

places.quote: A CDF of $2.27$ means more than half the ultimate estimate is unreported.

requirements.statement: Both the Bornhuetter-Ferguson and Cape Cod methods estimate ultimate claims as reported (or paid) claims to date plus expected ultimate claims times the percent unreported (unpaid), i.e. IBNR = ELR x exposure/premium x (1 - 1/CDF).

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}$$
$$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$

requirements.statement: Both BF and Cape Cod are credibility-weighted blends of the development (chain ladder) technique and the expected claims technique, with weights based on percent reported/paid, and both take the unreported/unpaid portion from the expected claims method.

places.quote: BF is a **credibility weighting** in disguise: it equals $Z \, U_{\text{CL}} + (1-Z)\,U_0$ with $Z = 1/\text{CDF}$.

Cape Cod converges to the [[Chain Ladder Method|chain ladder]] as cohorts mature and to the [[Expected Loss Method|expected claims]] technique for very immature ones — the same limiting behaviour as BF.

It is one end of the spectrum the reserving methods occupy: **expected claims** puts $100\%$ weight on the a priori, the [[Chain Ladder Method|chain ladder]] puts $100\%$ on actual emergence, and the [[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method|BF]] method blends them by the percentage reported.

requirements.statement: In the Cape Cod method the ELR is calculated from the historical data as total reported claims divided by total used-up on-level premium (on-level premium times percent reported), whereas in the BF method the ELR is an a priori estimate selected independently (e.g. from pricing or industry data).

places.quote: Where no reliable external ELR exists, the [[Cape Cod Method|Cape Cod]] technique derives one from the data instead.
The ELR is estimated as total reported losses over total *used-up* (on-level, developed) premium across all years.

requirements.statement: Because the Cape Cod ELR is computed from the experience directly, it responds automatically to a changing claims environment (if recent years are included), while the BF a priori ELR does not respond unless it is manually adjusted.

places.quote: A stale ELR that ignores [[Rate Level Change|rate changes]] and [[Loss Trend|trend]] produces a systematically biased reserve — and the bias persists year after year without ever showing up as instability.
The cost is that the estimate is no longer independent of the data: a systematically distorted triangle now corrupts the a priori as well as the development.

requirements.statement: Historical claims used to derive the ELR must be adjusted to be comparable to the claims expected in the projected year, e.g. trend for frequency/severity, adjust for benefit level or tort changes, remove or cap shock/large losses, and adjust for changes in case reserve adequacy or payment patterns.

places.quote: Premium **must be on level** and losses must be trended to a common cost level before the ELR is computed, or the derived ratio blends years written at different rate levels and different cost levels into one number.
Adequacy also affects the a priori methods indirectly: the [[Cape Cod Method|Cape Cod]] ELR is computed from reported losses, so a strengthening inflates it and the distortion enters twice.
Premium must be [[On-Leveling|on level]], claims must be [[Loss Trend|trended]] and adjusted for changes such as tort reform, and the development factors must be sound.

requirements.statement: Historical earned premium must be adjusted to the premium level of the projected year by on-leveling for past rate changes and trending for premium (exposure/inflation) changes.

places.quote: Historical premium was charged at the rates of its time, and [[On-Leveling|on-leveling]] restates it at current rates.

On-levelling adjusts for **rate changes only**. Drift in average premium from changing amounts of insurance, limits, deductibles or mix is a separate adjustment — see [[Premium Trend]] — and applying one in place of the other either double-counts or misses the effect entirely.
$$\text{Premium Trend Factor} = (1 + t_P)^{n}$$

requirements.statement: When a one-time event (e.g. court decision) distorts one historical year, BF with an unadjusted ELR is appropriate if it is an anomaly; if it persists, BF with a judgmentally adjusted ELR or Cape Cod (with its responsive ELR) is appropriate, since unadjusted Cape Cod would understate the ELR by averaging in older years.

places.quote: BF does not respond to bad news. If emergence runs far ahead of the a priori, BF holds most of its estimate anchored — which is exactly right when the emergence is noise and exactly wrong when it is signal.
When the data is the thing that is wrong, an external a priori is worth more than a self-consistent one.
With $D = 1$, every year gets the same weights and the method is the [[Cape Cod Method|Cape Cod method]], whose single ratio differs between years only by trend.

requirements.statement: Frequency-severity techniques are especially useful for long-tailed lines because they avoid the highly leveraged, unreliable development factors that development methods produce for immature years.

places.quote: **Counts and trended severity.** Develop counts, but estimate severity by **trending** a mature year's severity forward rather than developing an immature one — useful where severity development is unstable but severity trend is well understood.
Because the [[Cumulative Development Factor|CDF]] at early maturities is large, estimates are highly **leveraged**: a small proportional change in a factor moves ultimate by a large dollar amount.
Count factors are **smaller** than dollar factors at the same age, because a claim is counted as soon as it is reported while its dollars accrue for years afterward.

requirements.statement: Frequency-severity methods require a clear, consistent definition of claim counts; significant reopened claims make the count definition ambiguous and distort frequency and severity, making the methods unsuitable unless reopenings are handled consistently.

places.quote: The method needs **consistent count definitions** across the whole triangle, and it is sensitive to [[Large Loss|large losses]] in the severity series, so severities are usually capped and the excess layer added back separately.
**Claim count definitions** are the most common casualty: counting per claimant instead of per claim, beginning or ceasing to count claims closed without payment, or treating a reopened claim as new.
Counts must be **defined consistently**: per claim or per claimant, counting claims closed without payment or not, treating reopened claims as new or as continuing.

requirements.statement: Frequency-severity methods assume a stable mix of claim types, so a recent increase in high-severity claims violates the assumption unless severities are adjusted.

places.quote: The method needs **consistent count definitions** across the whole triangle, and it is sensitive to [[Large Loss|large losses]] in the severity series, so severities are usually capped and the excess layer added back separately.

requirements.statement: To handle a shift in severity, adjust the severity selections for affected years (e.g., restate past severities with a new trend, select incremental severities judgmentally for recent years in the disposal rate technique, or use Bornhuetter-Ferguson adjustments) while keeping the frequency selection.
