places.quote: **Counts and trended severity.** Develop counts, but estimate severity by **trending** a mature year's severity forward rather than developing an immature one — useful where severity development is unstable but severity trend is well understood.

resolution.quote: select severity from developed severities trended to the latest year's cost level
resolution.note: Re-quoted after the page was edited today: severity selected by trending rather than developing.

requirements.statement: Frequency-severity techniques can be based on either paid or reported data, and paid-data methods (such as the disposal rate method using closed counts and incremental paid severities) are not affected by changes in case reserving philosophy, whereas methods using reported data are distorted by such changes.

places.quote: **Paid data is immune**, so a divergence between paid and reported chain ladder estimates is the corroborating evidence.

requirements.statement: Frequency-severity techniques let frequency and severity be selected and trended separately, helping diagnose changes over time and allowing selections based on long-term trends.

places.quote: Counts are more **credible** and less inflation-sensitive; severity is where the trend lives. Projecting each with the tool it suits — development for counts, trend for severity — is often better than developing either alone.

Frequency is also **less inflation-sensitive**. Severity tracks medical, wage and repair-cost inflation; frequency responds to behaviour, exposure quality, weather and coverage terms. This is why the two are trended separately (see [[Loss Trend]]).

requirements.statement: Written premium for a calendar year is the premium for policies and transactions (new, cancellations, endorsements) whose effective dates fall in that year, regardless of when it is earned.

places.quote: Written premium is recorded when the policy takes effect, not when it is collected.
Additional premium for an endorsement is recorded on the endorsement's effective date and earned in the same way.

requirements.statement: Earned premium for a period is the portion of written premium corresponding to the part of the policy term that has expired within that period (written premium minus unearned premium).

places.quote: **Earned Premium** is the portion of premium corresponding to coverage the insurer has actually provided — the premium it has earned the right to keep, recognized pro rata as the policy term elapses.

requirements.statement: In-force premium at a date is the full-term annualized premium of all policies in effect on that date, using the characteristics in force then and excluding canceled or expired policies.

places.quote: [[In-Force|In-force]] premium is the annual premium of policies in force on a given date.
In-force premium is the **full-term** premium of each policy in effect at the date — the policy's own term, not an annualized one

requirements.statement: Full-term written premium applies to the policy's whole term (6 or 12 months from effective to expiration dates), so premium for a partial period equals full-term premium times the fraction of the term in that period.

places.quote: $$\text{EP for one policy} = \text{Full premium} \times \frac{\text{days elapsed}}{\text{policy term}}$$
$$\text{UEP for one policy} = \text{Full premium} \times \frac{\text{days remaining}}{\text{policy term}}$$

requirements.statement: A mid-term cancellation (pro rata) is recorded as negative written premium for the unexpired portion, and only the premium for the expired portion is earned.

places.quote: Written premium may still change after issuance — endorsements, cancellations and [[Premium Audit|audits]] all book additional or return premium into a later period
**Pro rata** cancellation returns the full unearned premium

requirements.statement: A mid-term change such as a territory relocation is treated as canceling the remaining term at the old premium and rewriting it at the new full-term premium; written and earned premium are split by the time spent under each characteristic.

places.quote: After a mid-term change, in-force premium is the full-term premium applicable on the date.
Additional premium for an endorsement is recorded on the endorsement's effective date and earned in the same way.

requirements.statement: Earned exposure is the exposure units (e.g., car-years, where a 12-month policy is 1.0 car-year) for the portion of the policy term expired in the period, allocated to the territory in effect during that time.

places.quote: A $12$-month policy contributes **one** earned car-year in total, spread pro rata over its term: written the day it is issued, earned $1/12$ per month, in force from effective date to expiry.

requirements.statement: In the Berquist-Sherman paid claim adjustment, adjust cumulative closed claim counts by multiplying each accident year's estimated ultimate claim count by the selected disposal rate for each age (disposal rate = closed claim count divided by ultimate claim count).

places.quote: Compute **disposal rates** — closed claims ÷ ultimate (or reported) claims — at each accident year and maturity.
$$\text{Disposal Rate}_n = \frac{\text{Closed claims at age } n}{\text{Ultimate claim counts}}$$

requirements.statement: The Berquist-Sherman paid adjustment models the relationship between cumulative paid claims Y and cumulative closed claim counts X with an exponential curve Y = a·e^(bX), whose parameters a and b are fit (e.g., by a two-point fit) between successive ages.

Restate historical cumulative paid claims by plugging the adjusted closed claim count into the fitted exponential curve, using the parameters of the next age's fit for interpolation (e.g., age 12 uses the 12-24 fit) and the age's own parameters for the 36 (last-fitted) age by extrapolation.

places.quote: For each historical cell, interpolate the paid losses that *would* have been paid had that year closed claims at the current rate — reading along the row's paid-versus-disposal-rate relationship.
restate each historical year's paid losses to what they would have been at the *current* disposal pattern, by interpolating along each year's paid-versus-disposal-rate relationship

requirements.statement: The latest calendar-year diagonal of the paid claim triangle is not adjusted in the Berquist-Sherman method; the adjusted values on that diagonal equal the unadjusted values.

places.quote: Berquist-Sherman does not fix the diagonal itself. Strengthened reserves are on the books and belong in the estimate; what the restatement fixes is the *factors*, which would otherwise develop the strengthening a second time.

requirements.statement: A volume-weighted all-year age-to-age factor is the sum of the later-age values divided by the sum of the earlier-age values over all accident years that have both; age-to-ultimate factors are cumulative products of the age-to-age factors (with a tail factor).

places.quote: $$f_{k \to k+1} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k}}$$
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \left(\prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1}\right) \times \text{Tail}$$
$$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{vol-wtd}} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$

requirements.statement: Estimate ultimate claims for an accident year by multiplying its latest diagonal value (here the unadjusted paid claims) by the age-to-ultimate factor derived from the adjusted paid triangle.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate} = C_n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: The paid-to-reported (case-incurred) claims ratio is cumulative paid claims divided by cumulative reported claims at each maturity; it is a diagnostic of case reserve adequacy.
Average case outstanding equals (cumulative reported claims minus cumulative paid claims) divided by open claim counts at the same maturity.

places.quote: $$\bar O_{w,d} = \frac{L^{\text{rep}}_{w,d} - L^{\text{paid}}_{w,d}}{N^{\text{open}}_{w,d}}$$
$$\text{Avg Case Outstanding} = \frac{\text{Case Reserves}}{\text{Open Claim Counts}}$$

requirements.statement: A paid-to-reported ratio that declines down a column (for later accident years at the same age) and a rising average case outstanding on the latest diagonal both indicate that case reserve adequacy has strengthened (increased).

places.quote: **[[Case Adequacy|Case strengthening]]:** average case outstanding rises faster than trend on the latest diagonals, and paid-to-reported falls.
A jump concentrated on one **diagonal**, appearing at every maturity at once, is a change in reserving practice, not in claim cost.

a change in the paid-to-reported ratio signals a change in settlement patterns or in case adequacy — a rising ratio is consistent with faster settlement or weaker case reserves, a falling one with slower settlement or stronger case reserves

requirements.statement: A strengthening of case reserve adequacy distorts reported (case incurred) development, overstating loss development factors and ultimate claims if unadjusted.

places.quote: Applying historical factors — built under weaker reserving — to a strengthened diagonal **over-states** ultimate, because the strengthening is developed a second time.
The consequence is that the reported chain ladder will apply historical factors, earned on weaker reserves, to a stronger diagonal and overstate ultimates.

The reserving consequence is that reported development factors are now biased high, and applying them unadjusted would develop the strengthening a second time — the [[Berquist-Sherman Method|Berquist-Sherman]] situation.

requirements.statement: The Berquist-Sherman case outstanding adjustment restates historical diagonals' case outstanding to the current level of case reserve adequacy, so that development factors are not distorted before applying the reported development method.

places.quote: **Berquist-Sherman Method** restates a historical [[Development Triangle|triangle]] so that every year reflects **current** claims practice, removing the distortion caused by a change in [[Case Adequacy|case reserve adequacy]] or in [[Settlement Rate|claim settlement rates]].

The remedy is the [[Berquist-Sherman Method|Berquist-Sherman]] case adjustment: restate historical average case outstanding to the current adequacy level using a selected severity trend, rebuild the reported triangle, and select factors from the restated history.

requirements.statement: The expected claims technique (and paid development, when settlement rates are stable) is not affected by changes in case reserve adequacy, so it can be used to estimate ultimate claims when case reserve adequacy has changed.

places.quote: **Paid data is immune**, so a divergence between paid and reported chain ladder estimates is the corroborating evidence.

Paid data is **objective**. It carries no adjuster judgment, so a paid triangle is immune to changes in [[Case Adequacy|case reserve adequacy]] — the single most common distortion in reported triangles.

**Expected Loss Method** (expected claims technique) estimates ultimate losses entirely from an a priori expectation — usually an expected loss ratio applied to earned premium — giving **no weight** to what has actually been reported.

requirements.statement: When a calendar-year change in the claims process distorts the latest diagonal, do not relate unpaid to paid-to-date; use a method such as Bornhuetter-Ferguson or incremental payments that adjusts expected future amounts for the change across all accident years.

places.quote: The chain ladder instead scales the whole diagonal, so a distorted diagonal is multiplied by the full CDF.

requirements.statement: Bornhuetter-Ferguson unpaid = (1 - 1/CDF) × expected ultimate, where CDF is the age-to-ultimate development factor.

places.quote: \text{IBNR} = \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}

requirements.statement: Age-to-ultimate factors are obtained by multiplying age-to-age factors selected from steady-state (pre-change) years, from the tail back to each age.

places.quote: \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}
chaining them together produces the [[Cumulative Development Factor]] to ultimate

**The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.

requirements.statement: Expected ALAE or ULAE must be restated to reflect a known expense change (e.g. a 50% decline in ALAE), and historical ratios that predate the change should not be averaged with post-change ratios.

places.quote: Selecting the three-year average of $6.6\%$ would understate the cost of running off the remaining claims.

requirements.statement: The classical technique for unpaid ULAE assumes ULAE is 50% incurred when a claim is opened/reported and 50% when it is closed, and applies the ratio of paid ULAE to paid claims to 50% of case outstanding plus 100% of IBNR.

places.quote: If ULAE is assumed to be spent half at reporting and half at settlement, only $50\%$ remains on reported-but-unpaid claims while $100\%$ remains on [[IBNR]]

requirements.statement: Unpaid ULAE (classical) = ULAE-to-paid-claims ratio × [50% × case outstanding + IBNR].

places.quote: \text{ULAE Reserve} = R \times \left(0.5 \times \text{Case} + 1.0 \times \text{IBNR}\right)

requirements.statement: If ULAE shifts to being incurred later in a claim's life (e.g. in-house legal costs after reporting), the 50/50 assumption fails and the classical technique understates unpaid ULAE because more weight belongs on case outstanding.

places.quote: If ULAE is assumed to be spent half at reporting and half at settlement, only $50\%$ remains on reported-but-unpaid claims while $100\%$ remains on [[IBNR]] — the formula above. Assuming ULAE is spent purely with payments instead gives $R \times (\text{Case} + \text{IBNR})$.

requirements.statement: The Kittel method adjusts the ULAE ratio by using reported (incurred) losses alongside paid, but keeps the same reported/settled split assumption, so it does not fix a change in the timing of ULAE.
requirements.concept: Kittel Refinement of Classical ULAE Technique

places.quote: Kittel divides by the **average of paid and incurred** loss instead:

requirements.statement: In the paid ALAE-to-paid claims development technique, compute the ratio of cumulative paid ALAE to cumulative paid claims for each accident year at each age, then project each accident year's ratio to its ultimate ratio (additively via differences between ages, or multiplicatively via ratio link factors).
requirements.concept: Ratio Development of ALAE to Claims

requirements.statement: Develop paid claims to ultimate by selecting age-to-age factors from the triangle (e.g., averages of observed link ratios) and multiplying them into cumulative factors applied to the latest diagonal.

places.quote: **The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: Ultimate ALAE equals ultimate claims times the ultimate ALAE-to-claims ratio, and unpaid ALAE equals ultimate ALAE minus paid ALAE to date, summed across accident years for the total.

places.quote: or develop a **ratio of ALAE to loss** and apply it to projected losses.
$$\text{Unpaid} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Paid to date}$$

requirements.statement: When there is no development beyond the last observed age, the tail factor is 1.00 and the latest ratio/claims are treated as ultimate for the oldest accident year.

places.quote: A tail of exactly $1.000$ is itself an assumption — that development is complete — and it is the wrong one for any casualty line.

requirements.statement: Advantage of the paid ALAE-to-paid claims method: it uses the inherent relationship between ALAE and claims, and its ratio development is less leveraged/more stable than developing ALAE alone, with ratios able to be judgmentally selected.
requirements.concept: Ratio Development of ALAE to Claims

requirements.statement: Disadvantage of the paid ALAE-to-paid claims method under a change in business mix: the historical ALAE-to-claims ratio may no longer apply to the new mix, and errors in the ultimate claims estimate (e.g., from changed settlement patterns) flow directly into ultimate ALAE.
requirements.concept: Ratio Development of ALAE to Claims

places.quote: In **reserving**, a mix shift breaks the [[Homogeneity|homogeneity]] assumption behind the [[Development Triangle|triangle]].
- **Each cohort develops in the same pattern.** Violated by a change in [[Mix of Business|mix]], limits or coverage.

requirements.statement: Age-to-age (link ratio) factors are computed as the ratio of cumulative reported claims at one maturity to those at the prior maturity for each accident year, and an all-year average is selected for each development interval.

places.quote: $$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{AY}} = \frac{C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$
$$f_{k \to k+1} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k}}$$

requirements.statement: Age-to-ultimate factors are obtained by cumulating the selected age-to-age factors from the latest age to ultimate, using a tail factor (1.00 if no development after the last age); the percent reported is the inverse of the age-to-ultimate factor.

places.quote: The reciprocal is the **percentage reported** (or paid): $p_n = 1/\text{CDF}_n$, and $1 - p_n$ is the percentage unreported.
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: IBNR (unreported claims) for an accident year equals the selected ultimate claims minus claims reported to date.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = U - \text{Reported}$$
$$\text{IBNR} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Reported}$$

requirements.statement: Expected emergence in the next calendar period equals the current IBNR times (percent reported at the end of the period minus percent reported at the start) divided by (1 minus percent reported at the start), i.e. the share of expected future unreported claims that emerges in the period.
requirements.concept: Expected Claim Emergence (Actual vs Expected Analysis)

places.quote: $$\text{Expected emergence} = U_{\text{prior}} \times \left(\frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n+1}} - \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n}}\right)$$

resolution.quote: \text{Expected emergence} = \frac{U_{\text{prior}} - \text{Reported}_{n}}{1 - 1/\text{CDF}_{n}}
resolution.note: Re-quoted after the page was edited today: expected emergence from IBNR and the change in % reported.

requirements.statement: Actual emergence in a calendar year is the change in reported claims over the year (latest diagonal minus prior diagonal) and is compared with expected emergence; actual below expected indicates favorable development.
requirements.concept: Expected Claim Emergence (Actual vs Expected Analysis)

places.quote: $$\text{A/E} = \frac{\text{Actual emergence}}{\text{Expected emergence}}$$

requirements.statement: The reported (or paid) development technique relies fully on historical data with no a priori complement, so lower-than-expected actual emergence flows through to a lower ultimate and reduced unpaid claims.

places.quote: This is the strong one: the method takes whatever sits on the diagonal at face value and scales it.
The chain ladder instead scales the whole diagonal, so a distorted diagonal is multiplied by the full CDF.

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson technique, with unreported percentage as weight, projects unpaid claims as expected ultimate times percent unreported, so unpaid is unaffected by actual emergence deviations.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}$$
It assumes losses reported to date say nothing about those still to come.

requirements.statement: The expected claims technique holds ultimate claims at the a priori expected value, so lower-than-expected actual emergence implies higher unpaid claims (deviations are assumed to reverse).

places.quote: The $\$50{,}000$ reported is used only to split the estimate between reported and IBNR — it plays no part in setting the ultimate.
**Expected.** The usual estimate is an expected loss ratio times earned premium.

requirements.statement: A large paid or reported claim at an early maturity inflates the paid or reported development (chain ladder) estimate because historical LDFs are applied to an abnormally high amount, while the Bornhuetter-Ferguson method adds only expected unreported or unpaid claims to actual losses and is therefore less distorted.

places.quote: The chain ladder instead scales the whole diagonal, so a distorted diagonal is multiplied by the full CDF.
A [[Large Loss|shock loss]] reported early is multiplied by the full CDF.

requirements.statement: An increase in case reserve adequacy inflates reported (and case outstanding-based) development estimates, but leaves paid methods unaffected, so paid methods are preferred.

places.quote: *Case strengthening*: reported development overstates, reported BF and Cape Cod overstate less; paid methods and expected claims are unaffected.
**Paid data is immune**, so a divergence between paid and reported chain ladder estimates is the corroborating evidence.

requirements.statement: A slowdown in settlement rates makes paid development methods understate ultimate claims (historical LDFs applied to lower paid amounts), while an increase in settlement rates makes them overstate; reported methods are unaffected, so reported methods are preferred.

places.quote: **Slower settlement** does the reverse and understates ultimate from paid data.
*Faster settlement*: paid development overstates; reported methods are largely unaffected.
Faster closing inflates the recent paid diagonal, so historical paid factors **over-develop** it. Slower closing does the reverse.

requirements.statement: When the expected loss ratio is increasing (deteriorating), the expected claims method understates ultimate claims and the BF method, which relies partly on the expected claims, also understates; the development method reflects the actual experience and is preferred.
requirements.concept: Expected Claims Method and Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method

places.quote: *Rising claim ratios*: development techniques still work; the [[Expected Loss Method|expected claims]] technique fails unless its ratio is updated; [[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method|BF]] and [[Cape Cod Method|Cape Cod]] understate, partially.

A stale ELR that ignores [[Rate Level Change|rate changes]] and [[Loss Trend|trend]] produces a systematically biased reserve — and the bias persists year after year without ever showing up as instability.

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson method is a credibility-weighted blend of the development method and the expected claims method, giving more stable estimates when data are distorted.

places.quote: BF is a **credibility weighting** in disguise: it equals $Z \, U_{\text{CL}} + (1-Z)\,U_0$ with $Z = 1/\text{CDF}$.

It is one end of the spectrum the reserving methods occupy: **expected claims** puts $100\%$ weight on the a priori, the [[Chain Ladder Method|chain ladder]] puts $100\%$ on actual emergence, and the [[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method|BF]] method blends them by the percentage reported.

requirements.statement: Diagnose the cause of differences among reserving method estimates by comparing which methods (paid vs reported, development vs BF vs expected claims) are higher or lower, propose a scenario consistent with the pattern, and select the method least distorted by that scenario.

places.quote: **Responses:** detect the change (interview plus [[Data Diagnostic Analysis|diagnostics]] — average case outstanding, closed-to-reported counts, paid-to-reported ratios); lean on methods the change does not touch;
The two answers rest on the same claims, so their difference is a diagnostic about case adequacy and settlement rates, not a menu to average.

The two diagnostics above separate the two kinds of change. A moving **disposal rate** is a [[Settlement Rate|settlement speed]] change and distorts **paid** development; a jump in **average case outstanding** is a [[Case Adequacy|case adequacy]] change and distorts **reported** development.

requirements.statement: The three criteria of a good exposure base are that it is proportional to expected loss, practical, and has historical precedence.

places.quote: **Proportional to expected loss.** All else equal, a policy with two exposures should have twice the expected loss of a similar policy with one.

requirements.statement: An exposure base is proportional to expected loss when a change in the amount of exposure units corresponds to a proportional change in expected losses, so a base with a causal relationship to loss meets this criterion.

places.quote: All else equal, a policy with two exposures should have twice the expected loss of a similar policy with one.

requirements.statement: An exposure base is practical if it is objectively defined, easy and inexpensive to obtain and verify, and not subject to manipulation (e.g., self-reported data).

places.quote: Objective, and relatively easy and inexpensive to obtain and verify — which also keeps policyholders and producers from manipulating it (declared annual mileage invites more dishonesty than car-years).
**Operational** — objective, inexpensive to obtain and verify, not manipulable by the insured.

**Standard criteria** for whether a classification variable is acceptable: actuarial (statistically significant, homogeneous, credible), operational (objective, cheap to verify, not manipulable), social (privacy, causality, affordability, controllability) and legal (permitted in the jurisdiction).

requirements.statement: Historical precedence means the exposure base is consistent with past practice and industry use, so changing it can cause IT/system costs, restated historical data, premium swings for policyholders, and loss of industry benchmarks.

places.quote: A change of base can cause large premium swings for individual insureds, requires a change in the rating algorithm and systems, and may force significant adjustments to the several years of data a ratemaking analysis uses.

requirements.statement: ASOP 12 lists considerations for evaluating a risk characteristic used in risk classification: relationship to expected outcomes, causality, objectivity, practicality/cost, applicable law, industry practice, business practice (e.g., privacy, controllability, affordability), homogeneity, credibility, and avoiding adverse selection.

places.quote: ASOP 12 also asks the actuary to comply with applicable law, consider industry and business practices, and consider the reasonableness of the results, such as the consistency of the pattern of rates among classes (§3.3.3–3.3.4).

requirements.statement: To evaluate a proposed risk characteristic under ASOP 12, pick distinct considerations and explain how the characteristic does or does not satisfy each (e.g., relationship to expected loss, objectivity, privacy, controllability, legality, adverse selection).

places.quote: Once risk characteristics are chosen, the actuary forming the classes weighs three considerations, which are often interrelated:

**Standard criteria** for whether a classification variable is acceptable: actuarial (statistically significant, homogeneous, credible), operational (objective, cheap to verify, not manipulable), social (privacy, causality, affordability, controllability) and legal (permitted in the jurisdiction).

requirements.statement: Case incurred loss equals loss payments plus the change in case reserves (i.e., paid loss plus change in outstanding case reserve).

places.quote: $$\text{CY Reported Losses} = \text{Paid} + \Delta\text{Case Reserves}$$
Werner & Modlin and Friedland both define calendar-year **reported** losses as paid losses plus the change in case reserves.

requirements.statement: Calendar year losses are aggregated by summing all loss payments and case reserve changes with transaction dates falling within that calendar year, regardless of accident or policy date.

places.quote: groups every transaction by the calendar year in which it is *booked* — premium as it is earned, losses as they are paid or as case reserves change — without regard to the policy's effective date or the claim's accident date.

requirements.statement: Policy year losses include all transactions on claims whose policy effective date falls in the policy year, limited to transactions on or before the evaluation date.

places.quote: groups every premium and loss transaction belonging to policies *incepting* in a given calendar year, and follows that cohort until the last claim closes.

requirements.statement: Accident year losses include all transactions on claims whose accident date falls in the accident year, limited to transactions on or before the evaluation date.

places.quote: groups losses by the calendar year in which the loss event *occurred*, and matches them against the [[Earned Premium|premium earned]] in that same year — regardless of when the policy was written, when the claim was reported, or when it was paid.

requirements.statement: A loss ratio equals losses divided by premium, and an accident year loss ratio uses the earned premium for the matching year (calendar year earned premium for the accident year).

places.quote: Accident-year aggregation takes its premium and exposures on the calendar-year basis — Werner & Modlin note the method is often called *calendar-accident year*
$$\text{AY } n \text{ Loss Ratio} = \frac{\text{Losses occurring in year } n}{\text{Premium earned in year } n}$$
$$\text{Loss Ratio} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Premium}}$$

requirements.statement: Advantage of policy year data: it gives the best match of premium and losses (exposures to losses), and it isolates the effect of changes in policy limits or underwriting guidelines.

places.quote: **[[Policy Year]]** — every transaction on policies incepting in the year. The best match of premium to loss, and particularly useful when underwriting or pricing changes occur (Friedland's example: a shift to large-deductible policies), but its exposures are not fully earned until 24 months after it starts, so its data takes longer to develop.

requirements.statement: Disadvantage of policy year data: it takes the longest to become fully developed and available, so it is the least responsive, and its premium and losses must be developed to ultimate.

places.quote: The price of that match is **time**. With annual policies a PY cohort is not fully written until $12$ months after the year begins and not fully earned until $24$ months, so PY data is roughly a year less mature than the corresponding [[Accident Year]] at the same valuation date.

requirements.statement: A claims-made policy covers claims that are reported during the policy period (and occur on or after the retroactive date), regardless of when the accident occurred.

places.quote: **Claims-Made Coverage** is a policy trigger under which the policy responds to claims *reported* during the policy period, provided the underlying loss occurred on or after the policy's **retroactive date**.

requirements.statement: An occurrence policy covers losses that occur (accident date) during the policy period, regardless of when they are reported.

places.quote: **Occurrence Coverage** is a policy trigger under which the policy responds to losses that *occur* during the policy period, however long afterwards the claim is reported.

requirements.statement: Tail coverage (extended reporting endorsement) covers claims reported after a claims-made policy ends for accidents that occurred during the claims-made coverage period.

places.quote: An **extended reporting endorsement** (ERP, or "tail coverage") covers claims that occurred during the claims-made coverage period but are reported after the last policy expires

requirements.statement: To assign claims to insurers when switching from claims-made to occurrence, allocate each claim to the claims-made insurer if reported in its policy period (and after any retro date), and to the occurrence insurer if the accident date falls in its policy period.

places.quote: $$\text{Covered if } \; \text{accident date} \ge \text{retro date} \; \text{ and } \; \text{report date} \in \text{policy period}$$
$$\text{Covered if } \; \text{effective date} \le \text{accident date} \le \text{expiration date}$$

requirements.statement: Occurrence policy ultimate losses are more volatile than claims-made because occurrence policies have a report lag (pure IBNR) plus settlement lag, giving a longer development period, while claims-made policies have essentially no report lag.

places.quote: Because the trigger is the report date, a claims-made policy has **no pure IBNR** — only IBNER on claims already reported — so the risk of reserve inadequacy is greatly reduced relative to the [[Occurrence Coverage|occurrence]] form.
It must reserve for **pure [[IBNR]]** — claims it has no knowledge of — for as long as claims from expired policies can still emerge, which for a product like medical malpractice can be many years.

requirements.statement: Unexpected changes in loss trend or reporting/settlement patterns affect occurrence policy estimates more than claims-made estimates because occurrence claims are exposed to trend and pattern shifts over a longer time before payment.

places.quote: If there is a sudden, unpredictable change in the underlying trends, the claims-made policy priced on the prior trend will be closer to the correct price than an occurrence policy priced on the prior trend.

requirements.statement: Occurrence policies earn more investment income than claims-made policies because the longer lag between premium receipt and loss payment (report lag plus settlement lag, with larger reserves including IBNR) leaves funds invested longer.

places.quote: The investment income earned from claims-made policies is substantially less than under occurrence policies — which the target underwriting profit provision must reflect, along with the reduced pricing risk.
Premiums are collected before claims are paid, and reserves are held until the claims fall due, so the insurer invests money that it will later pay to policyholders.

requirements.statement: Report lag is the time from claim occurrence to when it is reported; settlement lag is the time from report to claim closure.

places.quote: $$\text{Report lag} = \text{Report date} - \text{Accident date}$$

requirements.statement: Square root rule for partial credibility: Z = sqrt(number of claims / claims required for full credibility), capped at 1.

places.quote: Partial credibility uses the **square root rule**: $Z = \sqrt{n/n_{\text{full}}}$ when $n < n_{\text{full}}$
$$Z = \min\left(\sqrt{\frac{n}{n_F}},\; 1\right)$$
Partial credibility uses the **square root rule**, $Z = \sqrt{n / n_{\text{full}}}$, capped at $1$ — a class with a quarter of the required claims gets $Z = 0.50$.

requirements.statement: Credibility-weighted estimate = Z × (state indication) + (1 − Z) × (complement of credibility), where the complement for a state's rate change can be the countrywide indicated rate change.

places.quote: $$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$
$$\text{Estimate} = Z \cdot \bar{X} + (1-Z) \cdot \mu_0$$
$Z$ multiplies the observed experience; $1 - Z$ goes to the [[Complement of Credibility]]

requirements.statement: Loss ratio method indicated rate change with all-variable expenses = (loss and ALAE ratio) / (1 − variable expense ratio − profit provision) − 1.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss Ratio}}{\text{PLR}} - 1 \quad \text{(all-variable form)}$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio}}{\text{PLR}} - 1$$

requirements.statement: Loss ratio method indicated rate change with fixed expenses = (loss and ALAE ratio + fixed expense ratio) / (1 − variable expense ratio − profit provision) − 1.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + \text{Fixed Expense Ratio}}{1 - V - Q} - 1$$

requirements.statement: The target profit and contingency provision is a choice made by the insurer (or constrained by regulation); a negative provision may be used for long-tailed lines with substantial investment income, to compete for new business, or when regulation requires it.

places.quote: [[Long Tail Lines|Long-tail lines]] hold reserves for years and earn substantial investment income on them, so they can support a low or even negative underwriting provision and still return the target on equity

In long-tailed lines (personal auto bodily injury, workers compensation) years may pass between the premium and the settlement of all claims, and the investment income can be large enough to accept an underwriting loss and still achieve the target total return

requirements.statement: The pure premium method is preferable to the loss ratio method for new business with no existing rates, since there is no premium to on-level.

places.quote: The method produces an **absolute rate**, which is why it is the only choice for a **new** line or programme where there is no current rate to change.
It produces a **change**, not a rate — so it cannot price a new line of business with no current rates to adjust.

requirements.statement: The pure premium method is preferable when new rating variables are introduced that are not in the historical data, because premium cannot be put on-level for the loss ratio method.

places.quote: Its requirement is premium at current rate level, which is hard to calculate accurately after many changes to a complex rating algorithm.
The [[Pure Premium Method]] needs no on-levelling at all, because it never divides by premium. That is its principal practical advantage where rate history is messy or the book has been re-tiered.
That makes it the natural measure for a new book, a re-tiered book, or any analysis where premium data is unreliable.

requirements.statement: Under the premium-based projection method with fixed and variable expenses, the indicated average rate = (pure premium including LAE + fixed expense per exposure) / (1 - variable expense ratio - underwriting profit provision).

places.quote: $$\text{Rate} = \frac{\text{Pure Premium} + \text{Fixed Expense per Exposure}}{1 - V - Q_T}$$
$$\text{Rate} = \frac{\text{Pure Premium} + F}{1 - V - Q_T}$$

requirements.statement: Split each selected expense ratio into fixed and variable portions by multiplying it by the % fixed and (1 - % fixed), then sum fixed portions and variable portions across categories.
requirements.concept: Fixed and Variable Expenses in Ratemaking

requirements.statement: Convert a fixed expense ratio (a percentage of premium) to a fixed dollar expense per exposure by multiplying it by the projected average premium per exposure.

places.quote: The fixed dollars are then put per exposure either by multiplying the fixed expense ratio by the projected average premium, or by dividing fixed expenses directly by exposures or policy count.
$$F = 6.5\% \times \$800 = \$52.00 \text{ per exposure}$$

requirements.statement: Select each expense ratio based on its trend: if ratios show a consistent trend, select the most recent year to remain responsive; if there is no clear pattern or the ratios are volatile, select an average of the years.
Selections should be made on each expense category's total ratio before splitting into fixed and variable, so that volatility in one component does not mask a trend in another.

Fundamental insurance equation: premium = losses and LAE + expenses + underwriting profit, so a target profit without a rate change requires lower expenses or lower losses; if the indicated rate exceeds the current rate and expense ratios are rising, keeping rates unchanged makes the profit target unlikely.

places.quote: $$\text{UW Profit} = \text{EP} - \text{Losses} - \text{LAE} - \text{UW Expenses}$$
**Non-Pricing Solutions** are actions that bring the fundamental insurance equation back into balance by **reducing costs** — expenses or expected losses — rather than by raising rates.

requirements.statement: Compute on-level factors with the parallelogram method: determine the fraction of each year's earned premium written at each rate level (given the policy term and rate change effective dates), form the average rate level, and divide the current rate level by it.

places.quote: $$\text{OLF}_Y = \frac{I_{\text{current}}}{\sum_k A_{Y,k}\, I_k}$$
$$\text{On-Level Factor} = \frac{\text{Current cumulative index}}{\text{Average index for the year}}$$

requirements.statement: With semi-annual policies, a rate change takes six months to be fully earned in, so the parallelogram uses a 6-month policy term rather than a 12-month one.

places.quote: With a six-month term the diagonal runs from $4/1$ at the bottom of the square to $10/1$ at the top.

requirements.statement: Trend premium (and losses) from each experience period's average written/earned/accident date to the average date for the future period when the rates will be in effect (effective date plus half the policy-term-adjusted rate period), using the number of years between those dates as the exponent.

places.quote: The trend period runs from the average date of historical losses (midpoint of the accident year) to the average date of future losses (midpoint of the prospective rating period)
with six-month policies the trend-from date moves to $4/1/2011$ and the period is $2.25$ years.
measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period

requirements.statement: Combine frequency and severity trends multiplicatively, (1 + frequency trend)(1 + severity trend), to obtain the loss trend (pure premium trend).

places.quote: $$1 + t_{PP} = (1 + t_{\text{freq}})(1 + t_{\text{sev}})$$
Separately selected frequency and severity trends combine multiplicatively: $1 + T_{PP} = (1 + T_F)(1 + T_S)$.

requirements.statement: Develop losses with the chain-ladder method: select age-to-age factors from the triangle (e.g. averages of observed link ratios), multiply them to get age-to-ultimate factors (including a tail factor), and apply them to the latest reported losses.

places.quote: $$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$
$$f_{k \to k+1} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k}}$$

requirements.statement: Handle catastrophes separately: remove catastrophe losses from the development and trend analysis, then add a projected catastrophe load, converted to a ratio by dividing the per-exposure load by the trended on-level premium per exposure.

places.quote: Catastrophe losses are … from the experience period and replaced with a long-run expected load.
it becomes the catastrophe provision in a rate in place of whatever catastrophe losses happened to occur in the experience period.

requirements.statement: Loss ratio indicated rate change = [(loss & ALAE ratio × (1 + ULAE provision)) + fixed expense ratio] / (1 − variable expense ratio − profit & contingencies provision) − 1.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{VPLR} = 1 - V - Q_T \quad \text{(variable permissible loss ratio)}$$

requirements.statement: Under full credibility, the indication is based entirely on the experience-period loss ratio, with no complement of credibility.

places.quote: $$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$
the volume of experience at which … assigns $Z = 1$.

requirements.statement: The loss elimination ratio (LER) at a given deductible or loss limit is the fraction of ground-up losses that fall below that amount (eliminated by the deductible); the excess ratio is its complement, the fraction of losses above it.

places.quote: $E[X]$ is expected ground-up loss, $\text{LER}(d)$ the [[Loss Elimination Ratio|loss elimination ratio]] at deductible $d$ (so $1 - \text{LER}$ is the excess ratio)
**Loss Elimination Ratio** (LER) is the proportion of ground-up losses removed by a deductible — the share of expected loss that the insured retains rather than transfers.
The share of expected loss that stays under the cap is $E[X \wedge L]/E[X] = 1 - R(L)$, the loss elimination ratio of a deductible at $L$.

requirements.statement: To split expected ground-up losses for a large deductible policy, select the LER and excess ratio at the deductible amount and multiply them by ground-up losses to get losses below the deductible (insured-retained) and excess losses (insurer-paid).

places.quote: $$\text{Excess Losses} = E[X] \times \big(1 - \text{LER}(d)\big)$$
The LER is the bridge from a full-coverage rate to a deductible rate: multiply the full-coverage loss cost by $(1 - \text{LER})$ to get the loss cost net of the deductible.

requirements.statement: When the deductible applies to loss only and not to ALAE, the insurer bears the full ALAE (a percentage of total ground-up losses), so all ALAE is included in the premium.

places.quote: ALAE is $9\%$ of ground-up losses and is not reduced by the deductible.

requirements.statement: Large deductible premium = (excess losses + ALAE + fixed expenses + risk margin + cost of processing losses below deductible + credit risk charge) / (1 − variable expense ratio − profit provision), where risk margin is a percentage of excess losses and the processing cost and credit risk are percentages of losses below the deductible (expected deductible payments).

places.quote: $$\text{Premium} = \frac{\text{Excess Losses} + \text{ALAE} + F + \text{CR} + \text{RM}}{1 - V - Q}$$

requirements.statement: Variable expenses and the underwriting profit provision are expressed as percentages of premium, so they go in the denominator as (1 − V − profit), while fixed and loss-based loads go in the numerator.

places.quote: $$\text{Premium} = \frac{\text{Excess Losses} + \text{ALAE} + F + \text{CR} + \text{RM}}{1 - V - Q}$$
They are expressed as a percentage and enter the **denominator** of the rate formula, so they gross up the rate rather than being added to it.
- $F$ enters the **numerator** of the rate; [[Variable Expenses|variable expenses]] $V$ and the profit provision $Q_T$ enter the **denominator**.

requirements.statement: Written exposures for a calendar year are the exposures of all policies written (effective) in that year, counted for the full policy term at inception.

places.quote: A $12$-month policy contributes **one** earned car-year in total, spread pro rata over its term: written the day it is issued, earned $1/12$ per month, in force from effective date to expiry.
**Written Premium** is the full premium booked when a policy is issued, for the entire policy term, regardless of how much of the coverage period has elapsed.

requirements.statement: Earned exposures for a calendar year are the portion of policy exposure that has expired (been in force) during that year, recognized pro rata over the policy term.

places.quote: **Earned Exposure** is the portion of written exposure for which coverage has actually been provided during the period — the exposure analogue of [[Earned Premium|earned premium]], and the correct denominator for a pure premium.

requirements.statement: A policy with a term longer than one year carries one exposure unit per year of term (e.g., a two-year policy counts as two exposures).
Compute a policy's earned exposures in a calendar year as its total exposure times the fraction of its term (months in force) that falls within that calendar year, assuming even earning.

places.quote: A $12$-month policy contributes **one** earned car-year in total, spread pro rata over its term: written the day it is issued, earned $1/12$ per month, in force from effective date to expiry.
$$\text{EP for one policy} = \text{Full premium} \times \frac{\text{days elapsed}}{\text{policy term}}$$

requirements.statement: Over the life of a policy, total earned exposures across calendar years equal the written exposures, so earned amounts in successive years sum to the written total.

places.quote: A $12$-month policy contributes **one** earned car-year in total, spread pro rata over its term: written the day it is issued, earned $1/12$ per month, in force from effective date to expiry.
Both calendar years draw on one written premium transaction of $\$1{,}200$ booked in $2024$.

requirements.statement: Premium under a rating algorithm equals base rate times the territory factor, plus any additive policy fee added last, multiplied by exposures and summed across territories.

places.quote: $$\text{Premium} = \left[\text{Base Rate} \times \prod_i R_i + \sum_j A_j\right] \times (1 - D) + \text{Fees}$$

requirements.statement: Underwriting profit equals premium minus loss and LAE, minus fixed expenses, minus variable expenses.

places.quote: $$\text{UW Profit} = \text{EP} - \text{Losses} - \text{LAE} - \text{UW Expenses}$$

requirements.statement: LAE provided as a percentage of loss cost is a load applied to loss (loss times one plus the LAE percentage), and loss costs per exposure are multiplied by exposures to get total loss.

places.quote: $$\text{Pure Premium} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Exposures}}$$

It cannot be traced to a claim, so it is estimated in aggregate — classically as the ratio of calendar-year paid ULAE to calendar-year paid loss plus ALAE, applied to loss plus ALAE that has been adjusted for extraordinary events, development and trend.

requirements.statement: Fixed expense is a per-exposure cost, distinct from a policy fee, which is a premium component; the variable expense ratio applies to total premium including the policy fee.

places.quote: They cost roughly the same on a $\$500$ policy as on a $\$5{,}000$ one, so they are recovered as a **dollar amount per exposure**, not as a percentage of premium.
They are expressed as a percentage and enter the **denominator** of the rate formula, so they gross up the rate rather than being added to it.

requirements.statement: The indicated policy fee equals fixed expense per exposure divided by (1 minus variable expense ratio minus profit provision).

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Rate} = \frac{\text{Pure Premium} + F}{1 - V - Q_T}$$
$$\text{Rate} = \frac{\text{Pure Premium} + \text{Fixed Expense per Exposure}}{1 - V - Q_T}$$

requirements.statement: Indicated territory relativities are each territory's loss cost per exposure divided by the base territory's loss cost per exposure, with the base territory having factor 1.000.

places.quote: $$\text{Territory Relativity}_i = \frac{\text{Pure Premium}_i}{\text{Pure Premium}_{\text{base}}}$$
$$\text{Territory relativity} = \frac{\text{Territory pure premium}}{\text{Overall pure premium}}$$

requirements.statement: The indicated base rate equals the base territory's loss cost times (1 plus LAE load) divided by (1 minus variable expense ratio minus profit provision), excluding fixed expenses which the policy fee covers.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Rate} = \frac{\text{Pure Premium} + F}{1 - V - Q_T}$$

requirements.statement: Changing only the base rate leaves inaccurate territory relativities and policy fee in place, so underpriced classes remain subsidized by others, causing adverse selection, deteriorating profitability and reduced equity.

places.quote: **Flattening a territory differential** has the effect Werner & Modlin describe for any rating variable: risks with different expected costs pay the same rate, so the low-cost risks subsidise the high-cost ones, and a company doing this while competitors differentiate faces [[Adverse Selection|adverse selection]]

resolution.quote: an insurer that charges one average rate to a heterogeneous group loses the better risks to competitors that price them properly, and retains the worse ones
resolution.note: Classification Ratemaking (one link from Territory Ratemaking) teaches the subsidy and adverse selection that inaccurate relativities cause (Werner Ch.9).

requirements.statement: The homeowners rate per $1,000 of coverage equals expected frequency times expected severity limited to the amount of insurance (pure premium), divided by the amount of insurance in thousands.
requirements.concept: Homeowners Insurance Rating by Amount of Insurance

resolution.quote: is set by the face amount chosen, as expected indemnity divided by face value
resolution.note: Taught on the tagged Coinsurance Rating page: rate per amount of insurance = f x E[min(L,F)] / F (Werner Ch.11 p.212); the check missed it.

requirements.statement: To find expected severity at an amount of insurance below the home's value, cap each loss band's average at the amount of insurance and weight by the band probabilities (limited expected value), so losses above the limit contribute the limit.

places.quote: It equals the expected value of $\min(X, u)$.

Under a limit $u$ and no other modification, the insurer pays the whole loss $X$ when it is below $u$ and pays $u$ when it is not, so the payment is the limited loss variable $X \wedge u$, whose mean is the [[Limited Expected Value|limited expected value]].

requirements.statement: The rate per $1,000 of coverage decreases as the amount of insurance increases, because the lower layers of coverage are the most likely to be hit by losses.

places.quote: Each successive layer is cheaper per dollar of limit — which is exactly the consistency property.

requirements.statement: Underinsurance harms the insured, who retains losses above the limit and bears coinsurance penalties on partial losses, and harms the insurer, who collects inadequate premium if rates assume insurance to value, since the rate per $1,000 is higher for underinsured homes; those insured to value pay an adequate rate and do not subsidize others.

places.quote: Fall short and every partial loss is settled at the ratio of insurance carried to insurance required.

Property rates are charged per \$100 of insurance, but expected losses depend on the property and hardly at all on the limit chosen. A book insured below value therefore collects too little premium at the filed rate.

requirements.statement: The coinsurance apportionment ratio is the lesser of 1 and the amount of insurance divided by the product of the coinsurance percentage and the property value.

places.quote: $$a = \min\!\left(\frac{F}{cV},\ 1.0\right)$$
$$R = \min\left(\frac{C}{p \times V},\ 1\right)$$
$$\text{Property payment} = \min\left(\min\left(\frac{C}{p \times V},\ 1\right) \times L - D,\ C\right)$$

requirements.statement: The indemnity payment is the lesser of the amount of insurance and the apportionment ratio times the loss (with no deductible).

places.quote: $$I = L \times \frac{F}{cV}, \quad \text{where } I \le F \text{ and } I \le L$$
$$\text{Payment} = \min\big(R \times L - D,\ C\big)$$

requirements.statement: The coinsurance penalty is the amount that would have been paid without the coinsurance provision (the loss capped at the amount of insurance) minus the actual indemnity payment; it is zero when the policy limit binds.

places.quote: The insured absorbs $\$50{,}000$ — a penalty for under-insurance, not a deductible.
on a total loss the insurer pays the full limit whether or not the requirement is met. The penalty therefore matters only for partial losses.
With at least \$450,000 of insurance the insurer would have paid \$79,000, so the penalty costs the insured \$16,000.

requirements.statement: The experience rating modification factor equals 1 + Z × (AER − EER)/EER, where AER is the actual experience ratio, EER is the expected experience ratio, and Z is the credibility.

places.quote: $M = Z \times \frac{A}{E} + (1 - Z)$
$M = Z\,\frac{A}{E} + (1 - Z) = \frac{A + K}{E + K}$

requirements.statement: Expected unreported basic limit loss and ALAE equals company subject basic limit loss and ALAE times the expected experience ratio times the expected percentage unreported.

places.quote: For each experience year and sub-line, the expected future development is that row's company subject loss cost times the expected experience ratio times a loss development factor from Rule 15, and the rows are summed.

requirements.statement: The actual experience ratio equals the risk's reported basic limit loss and ALAE plus expected unreported loss and ALAE, divided by company subject basic limit loss and ALAE.

places.quote: The actual experience ratio is built from the loss history and the expected future development.

requirements.statement: Experience rating uses losses limited to basic limits and the maximum single limit per occurrence, not unlimited reported losses.

places.quote: For each experience year and sub-line, the loss history is the incurred loss excluding ALAE capped at the basic per-occurrence limit, plus the ALAE, then capped at the Maximum Single Loss.
It is capped per claim, or split into primary and excess.

requirements.statement: Schedule rating applies to individual risk characteristics expected to materially affect future losses but not yet reflected in the historical experience used by experience rating, such as a newly implemented safety program; applying it to characteristics already reflected in experience double counts.

places.quote: If a risk has made a recent change that will likely impact its loss experience, then it is appropriate to use a schedule credit or debit, because the change is not yet reflected in the experience period.
Whatever already shows in a risk's past losses is already reflected in its experience mod.

requirements.statement: Compute age-to-age development factors as ratios of reported loss at successive maturities from a loss triangle, and select a factor for each interval by averaging the observed factors.

resolution.quote: is the ratio of a cohort's cumulative amount at one maturity to its amount at the previous maturity
resolution.note: Age to Age Factor (a syllabus page) defines the factor and its selection by averaging the column; the check missed it.

requirements.statement: Obtain cumulative development factors by multiplying the selected age-to-age factors from a given maturity through the tail factor, then multiply each accident year's reported loss at its current maturity by its own CDF to get ultimate loss.

places.quote: CDFs are built **backwards from the tail**: start with the tail factor, multiply in each successive age-to-age factor moving toward younger ages.
$$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: Determine the trend period for each experience year as the time from its average accident (or earned) date to the average accident (or earned) date of the period the proposed rates will be in effect; for annual policies written evenly, that future date is the effective date plus one year (the midpoint of the period rates are in effect plus half the policy term).

places.quote: The trend period $n$ runs from the average written date of the policies earning premium in the experience period to the **average written date of the policies in effect while the new rates are** — for calendar-year 2011 earned premium and annual policies written in 2013, $1/1/2011$ to $6/30/2013$, or $2.5$ years.
$t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.

requirements.statement: Use the parallelogram method to find the average rate level for each experience year (areas of the policy-writing parallelogram at each rate level for annual policies written evenly), and compute the on-level factor as the current rate level divided by that year's average rate level.

places.quote: $$\text{OLF}_Y = \frac{I_{\text{current}}}{\sum_k A_{Y,k}\, I_k}$$

For **annual** policies written uniformly, a rate change effective at time $p$ through year $Y$ earns over a triangle of area $\tfrac{1}{2}(1-p)^2$ in year $Y$ — so a $7/1$ change affects only $0.125$ of that year's earned premium, and a $1/1$ change affects $0.500$.

requirements.statement: Apply annual premium trend to on-level earned premium over the trend period, and apply loss trend compounded over the trend period to ultimate losses, where the pure premium trend is the product of the frequency trend factor and the severity trend factor.

places.quote: $$\text{Premium Trend Factor} = (1 + t_P)^{n}$$
$$1 + t_{PP} = (1 + t_{\text{freq}})(1 + t_{\text{sev}})$$

requirements.statement: When losses are capped at a basic limit, build an excess loss factor as 1 plus the ratio of long-term historical excess losses to capped losses (capped = unlimited minus excess), and multiply the trended capped losses by it to load for excess losses.

places.quote: $$\text{ELF} = 1 + \frac{\sum \text{Excess losses}}{\sum \text{Non-excess losses}}$$
$$\text{Excess Load} = \frac{\text{Expected losses above } M}{\text{Expected losses below } M}$$

requirements.statement: Loss ratio indicated rate change = (trended loss & LAE ratio including ULAE + fixed expense ratio) / (1 − variable expense ratio − profit and contingencies provision) − 1, with ULAE loaded as a percentage of loss and ALAE.
requirements.concept: Loss Ratio Method (Overall Rate Level Indication)

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + \text{Fixed Expense Ratio}}{1 - V - Q} - 1$$

requirements.statement: An insurer may not take the full indicated rate change because of marketplace/competitive considerations, regulatory constraints, or customer disruption and retention concerns from a large increase.
requirements.concept: Rate Change Selection and Implementation Constraints

places.quote: The **selected** change may differ for reasons that are legitimate and must be documented: [[Credibility|credibility]] weighting against a [[Complement of Credibility|complement]], [[Ratemaking Constraints|regulatory caps]], rate capping to limit policyholder disruption, competitive position, and [[Lifetime Value|retention economics]].

requirements.statement: Total IBNR equals IBNER plus IBNYR, so IBNYR equals total IBNR minus IBNER.

places.quote: \text{IBNR} = \underbrace{\text{Pure IBNR}}_{\text{unreported claims}} + \underbrace{\text{IBNER}}_{\text{development on known claims}}
Development has two drivers: **pure IBNR** (claims that occurred but have not yet been reported)…Reported triangles capture both

requirements.statement: An accident year triangle groups claims by occurrence date, so developing it to ultimate captures both development on known claims and late-reported claims (total IBNR).

places.quote: An AY cohort is **not final** at year end: losses still develop as claims are reported and case reserves are re-estimated, so an AY must be brought to ultimate with a [[Cumulative Development Factor|CDF]] before it can be compared with a mature year.
Development has two drivers: **pure IBNR** (claims that occurred but have not yet been reported)…Reported triangles capture both

requirements.statement: A report year triangle groups claims by report date, so no new claims enter a closed report year; developing it to ultimate captures only development on known claims (IBNER).

places.quote: **A claims-made book has no pure IBNR** by construction — every claim in a [[Report Year|report year]] is already reported — so its IBNR is entirely IBNER.

A report year **closes to new claims** at year end — pure [[IBNR]] is zero by construction, since every claim in the cohort is already known. All remaining development is **IBNER**: re-estimation of claims already reported.

requirements.statement: Compute age-to-age factors from a cumulative triangle as ratios of successive cumulative values, select a factor for each age, and multiply the selected factors (with any tail factor) to get cumulative development factors to ultimate.

places.quote: **The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.
CDFs are built **backwards from the tail**: start with the tail factor, multiply in each successive age-to-age factor moving toward younger ages.

requirements.statement: Ultimate claims for each year equal reported-to-date claims times the cumulative development factor to ultimate.

places.quote: \text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}
U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}
\text{Ultimate} = C_n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}

requirements.statement: Apply a tail factor only to a triangle that is still developing past the last observed age; a report year triangle with no claims reported beyond the last age needs no tail.

places.quote: A report year **closes to new claims** at year end — pure [[IBNR]] is zero by construction, since every claim in the cohort is already known. All remaining development is **IBNER**: re-estimation of claims already reported.
**Tail Factor** is the development factor applied beyond the last maturity observable in the triangle — the estimate of all emergence that will occur after the data runs out.

requirements.statement: Frequency-severity alternative: project cumulative claim counts to ultimate, subtract reported counts to get pure IBNR counts, and multiply by a selected severity developed to ultimate.

places.quote: Splitting the two requires a [[Claim Count Triangle|claim count triangle]]: develop counts to ultimate, subtract reported counts to get unreported claims, and value them at an expected severity. Pure IBNR falls out; IBNER is the remainder.
Counts split broad IBNR into its two parts: **pure IBNR** (unreported claims, valued at an expected severity) and **IBNER** (development on known claims).

requirements.statement: Diagnostic triangles are interpreted by reading down the columns, comparing the same maturity across accident years, not across rows, since movement along a row only reflects normal maturing.

places.quote: Reading **down a column** compares years at the same age, which shows trends and mix.
**Down a column** — how successive cohorts compare at the *same* maturity.

requirements.statement: The paid to reported claim ratio at each age is cumulative paid claims divided by cumulative reported claims (equivalently paid/(paid + case outstanding)).

places.quote: Paid ÷ reported losses

requirements.statement: A rising paid-to-reported ratio down a column can result from faster settlement of claims, weaker case reserve adequacy, or both, so this ratio alone cannot distinguish the two causes.

places.quote: **Faster [[Settlement Rate|settlement]]:** closure rates and paid-to-reported rise together.
Paid ultimates above reported ultimates suggest case reserves are inadequate; the reverse suggests they are strengthening (or claims are closing slowly).

requirements.statement: Closed claim counts are obtained as cumulative reported claim counts less open claim counts, and the closed to reported count ratio is closed counts divided by reported counts.
requirements.concept: Closed to Reported Claim Count Ratio

places.quote: The [[Settlement Rate|disposal rate]] is closed counts over ultimate (or reported) counts.
Compute **disposal rates** — closed claims ÷ ultimate (or reported) claims — at each accident year and maturity.

requirements.statement: A rising closed-to-reported count ratio down a column indicates claims are being settled faster, i.e., an increase in settlement rates.
requirements.concept: Closed to Reported Claim Count Ratio

places.quote: **Faster [[Settlement Rate|settlement]]:** closure rates and paid-to-reported rise together.
Closure at $24$ months has risen from $45\%$ to $63\%$ — claims are settling substantially faster, and the trend is steady rather than a one-off.

requirements.statement: Average case outstanding equals (cumulative reported claims minus cumulative paid claims) divided by open claim count.

places.quote: $$\text{Avg Case Outstanding} = \frac{\text{Case Reserves}}{\text{Open Claim Counts}}$$
The first block is the **average case outstanding** for accident year $w$ at age $d$: reported less paid losses, per open claim.

requirements.statement: With no claim cost inflation, average case outstanding is unaffected by closure speed, so a flat pattern down a column indicates unchanged case reserve adequacy while rising or falling values indicate strengthening or weakening.

places.quote: **The diagnostic is average case outstanding per open claim**, compared *down each column* of the triangle. It should grow at roughly the severity trend.

requirements.statement: Put historical earned premium on the current rate level by multiplying each year's earned premium by its premium on-level adjustment factor, so that premium is comparable across years.

places.quote: $$\text{On-Level Premium} = \text{Historical EP} \times \text{On-Level Factor}$$
$\text{OLF}$ is the current rate level divided by the average historical rate level.

requirements.statement: Trend historical ultimate claim counts to a common target year by applying the annual claim count trend compounded for the number of years between each accident year and the target year.

places.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.
The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: Frequency equals trended ultimate claim counts divided by on-level earned premium, which removes the effects of rate changes, count trend and book growth.
Select a frequency from the historical trended frequencies, excluding or discounting outliers, and apply it to the target year's on-level premium to get its claim count at the target trend level.

places.quote: $$U = \text{Exposures} \times \text{Frequency}_{\text{ult}} \times S_{\text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: De-trend a selected frequency (claim count) and a selected severity from the level of one year back to the earlier accident year by dividing by the respective annual trend factors for the years between them.
Ultimate claims equal ultimate claim count times ultimate average severity, and IBNR equals ultimate claims minus reported (cumulative) claims.

places.quote: $$U = N_{\text{ult}} \times S_{\text{ult}}$$
IBNR is the portion of ultimate not yet reported:

requirements.statement: Frequency-severity methods are useful when frequency and severity move at different rates or when development factors on long-tailed lines are highly leveraged at early maturities, since counts and severities can be projected and trended separately.

places.quote: The value of the split is **diagnostic**. A dollar triangle tells you losses grew; frequency and severity tell you *why*, and the two causes call for different responses and carry different persistence.
**Long-tail lines** ([[Long Tail Lines|liability, workers compensation]]) have large CDFs at early maturities and need a [[Tail Factor]] beyond the observed triangle

requirements.statement: Frequency-severity methods are not useful when the claim count definition is inconsistent over time (for example changes in treatment of closed-without-payment claims, reopened claims, or significant partial payments), because counts and severities become distorted.

places.quote: The method needs **consistent count definitions** across the whole triangle, and it is sensitive to [[Large Loss|large losses]] in the severity series

Counts must be **defined consistently**: per claim or per claimant, counting claims closed without payment or not, treating reopened claims as new or as continuing. A definition change mid-triangle looks exactly like a frequency trend.

requirements.statement: In the frequency-severity technique, develop reported claim counts to ultimate and develop severity (claims divided by counts) to ultimate separately, then multiply ultimate counts by ultimate severity to get ultimate claims.

places.quote: Develop the count triangle to ultimate counts; develop an average severity triangle (dollars ÷ counts at each age) to ultimate severity; multiply.

requirements.statement: Age-to-age development factors are the ratio of cumulative values at successive maturities for the same accident year; a selected factor is an average (e.g. straight average) of the observed factors, and the cumulative development factor is the product of selected factors times the tail factor.

places.quote: **Simple average**: unweighted mean of all individual year factors

build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.
**Age-to-Age Factor** (link ratio) is the ratio of a cohort's cumulative amount at one maturity to its amount at the previous maturity — the observed development between two ages.

requirements.statement: Average reported severity at a given maturity equals cumulative reported claims divided by cumulative reported claim counts, and a severity triangle is built from these ratios.

places.quote: develop an average severity triangle (dollars ÷ counts at each age) to ultimate severity
$$\text{Average Severity} = \frac{\text{Losses}}{\text{Claim Counts}}$$
$$\text{Severity} = \frac{\text{Total Losses}}{\text{Number of Claims}}$$

requirements.statement: When a benefit-level change affects claims by accident date, restate the accident years not subject to the change to the common benefit level by multiplying by (1 − stated reduction), and do not adjust accident years already reflecting the change.

places.quote: A benefit-level change is restated in the data, or allowed for in the selection, so that it is not double counted.

**Benefit-level changes** in statutory lines (workers compensation reform, auto no-fault changes) are the same problem at industry scale, and are handled by a law-level adjustment factor applied to historical losses before trend

requirements.statement: A law limiting benefits changes claim severity but not claim counts, so the claim count triangle needs no adjustment for it.

resolution.note: Data the question gives: it states the law's expected impact is a 25% reduction in claim severity, so the count triangle needs no adjustment.

requirements.statement: With no development beyond the last observed maturity, the tail factor is 1.000, and with no loss trend severities need no trend adjustment across accident years.

resolution.note: Data the question gives: it states there is no development after 36 months and no loss trend.

requirements.statement: Under the expected claims technique, ultimate claims equal earned premium times the a priori expected claim ratio, ignoring the year's own emerged experience.

places.quote: **Expected Loss Method** (expected claims technique) estimates ultimate losses entirely from an a priori expectation — usually an expected loss ratio applied to earned premium — giving **no weight** to what has actually been reported.

requirements.statement: IBNR is the portion of ultimate claims not yet reported, so it equals ultimate claims minus reported claims.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Reported}$$
$$\text{IBNR} = U_{\text{AY}} - C_{\text{AY},\,n}$$

requirements.statement: Total unpaid claims are ultimate claims not yet paid, equal to ultimate minus paid claims, i.e. case reserves (reported minus paid) plus IBNR.

places.quote: $$\text{Unpaid} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Paid to date}$$
$$\text{Reported Losses} = \text{Paid Losses} + \text{Case Reserves}$$

requirements.statement: In the reported Bornhuetter-Ferguson technique, IBNR equals expected claims (premium times expected claim ratio) times (1 − 1/CDF), where 1/CDF is the percent reported; the ultimate is reported claims plus this IBNR.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}$$
$$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$

requirements.statement: Select age-to-age factors from the triangle (e.g. an average of the observed individual factors) for each development period.

places.quote: **The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.
- **Simple average** — equal weight to each year, so a small, volatile year counts as much as a large one.

requirements.statement: Compute age-to-ultimate cumulative development factors by multiplying selected age-to-age factors from the given age through the last age, including a tail factor (1.000 if no development after the last age).

places.quote: $$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \left(\prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1}\right) \times \text{Tail}$$
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: The percent unreported for BF must use the age-to-ultimate CDF for the accident year's current age, not just the next age-to-age factor.

places.quote: $$\text{Reported \%} = \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}}$$
The reciprocal is the **percentage reported** (or paid): $p_n = 1/\text{CDF}_n$, and $1 - p_n$ is the percentage unreported.

requirements.statement: In the reported claim development technique, compute age-to-age factors as ratios of successive cumulative reported claims, select a factor for each age (e.g., an all-year average), and multiply the latest reported amount by successive selected factors to project it to later ages.

places.quote: **The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.
CDFs are built **backwards from the tail**: start with the tail factor, multiply in each successive age-to-age factor moving toward younger ages.
$$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{AY}} = \frac{C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$
