requirements.statement: The expected incremental claims in a given calendar year equal the difference between projected cumulative amounts at the end and the start of the development period that falls in that calendar year (a diagonal of the triangle), not the projection to ultimate.

resolution.quote: the share of ultimate the pattern says should report (or be paid) between the two valuations
resolution.note: Actual vs Expected Analysis (syllabus page) teaches expected emergence between two valuations from the pattern (Friedland Ch.15 pp.350-351).

requirements.statement: Reported claims equal paid claims plus case outstanding, so incremental reported claims over a period equal incremental paid claims plus the change in case outstanding.
requirements.concept: Incremental Paid to Previous Case Outstanding Technique

places.quote: $$\text{CY Reported Losses} = \text{Paid} + \Delta\text{Case Reserves}$$
$$\text{Reported Losses} = \text{Paid Losses} + \text{Case Reserves}$$

requirements.statement: Build the incremental paid triangle by differencing cumulative paid claims, and divide each incremental payment by the case outstanding at the start of that period to get incremental paid to previous case outstanding ratios, from which a ratio is selected for each period.
requirements.concept: Incremental Paid to Previous Case Outstanding Technique

places.quote: Friedland's fuller version works period by period, using two ratios estimated from history: **paid in the next period ÷ case outstanding at the start**, and **case outstanding at the end ÷ case outstanding at the start**.

requirements.statement: Compute case outstanding development ratios as case outstanding at the end of a period divided by case outstanding at its start, select ratios, and project future case outstanding by applying them successively to the latest case reserve.
requirements.concept: Incremental Paid to Previous Case Outstanding Technique

places.quote: Friedland's fuller version works period by period, using two ratios estimated from history: **paid in the next period ÷ case outstanding at the start**, and **case outstanding at the end ÷ case outstanding at the start**.

requirements.statement: To project incremental reported claims for a future period, apply the paid-to-previous-case ratio to the projected case outstanding at the start of the period to get the payment, and add the change in projected case outstanding over the period.
requirements.concept: Incremental Paid to Previous Case Outstanding Technique

places.quote: Rolling these forward generates a payment stream and runs the case balance down to zero.
$$\text{CY Reported Losses} = \text{Paid} + \Delta\text{Case Reserves}$$

requirements.statement: The case outstanding technique projects development only on claims that already have case reserves (IBNER) and cannot capture pure IBNR; it is therefore appropriate on a report-year basis, where all claims are already reported, but generally not on an accident-year basis, where unreported claims carry no case reserve and ultimate would be understated (except for short-tailed lines with nearly all claims reported at the first maturity).
requirements.concept: Incremental Paid to Previous Case Outstanding Technique

places.quote: **Case reserves** (also called case outstanding) are claim-specific estimates of the expected future payments on individual reported claims, established by claims adjusters based on the known facts of each loss.
A report year **closes to new claims** at year end — pure [[IBNR]] is zero by construction, since every claim in the cohort is already known.
**Pure IBNR** (narrow IBNR) covers claims that have occurred but are unknown to the insurer.

requirements.statement: Cumulate successive rate changes multiplicatively into a rate level index (each change applies on top of prior changes), with an arbitrary base since only ratios matter.

places.quote: Rate level indices **compound**: successive changes of $+8\%$ and $+5\%$ give a cumulative index of $1.08 \times 1.05 = 1.134$, not $1.13$.

$I_k$ is the cumulative rate level index of rate level group $k$ (each index is the previous one times $1 +$ that change), $I_{\text{current}}$ the latest index — even if the change came after the experience period — and $A_{Y,k}$ the share (area) of year $Y$'s earned premium written at level $k$.

requirements.statement: Under the parallelogram method, the on-level factor equals the current rate level divided by the average rate level in effect over the experience period, where each rate level is weighted by the share of the period (area of the parallelogram) it was in effect; on-level premium is earned premium times the on-level factor.

places.quote: $$\text{On-Level Factor} = \frac{\text{Current cumulative rate level index}}{\text{Average rate level index for the period}}$$
$$\text{OLF}_Y = \frac{I_{\text{current}}}{\sum_k A_{Y,k}\, I_k}$$
The areas are still found by geometry, and the on-level factor is still the current cumulative index over the year's average index.

requirements.statement: For a policy year (policies written during the year) with annual policies, the parallelogram collapses to a rectangle, so each rate level is weighted by the fraction of the writing year it was in effect, unlike a calendar year where policies written over two years earn in the period.

places.quote: **Policy-year and written premium** are grouped by write date, so the rate level boundary cuts them cleanly: a change effective a fraction $p$ into the year affects the share $1 - p$.

requirements.statement: The loss ratio method indicated rate change factor is (loss & LAE ratio + fixed expense ratio) / (1 − variable expense ratio − profit and contingency provision); loss ratio uses premium at current rate level, and an indication of zero change means the factor equals 1.0.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$

requirements.statement: The parallelogram method assumes policies are written uniformly throughout the period; if exposures grow rapidly, more policies are written at later, higher rate levels, so the true average rate level is higher, the true on-level factor lower, and the method overstates on-level premium, understating the loss ratio and the indicated rate change.

places.quote: **Two weaknesses.** It assumes uniform writing — false for seasonal business such as boat owners, whose policies are bought ahead of the season; refining to quarters or months, or weighting by the actual distribution of writings, helps.

The general rule: the parallelogram method is a shortcut that substitutes geometry for data. When the writing pattern is known to violate uniformity — seasonal lines, a book in rapid growth, a mid-year change in policy term — use the data instead.

requirements.statement: Policy year premium can develop after the policy year ends because of premium audits (exposure bases such as payroll or sales measured after expiration) and retrospectively rated policies whose premium depends on emerging losses.

places.quote: Audits break the tidy relationship between transaction date and cohort. An audit on a policy written in $2023$ books premium in $2025$, so **[[Policy Year]] premium keeps changing** for two or three years and [[Calendar Year|calendar year]] premium contains audit adjustments belonging to prior years.
**Retrospective Rating** adjusts a policy's premium *after* the period, based on the insured's own losses during that period, within a guaranteed minimum and maximum.

On a [[Retrospective Rating|retrospectively rated]] policy the final premium depends on the insured's own losses, so the insurer estimates the adjustment for the expired part of the term by actuarially accepted methods.

requirements.statement: Age-to-age (link ratio) development factors are computed as the cumulative claims at a later age divided by the cumulative claims at the prior age for the same accident year.

places.quote: $$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{AY}} = \frac{C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$

requirements.statement: An all-year simple average selects each age-to-age factor as the unweighted arithmetic mean of all available observed factors for that development interval.

places.quote: **Simple average** — equal weight to each year, so a small, volatile year counts as much as a large one.

requirements.statement: The cumulative development factor to ultimate is the product of the selected age-to-age factors from the current age through the last age, and ultimate claims equal the latest cumulative claims times this factor (with no development beyond the final age, the tail factor is 1.0).

places.quote: $$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \left(\prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1}\right) \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: IBNR equals ultimate claims minus reported (case-incurred) claims, not ultimate minus paid claims.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Reported}$$
$$\text{IBNR} = U_{\text{AY}} - C_{\text{AY},\,n}$$

requirements.statement: Calendar year payments are incremental paid amounts: the latest diagonal of the cumulative paid triangle minus the prior diagonal, with the first-age cell of the latest accident year counted in full.

requirements.statement: In the reported claim development technique, ultimate claims are estimated by applying a cumulative development factor (from volume-weighted average age-to-age factors on the reported triangle) to the latest diagonal of reported claims.

places.quote: **Cumulative Development Factor** (CDF, or age-to-ultimate factor) is the product of all selected [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] from a given maturity through to ultimate, including the [[Tail Factor|tail]].

**The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.

requirements.statement: In the paid claim development technique, ultimate claims are estimated by applying a cumulative development factor (from volume-weighted average age-to-age factors on the paid triangle) to the latest diagonal of paid claims.

places.quote: A CDF is specific to the triangle it came from: paid CDFs differ from reported CDFs, count CDFs from dollar CDFs, and a CDF built on data capped at a retention differs from a gross one.
Run it on **paid and reported** data both.

requirements.statement: The reported development technique assumes a consistent case reserve adequacy over time; a strengthening of case reserves raises the latest reported diagonal and the reported factors, overstating reported ultimates (most for the least mature years), while paid ultimates are unaffected.

places.quote: Applying historical factors — built under weaker reserving — to a strengthened diagonal **over-states** ultimate, because the strengthening is developed a second time.
Changes in case reserving adequacy over time (systematic strengthening or weakening) distort development triangle patterns
**The pattern is stable over calendar time.** Violated by a change in [[Case Adequacy|case adequacy]], [[Settlement Rate|settlement speed]] or [[Inflation|inflation]] — the diagonal effects.

requirements.statement: A change in the speed of claim reporting (faster reporting with unchanged payment pace) distorts reported development factors and reported ultimates but not paid ultimates.

A large reported but unpaid claim in a single immature accident year inflates that year's reported claims, and applying the age-to-age factor leverages it into an overstated reported ultimate, while the paid technique is unaffected.

places.quote: The chain ladder instead scales the whole diagonal, so a distorted diagonal is multiplied by the full CDF. BF's answer moves dollar-for-dollar with a reporting anomaly; the chain ladder's moves by CDF-times.
Leaving a $\$2$M claim in an immature diagonal and multiplying it by a CDF of $4$ produces an $\$8$M estimate from one claim.

**Future development is proportional to what has emerged.** This is the strong one: the method takes whatever sits on the diagonal at face value and scales it. A [[Large Loss|shock loss]] reported early is multiplied by the full CDF.

requirements.statement: The Berquist-Sherman case outstanding adjustment restates historical average case outstanding to the current adequacy level by detrending the latest-diagonal average case outstanding, then rebuilds reported claims as paid claims plus adjusted case outstanding before developing.

places.quote: The remedy is the [[Berquist-Sherman Method|Berquist-Sherman]] case adjustment: restate historical average case outstanding to the current adequacy level using a selected severity trend, rebuild the reported triangle, and select factors from the restated history.
**Trend the latest diagonal's** average case outstanding backwards at $t$ to restate each historical cell at today's adequacy level.

requirements.statement: The expected claims method estimates ultimate claims from an a priori loss ratio or exposure-based expectation, independent of the company's own development history.

places.quote: **Expected Loss Method** (expected claims technique) estimates ultimate losses entirely from an a priori expectation — usually an expected loss ratio applied to earned premium — giving **no weight** to what has actually been reported.

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson method estimates ultimate claims as actual reported (or paid) claims plus expected claims times the percent unreported (or unpaid), so actual claims are not leveraged by a development factor.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$

requirements.statement: A large claim can be handled separately by removing it from the triangle, developing the remaining claims, and adding the claim department's estimate of ultimate for the large claim.
requirements.concept: Large Claim Adjustment in Claim Development

places.quote: In **reserving** the parallel treatment applies: the actuary may exclude large claims from the initial projection, then add back a case-specific projection for the reported large claims and a smoothed provision for the IBNR portion of large claims

requirements.statement: The disposal rate is the ratio of cumulative closed claim counts at a given maturity to the ultimate claim count for that accident year.

places.quote: $$\text{Disposal Rate}_n = \frac{\text{Closed claims at age } n}{\text{Ultimate claim counts}}$$
measuring the [[Settlement Rate|disposal rate]] (in Friedland, cumulative closed claim counts divided by the selected ultimate claim count for the accident year; other authors define it differently)

requirements.statement: The Berquist-Sherman settlement-rate (paid claim development) adjustment restates all accident years to the current settlement rate, using the disposal rate of the latest diagonal at each maturity as the target.

places.quote: 2. Select the current disposal rate pattern as the target.

The remedy is the [[Berquist-Sherman Method|Berquist-Sherman]] paid adjustment: restate each historical year's paid losses to what they would have been at the *current* disposal pattern, by interpolating along each year's paid-versus-disposal-rate relationship, then select factors from the restated triangle.

requirements.statement: Adjusted closed claim counts at a maturity equal the selected (latest diagonal) disposal rate times each accident year's ultimate claim count.

places.quote: Select the current disposal rate pattern as the target.
$$\text{Disposal Rate}_n = \frac{\text{Closed claims at age } n}{\text{Ultimate claim counts}}$$

requirements.statement: An accident year whose disposal rate exceeds the target rate settled claims faster than current practice and its closed counts are adjusted downward; a year with a lower rate is adjusted upward; a year equal to the target (including the latest diagonal) is not adjusted.

places.quote: AY 2021's restated $24$-month paid figure is $\$4{,}977{,}800$ instead of $\$4{,}000{,}000$ — what it would have shown had it been closing claims at today's pace.

requirements.statement: Ultimate claim counts are estimated by applying the chain ladder method to the reported claim count triangle: compute age-to-age factors, select averages, form cumulative development factors, and multiply by the latest reported counts (not the closed count triangle).

places.quote: **The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.
- **Reported counts** — how fast claims come in. Develops to ultimate; the basis for pure [[IBNR]] counts.

requirements.statement: To restate claims for a change in severity (e.g., a court decision) that applies to payments made after a date, de-cumulate the triangle into incremental payments, because each incremental cell is paid in a single calendar year, and multiply the incremental payments made before the change by the severity factor to bring them to the current severity level.

requirements.statement: Incremental payments in a triangle are on the calendar-year diagonals: the cell for accident year a at age m months was paid in calendar year a + m/12 - 1, so payments in calendar years after the effective date are already at the new severity level and need no adjustment.

places.quote: **Along a diagonal** — everything that happened in one calendar period.

**Calendar Year Effect** (diagonal effect) is an influence that acts on every accident year in the same calendar period, and so on one diagonal $w + d = \text{constant}$ of a [[Development Triangle|development triangle]].

requirements.statement: After adjusting the triangle, re-cumulate the incremental payments, compute age-to-age factors as ratios of successive cumulative values, select factors from all adjusted data, and apply a tail factor (1.00 if no development beyond the last age).

places.quote: **The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.
**Age-to-Age Factor** (link ratio) is the ratio of a cohort's cumulative amount at one maturity to its amount at the previous maturity — the observed development between two ages.

requirements.statement: Paid development ultimate claims = cumulative paid claims to date × cumulative development factor to ultimate (the product of the remaining age-to-age factors and the tail).

places.quote: $$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate} = C_n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: On-level factor by the parallelogram method: compute each year's average rate level from the share of the year's earned premium written at each rate level (annual policies written evenly), then divide the current rate level by that average rate level.

places.quote: $$\text{On-Level Factor} = \frac{\text{Current cumulative rate level index}}{\text{Average rate level index for the period}}$$

**Werner's six steps:** date the changes and form rate level groups; find each group's area in each year; build cumulative indices; take the area-weighted average index; divide it into the current index; apply the factor to the year's earned premium.

requirements.statement: Cape Cod used-up (on-level) premium for each accident year = on-level earned premium / cumulative development factor (i.e., × percent developed).

places.quote: **Used-up premium** $\text{EP}_i / \text{CDF}_i$ is the share of each year's premium "exposed" to the losses reported so far.
$P_i / \text{CDF}_i$ is the **used-up premium**, the share of the premium that the claims reported so far correspond to.

requirements.statement: The Cape Cod expected loss ratio is the total of adjusted (on-level) reported or paid claims across all accident years divided by the total used-up on-level premium; claims and premium must be on a common basis.

places.quote: The ELR is estimated as total reported losses over total *used-up* (on-level, developed) premium across all years.
**Inputs it needs:** Premium must be [[On-Leveling|on level]], claims must be [[Loss Trend|trended]] and adjusted for changes such as tort reform, and the development factors must be sound.

requirements.statement: Cape Cod ultimate claims = claims paid to date + on-level premium × Cape Cod loss ratio × (1 − 1/CDF), i.e., actual paid plus expected unpaid claims.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$
$$\hat U_j = C_j + \text{IBNR}_j$$

requirements.statement: The classical ULAE technique uses a ratio of calendar-year paid ULAE to calendar-year paid claims, applied to unpaid claims to estimate the ULAE reserve, and assumes paid ULAE and paid claims move together.

places.quote: Compute the ratio $R$ of calendar-year paid ULAE to calendar-year paid loss, review it for trend, and apply it to unpaid claims.

requirements.statement: The classical ULAE reserve equals the ratio times (50% of case outstanding reserves plus 100% of IBNR), reflecting the assumption that half of a claim's ULAE is spent at opening and half at closing.

places.quote: If ULAE is assumed to be spent half at reporting and half at settlement, only $50\%$ remains on reported-but-unpaid claims while $100\%$ remains on [[IBNR]] — the formula above.

requirements.statement: In a rapidly growing book, ULAE is spent as claims are reported while paid claims lag, so the paid-to-paid ratio is distorted upward and the classical method overstates the ULAE reserve.

places.quote: The classical method's central weakness is **growth**: in a rapidly growing book, current paid ULAE supports a claim inventory much larger than current paid losses reflect, so the ratio overstates the true cost per dollar of loss; in a shrinking or runoff book, it understates it.

requirements.statement: Kittel's refinement divides calendar-year paid ULAE by the average of paid claims and incurred claims (0.5 paid + 0.5 incurred) to correct the classical ratio when volume is changing.

places.quote: $$R_{\text{Kittel}} = \frac{\text{Paid ULAE}}{0.5(\text{Paid Loss}) + 0.5(\text{Incurred Loss})}$$

requirements.statement: In a catastrophe-prone area, catastrophe years produce volatile spikes in paid claims that are not matched by ULAE, so the paid-to-paid ratio swings with catastrophe experience; Kittel and the generalized approach, which also rely on volatile paid ratios, do not fix this.

places.quote: Where calendar-year paid losses are volatile, replace them with *expected* losses — apply reporting and payment patterns to accident-year ultimate estimates — so the denominator is smoothed rather than driven by one year's payment timing.

requirements.statement: The Mango-Allen bootstrap smooths the ratio by dividing paid ULAE by expected paid claims (accident year ultimates run through a payment pattern) rather than by actual calendar-year paid claims.

places.quote: Where calendar-year paid losses are volatile, replace them with *expected* losses — apply reporting and payment patterns to accident-year ultimate estimates — so the denominator is smoothed rather than driven by one year's payment timing.

requirements.statement: For long-tail lines the 50/50 assumption fails because claims stay open for years and incur substantial maintenance ULAE after opening, so the classical method understates the ULAE reserve on case outstanding.

places.quote: Drops the $50/50$ assumption entirely: ULAE is allocated to claim events (opening, maintenance, closing) with selected weights, and the resulting ratio is applied to the corresponding unpaid counts or dollars.

requirements.statement: The Conger-Nolibos generalized approach attributes ULAE to opening, maintaining and closing a claim with separately selected weights, and applies each weight to the corresponding unpaid claim dollars, dropping the 50/50 split.

places.quote: Drops the $50/50$ assumption entirely: ULAE is allocated to claim events (opening, maintenance, closing) with selected weights, and the resulting ratio is applied to the corresponding unpaid counts or dollars.

resolution.quote: ULAE is allocated to claim events (opening, maintenance, closing) with selected weights, and the resulting ratio is applied to the corresponding unpaid dollars

places.quote: the actuary may exclude large claims from the initial projection, then add back a case-specific projection for the reported large claims
**1. Remove the shock loss** before developing — a [[Large Loss|large loss]] does not develop like ordinary claims and would be multiplied by the CDF:

requirements.statement: Adjusted ultimate ALAE by the paid ALAE development technique: develop paid ALAE excluding the large claim with the paid ALAE CDF, then add the large claim's ultimate ALAE.

places.quote: Friedland gives three approaches: develop a **combined** loss-and-ALAE triangle, develop **ALAE separately** in its own triangle, or develop a **ratio of ALAE to loss** and apply it to projected losses.

the actuary may exclude large claims from the initial projection, then add back a case-specific projection for the reported large claims and a smoothed provision for the IBNR portion of large claims (Friedland)

requirements.statement: The implied paid ALAE development factor equals the unadjusted ultimate ALAE estimate divided by the paid ALAE to date.

places.quote: $$\text{Ultimate} = C_n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate}_{\text{paid}} = \text{Paid}_n \times \text{CDF}^{\text{paid}}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: In the paid ALAE to paid claims ratio technique, the development factor is the ultimate ALAE-to-claims ratio divided by the paid ALAE-to-paid claims ratio.

resolution.quote: develop a ratio of ALAE to loss and apply it to projected losses

requirements.statement: Adjusted ultimate ALAE by the ratio technique: develop the paid ALAE-to-paid claims ratio excluding the large claim to an ultimate ratio, multiply by ultimate claims excluding the large claim, then add the large claim's ultimate ALAE.

the actuary may exclude large claims from the initial projection, then add back a case-specific projection for the reported large claims and a smoothed provision for the IBNR portion of large claims (Friedland)

requirements.statement: At early maturities the paid and reported development methods are highly leveraged, because the large cumulative development factor magnifies small distortions (e.g. a single large claim or a change in case reserve adequacy) in the little-developed actual data.

places.quote: The chain ladder instead scales the whole diagonal, so a distorted diagonal is multiplied by the full CDF.
Because the [[Cumulative Development Factor|CDF]] at early maturities is large, estimates are highly **leveraged**: a small proportional change in a factor moves ultimate by a large dollar amount.

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson method blends actual emerged claims with expected claims for the unreported (or unpaid) portion, so it is more stable than development methods at immature ages and is not distorted by a single large claim in the actual data.

places.quote: The key structural property: **actual emergence is taken at face value and only the unemerged portion is estimated**.

BF applies the development factor only to the *unreported* portion and anchors the rest on an a priori expectation, so a one-off reserve entry moves the answer by its own amount rather than by five times its amount.

requirements.statement: A large gap between paid and reported indications signals that case reserves or settlement patterns differ from history, such as a large claim reported but not yet settled, or a change in case reserve adequacy.

places.quote: Changes in case reserving adequacy over time (systematic strengthening or weakening) distort development triangle patterns
*Faster settlement*: paid development overstates; reported methods are largely unaffected.

requirements.statement: The Benktander ultimate equals reported (or paid) claims plus (1 - p) times the B-F ultimate, where p is the percentage reported (or paid), i.e. 1/CDF.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{GB}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) U_{\text{BF}}$$

requirements.statement: The Benktander ultimate is a credibility-weighted average of the development ultimate (weight p) and the B-F ultimate (weight 1-p), so it lies between them and is closer to B-F when p is small.

places.quote: - **Credibility $Z = p$.** The second identity is the useful one. Benktander weights chain ladder against BF with $Z = p$: the more of the year that has emerged, the more the answer leans on the data.
Benktander credibility-weights the development and BF ultimates for the same year, giving the development method weight equal to the year's percent reported.

requirements.statement: When ultimate estimates for an accident year shift across successive evaluations, the actuary should ask management about operational changes that could explain the pattern, such as changes in case reserve adequacy, claim settlement or closure speed, or handling of large claims.

places.quote: **Understand the business.** Meet claims, underwriting and operations to identify changes in coding, processing, case reserving, underwriting, policy provisions, marketing and reinsurance.
**Responses:** detect the change (interview plus [[Data Diagnostic Analysis|diagnostics]] — average case outstanding, closed-to-reported counts, paid-to-reported ratios)

requirements.statement: Accident year incurred losses as of a valuation date equal cumulative paid losses plus case reserves outstanding at that date, for claims with accident dates in that year.

places.quote: **Incurred Losses** — more precisely **reported losses** — are cumulative [[Paid Losses|payments]] plus [[Case Reserves|case outstanding]] on known claims at a valuation date.
$$= \text{Paid Losses} + \text{Case Reserves}$$

requirements.statement: Assign each claim to an accident year by its accident date, and for the case reserve use only the latest reserve at the valuation date for each claim rather than summing successive ending reserves.

places.quote: The **occurrence date** alone decides the year. A policy written $10/1/2023$ with a loss on $2/4/2024$ paid in $2026$ is Accident Year $2024$.
Case reserves reflect the adjuster's current best estimate and are updated as new information emerges

requirements.statement: Calendar year incurred losses = payments during the calendar year + ending case reserves − beginning case reserves.

places.quote: $$\text{CY Reported Losses} = \text{Paid} + \Delta\text{Case Reserves}$$

requirements.statement: Calendar year aggregation counts only transactions occurring in that year regardless of accident date, and a claim not yet reported has a beginning case reserve of zero in its first calendar year.

places.quote: **Calendar Year** (CY) is a data aggregation method that groups every transaction by the calendar year in which it is *booked* — premium as it is earned, losses as they are paid or as case reserves change — without regard to the policy's effective date or the claim's accident date.

requirements.statement: An advantage of calendar year aggregation is that its data are final once the year closes (no later development), so they are immediately available and tie to financial reporting.

places.quote: CY is the **financial reporting** basis: most insurers report financially by calendar year, so the data is available quickly once the year ends and costs nothing extra to aggregate for ratemaking.

requirements.statement: A disadvantage of calendar year aggregation is that losses include transactions from all prior accident years while premium is earned only from current exposures, mismatching losses and premium and making it poor for IBNR estimation, especially for long-tailed lines.

places.quote: CY incurred losses **mix accident years**: a CY 2024 figure contains payments and reserve changes on claims from $2024$ and from every prior year.
but its losses include payments and reserve changes on claims from policies issued years ago, a mismatch with the premium earned in the year.

requirements.statement: The fundamental insurance equation in ratio form: permissible loss and LAE ratio = 1 − total variable expense ratio − underwriting profit and contingencies provision (a negative profit provision raises the permissible loss ratio).

places.quote: $$\text{VPLR} = 1 - V - Q_T \quad \text{(variable permissible loss ratio)}$$
$$\text{Target LR} = 1 - V - F - Q$$

requirements.statement: Compute an expense ratio by dividing the expense by the premium base that matches how the expense is incurred: written premium for expenses incurred at policy issuance (commissions, other acquisition costs, taxes, licenses and fees), earned premium for expenses incurred evenly over the policy term (general expenses).

places.quote: **Premium-based ratios use different denominators.** Expenses incurred at the onset of the policy — commissions, other acquisition, and taxes, licenses and fees — are calculated on [[Written Premium]]; general expenses, incurred throughout the policy, on [[Earned Premium]].

Because commissions and taxes attach when a policy is **written**, these ratios are computed against [[Written Premium|written premium]]; expenses incurred as coverage is provided use [[Earned Premium|earned premium]].

requirements.statement: Commissions, other acquisition costs, and taxes, licenses and fees are incurred when the policy is written, so they are related to written premium, while general expenses are incurred as the policy is in force, matching earned premium.

places.quote: **Premium-based ratios use different denominators.** Expenses incurred at the onset of the policy — commissions, other acquisition, and taxes, licenses and fees — are calculated on [[Written Premium]]; general expenses, incurred throughout the policy, on [[Earned Premium]].

Because commissions and taxes attach when a policy is **written**, these ratios are computed against [[Written Premium|written premium]]; expenses incurred as coverage is provided use [[Earned Premium|earned premium]].

requirements.statement: A negative underwriting profit provision does not imply an overall loss; investment income on loss reserves and unearned premium (float) can offset an underwriting loss and produce a positive total return.

places.quote: Underwriting profit is **not** total profit. An insurer holds policyholder-supplied funds — [[Unearned Premium|unearned premium]] and loss reserves — between collecting premium and paying claims, and the investment income on those funds is a real part of the return.

Because it excludes investment income, a combined ratio above $100\%$ is not automatically unprofitable. [[Long Tail Lines|Long-tail lines]] hold premium for years before paying claims, so they can sustain combined ratios well above $100\%$

requirements.statement: Test whether underwriting profit expectations were met by comparing the actual loss and LAE ratio (ultimate losses and LAE divided by earned premium) with the permissible loss and LAE ratio; an actual ratio above the permissible ratio means the profit target was missed.

places.quote: Rate adequacy is judged against the [[Permissible Loss Ratio]], not against $100\%$: a projected loss ratio above the PLR means rates are inadequate even when the book appears to be making money.
When the projected loss ratio exceeds the target, rates are inadequate; when it falls below, rates are excessive; the ratio of projected to target drives the indicated change

requirements.statement: Under the loss ratio method, the indicated rate level change factor equals (projected loss and LAE ratio + fixed expense ratio) divided by (1 − variable expense provision − profit and contingency provision), with the fixed expense ratio added in the numerator.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + \text{Fixed Expense Ratio}}{1 - V - Q} - 1$$

requirements.statement: In the loss ratio method, compute the loss and LAE ratio and the fixed expense ratio by dividing trended and developed losses and fixed expenses by on-level trended earned premium; exposures are not used, and the indicated change is the factor minus 1.

places.quote: **Premium** — historical earned premium, brought to [[On Level Premium|current rate level]], developed to ultimate where it is still changing, and [[Premium Trend|trended]].
It works entirely in ratios, so it needs premium on level rather than exposure counts.

requirements.statement: Under the pure premium method, the indicated average rate equals (pure premium + fixed expense per exposure) divided by (1 − variable expense provision − profit and contingency provision).

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Rate} = \frac{\text{Pure Premium} + F}{1 - V - Q_T}$$
$$\text{Rate} = \frac{\text{Pure Premium} + F}{1 - V - Q_T}$$
$$\text{Rate} = \frac{\text{Pure Premium} + \text{Fixed Expense per Exposure}}{1 - V - Q_T}$$

requirements.statement: Pure premium is trended and developed losses and LAE divided by earned exposures; the pure premium method uses losses and exposures but not premium.

places.quote: project loss and LAE per exposure, add the fixed expense per exposure, and gross up for variable expenses and profit.
$$\text{Pure Premium} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Exposures}}$$

requirements.statement: The loss ratio method cannot be used when there is no premium at current rate level or rate history to on-level (e.g., a new line of business or territory), because it produces a change to an existing rate.

places.quote: It produces a **change**, not a rate — so it cannot price a new line of business with no current rates to adjust.

The method produces an **absolute rate**, which is why it is the only choice for a **new** line or programme where there is no current rate to change. The [[Loss Ratio Method]] can only produce a change to something that already exists.

requirements.statement: The pure premium method cannot be used when there is no well-defined or consistently measured exposure base, since losses must be divided by exposures.

places.quote: The method's advantage is that it needs no exposure data, which makes it preferable where exposure data is unavailable or the product has no clearly defined [[Exposure Base|exposure base]]

The method's requirement is a **well-defined, stable exposure base**. Where exposures are not consistently recorded, or where the base changed mid-history, the pure premium is unreliable and the loss ratio method is preferred.

requirements.statement: Expected profit equals the sum over classes of (rate charged minus true expected cost) times projected exposures.

places.quote: $$\text{UW Profit} = \text{EP} - \text{Losses} - \text{LAE} - \text{UW Expenses}$$

requirements.statement: With a 0% profit provision in the indicated rate, the true expected cost is the break-even rate, so profit is the margin of charged rate above expected cost.

places.quote: $$\text{Rate} = \frac{\text{Pure Premium} + F}{1 - V - Q_T}$$

requirements.statement: To evaluate a rating plan scenario, use the rates charged under that scenario together with the projected exposures that result from those rates, not the current exposures.

places.quote: If the relativity change is large enough to shift the mix — insureds receiving large increases non-renew — the realized average premium change may differ from $+6.0\%$, and if the risks that leave are not equally profitable, the shift affects the adequacy of the overall rates.

requirements.statement: Adverse selection: underpriced classes attract more exposures and overpriced classes lose exposures, so exposure shifts toward classes subsidized by others when rates do not reflect true cost.

places.quote: **Adverse Selection** is the tendency for those who know they are worse-than-average risks to buy more insurance, and better-than-average risks to buy less, when the insurer cannot distinguish between them.
In a competitive market an insurer that charges one average rate to a heterogeneous group loses the better risks to competitors that price them properly, and retains the worse ones

requirements.statement: To decide whether to implement a rate change, net the one-time implementation cost against only the scenario that implements the change, then compare it to the profit of the alternative scenario.

resolution.note: A step of this solution's plan: netting the one-time cost the question gives against the scenario that incurs it and comparing profits.

requirements.statement: A one-time implementation cost can be evaluated over a short-term view (first-year net) or long-term view (payback period equals cost divided by recurring annual gain), and rates closer to true cost are more equitable and reduce adverse selection.

places.quote: **Classification.** Charge $\$200$ and $\$1{,}000$ respectively; both groups buy; everyone is insured. This is the efficiency argument for risk-based pricing.

requirements.statement: The indicated relativity for a class from loss experience is the class's pure premium (loss and ALAE per exposure) divided by the pure premium of the total book; this is normalized so its exposure-weighted average is 1.000.

places.quote: $$\text{Territory relativity} = \frac{\text{Territory pure premium}}{\text{Overall pure premium}}$$

requirements.statement: When the complement of credibility is 'no change', current relativities must be rebased by dividing each by their exposure-weighted average so they are on the same normalized basis as the indicated relativities, and used as the complement.
Under the square root rule, partial credibility is Z = min(sqrt(n / full credibility standard), 1).

places.quote: $$Z = \min\left(\sqrt{\frac{n}{n_F}},\; 1\right)$$
$$Z = \min\!\left(1,\, \sqrt{\frac{n}{n_{\text{full}}}}\right)$$

requirements.statement: The credibility-weighted relativity is Z times the indicated relativity plus (1 − Z) times the complement relativity.

places.quote: $$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$
$$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$

requirements.statement: To make class changes revenue neutral, off-balance the credibility-weighted relativities by dividing by their exposure-weighted average so the new average equals the current average at an unchanged base rate.

places.quote: **Off-balance.** Relativity changes almost always change the average rate. The base rate must be adjusted so that the combined effect equals the intended [[Overall Rate Level Indication|overall indication]] — see [[Rate Change]].
any simultaneous change to classification relativities must be **off-balanced** so the two together produce the intended overall effect, not the sum of both.

requirements.statement: The indicated class rate change is the new relativity divided by the current relativity minus 1, with both relativities on the same basis (both raw, both rebased, or both relative to the weighted average).

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Indicated Rate}}{\text{Current Rate}} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Indicated Rate}}{\text{Current Rate}} - 1$$

requirements.statement: To judge whether a GLM rating variable is worth adding, check that the indicated relativities show a sensible (e.g. monotonic, intuitive) trend and that the plus/minus two standard error bands are narrow enough that adjacent levels are statistically distinguishable.
requirements.concept: GLM Output Interpretation and Variable Selection

places.quote: Output is judged on more than significance: consistency of the pattern across levels, standard errors, the effect of removing the variable (analysis of deviance), and validation on a holdout period.

requirements.statement: Check consistency of a variable's fitted relativities across individual years (by-year test); relativities that are stable over time indicate a persistent effect rather than overfitting or one-year noise.

places.quote: Stability is assessed by refitting without the most influential records (the highest Cook's distance), by comparing the parameter estimates across cross-validation runs, since the model should give similar results on separate subsets of the data, and by bootstrapping each estimate.
the differences between groups should be statistically significant and stable from year to year

requirements.statement: A variable's chi-squared (p-value) percentage below the significance threshold (e.g. 5%) means the null hypothesis that the variable adds nothing is rejected, so the variable is statistically significant in the model.

places.quote: Since $9.4 > 7.81$, reject the smaller model at 5%: the variable is significant.

requirements.statement: Levels with little exposure have low credibility, producing wide standard error bands, volatile year-to-year relativities and counterintuitive reversals; this is remedied by grouping sparse levels with adjacent levels rather than rejecting the variable.
requirements.concept: Credibility and Level Grouping in GLM Rating Variables

places.quote: Where a level is too thin, combine similar levels or find more data.
A GLM gives each level the estimate that best fits its own data, whatever the volume, so thin levels get extreme coefficients with wide standard errors.

requirements.statement: A good rating variable should also meet practical criteria: it is objective and easy to administer, intuitively related to the loss, socially acceptable, and compliant with regulations.

places.quote: **Operational** — objective, inexpensive to obtain and verify, not manipulable by the insured.
It should be objective and hard to manipulate, practical to collect and verify, and legal ([[Risk Classification Restrictions]], [[Unfair Discrimination]]) and socially acceptable.

requirements.statement: Multivariate methods are discouraged in heavily regulated markets where the regulator mandates a different ratemaking method (e.g. California private passenger auto using univariate sequential factor selection and adjusted pure premium), whereas merely restricting allowable variables does not preclude multivariate methods.

Multivariate methods are discouraged when data is insufficient (new line or territory) or too heterogeneous (large commercial, large-deductible or retrospectively rated, individually underwritten risks) to build a credible model dataset.

Multivariate methods may also be discouraged by operational constraints (lack of systems, data infrastructure or expertise where cost exceeds benefit) or by little competitive pressure (no adverse selection threat from rivals).
requirements.concept: Multivariate Methods: Operational and Competitive Environment

requirements.statement: Harwayne's method first restates each other state's overall pure premium at the subject state's class exposure distribution, by weighting that state's class pure premiums by the subject state's class exposures.

places.quote: **Step 2 — Y's and Z's average pure premiums on State X's class mix** (X's exposures, each state's own class pure premiums)

requirements.statement: The state adjustment factor for each other state equals the subject state's overall pure premium divided by that other state's overall pure premium restated at the subject state's class distribution.

The Harwayne complement for a class equals the average of the other states' class pure premiums, each multiplied by its state adjustment factor, weighted by each other state's exposures in that class.
Under classical (limited fluctuation) credibility, Z = min(1, sqrt(n / full credibility standard)), the square root rule, with n the exposures of the experience being weighted.

places.quote: Z = \min\left(\sqrt{\frac{n}{n_F}},\; 1\right)
Z = \min\!\left(1,\, \sqrt{\frac{n}{n_{\text{full}}}}\right)

requirements.statement: The credibility-weighted estimate equals Z times the subject's own experience plus (1 − Z) times the complement of credibility.

places.quote: \text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}
\text{Estimate} = Z \cdot \bar{X} + (1-Z) \cdot \mu_0

requirements.statement: Harwayne's method corrects for distributional bias from differing class mixes across states, so it suits situations where class distributions differ by state, and low volume does not make it inappropriate.

places.quote: the complement is unbiased because it adjusts for the distributional differences, reasonably accurate when there is enough multi-state data

requirements.statement: Desirable qualities of a complement of credibility are: unbiased, statistically independent of the base statistic, available, accurate, easy to compute, and having a logical relationship to the base statistic.
requirements.concept: Qualities of a Complement of Credibility

places.quote: It should be (1) **accurate** — as low an error variance as possible around the future expected losses; (2) **unbiased** — not routinely higher or lower than the observed experience; … (6) **logically related** to the base statistic, so that its use is easy to support.

requirements.statement: Two-step premium trending: step 1 trends historical average premium at current rate level from its experience period to the latest available data point, and step 2 projects from that point to the average date of the future period, with the end date of step 1 being the start date of step 2.

places.quote: Step one brings historical average earned premium up to the **current** average written premium level (a known, observed figure); step two projects forward from there at a selected prospective trend:

requirements.statement: The step 1 trend factor equals the latest quarter's average written premium at current rate level divided by the calendar year's average earned premium at current rate level, carrying earned-date premium to the average written date.

places.quote: $$\text{Step 1} = \frac{\text{Latest avg written premium at CRL}}{\text{Historical avg earned premium at CRL}}$$

requirements.statement: The projected trend period runs from the average written date of the latest data quarter (midpoint of the quarter) to the average written date of policies written during the period the new rates are in effect (the midpoint of the policy writing period, e.g., one year after the effective date for annual policies).

places.quote: The trend period $n$ runs from the average written date of the policies earning premium in the experience period to the **average written date of the policies in effect while the new rates are** — for calendar-year 2011 earned premium and annual policies written in 2013, $1/1/2011$ to $6/30/2013$, or $2.5$ years.

requirements.statement: The step 2 projection factor is (1 + annual trend rate) raised to the length of the trend period in years.

places.quote: $$\text{Trend Factor} = (1 + t)^{n}$$
The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: Because premium is at current rate level, rate changes are excluded, so negative premium trend arises from changes in the characteristics of the business, such as a shift in mix toward lower-premium classes or territories, or insureds choosing higher deductibles or lower limits.

places.quote: **Premium Trend** is the change over time in the average premium per exposure at a *constant rate level* — the drift caused by distributional shifts in the policies written (amounts of insurance, limits, deductibles, [[Mix of Business|mix of business]])
In **ratemaking**, a mix shift shows up as premium trend (average premium moving without a rate change), as apparent loss trend, and as a change in the overall loss ratio.
Average premium drifts even when rates are unchanged, as the mix shifts toward higher deductibles, newer cars or higher insured values.

requirements.statement: Falling price levels (deflation) reduce premium per policy when the exposure base is inflation-sensitive, such as payroll or receipts, producing a negative premium trend; a mere decrease in the inflation rate does not.

places.quote: Under the [[Loss Ratio Method]] the effect enters through [[Premium Trend|premium trend]] instead: the premium at current rates grows with the exposure base even with no rate change, so the two methods handle the same phenomenon in different places and must not both be applied.
Some bases, such as payroll and sales revenue, are highly influenced by inflation, which is what [[Exposure Trend]] measures; count-based bases (car-years, house-years) are not.

requirements.statement: The univariate (one-way) relativity method estimates each level of a rating variable from that level's own pure premium or loss ratio, ignoring the effect of other rating variables.

places.quote: A **univariate** (one-way) pure premium or loss ratio analysis attributes to a variable the effect of everything correlated with it.
because a univariate pure premium picks up the effect of every correlated variable — checked against a multivariate ([[Generalized Linear Model|GLM]]) result before use.

requirements.statement: Univariate methods implicitly assume exposures are distributed uniformly across other rating variables; when exposures are correlated across variables (e.g., territory and class mix), the univariate indications are distorted by double-counting the other variable's effect.

places.quote: Urban territories carry different vehicle mixes, limit selections and driver populations, and a one-way territorial relativity absorbs all of it
The two variables are **correlated**: youthful drivers disproportionately drive old vehicles.
A univariate analysis assigns the whole effect to territory and would double-count when the other variables are rated too

requirements.statement: Test whether the univariate assumption holds by comparing the distribution of exposures across other rating variables (e.g., class mix) in each level of the variable being analyzed; a lower-rated class concentration biases the indication downward and a higher-rated class concentration biases it upward.

places.quote: **Correlation.** If urban policyholders also skew toward younger drivers or higher limits, part of the $2.00$ belongs to those variables rather than to geography.

requirements.statement: In the adjusted pure premium method, compute adjusted exposures for each level by multiplying exposures in each level of the other rating variable by that variable's current charged relativity and summing, to put exposures on an equivalent-base basis.

places.quote: When other rating variables also apply, each class's exposures are first multiplied by their average relativity for those other variables, so that the factor measures only this variable's effect on the average premium.

requirements.statement: Adjusted pure premium = loss (and ALAE) divided by adjusted exposures for the level.

places.quote: $$\text{Pure Premium} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Exposures}}$$
$$\text{Pure Premium} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Exposures}} = \text{Frequency} \times \text{Severity}$$

requirements.statement: Indicated relativity equals a level's adjusted pure premium divided by the base level's adjusted pure premium, so the base level has a relativity of 1.000.

places.quote: $$\text{Territory Relativity}_i = \frac{\text{Pure Premium}_i}{\text{Pure Premium}_{\text{base}}}$$
$$\text{Relativity}_i = \frac{\text{Pure Premium}_i}{\text{Pure Premium}_{\text{base}}}$$
$$\text{Relativity}_i = \frac{\text{Pure Premium}_i}{\text{Pure Premium}_{\text{base}}}$$

requirements.statement: In GLM output, a variable's chi-square percentage (p-value) below a conventional threshold such as 5% indicates the variable is statistically significant and supports including it as a rating variable.

places.quote: With a log link, a class coefficient $\hat{\beta}$ is a relativity of $e^{\hat{\beta}}$, and the [[p-Value|p-value]] behind $z$ is the chance of an estimate that far from zero if the class truly had no effect.

requirements.statement: Narrow standard error bands around GLM relativity estimates indicate the level estimates are precise, while wide bands (typically from thin data) indicate unreliable estimates.

places.quote: A sparse base widens every other level's interval, so the [[Generalized Linear Models for Insurance Rating (Goldburd et al. - 2020)|GLM monograph]] advises a base level with plenty of data.

requirements.statement: Substantial, ordered differences in fitted relativities across the levels of a variable show that the variable differentiates expected cost and supports its use in rating.

places.quote: In classification ratemaking it is the first actuarial test of whether a [[Rating Class|rate class]] has earned its own rate.
It must be statistically related to expected losses; a causal story strengthens the case, but ASOP No. 12 does not require one.

resolution.quote: Output is judged on more than significance: consistency of the pattern across levels, standard errors
resolution.note: The GLM page (tagged, syllabus) teaches judging a variable by the consistency of its pattern across levels (Werner Ch.10 p.179).

requirements.statement: Multivariate methods account for correlation among rating variables by evaluating all variables simultaneously, whereas univariate methods double-count effects shared by correlated variables.

places.quote: because it estimates every rating variable *simultaneously* and so reports each one net of the others — solving the correlation problem that makes univariate relativities double-count.

A **univariate** (one-way) pure premium or loss ratio analysis attributes to a variable the effect of everything correlated with it. If young drivers also drive older cars, a one-way age relativity contains part of the vehicle-age effect, and rating both double-counts.

requirements.statement: Multivariate methods can capture interactions between rating variables, where the effect of one variable depends on the level of another, which univariate methods cannot represent.

places.quote: A coefficient on a variable that is interacted with a continuous predictor $x$ describes the effect where $x = 0$.

requirements.statement: Multivariate methods provide statistical diagnostics (standard errors, significance tests, residuals) and separate systematic signal from random noise, giving more stable relativities than univariate methods.

places.quote: Output is judged on more than significance: consistency of the pattern across levels, standard errors, the effect of removing the variable (analysis of deviance), and validation on a holdout period.
**Model diagnostics** are the plots and statistics used *after* fitting to check whether a model's assumptions hold and, where they fail, how.

requirements.statement: Spatial smoothing improves territory relativity estimates by credibility-weighting a territory's own experience with the experience of nearby territories, using distance-based weights that decline with distance or adjacency-based weights from bordering territories.

places.quote: **Spatial smoothing** is what makes fine granularity workable: because loss cost varies continuously across space, a cell's estimate can borrow strength from its neighbours. Werner describes distance-based and adjacency-based smoothing, applied *before* territories are grouped.

Because geographic risk is similar for nearby units, actuaries smooth spatially: *distance-based* smoothing suits weather perils, *adjacency-based* smoothing suits perils driven by socio-demographic characteristics such as theft

requirements.statement: Spatial smoothing borrows information from neighboring territories, increasing effective data volume, narrowing confidence intervals, and producing relativities that vary smoothly across geography, which helps sparsely populated territories.

places.quote: because loss cost varies continuously across space, a cell's estimate can borrow strength from its neighbours.
too much or too little smoothing either masks real variation or leaves noise

requirements.statement: An increased limits factor (ILF) for a limit is the ratio of expected losses limited to that limit to expected losses limited to the basic limit.

places.quote: $$\text{ILF}(L) = \frac{E[X \wedge L]}{E[X \wedge B]}$$
Under its simplifying assumptions, the increased limit factor for limit $H$ over basic limit $B$ is $\text{ILF}(H) = \text{LAS}(H)/\text{LAS}(B)$

requirements.statement: Expected losses in a layer between two limits equal the expected basic limit losses times the difference between the ILFs at the upper and lower limits.

places.quote: $$\text{Layer } (M, L] \text{ cost} = \text{Basic LC} \times \left[\text{ILF}(L) - \text{ILF}(M)\right]$$
In [[Increased Limits|ILF]] form, it is the basic-limits loss cost $\times\,[\text{ILF}(b) - \text{ILF}(a)]$.

requirements.statement: Equal ILFs at two different limits imply zero expected loss, and therefore no premium, for the layer between them, which is inadequate and typically reflects a lack of credible loss experience in that high layer rather than truly zero expected loss.

places.quote: Flat is acceptable only in a degenerate case: it implies the expected loss in the $\$500$K–$\$1$M layer is the same per dollar as in the $\$250$K–$\$500$K layer, so $S(x)$ could not fall anywhere between $\$250$K and $\$1$M — no loss could end in that range.

requirements.statement: ILFs should increase with the limit but at a decreasing rate, so the indicated ILFs must be checked for consistency (monotonic, no zero-charge layers) before implementation.

places.quote: So the *marginal* indemnity cost per dollar of additional limit must not increase as the limit rises; an indemnity ILF table whose marginal cost increases is not consistent with any size-of-loss distribution.
Expected cost per dollar of limit falls as the layer rises (the consistency test).

requirements.statement: To derive ILFs for limits above those with experience, fit a parametric severity distribution to ground-up loss data, compute limited expected values at each limit from the fitted curve, and take ratios to the basic limit LEV.

places.quote: ILFs are estimated from a **size-of-loss distribution** — empirically, building the limited average severity layer by layer so that losses censored at policy limits introduce no bias, or from a fitted curve (lognormal, Pareto, truncated Pareto)
Under its simplifying assumptions, the increased limit factor for limit $H$ over basic limit $B$ is $\text{ILF}(H) = \text{LAS}(H)/\text{LAS}(B)$

requirements.statement: Alternative ways to get ILFs for new higher limits include using industry or bureau ILFs, or credibility-weighting the company's own indicated ILFs with industry ILFs.

places.quote: Data at high limits is sparse and volatile, which is why ILFs are calculated from a broader body of experience (class group, state group or countrywide) and applied to class-, state- and territory-specific basic limit loss costs.

**Excess (increased-limits) complements:** increased limits analysis, lower limits analysis, limits analysis, and the fitted-curve approach — all built on the fact that excess layers have too few claims ever to be credible on their own.

requirements.statement: Challenges in setting higher-limit ILFs include selecting a severity curve for the tail, loss data being censored at current policy limits so the tail is extrapolated with limited credibility, and the need for additional capital or reinsurance due to greater volatility.

places.quote: Data at high limits is sparse and volatile, which is why ILFs are calculated from a broader body of experience (class group, state group or countrywide) and applied to class-, state- and territory-specific basic limit loss costs.
**Right-censoring**: true value exceeds $c$ (e.g., policy limit reached, study ends before claim settles)

**The tail decides the excess layers.** Two severity distributions with the same mean can put very different amounts above a high attachment point. Excess pricing depends on how well the tail is fitted, and the mean says little about it.

requirements.statement: The change in a territory's relativity equals its indicated relativity divided by its current relativity.

places.quote: A class's rate change is $(1 + \Delta)\,\text{OBF}\,r_i^{\text{new}}/r_i^{\text{old}} - 1$.

requirements.statement: Because moving to indicated relativities changes the average rate level, compute an off-balance factor as the reciprocal of the premium-weighted average of the relativity changes, so the overall rate change still hits the target.

places.quote: must be **off-balanced** against any simultaneous change in relativities so the two together deliver the intended effect.
OBF, the off-balance factor, is the average relativity before the change divided by the average relativity after it.

requirements.statement: A territory's total rate change is the product of its relativity change, the off-balance factor, and one plus the overall target rate change.

places.quote: A class's rate change is $(1 + \Delta)\,\text{OBF}\,r_i^{\text{new}}/r_i^{\text{old}} - 1$.

requirements.statement: When a territory's change exceeds a cap, set it at the cap and recover the resulting premium shortfall by scaling up the changes of the uncapped territories by a common redistribution factor, so total premium still meets the target.

places.quote: a cap on the change for any level of a rating variable is made up by adjusting the base rate and the other relativities
The base rate has to be adjusted to make up the capped premium

requirements.statement: To convert capped rate changes back to relativities, multiply each territory's capped change by its current relativity, then divide by the base territory's resulting value so the base territory's relativity equals 1.00.

places.quote: Relative to class A, the new relativities are $1.25(0.660/0.600) = 1.375$ for B and $1.60(0.750/0.600) = 2.000$ for C.

requirements.statement: Under a coinsurance clause, the apportionment ratio equals the amount of insurance carried divided by the amount required (coinsurance percentage times property value).

places.quote: $$a = \min\!\left(\frac{F}{cV},\ 1.0\right)$$
$$R = \min\left(\frac{C}{p \times V},\ 1\right)$$

requirements.statement: The insurer's indemnity equals the apportionment ratio times the loss (less any deductible), capped at the policy limit; the coinsurance penalty is the loss amount the insurer does not pay because of underinsurance.

places.quote: Fall short and every partial loss is settled at the ratio of insurance carried to insurance required.
$$\text{Payment} = \min\big(R \times L - D,\ C\big)$$

requirements.statement: With no deductible, the amount of loss equals the indemnity payment plus the coinsurance penalty.

places.quote: The insured absorbs the rest or relies on other insurance.
The insured absorbs $\$50{,}000$ — a penalty for under-insurance, not a deductible.

requirements.statement: An inflation guard endorsement automatically increases the amount of insurance periodically by a set percentage or construction cost index, keeping coverage in step with replacement cost.

places.quote: or an inflation guard, which raises the limit through the year.
The limit increases automatically by the annual percentage shown in the declarations, pro rata by days, from the most recent of the inception, anniversary or limit-changing date.

requirements.statement: Insurers can encourage insurance to value by offering guaranteed replacement cost only to insureds who insure to a specified percentage of estimated replacement cost.

places.quote: The homeowners replacement cost condition pays full replacement cost only when the dwelling is insured for at least 80% of its replacement cost (see the second example on [[Replacement Cost]]).
The homeowners form also pays replacement cost only when the dwelling is insured for at least 80% of its full replacement cost, which is an [[Insurance to Value|insurance to value]] provision.

requirements.statement: Other insurance-to-value initiatives include property valuation software to identify underinsured homes, inspections or appraisals to establish replacement cost, and education about coinsurance penalties and underinsurance.

places.quote: That is why underwriters verify property values with appraisals and building cost estimates

requirements.statement: The cumulative development factor at a given maturity is the product of the age-to-age factors from that maturity to ultimate (with a tail factor of 1.000 if there is no development beyond the last age).

places.quote: $$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \left(\prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1}\right) \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: The loss development method estimates ultimate loss as reported (or paid) loss to date times the cumulative development factor.

places.quote: $$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate} = C_n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson method estimates ultimate loss as reported loss plus expected loss (expected loss ratio times premium) times the percent unreported, where percent unreported is 1 - 1/CDF.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$
$$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$

requirements.statement: The BF a priori expected loss uses unadjusted earned premium; on-leveling and trending are done in the rate indication, not in the BF expected loss calculation.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}$$

requirements.statement: The development method is highly leveraged for immature years because reported losses are multiplied by a large CDF, making it volatile; BF is more stable for immature years, while for mature years the methods converge and either is acceptable.

places.quote: It is therefore the method of choice at **immature maturities** and for [[Long Tail Lines|long-tail lines]], converging to the chain ladder as the cohort matures.

At a CDF of $4$, a dollar of distortion on the diagonal becomes four dollars of ultimate — which is why the chain ladder is unreliable at immature ages in [[Long Tail Lines|long-tail lines]] and why methods that develop only the *unreported* portion are preferred there.

requirements.statement: On-level factors are found with the parallelogram method: for annual policies written evenly, a mid-year rate change affects 12.5% of that year's earned premium and 87.5% of the next year's; the OLF is the current rate level divided by the calendar year's average rate level.

places.quote: $$\text{OLF}_Y = \frac{I_{\text{current}}}{\sum_k A_{Y,k}\, I_k}$$

For **annual** policies written uniformly, a rate change effective at time $p$ through year $Y$ earns over a triangle of area $\tfrac{1}{2}(1-p)^2$ in year $Y$ — so a $7/1$ change affects only $0.125$ of that year's earned premium, and a $1/1$ change affects $0.500$.

requirements.statement: Trend periods run from the average date of each historical period (average earned date for premium, average accident date for losses) to the average date the proposed rates will be in effect (for annual policies, one year after the effective date plus half the policy term to reach average accident date); losses and premium are trended using compound annual trend factors over those periods.

places.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.
$$\text{Premium Trend Factor} = (1 + t_P)^{n}$$

requirements.statement: The projected loss ratio is trended ultimate loss and ALAE divided by on-level trended earned premium, summed across years, then loaded for ULAE as a percentage of loss and ALAE.

places.quote: The numerator's loss ratio must be **projected**: ultimate losses (developed), trended to the future policy period, over earned premium brought to **current rate level** ([[On-Leveling]]) and trended ([[Premium Trend]]).

It cannot be traced to a claim, so it is estimated in aggregate — classically as the ratio of calendar-year paid ULAE to calendar-year paid loss plus ALAE, applied to loss plus ALAE that has been adjusted for extraordinary events, development and trend.

requirements.statement: The indicated rate change is (projected loss and LAE ratio + fixed expense ratio) / (1 - variable expense ratio - profit and contingencies provision) minus 1.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$

requirements.statement: With full credibility, the indicated rate change is based entirely on the experience-period indication with no complement of credibility.
Earned premium for a period is the portion of a policy's written premium corresponding to the part of its term that has expired within that period.

places.quote: **Earned Premium** is the portion of premium corresponding to coverage the insurer has actually provided — the premium it has earned the right to keep, recognized pro rata as the policy term elapses.

requirements.statement: Compute a policy's earned premium in a period by pro rata allocation: written premium times months of the policy's own term falling in the period divided by the total months of that policy's term.

places.quote: $$\text{EP for one policy} = \text{Full premium} \times \frac{\text{days elapsed}}{\text{policy term}}$$

requirements.statement: Policies that expired before the start of the period contribute no earned premium to that period, and a policy whose whole term lies within the period earns its full premium.

places.quote: $$\text{EP for one policy} = \text{Full premium} \times \frac{\text{days elapsed}}{\text{policy term}}$$
The January cohort earns $12/12$ of a year, the February cohort $11/12$, and so on down to the December cohort's $1/12$:

requirements.statement: Unearned premium at a valuation date is the portion of written premium for the unexpired part of policies still in force at that date (written premium minus earned premium).

places.quote: **Unearned Premium** is the portion of written premium corresponding to coverage not yet provided — the insurer's obligation to either provide the remaining coverage or return the premium.
The unbooked remainder sits in the [[Unearned Premium|unearned premium reserve]].

requirements.statement: Accident year groups claims by the date of the accident (occurrence), regardless of when the claim is reported or paid.

places.quote: **Accident Year** (AY) is a data aggregation method that groups losses by the calendar year in which the loss event *occurred*, and matches them against the [[Earned Premium|premium earned]] in that same year — regardless of when the policy was written, when the claim was reported, or when it was paid.

requirements.statement: Reported claims (losses) net of reinsurance equal gross paid claims plus gross case reserves minus reinsurance recoveries.

places.quote: $$\text{Net} = \text{Gross} - \text{Ceded} - \text{S\&S} - \text{Deductible Recoveries}$$
$$\text{CY Reported Losses} = \text{Paid} + \Delta\text{Case Reserves}$$

requirements.statement: Development techniques assume the historical development pattern applies to immature years, so data grouped with differing development patterns (e.g., short-tail and long-tail coverages) must be separated into homogeneous groups to give accurate unpaid claim estimates.

places.quote: Two coverages may have similar loss ratios and completely different reporting and settlement speeds; combining them into one triangle produces development factors that describe neither.
Combining them would average a multi-year liability pattern with an essentially immediate property pattern, producing development factors that fit neither.

requirements.statement: A combined triangle blending segments with different development patterns yields a biased estimate when the mix of business between segments shifts (e.g., coverage changes, legislative changes affecting one segment).

places.quote: If the insurer grows the liability side to $55\%$ of premium, the true blended factor rises, but the historical triangle still reports $1.28$ — the estimate is now biased low, and nothing in the triangle reveals why.
If the segments have different emergence patterns, the blended development factors drift as the weights drift — and the triangle gives no signal that this is what is happening.

requirements.statement: Analyzing segments separately lets changes in frequency, severity, settlement rates or case reserve adequacy be attributed to the segment where they occur rather than being masked, revealing emerging trends earlier.

places.quote: Diagnosing which has moved requires segment-level data; the aggregate alone cannot distinguish them.

requirements.statement: External or industry data reflects other companies' business mix, underwriting, claim handling, case reserve adequacy and settlement practices, so its patterns may not be relevant to the insurer's own book; internal data is more relevant.
requirements.concept: Use of External Data in Reserving

places.quote: **Never use external data unadjusted.** It must be reconciled to the subject book on the dimensions that actually drive development: coverage and [[Line of Business|line of business]] definitions, policy limits and attachment points, [[Mix of Business|mix of business]], jurisdiction and legal environment, [[Case Adequacy|case-reserve adequacy]] philosophy, and [[Settlement Rate|settlement speed]].
The combined experience may not reflect any one reinsurer's markets, terms and operations.

requirements.statement: Long-tailed coverages like bodily injury need many years of history to observe ultimate development; with limited history, internal data lacks credibility and the tail must be extrapolated or supplied by external data.

places.quote: **When external data is needed:** a new line or new company with no history; a small or newly segmented book whose triangle is too volatile to be [[Credibility|credible]]; the immature end of a long-tail triangle where a [[Tail Factor]] must be chosen; and as an independent reasonableness check on a selection driven entirely by internal data.

The tail is the one factor with **no data behind it**, and in [[Long Tail Lines|long-tail lines]] it is often the single largest assumption in the analysis. A triangle that runs ten years still misses decades of workers compensation medical payments.
