requirements.statement: Splitting data into more segments reduces the volume in each, increasing the variability of link ratios and lowering credibility, so there is a trade-off between homogeneity and credibility.

places.quote: Homogeneity is always traded against [[Credibility]]. Splitting a book finer makes each group more alike but leaves each with less data;
Credibility governs the **homogeneity trade-off**: splitting a book finer improves [[Homogeneity|homogeneity]] but shrinks $n$ in each cell, lowering $Z$ and handing the answer to the complement.
The trade-off is in the formula: every further split makes the groups more alike but shrinks $n_g$, so more of each group's estimate is handed to the [[Complement of Credibility|complement]].

requirements.statement: Separate analyses by segment require more data preparation, selections and review, and volatile reserve estimates can cause swings in reported results and key financial metrics watched by investors, rating agencies and regulators.

places.quote: **Practical limits:** a segment needs a field the systems actually capture; separate analyses cost time; and a small, stable component may not justify its own study.
**Investors and rating agencies** — reserve development history, volatility, and the effect on reported earnings; adverse development is a disclosure item. See [[Stakeholder Reporting]].

requirements.statement: Ultimate claims equal ultimate claim counts times ultimate severity (average claim size), computed separately for each accident period.

places.quote: $$U = N_{\text{ult}} \times S_{\text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: Severity is an average, so severities of sub-periods (e.g., half-years) cannot be summed to get an annual severity; compute ultimate claims for each sub-period and add the dollars.

resolution.note: Arithmetic: a severity is an average, so sub-period severities are not summed; ultimate dollars are added instead.

requirements.statement: Apply the chain ladder method to the reported count and reported severity triangles: compute age-to-age factors, select factors, form cumulative development factors to ultimate (including a tail), and multiply the latest diagonal value by the CDF for its age.

places.quote: **The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: When development factors differ systematically by season (e.g., first versus second half of the year), select separate development patterns for each season rather than averaging across all periods.

resolution.note: A selection judgment on the question's own half-year data; Friedland gives no seasonal rule (Development Triangle, in reach, notes finer periods show seasonality).

requirements.statement: Use the CDF matching each accident period's current age (e.g., the 12-to-ultimate CDF for a period evaluated at 12 months), applied to the value at that age.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: Reported claim counts excluding claims closed with no payment can develop downward because claims counted at early maturities are removed when later closed without payment, and this outweighs newly reported claims.
requirements.concept: Claim Count Development / Closed Without Payment

requirements.statement: Seasonality can only be detected with data at a finer granularity than annual (monthly, quarterly, semi-annual), by comparing the same sub-periods across years; diagnostics include triangles of closed-to-reported count ratios, implied frequency, or each quarter's share of the annual total by maturity.

places.quote: Signature on the [[Autocorrelation Function|ACF]]: significant spikes at lags $s, 2s, 3s, \dots$ that do not die away

requirements.statement: Age-to-age (link ratio) development factors are the ratio of cumulative claims at a later age to cumulative claims at the prior age for the same accident year, and the age-to-ultimate factor is the product of the subsequent age-to-age factors including the tail factor.

places.quote: **Age-to-Age Factor** (link ratio) is the ratio of a cohort's cumulative amount at one maturity to its amount at the previous maturity — the observed development between two ages.

**Cumulative Development Factor** (CDF, or age-to-ultimate factor) is the product of all selected [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] from a given maturity through to ultimate, including the [[Tail Factor|tail]].

requirements.statement: In the reported claims development technique, ultimate claims equal the latest cumulative reported claims multiplied by the age-to-ultimate factor for that maturity.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate} = C_n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: A tail factor (the oldest age-to-ultimate factor) can be derived from the ultimate claims already estimated for the oldest accident year divided by its latest reported claims.

resolution.quote: projects each cohort to ultimate by multiplying its latest cumulative amount by a
resolution.note: The chain-ladder relation U = C x CDF (syllabus page), read backwards with the question's own ultimate for the oldest year, gives the tail.

requirements.statement: Age-to-age factors are selected from the triangle, for example as an all-year weighted average or from consistent observed link ratios, and applied to less mature accident years.

places.quote: **The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.
- **Volume-weighted (all-year)** — the ratio of column sums. Weights each year by its size, so it is stable and dominated by the large years. The default choice.
- **Volume-weighted average**: $\Sigma(\text{col }n{+}1) / \Sigma(\text{col }n)$ — gives more credibility to larger accident years; the standard default selection

requirements.statement: A triangle of cumulative paid claims divided by cumulative reported claims (paid-to-reported ratios) is a diagnostic used to detect changes in claim settlement speed or case reserve adequacy.

places.quote: **[[Case Adequacy|Case strengthening]]:** average case outstanding rises faster than trend on the latest diagonals, and paid-to-reported falls.

Comparing the two is a standard diagnostic: a change in the paid-to-reported ratio signals a change in settlement patterns or in case adequacy … a rising ratio is consistent with faster settlement or weaker case reserves, a falling one with slower settlement or stronger case reserves

requirements.statement: A decline in paid-to-reported ratios in recent accident years at the same age indicates slower claim settlement (e.g. tighter claims handling) or stronger case reserves, which violates the stable-development assumption of the reported and paid development techniques.

places.quote: **The pattern is stable over calendar time.** Violated by a change in [[Case Adequacy|case adequacy]], [[Settlement Rate|settlement speed]] or [[Inflation|inflation]] — the diagonal effects.
**[[Case Adequacy|Case strengthening]]:** average case outstanding rises faster than trend on the latest diagonals, and paid-to-reported falls.
a falling one with slower settlement or stronger case reserves

requirements.statement: Understated unpaid claims overstate profitability, which can mislead investors into investing, lead regulators to set lower target profit or fail to detect insolvency risk, and cause management to make poor expansion or pricing decisions.

places.quote: Redundancy is a profit deferral; deficiency understates the loss ratio, overstates surplus, and feeds an inadequate rate indication back into pricing, so the same error appears again in next year's business.

Accuracy matters beyond the balance sheet: unpaid claim estimates drive solvency assessment, [[Ratemaking|ratemaking]] (through ultimate loss ratios), reinsurance commutations, collateral requirements, and the price of the company itself in a transaction.

requirements.statement: On-level premium (earned premium at current rate level) is historical earned premium restated as if all policies had been written at the current rate level; the on-level factor is the current rate level divided by the average rate level earned during the period.

places.quote: **On-Level Premium** is historical earned premium restated as though every policy had been written at the rate level currently in effect.
$$\text{On-Level Factor} = \frac{\text{Current cumulative index}}{\text{Average index for the year}}$$

requirements.statement: Use the parallelogram method for annual policies written uniformly: a rate change effective a fraction p through the year leaves p^2/2 of the following year's earned premium at the old level and puts (1-p)^2/2 of its own year at the new level; the area between is at the intermediate level, and every rate change affecting the year must be included.

places.quote: The second formula is the area earned in the same calendar year at a new level effective a fraction $p$ of the way through it, for annual policies.

For **annual** policies written uniformly, a rate change effective at time $p$ through year $Y$ earns over a triangle of area $\tfrac{1}{2}(1-p)^2$ in year $Y$ — so a $7/1$ change affects only $0.125$ of that year's earned premium, and a $1/1$ change affects $0.500$.

requirements.statement: The cumulative rate level index is the product of (1 + rate change) over successive rate changes, and the current rate level is the index after the latest change.

places.quote: Rate level indices **compound**: successive changes of $+8\%$ and $+5\%$ give a cumulative index of $1.08 \times 1.05 = 1.134$, not $1.13$.
$I_k$ is the cumulative rate level index of rate level group $k$ (each index is the previous one times $1 +$ that change)

requirements.statement: Trend on-level premium from each year's average earned date (July 1 for a calendar year) to the average earned date of the projected period, using (1+trend)^years; for annual policies with rates in effect one year, the average earned date is one year after the effective date (six months after the average written date).

places.quote: The trend period $n$ runs from the average written date of the policies earning premium in the experience period to the **average written date of the policies in effect while the new rates are** — for calendar-year 2011 earned premium and annual policies written in 2013, $1/1/2011$ to $6/30/2013$, or $2.5$ years.
$t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.

requirements.statement: With fixed expenses as a percentage of premium, the loss ratio indicated rate change is (projected loss & LAE ratio + fixed expense provision) / (1 − variable expense provision − profit provision) − 1.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$

requirements.statement: The projected loss and LAE ratio equals projected ultimate loss and LAE divided by projected earned premium at current rate level.

places.quote: The numerator's loss ratio must be **projected**: ultimate losses (developed), trended to the future policy period, over earned premium brought to **current rate level** ([[On-Leveling]]) and trended ([[Premium Trend]]).

requirements.statement: Frequency in the frequency-severity technique is ultimate claim counts divided by an exposure base (e.g., payroll), expressed as claims per unit of exposure.

places.quote: **Frequency** is the number of claims per unit of exposure — how often losses happen, as distinct from [[Severity|how much they cost]].

requirements.statement: To compare frequencies across accident years, trend both the claim counts (at the claim count trend rate) and the inflation-sensitive exposure base (at its inflation rate) from each accident year to the target year's level, with trend periods equal to the number of years from each accident year to the target year, before dividing.

places.quote: Exposure trend applies **only** to inflation-sensitive bases. Car-years and house-years do not inflate; payroll, receipts and amount of insurance do.
The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: Select an ultimate frequency from the trended historical frequencies by judging their pattern: if frequencies show a consistent increasing trend, weight recent years more heavily (e.g., latest year or short average), and justify the selection.

places.quote: The series is not a constant trend — it **accelerated** around $2022$. The five-year figure averages the old regime with the new one and understates the current level of inflation; the two-year figure is responsive but rests on three observations.

requirements.statement: Select an ultimate severity for the projected year by trending each available selected ultimate severity to the projected year's level at the severity trend rate and averaging them; severity is selected independently of the selected frequency.

places.quote: **Counts and trended severity.** Develop counts, but estimate severity by **trending** a mature year's severity forward rather than developing an immature one — useful where severity development is unstable but severity trend is well understood.
$$\text{Trend Factor} = (1 + t)^{n}$$

requirements.statement: The frequency-severity ultimate claims equals the selected frequency times the projected year's exposure base times the selected severity (watching units of the exposure base).

places.quote: $$U = \text{Exposures} \times \text{Frequency}_{\text{ult}} \times S_{\text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Pure Premium} = \text{Frequency} \times \text{Severity}$$

requirements.statement: The percent unreported equals 1 minus 1/CDF, where the CDF is the cumulative reported claims development factor at the evaluation age.

places.quote: - $C$ is reported (or paid) losses to date, $U_0 = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}$ the a priori expectation, and $1 - 1/\text{CDF}$ the percentage unreported from the [[Development Triangle|development pattern]].
The reciprocal is the **percentage reported** (or paid): $p_n = 1/\text{CDF}_n$, and $1 - p_n$ is the percentage unreported.

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson ultimate equals actual reported claims plus the expected ultimate claims (a priori, here from the frequency-severity technique) times the percent unreported.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$
$$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$

requirements.statement: The Cape Cod technique is a Bornhuetter-Ferguson method in which the expected claim ratio is derived from the data (reported claims relative to used-up premium across all years) rather than selected externally.

places.quote: **Cape Cod Method** (Stanard-Bühlmann) is the [[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method|Bornhuetter-Ferguson]] technique with the a priori loss ratio **derived from the data itself** rather than supplied externally.
Where no reliable external ELR exists, the [[Cape Cod Method|Cape Cod]] technique derives one from the data instead.

requirements.statement: Used-up premium for an accident year equals on-level earned premium divided by the reported claims development factor (CDF) to ultimate.

places.quote: **Used-up premium** $\text{EP}_i / \text{CDF}_i$ is the share of each year's premium "exposed" to the losses reported so far.
$P_i / \text{CDF}_i$ is the **used-up premium**, the share of the premium that the claims reported so far correspond to.

requirements.statement: The Cape Cod expected claim ratio equals total (adjusted) reported claims across all years divided by total used-up premium across all years, using undeveloped claims in the numerator.

places.quote: $$\text{ELR} = \frac{\sum_i C_i}{\sum_i \text{EP}_i \times \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}}$$

requirements.statement: Developed (ultimate) claims must not be paired with used-up premium; developed claims pair with full on-level premium and undeveloped reported claims pair with used-up premium, otherwise development is double-counted.

places.quote: Weighting the developed loss ratios by full premium gives immature years far too much say.

resolution.quote: is the share of each year's premium "exposed" to the losses reported so far.
resolution.note: The tagged Cape Cod page teaches that used-up premium pairs with reported (undeveloped) losses (Friedland Ch.10).

requirements.statement: To adjust for a legislative change that alters claim costs, restate each accident year's claims to a common cost level by applying a reform factor of (1 − change) to years before the effective date and no adjustment to years fully after it.
requirements.concept: Claims Adjustment for Benefit Level Changes

places.quote: Split accident years at the effective date and adjust expected claim ratios with a law-change estimate.

**Benefit-level changes** in statutory lines (workers compensation reform, auto no-fault changes) are the same problem at industry scale, and are handled by a law-level adjustment factor applied to historical losses before trend — deliberately kept separate from trend so the two are not confused.
Premium must be [[On-Leveling|on level]], claims must be [[Loss Trend|trended]] and adjusted for changes such as tort reform, and the development factors must be sound.

requirements.statement: Bornhuetter-Ferguson ultimate claims = reported claims + expected claim ratio × on-level earned premium × (1 − 1/CDF), i.e., reported plus expected unreported claims.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$
$$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$

requirements.statement: When the expected claim ratio is stated at a common cost level, the expected-claims term must be restated back to a given accident year's own cost level (e.g., dividing by the reform factor) if that year is not at the common level.
requirements.concept: Claims Adjustment for Benefit Level Changes

places.quote: $$\text{Adjusted ELR}_i = \text{ELR}_{\text{base}} \times \frac{\text{Rate level}_{\text{base}}}{\text{Rate level}_i} \times \frac{\text{Loss trend}_i}{\text{Loss trend}_{\text{base}}}$$

requirements.statement: Paid claims equal reported (incurred) claims minus case outstanding, so a paid triangle can be derived from reported and case outstanding triangles.

places.quote: $$\text{Reported Losses} = \text{Paid Losses} + \text{Case Reserves}$$
$$= \text{Paid Losses} + \text{Case Reserves}$$

requirements.statement: Compute age-to-age development factors from a cumulative triangle as ratios of successive maturities, select a factor for each period (e.g., an average of the observed factors), and multiply selected factors with a tail factor to obtain the cumulative development factor to ultimate.

places.quote: $$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{AY}} = \frac{C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \left(\prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1}\right) \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: When there is no development after the last observed maturity, the tail factor equals 1.000.

places.quote: A tail of exactly $1.000$ is itself an assumption — that development is complete

requirements.statement: Ultimate claims equal reported claims times the reported CDF and also equal paid claims times the paid CDF, so reported = U/reported CDF and paid = U/paid CDF; case outstanding = reported − paid and unpaid = ultimate − paid.

places.quote: $$\text{Ultimate}_{\text{paid}} = \text{Paid}_n \times \text{CDF}^{\text{paid}}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Unpaid} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Paid to date}$$

requirements.statement: The case outstanding development factor at a maturity equals industry unpaid claims divided by industry case outstanding, i.e., (1 − 1/paid CDF) / (1/reported CDF − 1/paid CDF), equivalently 1 + (reported CDF − 1)(paid CDF)/(paid CDF − reported CDF).

places.quote: $$f_{\text{case}} = \frac{\text{All future payments}}{\text{Current case outstanding}}$$

requirements.statement: In the case outstanding technique, the industry-derived factor for the accident year's maturity is applied to the company's own case outstanding to estimate the company's unpaid claims.

places.quote: $$U = \text{Paid to date} + \text{Case Outstanding} \times f_{\text{case}}$$

requirements.statement: Limitations of the case outstanding technique with industry factors: industry case reserving, settlement practices and business mix may differ from the company's; factors are highly leveraged at early maturities; it provides no explicit pure IBNR; and a large claim in case outstanding distorts the projection.

places.quote: It must be reconciled to the subject book on the dimensions that actually drive development
A [[Large Loss|shock loss]] reported early is multiplied by the full CDF.

requirements.statement: In the disposal-rate frequency-severity method, the tail severity at maturity m is the average severity of all claims closing at age m and later, i.e. pooled paid dollars divided by pooled closed claim counts for all cells at maturity m or beyond.
Compute a tail severity by summing trended incremental paid losses over all cells at maturity m or later and dividing by the sum of untrended incremental closed counts over those same cells.
Trend incremental paid claims to a target cost level by applying (1+trend)^(target year - accident year) to every cell in an accident year's row, regardless of maturity.

places.quote: **Loss Trend** is the annual rate of change in loss cost over time — driven by inflation, the legal environment, technology, safety and mix — applied to bring historical losses from the cost level of the experience period to the cost level of the **future policy period**.
The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: The tail severity at age m equals the count-weighted average of the severity of claims closing at age m and the tail severity at the next age, which allows building tail severities recursively from a later-age tail severity.

resolution.note: Arithmetic: a pooled average severity is the count-weighted average of its parts; the tail-severity definition itself is the write item r1/r2.

requirements.statement: To choose the maturity at which to combine data into a single tail severity, compare trended incremental severities by cell (paid x trend / counts) across accident years and pick the age where they stop being stable and credible, keeping earlier ages as their own steps.

Combining at too early an age discards usable development detail, while combining too late leaves the tail selection resting on few, volatile claims; late-maturity incremental severities based on small claim counts are erratic and noisy.

Diagnose a change in case reserve adequacy versus a change in settlement rate: flat closed-to-reported count ratios indicate no settlement rate change, while a sharply falling average case outstanding on the latest diagonal alongside steady average paid severity indicates weakened case reserves.

places.quote: A jump concentrated on one **diagonal**, appearing at every maturity at once, is a change in reserving practice, not in claim cost.
**[[Case Adequacy|Case strengthening]]:** average case outstanding rises faster than trend on the latest diagonals, and paid-to-reported falls.

**Reported data is largely immune**, because reported losses include the case reserve whether or not the claim has closed. So a paid-versus-reported divergence, together with a moving disposal rate, is the diagnostic pair.

requirements.statement: The Berquist-Sherman case outstanding adjustment restates the whole reported triangle to the case adequacy level of the latest diagonal, so the latest diagonal of reported claims is unchanged.

places.quote: Against the original reported figures ($\$1{,}300{,}000$, $\$1{,}350{,}000$, $\$1{,}675{,}000$), the older years have been raised by around $19\%$ while the latest is unchanged.

requirements.statement: Select a severity trend from year-over-year changes in average paid claim severity (unaffected by case reserving practice), not from total claims or average case outstanding.

places.quote: **Paid data is immune**, so a divergence between paid and reported chain ladder estimates is the corroborating evidence.
Severity triangles are read down the **column**, not across the row: comparing accident years at the *same* maturity isolates the change in cost level, while movement along a row is development.
$$\text{Annual Trend} = \left(\frac{S_n}{S_0}\right)^{1/n} - 1$$

requirements.statement: Adjusted average case outstanding for each accident year is the latest-diagonal average case outstanding in that maturity column de-trended backwards at the selected trend rate for each year of difference.

places.quote: $$\text{Adjusted Case}_{\text{AY},n} = \text{Case}_{\text{latest},n} \times \left(1 + t\right)^{-(\text{years before latest})}$$

resolution.quote: Trend the latest diagonal's average case outstanding backwards at
resolution.note: Stale: the tagged Berquist-Sherman page still teaches de-trending the latest diagonal's average case outstanding (Friedland Ch.13), now as a numbered step.

requirements.statement: Adjusted reported claims = actual paid claims + adjusted average case outstanding × actual open claim counts.

places.quote: $$\text{Adjusted Reported}_{\text{AY},n} = \text{Paid}_{\text{AY},n} + \text{Adjusted Case}_{\text{AY},n}$$

resolution.quote: Multiply the restated averages by the open claim counts to get adjusted case reserves, add paid, and rebuild the reported triangle.
resolution.note: Stale: the tagged Berquist-Sherman page still teaches adjusted reported = paid + adjusted average case x open counts (Friedland Ch.13).

requirements.statement: Develop the adjusted reported triangle to ultimate by selecting volume-weighted age-to-age factors, multiplying them into a cumulative development factor, and applying it to the latest reported claims.

places.quote: **Volume-weighted (all-year)** — the ratio of column sums. Weights each year by its size, so it is stable and dominated by the large years. The default choice.

**The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.

requirements.statement: IBNR (total, including development on known claims) = ultimate claims minus reported (case-incurred) claims, not minus paid claims.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Reported}$$
$$\text{IBNR} = \text{Ultimate Losses} - \text{Reported Losses}$$

requirements.statement: When case reserve adequacy changes, techniques that avoid case reserves (paid development, paid frequency-severity/disposal rate, expected claims) remain appropriate, whereas unadjusted reported development, reported Bornhuetter-Ferguson, or reported Cape Cod are distorted.
requirements.concept: Choosing Reserving Methods Under Changing Conditions

places.quote: **Paid data is immune**, so a divergence between paid and reported chain ladder estimates is the corroborating evidence.
*Case strengthening*: reported development overstates, reported BF and Cape Cod overstate less; paid methods and expected claims are unaffected.

requirements.statement: To apply the reported claims development technique to a reinsured book, first subtract ceded excess of loss reported claims from gross reported claims to build a net-of-XOL reported triangle, then develop that net triangle.

places.quote: $$\text{Net} = \text{Gross} - \text{Ceded}$$
Friedland does not prescribe one route: some actuaries analyze gross and ceded and derive net, others analyze gross and net, depending on data availability, the reinsurance programme and preference.

requirements.statement: Age-to-age factors are ratios of cumulative reported claims at successive ages, a selected factor is chosen (e.g. by averaging), and the cumulative development factor to ultimate is the product of the selected factors from that age onward (with a tail factor of 1.000 when there is no development beyond the last age).

places.quote: $$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$
$$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{AY}} = \frac{C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$

**The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.

requirements.statement: Projected ultimate claims equal latest cumulative reported claims multiplied by the cumulative development factor for that age.

places.quote: $$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ceded Ultimate} = \text{Ceded Reported} \times \text{CDF}^{\text{ceded}}$$

requirements.statement: An aggregate stop loss reinsurance caps an accident year's total net losses at the stop loss limit, so it applies to the projected ultimate (and to paid-to-date) after the per-occurrence excess of loss treaty has been netted out, not to the triangle used to derive development factors.

places.quote: Typically per-occurrence excess comes off first, then the quota share applies to what remains, and the stop-loss applies last to protect the final net result.
Over a stated period, the reinsurer pays the amount by which the total losses $S$ exceed a retention $d$, and the expected value of that payment, $E[(S - d)_+]$, is the **net stop-loss premium**.
**Aggregate Excess of Loss** reinsurance responds to the **total** of the cedant's losses over a period, usually a year, rather than to any single loss.

requirements.statement: Net ultimate after all reinsurance is the minimum of ultimate net of XOL and the stop loss limit (no cap for years without a stop loss), and paid claims net of XOL must likewise be capped at the stop loss limit before being subtracted.

places.quote: $$Y = \min\left(\max(S - A,\, 0),\; L_A\right)$$
$$\text{Ceded}_{\text{Agg}} = \min\left(\max(S - A,\,0),\; L_A\right)$$
**Stop-loss:** the ceded ultimate is $3{,}220 - 3{,}000 = 220$, and nothing is ceded on paid because $2{,}100 < 3{,}000$.

requirements.statement: Unpaid claims equal ultimate claims minus paid claims to date, with both measured on the same net-of-reinsurance basis.

places.quote: $$\text{Unpaid} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Paid to date}$$

requirements.statement: The classical (paid-to-paid) ULAE technique uses a ratio of calendar year paid ULAE to calendar year paid claims.

places.quote: **Classical (dollar-based, paid-to-paid).** Compute the ratio $R$ of calendar-year paid ULAE to calendar-year paid loss, review it for trend, and apply it to unpaid claims.

It cannot be traced to a claim, so it is estimated in aggregate — classically as the ratio of calendar-year paid ULAE to calendar-year paid loss plus ALAE, applied to loss plus ALAE that has been adjusted for extraordinary events, development and trend.

requirements.statement: The classical technique assumes half of ULAE is incurred when a claim is opened and half as it is closed/paid over its life, so ULAE for reported claims is 50% remaining and for unreported claims is 100% remaining.

places.quote: If ULAE is assumed to be spent half at reporting and half at settlement, only $50\%$ remains on reported-but-unpaid claims while $100\%$ remains on [[IBNR]] — the formula above.

requirements.statement: Unpaid ULAE under the classical technique = paid-to-paid ULAE ratio × (50% × case reserves + 100% × IBNR).

places.quote: $$\text{ULAE Reserve} = R \times \left(0.5 \times \text{Case} + 1.0 \times \text{IBNR}\right)$$

requirements.statement: Calendar year paid claims are obtained by summing incremental payments (differences between successive cumulative values) along each diagonal of the accident year triangle.

A multi-year weighted average ULAE ratio equals total paid ULAE divided by total paid claims over the period, so total ULAE equals ratio times total paid claims and a missing year's ULAE can be found by subtracting known years.

resolution.note: Arithmetic: a multi-year weighted ULAE ratio is total paid ULAE over total paid claims, with the ratio given by the question; the classical ratio is on the tagged ULAE page.

requirements.statement: The classical technique assumes a steady-state book; if paid-to-paid ratios trend over time (e.g., a start-up year or a growing book inflating an average), the historical average ratio is not representative and the unpaid ULAE estimate is biased, so a ratio from recent experience should be used.

places.quote: The classical method's central weakness is **growth**: in a rapidly growing book, current paid ULAE supports a claim inventory much larger than current paid losses reflect, so the ratio overstates the true cost per dollar of loss; in a shrinking or runoff book, it understates it.

requirements.statement: Strengthening case reserves is a calendar-year effect that raises reported claims on the latest diagonal of every accident year, while large losses affect only the accident year in which they occurred.

places.quote: A jump concentrated on one **diagonal**, appearing at every maturity at once, is a change in reserving practice, not in claim cost.

**Calendar Year Effect** (diagonal effect) is an influence that acts on every accident year in the same calendar period, and so on one diagonal $w + d = \text{constant}$ of a [[Development Triangle|development triangle]].

requirements.statement: Paid development methods use only paid claims and are not affected by changes in case reserve adequacy.

places.quote: **Paid data is immune**, so a divergence between paid and reported chain ladder estimates is the corroborating evidence.

Paid data is **objective**. It carries no adjuster judgment, so a paid triangle is immune to changes in [[Case Adequacy|case reserve adequacy]] — the single most common distortion in reported triangles.

requirements.statement: The reported development technique overstates ultimate claims when case reserves are strengthened but historical development factors are not adjusted, since factors reflecting the old case adequacy are applied to inflated reported claims.

places.quote: *Case strengthening*: reported development overstates, reported BF and Cape Cod overstate less; paid methods and expected claims are unaffected.
Applying historical factors — built under weaker reserving — to a strengthened diagonal **over-states** ultimate, because the strengthening is developed a second time.

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson estimate of ultimate equals actual claims (paid or reported) plus (1 - 1/CDF) times a priori expected claims.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$
$$\text{Ultimate} = \text{Reported} + \text{Expected losses} \times \%\,\text{Unreported}$$

requirements.statement: The reported Bornhuetter-Ferguson technique is overstated when case reserves are strengthened without adjusting the CDF, because the percent unreported is too high, though the overstatement is smaller than under reported development.

places.quote: its IBNR comes from the a priori and the unreported *proportion*, so it takes no credit for the claims now booked in case.

requirements.statement: The disposal rate frequency-severity technique relies on closed claim counts and paid severities, so it is unaffected by case reserve strengthening and depends on a stable settlement (disposal) rate.

places.quote: **Disposal rate (Berquist-Sherman) approach.** Project the number of claims closing in each future period from historical **disposal rates**, value them at a trended severity for that maturity, and sum the future payments.
$$\text{Disposal Rate}_n = \frac{\text{Closed claims at age } n}{\text{Ultimate claim counts}}$$

requirements.statement: Paid development applied to an accident year containing unusually large paid claims overstates ultimate, since the development factor leverages the large closed losses as if they will keep developing.

places.quote: The paid method magnifies the same distortion nearly three times as much.

requirements.statement: The paid Bornhuetter-Ferguson technique handles large paid losses better than paid development because only the unpaid portion is estimated from the a priori expected claims, though it still overstates somewhat because the percent unpaid is too high.

places.quote: The key structural property: **actual emergence is taken at face value and only the unemerged portion is estimated**.

requirements.statement: To assess selected development factors, compare the ultimate claim ratios from the development technique with those from other techniques (e.g., frequency-severity) by accident year; a development estimate that departs from the other methods in one year points to the factor(s) used only for that year.

places.quote: Then test the *selected* ultimates by the ratios they imply: ultimate claim ratios, severities, frequencies and pure premiums by year

Standard practice is to run several methods on both paid and reported data, lay the results side by side by accident year, and select — leaning on a priori methods at immature ages and development methods at mature ones, with reasons recorded.

requirements.statement: The most recent (least mature) accident year's development estimate depends on the earliest age-to-age factor (e.g., 12-24 months), which is the most leveraged factor and magnifies reported claims into the ultimate, so an overstated early factor gives an overstated ultimate for that year.

places.quote: A $5\%$ error in the $12\text{–}24$ factor moves ultimate by roughly $\$480{,}000$
The CDF measures **leverage**. At a CDF of $4$, a dollar of distortion on the diagonal becomes four dollars of ultimate

requirements.statement: When business mix is unchanged and there are no unusually large losses, the true ultimate claim ratio should be roughly stable across accident years, so a single outlier year indicates an assumption problem rather than a real change.

places.quote: As a reserving diagnostic, the loss ratio series across accident years at a fixed maturity should move smoothly. A break in the series is a signal

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson ultimate equals reported claims plus expected claims times the percent unreported (1 - 1/CDF); equivalently it is a credibility weighting of the development estimate (weight 1/CDF) and the expected claims (weight 1 - 1/CDF).

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$
$$\text{Ultimate} = \text{Reported} + \text{Expected losses} \times \%\,\text{Unreported}$$

requirements.statement: In the Bornhuetter-Ferguson method, mature years put almost all weight on reported claims (so BF matches the development estimate), while immature years put more weight on the initial expected loss ratio, so BF results move toward the a priori assumption as maturity decreases.

places.quote: The more of the year that has emerged, the more the answer relies on the data — automatically, without a separate credibility judgment.

It is one end of the spectrum the reserving methods occupy: **expected claims** puts $100\%$ weight on the a priori, the [[Chain Ladder Method|chain ladder]] puts $100\%$ on actual emergence, and the [[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method|BF]] method blends them by the percentage reported.

requirements.statement: To assess the initial expected loss ratio, check whether BF results drift steadily away from the other techniques' stable estimates as maturity falls; a one-directional drift downward indicates the initial expected loss ratio is too low and should be raised toward the level indicated by mature years and other methods.

places.quote: The a priori is the weak point. A stale ELR that ignores [[Rate Level Change|rate changes]] and [[Loss Trend|trend]] produces a systematically biased reserve — and the bias persists year after year without ever showing up as instability.

The **ELR** is the whole method, and it must be derived, not assumed: from the pricing indication for that year, from mature years' ultimate loss ratios adjusted for [[Rate Level Change|rate level]] and [[Loss Trend|trend]], or from [[External Information in Reserving|industry benchmarks]].

requirements.statement: Calendar year aggregation assigns to a calendar year the premium earned during that year (and losses/transactions recorded in that year), regardless of when the policies were written.

places.quote: everything booked in the year. Available quickly and already collected for financial reporting

is a data aggregation method that groups every transaction by the calendar year in which it is *booked* — premium as it is earned, losses as they are paid or as case reserves change — without regard to the policy's effective date or the claim's accident date.

requirements.statement: Calendar year earned premium for a policy is its annual premium times the fraction of the policy term falling within the calendar year, summed over all policies including those written in prior years.

places.quote: $$\text{CY Earned Premium} = \text{Written Premium} - \Delta\text{UEP}$$
$$\text{EP for one policy} = \text{Full premium} \times \frac{\text{days elapsed}}{\text{policy term}}$$

requirements.statement: Written premium is the full policy premium assigned to the period containing the policy's effective date.

places.quote: is the full premium booked when a policy is issued, for the entire policy term, regardless of how much of the coverage period has elapsed.
It is recorded on the policy's effective date, and the full amount goes into the unearned premium reserve at that moment.

requirements.statement: Policy year aggregation groups policies by effective date within the year and follows each policy through the end of its term, so a policy year spans two calendar years of earning.

places.quote: its exposures are not fully earned until 24 months after it starts
is a data aggregation method that groups every premium and loss transaction belonging to policies *incepting* in a given calendar year, and follows that cohort until the last claim closes.

requirements.statement: When a policy is cancelled mid-term, its premium is reduced pro rata to the time in force, lowering both written and earned premium for its policy year.

places.quote: Cancellation returns the unearned portion. **Pro rata** cancellation returns the full unearned premium

requirements.statement: Once all policies in a policy year have expired or been cancelled, there is no unearned premium, so the policy year's written and earned premium are equal.

places.quote: its exposures are not fully earned until 24 months after it starts
is fully earned $24$ months after the policy year begins (for annual policies).

requirements.statement: Advantage of calendar year data: it is final at year end with no development, readily available, and reconciles to financial statements.

places.quote: Available quickly and already collected for financial reporting
A calendar year **never develops** — it is closed and fixed the moment the books close.

requirements.statement: Disadvantage of calendar year data: losses include claims from earlier accident years and premium comes from policies written in different years, so premium and losses are mismatched, distorting loss ratios.

places.quote: but its losses include payments and reserve changes on claims from policies issued years ago, a mismatch with the premium earned in the year.
a CY 2024 figure contains payments and reserve changes on claims from $2024$ and from every prior year.

requirements.statement: An occurrence policy covers claims that occur during the policy period, regardless of when they are reported, so its loss cost sums the costs of that accident period's claims across all subsequent report years (report lags).

places.quote: **Occurrence Coverage** is a policy trigger under which the policy responds to losses that *occur* during the policy period, however long afterwards the claim is reported.

requirements.statement: A claims-made policy covers claims reported during the policy period, subject to the retroactive date, which excludes claims that occurred before it.

places.quote: **Claims-Made Coverage** is a policy trigger under which the policy responds to claims *reported* during the policy period, provided the underlying loss occurred on or after the policy's **retroactive date**.

requirements.statement: To get a report-year total from the loss cost of one occurrence/report-lag component, divide that component by its lag percentage, then split the total into report-lag components using the lag distribution.

places.quote: Claims report $25\%$ in the accident year, then $35\%$, $25\%$ and $15\%$ in the following three.
Weight each accident year's cost by its share of the claims reported in $2026$:

requirements.statement: Trend loss costs by the annual trend rate compounded over the number of years between the base report year and the report year of the claim, since trend applies by report year rather than occurrence year.

places.quote: $$\text{Trend Factor} = (1 + t)^{n}$$

requirements.statement: When switching from claims-made to occurrence coverage, a gap exists for claims occurring before the occurrence policy's start but reported after the claims-made policy ends; this tail must be covered in addition to the occurrence policy.

places.quote: An **extended reporting endorsement** (ERP, or "tail coverage") covers claims that occurred during the claims-made coverage period but are reported after the last policy expires — what a retiring physician, or an insured switching to an occurrence policy, needs to avoid a gap.
If the insured let coverage lapse at the end of $2024$ and bought no extended reporting period, the claim is uninsured.

requirements.statement: Complete coverage without overlap when switching from claims-made to occurrence equals the occurrence policy loss cost plus the tail loss cost, where the tail is the sum of costs of pre-effective-date occurrences reported after the switch, trended by report year up to the maximum report lag.

places.quote: An **extended reporting endorsement** (ERP, or "tail coverage") covers claims that occurred during the claims-made coverage period but are reported after the last policy expires — what a retiring physician, or an insured switching to an occurrence policy, needs to avoid a gap.
The policy covers claims *reported* in $2026$, which arise from accidents in $2026$, $2025$, $2024$ and $2023$ in the proportions above.

requirements.statement: Bornhuetter-Ferguson ultimate loss = reported loss + expected loss ratio × premium × (1 − 1/CDF), where (1 − 1/CDF) is the percent unreported and the second term is the expected IBNR.

places.quote: $C$ is reported (or paid) losses to date, $U_0 = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}$ the a priori expectation, and $1 - 1/\text{CDF}$ the percentage unreported from the [[Development Triangle|development pattern]].
$$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$

requirements.statement: Develop reported losses to ultimate by multiplying them by the cumulative loss development factor for the accident year's maturity.

places.quote: $$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: Trend historical ultimate losses to the target accident year's cost level by compounding the annual loss cost trend over the number of years between each accident year and the target year.

places.quote: $$\text{Trend Factor} = (1 + t)^{n}$$

requirements.statement: Use the parallelogram method to on-level earned premium: with annual policies written uniformly and rate changes on January 1, each calendar year's average rate level is half the prior year's writings level plus half the current year's, and the on-level factor is the current rate level divided by the average rate level.

places.quote: The *average* index for a year is the earned-premium-weighted blend of the levels in force during that year.
$$\text{OLF}_Y = \frac{I_{\text{current}}}{\sum_k A_{Y,k}\, I_k}$$

For **annual** policies written uniformly, a rate change effective at time $p$ through year $Y$ earns over a triangle of area $\tfrac{1}{2}(1-p)^2$ in year $Y$ — so a $7/1$ change affects only $0.125$ of that year's earned premium, and a $1/1$ change affects $0.500$.

requirements.statement: Select the expected loss ratio as total trended ultimate losses divided by total on-level premium over the chosen experience years (a premium-weighted average), keeping losses and premium on a common cost and rate level basis.

places.quote: The **ELR** is the whole method, and it must be derived, not assumed: from the pricing indication for that year, from mature years' ultimate loss ratios adjusted for [[Rate Level Change|rate level]] and [[Loss Trend|trend]], or from [[External Information in Reserving|industry benchmarks]].

Premium **must be on level** and losses must be trended to a common cost level before the ELR is computed, or the derived ratio blends years written at different rate levels and different cost levels into one number.

requirements.statement: When applying BF to the target year, the premium used for expected losses must be on-level at the same basis as the ELR, and losses trended to the target year's cost level need no further trending for that year.

places.quote: The [[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method|BF]] and [[Expected Loss Method|expected claims]] techniques need an expected loss ratio per accident year, and a year written after a $+15\%$ rate change should carry a materially lower ELR than the year before it.

Premium **must be on level** and losses must be trended to a common cost level before the ELR is computed, or the derived ratio blends years written at different rate levels and different cost levels into one number.

requirements.statement: The minimum and maximum weekly indemnity benefits are set as stated percentages of the state average weekly wage (SAWW), so each limit equals the percentage times the SAWW.

places.quote: Texas, for example, publishes a maximum weekly income benefit tied to its state average weekly wage, \$1,271 for injuries from October 2025 through September 2026.

requirements.statement: A worker's weekly indemnity benefit equals the compensation rate times the pre-injury wage, floored at the minimum benefit and capped at the maximum benefit: min(max(rate x wage, minimum), maximum).

To estimate the direct impact of a benefit law change on losses, compute total benefits under the current and proposed structures (benefit per wage band times number of workers, summed), and express the impact as the percentage change of proposed over current benefits.
requirements.concept: Impact of Law Changes on Workers Compensation Losses

requirements.statement: When wages are grouped in bands, approximate each band's wage by its average (total wages divided by number of workers) when applying benefit rate and limits.
requirements.concept: Impact of Law Changes on Workers Compensation Losses

requirements.statement: Raising the minimum benefit reduces the financial incentive of low-wage workers to avoid injury claims and return to work, increasing claim frequency and duration among low-wage workers.
requirements.concept: Indirect Effects of Workers Compensation Benefit Changes

requirements.statement: Lowering the maximum benefit widens the gap between wage and benefit for high-wage workers, strengthening their incentive to avoid claims and return to work sooner, so claim frequency and duration fall among high-wage workers.
requirements.concept: Indirect Effects of Workers Compensation Benefit Changes

requirements.statement: Under the premium-based projection method, acquisition-type expenses (commission, other acquisition, premium tax and licensing fees) are incurred when policies are written and are ratioed to written premium.

places.quote: Expenses incurred at the onset of the policy — commissions, other acquisition, and taxes, licenses and fees — are calculated on [[Written Premium]]; general expenses, incurred throughout the policy, on [[Earned Premium]].

those incurred at the onset of the policy (commissions, other acquisition, taxes, licenses and fees) are measured against written premium, those incurred throughout the policy (general expenses) against [[Earned Premium|earned premium]], and the category ratios are added.

requirements.statement: Under the premium-based projection method, general expenses (and other costs incurred over the policy term) are ratioed to earned premium.

places.quote: Expenses incurred at the onset of the policy — commissions, other acquisition, and taxes, licenses and fees — are calculated on [[Written Premium]]; general expenses, incurred throughout the policy, on [[Earned Premium]].
Acquisition costs are incurred as policies are written, so they are related to written premium; general expenses are incurred through the policy term, so they are related to earned premium.

requirements.statement: The underwriting expense ratio is the sum of the commission, other acquisition, taxes/licenses/fees, and general expense ratios, and excludes loss adjustment expense.

places.quote: **Expense Ratio** is underwriting expenses as a share of premium — the non-claim cost of writing and servicing business.

requirements.statement: The operating expense ratio equals the underwriting expense ratio plus the loss adjustment expense ratio, with LAE ratioed to earned premium.

places.quote: $$\text{Operating Expense Ratio} = \text{UW Expense Ratio} + \frac{\text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Premium}}$$

requirements.statement: The total permissible loss ratio equals 1 minus the underwriting expense ratio minus the underwriting profit provision (if LAE is treated as a loss expense, it is included in this ratio; if LAE is treated as an operating expense, subtract the operating expense ratio instead).

places.quote: the **total permissible loss ratio** also takes out the fixed expense ratio, $\text{PLR} = 1 - F - V - Q_T$, and pays for loss and LAE alone.
$$\text{PLR} = 1 - V - F\% - Q_T \quad \text{(total permissible loss ratio)}$$

requirements.statement: With the premium-based projection method, indicated rate change = (projected loss & LAE ratio + fixed expense ratio) / (1 − variable expense ratio − profit provision) − 1.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{\text{VPLR}} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$

requirements.statement: When the projected loss ratio excludes LAE, add the LAE ratio to the loss ratio (not multiply by 1+LAE ratio) in the numerator of the indication, or alternatively treat LAE as a variable expense in the denominator, consistently.

places.quote: $$\text{Loss Ratio} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Premium}}$$
$$\text{Loss \& LAE Ratio} = \frac{\text{Loss} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Premium}}$$

requirements.statement: Fixed expenses do not vary with premium level and are kept separate from variable expenses (which vary with premium) in the premium-based projection indication.

places.quote: [[Fixed Expenses]] are assumed the same for each risk regardless of premium — typically home-office overhead, and per-policy costs such as printing and data entry.

**Fixed Expenses** are underwriting expenses assumed to be the same for each risk regardless of the size of the premium — typically home-office overhead, and per-policy costs such as printing and data entry.

requirements.statement: Lifetime value analysis sets the premium so that the policy breaks even (including the profit provision) over the customer's expected multi-period life rather than a single policy term, recovering up-front new business costs across later renewal years.

places.quote: **Lifetime Value** (LTV) is the present value of the expected profit from a customer relationship over its whole life, rather than over a single policy period.

requirements.statement: Weight each future year's entire net position (premium, loss, LAE and fixed expense) by the retention probability and discount it at the discount rate back to the first year, then set the sum of present values to zero to find the premium.

places.quote: $$\text{LTV} = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{\left(P_t - L_t - E_t\right) \times {}_{t}p}{(1 + r)^{t}}$$

requirements.statement: Required premium per exposure = (pure premium including LAE + fixed expense per exposure) / (1 - variable expense ratio - profit and contingencies provision).
requirements.concept: Premium Calculation (Loss Ratio and Fixed Expense Approach)

places.quote: $$\text{Rate} = \frac{\text{Pure Premium} + F}{1 - V - Q_T}$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + \text{Fixed Expense Ratio}}{1 - V - Q} - 1$$

requirements.statement: Load the pure premium for LAE by multiplying by (1 + LAE provision) when LAE is expressed as a percentage of loss.

places.quote: It cannot be traced to a claim, so it is estimated in aggregate — classically as the ratio of calendar-year paid ULAE to calendar-year paid loss plus ALAE, applied to loss plus ALAE that has been adjusted for extraordinary events, development and trend.

requirements.statement: In a multi-year projection, trend the loss cost by the annual loss trend for each later year and trend the premium by the annual premium trend; use the renewal fixed expense (not the new business amount) in renewal years.

places.quote: $$\text{Trend Factor} = (1 + t)^{n}$$
$$\text{Trend Factor} = (1 + r)^n$$

requirements.statement: The Statement of Principles Regarding Property and Casualty Ratemaking states that a rate is an estimate of the expected value of future costs, provides for all costs associated with the transfer of risk, provides for costs of an individual risk transfer, and is reasonable and not excessive, inadequate or unfairly discriminatory if actuarially sound.
requirements.concept: Statement of Principles Regarding Property and Casualty Ratemaking

places.quote: **Principle 1 — A rate is an estimate of the expected value of future costs.**
**Ratemaking** (May 1988): a rate is an estimate of the expected value of future costs and provides for all of them; see [[Principles of Ratemaking]].

requirements.statement: Justify lifetime value analysis under the Statement of Principles by tying its features (forward-looking multi-year projection, allocation of acquisition costs over customer life, individual-policy basis, supportable assumptions) to each of the four principles.
requirements.concept: Statement of Principles Regarding Property and Casualty Ratemaking

places.quote: The professional boundary matters: the **indication** is an actuarial estimate of expected cost; LTV is a **business decision layer** applied to it.
the departure from an indication for competitive or regulatory reasons is precisely where Principle 4 gets tested.

requirements.statement: A good exposure base is proportional to expected loss, practical (objective, easily measured and verifiable), and supported by historical precedent.

places.quote: **Proportional to expected loss.** All else equal, a policy with two exposures should have twice the expected loss of a similar policy with one.

requirements.statement: The social criteria for evaluating a rating variable are affordability, causality, controllability and privacy.

places.quote: social (privacy, causality, affordability, controllability) and legal (permitted in the jurisdiction)
**Social** — privacy, causality, controllability and affordability; these are where public and regulatory objections arise.

requirements.statement: A rating variable is socially acceptable on causality grounds if it has a direct causal link to loss rather than being merely a correlated proxy, and on controllability grounds if the insured can influence it to reduce premium or risk; a characteristic like age is not controllable.

places.quote: **Social:** it passes. The variable is controllable by the insured, causally intuitive and not a proxy for a protected class.

requirements.statement: Adverse selection (anti-selection) occurs when an insurer does not use a risk-differentiating variable that competitors use, so it attracts underpriced risks and loses overpriced risks.

places.quote: Every classification restriction reintroduces adverse selection by forcing a single price across risks the insurer knows differ

In a competitive market an insurer that charges one average rate to a heterogeneous group loses the better risks to competitors that price them properly, and retains the worse ones — the **adverse selection spiral**.

requirements.statement: An insurer that ignores a rating variable and has no expenses or profit charges every insured the average expected cost of its book (weighted by policy counts).

places.quote: In a competitive market an insurer that charges one average rate to a heterogeneous group loses the better risks to competitors that price them properly, and retains the worse ones — the **adverse selection spiral**.
The insurer cannot tell them apart and charges the average.

requirements.statement: To measure the effect of price-based switching, compare the insurer's rate to the competitor's rate for each risk class: the class where the insurer is cheaper gains a share of the competitor's policies and the class where it is more expensive loses that share of its own, then recompute the portfolio mix and profit as premium minus expected losses.

resolution.note: A step of this solution's plan on the switching shares the question gives; adverse selection itself is on the tagged Adverse Selection page.

requirements.statement: A good exposure base should be proportional to expected loss, meaning expected loss changes in direct proportion to the exposure units and has a logical relationship to the loss-producing hazard.

places.quote: All else equal, a policy with two exposures should have twice the expected loss of a similar policy with one.

requirements.statement: A good exposure base should be practical: objective, easy to obtain and verify, inexpensive to administer, and not subject to manipulation by the insured.

places.quote: Objective, and relatively easy and inexpensive to obtain and verify — which also keeps policyholders and producers from manipulating it (declared annual mileage invites more dishonesty than car-years).
objective, inexpensive to obtain and verify, not manipulable by the insured.

requirements.statement: A good exposure base should consider historical precedence: changing the base requires system, rating-algorithm and statistical-reporting changes and can cause premium disruption for insureds.

places.quote: A change of base can cause large premium swings for individual insureds, requires a change in the rating algorithm and systems, and may force significant adjustments to the several years of data a ratemaking analysis uses.

requirements.statement: For liability coverage, loss depends on third-party damages and injuries rather than the value of the insured's own property, so a value-based exposure base (insured value) is not proportional to liability expected loss.

places.quote: any condition or situation that presents the possibility of a claim alleging that a person or organization is legally responsible for injury or damage suffered by another party.

resolution.note: Applying the proportionality criterion (taught on the tagged Exposure Base page, Werner p.49) to the liability coverage the question describes.

requirements.statement: For physical damage coverage, repair and replacement costs rise with the value of the insured property, so insured value is proportional to expected physical damage loss.

places.quote: $\Delta V$ is the reduction in the value of the property, measured on whichever valuation basis applies.

resolution.note: Applying the proportionality criterion (taught on the tagged Exposure Base page, Werner p.49) to the physical damage coverage the question describes.

requirements.statement: Value-based exposure bases are harder to obtain and verify objectively than unit counts like boat-years (market value, purchase price and replacement cost differ), and are open to insured manipulation.

places.quote: Objective, and relatively easy and inexpensive to obtain and verify — which also keeps policyholders and producers from manipulating it (declared annual mileage invites more dishonesty than car-years).
objective, inexpensive to obtain and verify, not manipulable by the insured.

requirements.statement: Choose a recommended exposure base by weighing how well each candidate meets the three criteria for each coverage, retaining the existing base when the proposed one fails a criterion and the benefit does not justify the implementation cost and disruption.

places.quote: The proposal should be rejected; the AOI effect in the table is a case for an [[Classification Ratemaking|AOI relativity]], not a new base.

requirements.statement: Overly broad rating territories are heterogeneous, so a single average territorial relativity overcharges better risks and undercharges worse risks, exposing the insurer to adverse selection by competitors with finer territories.

places.quote: In **ratemaking**, a non-homogeneous class means systematic cross-subsidy: the better risks in the class are overcharged and leave (see [[Classification Ratemaking]]), while the worse risks stay — the adverse selection spiral that risk classification exists to prevent.

**Flattening a territory differential** has the effect Werner & Modlin describe for any rating variable: risks with different expected costs pay the same rate, so the low-cost risks subsidise the high-cost ones, and a company doing this while competitors differentiate faces [[Adverse Selection|adverse selection]] (Ch.9).

requirements.statement: Territory definitions based on a single peril (e.g., weather) fail to capture geographic variation in other perils such as theft, fire, water and liability, which follow different patterns such as population density.

places.quote: Geographic cost drivers: population and traffic density, crime, weather and catastrophe exposure, repair and medical costs, litigation propensity and local court behaviour, and — for property — building codes and fire protection class.

The CIA lists third-party data that can help find it: topography for some natural catastrophe perils, accident locations for auto, crime data for theft, weather data for water, sewer back-up, [[Flood Insurance|flood]] and hail, and public transportation data.

requirements.statement: Developing rating territories proceeds by defining basic geographic units, quantifying each unit's geographic risk, smoothing the residual geographic effect, and clustering the units into final rating territories.

places.quote: Territories are defined at some granularity (postal code, county, census tract) and then **grouped** into rating territories.

the CIA's steps are the same: build a non-territory model, compute residual loss costs at the building-block level (an FSA, say), model the residuals to group similar ones while balancing each block's credibility against its neighbours', then finalize the boundaries (CIA §2).

requirements.statement: Basic geographic units such as zip codes are granular but their boundaries change over time, whereas counties are stable but coarser, so unit choice trades off granularity against stability.

Geography is correlated with other rating variables, so a multivariate model such as a GLM that includes those variables is used to isolate the geographic effect from correlated variables and noise from thin data.

places.quote: Territory must be estimated **alongside** other rating variables, not before them.
location is heavily correlated with other rating variables, so a univariate analysis of territory is distorted, and the data in each small geographic unit is sparse (Werner & Modlin Ch.11).

requirements.statement: Spatial smoothing of residual geographic variation across neighboring units can be distance-based, which suits perils like weather, or adjacency-based, which suits perils following contiguous population patterns such as theft.

places.quote: Werner describes distance-based and adjacency-based smoothing, applied *before* territories are grouped.

Because geographic risk is similar for nearby units, actuaries smooth spatially: *distance-based* smoothing suits weather perils, *adjacency-based* smoothing suits perils driven by socio-demographic characteristics such as theft, and too much or too little smoothing either masks real variation or leaves noise (Werner & Modlin Ch.11).

requirements.statement: Clustering groups basic units with similar smoothed relativities into territories, using methods such as quantile-based (similar exposure per territory) or similarity-based clustering, and choosing the number of territories to balance within-territory homogeneity against credible volume.

places.quote: Too fine and no cell is [[Credibility|credible]]; too coarse and real cost differences are averaged away — the [[Homogeneity|homogeneity/credibility]] trade-off in its sharpest form.

**Clustering** is an unsupervised [[Statistical Learning]] technique that groups observations into clusters so that observations within a cluster are similar to each other and dissimilar from those in other clusters.

requirements.statement: The loss elimination ratio (LER) for a deductible is the fraction of ground-up losses that fall below the deductible (eliminated by it).

places.quote: **Loss Elimination Ratio** (LER) is the proportion of ground-up losses removed by a deductible — the share of expected loss that the insured retains rather than transfers.
$$\text{LER}(d) = \frac{E[X \wedge d]}{E[X]}$$

requirements.statement: Split ground-up losses into losses below the deductible (ground-up × LER) and excess losses above the deductible (ground-up × (1 − LER)); only excess losses are a loss cost to the insurer when the insured reimburses the below-deductible amounts.

places.quote: Under an ordinary deductible $d$ the loss splits in two: the part the policyholder keeps (is not reimbursed for) is the loss capped at the deductible, $\min(X, d) = X \wedge d$, and the insurer pays the excess $(X - d)_+$.
The LER is the bridge from a full-coverage rate to a deductible rate: multiply the full-coverage loss cost by $(1 - \text{LER})$ to get the loss cost net of the deductible.

requirements.statement: When the insurer pays all ALAE (deductible applies to loss only), ALAE is based on ground-up losses and is not reduced by the deductible, so the full ALAE is included in the premium.

places.quote: ALAE is $9\%$ of ground-up losses and is not reduced by the deductible.

requirements.statement: Deductible processing cost and credit risk charges are applied as percentages of the losses below the deductible, since the insurer fronts those payments and must recover them from the insured.

places.quote: so the premium must cover invoicing and monitoring and a provision for the credit risk that the insured cannot pay
deductible processing costs $3\%$ and credit risk $1.5\%$ of expected deductible reimbursements

requirements.statement: An additional risk margin is applied as a percentage of the excess (above-deductible) losses.

places.quote: the risk margin is $12\%$ of excess losses

requirements.statement: Premium = (expected losses + ALAE + fixed expenses + other fixed-dollar charges) / (1 − variable expense ratio − profit ratio); fixed-dollar costs go in the numerator and only premium-proportional variable expenses and profit go in the denominator.

places.quote: $$\text{Premium} = \frac{\text{Excess Losses} + \text{ALAE} + F + \text{CR} + \text{RM}}{1 - V - Q}$$
$F$ enters the **numerator** of the rate; [[Variable Expenses|variable expenses]] $V$ and the profit provision $Q_T$ enter the **denominator**.

requirements.statement: In the adjusted pure premium method, each cell's exposure is multiplied by the current rating factor of the other rating variable(s) to give adjusted exposures, which removes distortion from uneven distribution of exposures across the other variable.
requirements.concept: Adjusted Pure Premium Method for Class Relativities

places.quote: When other rating variables also apply, each class's exposures are first multiplied by their average relativity for those other variables, so that the factor measures only this variable's effect on the average premium.

requirements.statement: The adjusted pure premium for a segment equals the segment's total loss (and ALAE) divided by its adjusted exposures.
requirements.concept: Adjusted Pure Premium Method for Class Relativities

places.quote: $$\text{Pure Premium} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Exposures}} = \text{Frequency} \times \text{Severity}$$
$$\text{Pure Premium} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Exposures}}$$

requirements.statement: The indicated relativity for a segment equals its pure premium divided by the pure premium of the base class, so the base class has relativity 1.000.

places.quote: $$\text{Relativity}_i = \frac{\text{Pure Premium}_i}{\text{Pure Premium}_{\text{base}}}$$
$$\text{Relativity}_i = \frac{\text{Pure Premium}_i}{\text{Pure Premium}_{\text{base}}}$$

requirements.statement: When selecting relativities that move a fraction of the way from current to indicated, the selected relativity equals current plus that fraction times (indicated minus current).

places.quote: With, say, $Z = 0.45$, the credibility-weighted relativity is $0.45(1.56) + 0.55(1.00) = 1.25$

resolution.note: Arithmetic on the question's own instruction to move a stated fraction of the way from current to indicated.

requirements.statement: The off-balance factor is the exposure-weighted average current relativity divided by the exposure-weighted average selected relativity, using adjusted exposures as weights; it offsets the premium impact of changing relativities.

places.quote: $$\text{OBF} = \frac{\sum_i w_i\, r_i^{\text{old}}}{\sum_i w_i\, r_i^{\text{new}}}$$
$$B_{\text{new}} = B_{\text{old}} \times \frac{\bar{R}_{\text{old}}}{\bar{R}_{\text{new}}}$$

requirements.statement: The proposed base rate equals the current base rate times the off-balance factor (and times one plus the overall rate level change), so the base rate absorbs the off-balance.

places.quote: $$\text{Base Rate}_{\text{new}} = \text{Base Rate}_{\text{current}} \times \frac{1 + \text{overall change}}{1 + \text{change in average rate differential}}$$
$$B_{\text{new}} = B_{\text{old}} \times (1 + \Delta) \times \text{OBF}$$

requirements.statement: Social criteria for evaluating rating variables include affordability, causality, controllability, and privacy.

places.quote: **Social** — privacy, causality, controllability and affordability; these are where public and regulatory objections arise.

requirements.statement: Affordability means premiums should remain affordable, especially for compulsory coverage; controllability means the insured can influence the rating characteristic and thereby their premium, encouraging loss control.
When losses are uniformly distributed within a loss layer, the layer's average severity is its midpoint, so expected severity is the sum of layer probabilities times layer midpoints.

resolution.note: Prerequisite probability, not Exam 5 course content: a uniform distribution's mean is its midpoint, and the question states losses are uniform within each layer.

requirements.statement: Pure premium equals expected claim frequency times expected severity, and the rate per $1,000 of coverage is the pure premium divided by (amount of insurance / 1,000).
requirements.concept: Homeowners Insurance Rate per Amount of Insurance

places.quote: $E[\text{layer loss}] = E[N]\left(E[X \wedge b] - E[X \wedge a]\right)$

resolution.quote: is set by the face amount chosen, as expected indemnity divided by face value
resolution.note: Taught on the tagged Coinsurance Rating page: rate per amount of insurance = f x E[min(L,F)] / F (Werner Ch.11 p.212); the check missed it.

requirements.statement: For an amount of insurance below the home's value, losses are capped at the amount of insurance; expected severity is computed on capped losses, with a layer straddling the cap split proportionally into a part paid at layer values and a part capped at the limit, and layers above the cap valued at the cap.

places.quote: The **Limited Expected Value** (LEV) of a random variable $X$ at limit $u$ is the expected value of the payment under a policy that pays $X$ up to a maximum of $u$.
Under a limit $u$ and no other modification, the insurer pays the whole loss $X$ when it is below $u$ and pays $u$ when it is not

requirements.statement: Rate per $1,000 of coverage is higher at lower amounts of insurance because the first dollars of coverage are the most likely to be used (loss propensity is concentrated in lower layers).

places.quote: Each successive layer is cheaper per dollar of limit — which is exactly the consistency property.
Expected cost per dollar of limit falls as the layer rises (the consistency test).

requirements.statement: Underinsurance harms the insured because on a total or near-total loss they recover only the amount of insurance (short of rebuild cost), and under a coinsurance clause partial losses are also not fully indemnified due to a penalty.

places.quote: Fall short and every partial loss is settled at the ratio of insurance carried to insurance required.
The clause cannot raise the payment above the limit, and on a total loss the insurer pays the full limit whether or not the requirement is met.

requirements.statement: Rates are built assuming insurance to value, so underinsured homes pay inadequate premium for their loss propensity; across-the-board rate increases make properly insured policyholders subsidize underinsured ones, making rates inequitable.
