places.quote: Its purpose is **insurance-to-value**. Because most property losses are partial, an insured carrying $50\%$ of value would otherwise pay half the premium for nearly the same expected recovery, and the rate per $\$1{,}000$ would have to rise for everyone.
A book insured below value therefore collects too little premium at the filed rate.

requirements.statement: The coinsurance apportionment ratio is min(amount of insurance / (coinsurance % × property value), 1).

places.quote: \text{Recovery}_{\text{clause}} = \min\!\left(\frac{\text{Insurance Carried}}{\text{Coinsurance \% } \times \text{Value}},\, 1\right) \times \text{Loss}
a = \min\!\left(\frac{F}{cV},\ 1.0\right)
R = \min\left(\frac{C}{p \times V},\ 1\right)

requirements.statement: Indemnity under a coinsurance clause is the lesser of the policy limit and loss times the apportionment ratio; the coinsurance penalty is the lesser of the loss and the policy limit minus the indemnity, excluding any loss above the limit.

places.quote: \text{Recovery}_{\text{clause}} = \min\!\left(\frac{\text{Insurance Carried}}{\text{Coinsurance \% } \times \text{Value}},\, 1\right) \times \text{Loss}
\text{Payment} = \min\big(R \times L - D,\ C\big)
\text{Property payment} = \min\left(\min\left(\frac{C}{p \times V},\ 1\right) \times L - D,\ C\right)

requirements.statement: Management uses unpaid claim estimates in pricing, underwriting and strategic decisions, so under-reserving makes indicated rates look adequate and leads to writing business at inadequate rates, while over-reserving can lead to unnecessary rate increases or tightened underwriting that loses profitable business.

places.quote: The **direction of error is asymmetric in consequence**. Redundancy is a profit deferral; deficiency understates the loss ratio, overstates surplus, and feeds an inadequate rate indication back into pricing, so the same error appears again in next year's business.

Under-reserving can put **solvency** at risk: it presents the insurer as stronger than it is, and an inadequate estimate can lead it to cut rates on business already underpriced — worse still if the lower rates win market share (Friedland Ch. 1).

requirements.statement: Management relies on accurate unpaid claim estimates for decisions on reinsurance purchases and capital allocation.

places.quote: - Accuracy matters beyond the balance sheet: unpaid claim estimates drive solvency assessment, [[Ratemaking|ratemaking]] (through ultimate loss ratios), reinsurance commutations, collateral requirements, and the price of the company itself in a transaction.

requirements.statement: Investors use financial statements to judge earnings and financial strength, and the unpaid claim estimate is the largest liability on a P&C insurer's balance sheet, so an inaccurate estimate distorts reported income and surplus and misleads investors about the company's value.

places.quote: **Investors and rating agencies** — reserve development history, volatility, and the earnings effect. Adverse development is a disclosure item; a pattern of it affects the rating and the cost of capital.
The two are the largest liabilities on a property-casualty balance sheet: at the end of 2011, loss and LAE reserves were nearly 60% of U.S. industry liabilities and unearned premium about 20%.

requirements.statement: Investors use reserve levels, through their effect on reported earnings and surplus, to assess the dividends a company can sustainably pay.

resolution.quote: reserve development history, volatility, and the effect on reported earnings
resolution.note: The tagged Reserve Communication page teaches what investors take from reserves (Friedland Ch.1 pp.4-5); the dividend example is the sample answer's own illustration, not in Friedland.

requirements.statement: Regulators are principally concerned with insurer solvency to protect policyholders, and understated reserves overstate surplus and mask financial weakness, delaying regulatory intervention until the insurer may be insolvent and guaranty funds must absorb the shortfall.

places.quote: The **direction of error is asymmetric in consequence**. Redundancy is a profit deferral; deficiency understates the loss ratio, overstates surplus, and feeds an inadequate rate indication back into pricing, so the same error appears again in next year's business.
The cumulative development has been consuming surplus each year while reported results looked better than they were.

**Why insurers fail.** [[PACICC]]'s research is consistent: **inadequate pricing and deficient reserves** dominate, followed by rapid growth into unfamiliar lines, reinsurance failure or dispute, catastrophe exposure, and fraud.

requirements.statement: Regulators need accurate estimates of ultimate claim costs when reviewing rate filings because indicated rate levels depend directly on them.

places.quote: Accuracy matters beyond the balance sheet: unpaid claim estimates drive solvency assessment, [[Ratemaking|ratemaking]] (through ultimate loss ratios), reinsurance commutations, collateral requirements, and the price of the company itself in a transaction.
Understated reserves feed understated loss ratios into rate indications, so the business being written now is likely inadequately priced — the deficiency reproduces itself.

requirements.statement: Calendar year reported claims equal payments made during the calendar year plus the change in case outstanding reserves over that year (ending case minus beginning case).

places.quote: $$\text{CY Reported Losses} = \text{Paid} + \Delta\text{Case Reserves}$$

requirements.statement: Calendar year amounts are assigned by transaction date, not accident date, and a claim's case reserve before its first transaction is zero, so the first-year change in case equals the ending case.
requirements.concept: Calendar Year vs Accident Year Aggregation

places.quote: groups every transaction by the calendar year in which it is *booked* — premium as it is earned, losses as they are paid or as case reserves change — without regard to the policy's effective date or the claim's accident date.

requirements.statement: A decrease in case outstanding over the year gives a negative change in case that reduces calendar year reported claims, because payments partly release reserves already held.

places.quote: $\Delta$ terms are ending balance minus beginning balance.

requirements.statement: Under a quota share, the ceded amount is the ceded percentage times the gross loss, and the net amount is the retained percentage (one minus the ceded percentage) times gross; the treaty applies to claims by the period specified (e.g., accident date).

places.quote: $$\text{Ceded}_{\text{QS}} = a \times X$$
$$\text{Ceded}_{\text{QS}} = a\,X$$

resolution.quote: Under quota share, ceded is a fixed share
resolution.note: Ceded Losses (one link from the tagged Net of Reinsurance) teaches quota share cession as a fixed share of gross.

requirements.statement: Per-claim excess of loss reinsurance cedes the portion of each individual claim's cumulative amount above the retention, applied claim by claim and not on an aggregate basis; for paid claims, cumulative paid is compared to the retention.

places.quote: the reinsurer pays the part of each loss — per risk or per occurrence — above the cedant's retention $R$ (the attachment point)
[[Excess of Loss|Excess of loss]] reinsurance, by contrast, pays only the part of a loss above the retention.

resolution.quote: Under excess of loss, ceded responds only to claims piercing retention
resolution.note: Ceded Losses (one link from the tagged Net of Reinsurance) teaches per-claim excess of loss cession above the retention.

requirements.statement: For net reported (incurred) claims under excess of loss, the ceded amount in a calendar year is the change in cumulative ceded incurred (cumulative paid plus case above retention) from the prior year-end to the current year-end, and net reported equals gross reported minus that cession.

resolution.quote: Werner & Modlin and Friedland both define calendar-year reported losses as paid losses plus the change in case reserves.
resolution.note: The tagged Calendar Year page teaches CY reported = paid + change in case; applied to the ceded layer it gives the CY cession.

requirements.statement: An age-to-age (link ratio) factor is the reported claims at a later maturity divided by reported claims at the immediately adjacent earlier maturity for the same accident year.

places.quote: **Age-to-Age Factor** (link ratio) is the ratio of a cohort's cumulative amount at one maturity to its amount at the previous maturity — the observed development between two ages.

requirements.statement: Select an age-to-age factor from the available historical factors at that maturity (e.g., a simple average of the factors, or the only one available).

places.quote: - **Simple average** — equal weight to each year, so a small, volatile year counts as much as a large one.

requirements.statement: The cumulative development factor to ultimate at a given age is the product of the selected age-to-age factors from that age onward, including the tail factor to ultimate.

places.quote: **Cumulative Development Factor** (CDF, or age-to-ultimate factor) is the product of all selected [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] from a given maturity through to ultimate, including the [[Tail Factor|tail]].

requirements.statement: Under the reported development technique, ultimate claims equal reported claims to date multiplied by the cumulative development factor to ultimate.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate} = C_n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: Percent unreported equals 1 minus 1/CDF; percent reported is 1/CDF.

places.quote: The reciprocal is the **percentage reported** (or paid): $p_n = 1/\text{CDF}_n$, and $1 - p_n$ is the percentage unreported.

requirements.statement: Under the Bornhuetter-Ferguson technique, ultimate claims equal reported claims to date plus expected claims (earned premium times expected claims ratio) times the percent unreported.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$

requirements.statement: Under the expected claims technique, ultimate claims equal earned premium times the expected claims ratio, ignoring reported claims to date.

places.quote: **Expected Loss Method** (expected claims technique) estimates ultimate losses entirely from an a priori expectation — usually an expected loss ratio applied to earned premium — giving **no weight** to what has actually been reported.

requirements.statement: A small, volatile book gives unstable, low-credibility development factors, so techniques relying on its own development pattern are unreliable; a more stable pattern and expected claims ratio from a comparable larger book (same state and line) can be used, e.g., via Bornhuetter-Ferguson, which limits the leverage of volatile reported claims.
requirements.concept: Credibility and Technique Selection for Small Books

places.quote: Its virtue is **stability**: the estimate does not move with a thin diagonal, so a single early large claim or a slow month of reporting cannot swing it.
- **When external data is needed:** a new line or new company with no history; a small or newly segmented book whose triangle is too volatile to be [[Credibility|credible]];

requirements.statement: Ultimate claims under the frequency-severity technique equal selected frequency (claim counts per exposure) times exposure times selected ultimate severity per claim.

places.quote: $$U = \text{Exposures} \times \text{Frequency}_{\text{ult}} \times S_{\text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: When premium is used as the exposure base, restate historical earned premium to the current rate level by multiplying by the on-level adjustment factor, so that frequency is measured per on-level premium.

places.quote: $$\text{On-Level Premium} = \text{Historical EP} \times \text{On-Level Factor}$$
**On-Leveling** is the procedure that restates historical earned premium to the current rate level, producing [[On Level Premium|on-level premium]].

requirements.statement: Trend ultimate claim counts (frequency) and ultimate severities separately for each accident year, using compounded annual trend factors over the number of years from each accident year to the target year, then select a value such as the average of the trended years.

places.quote: $$\text{Trend Factor} = (1 + t)^{n}$$
The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: Adjust historical severities for a legislative (tort) change by applying the savings factor (one minus the savings) to periods before the change so all are at the post-reform level, and reverse this factor for accident years that predate the change; the adjustment applies only to claims occurring after the effective date.

places.quote: A benefit-level change is restated in the data, or allowed for in the selection, so that it is not double counted.
So historical loss costs are multiplied by $1 - 0.11 = 0.89$ to restate them at the post-reform benefit level, **before** trending forward.

requirements.statement: To move a selected frequency or severity from the target year level back to an earlier accident year, detrend it by dividing by one plus the annual trend for each year of difference (and reverse any law-change adjustment).

places.quote: $$\text{Adjusted ELR}_i = \text{ELR}_{\text{base}} \times \frac{\text{Rate level}_{\text{base}}}{\text{Rate level}_i} \times \frac{\text{Loss trend}_i}{\text{Loss trend}_{\text{base}}}$$

requirements.statement: Frequency-severity techniques assume claim counts are defined and reported consistently over time (a stable claim count definition), so past count patterns are a valid guide to the future.

places.quote: The method needs **consistent count definitions** across the whole triangle
Counts must be **defined consistently**: per claim or per claimant, counting claims closed without payment or not, treating reopened claims as new or as continuing.

requirements.statement: Frequency-severity techniques assume the claim settlement rate and case reserve adequacy are stable and the business mix is homogeneous, so observed severity development reflects underlying claim cost rather than changes in settlement speed or reserving.

places.quote: A *change* in adequacy over calendar time is one of the two distortions ([[Settlement Rate|settlement rate]] is the other) that make historical development factors misleading.
A change in it distorts **paid** development in the same way a change in [[Case Adequacy|case adequacy]] distorts reported development.

requirements.statement: An age-to-age development factor is the ratio of cumulative reported claims at one maturity to cumulative reported claims at the prior maturity for the same accident year; development factors are selected by averaging (straight, weighted, etc.) across accident years.

places.quote: **Age-to-Age Factor** (link ratio) is the ratio of a cohort's cumulative amount at one maturity to its amount at the previous maturity — the observed development between two ages.

requirements.statement: The cumulative development factor (CDF) to ultimate for a maturity is the product of the selected age-to-age factors from that maturity through the tail factor.

places.quote: $$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$

**Cumulative Development Factor** (CDF, or age-to-ultimate factor) is the product of all selected [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] from a given maturity through to ultimate, including the [[Tail Factor|tail]].

requirements.statement: Used-up premium for an accident year equals its earned premium multiplied by the percent reported (1/CDF to ultimate).

places.quote: **Used-up premium** $\text{EP}_i / \text{CDF}_i$ is the share of each year's premium "exposed" to the losses reported so far.
$P_i / \text{CDF}_i$ is the **used-up premium**, the share of the premium that the claims reported so far correspond to.

requirements.statement: The Cape Cod expected claims ratio equals total reported claims across all accident years divided by total used-up premium.

places.quote: The ELR is estimated as total reported losses over total *used-up* (on-level, developed) premium across all years.

requirements.statement: Cape Cod ultimate claims equal reported claims plus expected unreported claims, where expected unreported claims = premium × expected claims ratio × (1 − percent reported).

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$
$$U = \text{Reported} + \text{IBNR}$$
$$\hat U_j = C_j + \text{IBNR}_j$$

requirements.statement: A change in the mix of business that speeds up claim reporting lowers the observed development factors, so selected factors that include older, slower-reporting experience are too high, giving CDFs that are too high.

places.quote: If the segments have different emergence patterns, the blended development factors drift as the weights drift — and the triangle gives no signal that this is what is happening.
*Growth in a slower-developing segment*: every technique on the combined data understates.

requirements.statement: In the Cape Cod method, CDFs that are too high understate the percent reported and used-up premium, which overstates the expected claims ratio and the percent unreported, so ultimate claims and IBNR are overstated.

places.quote: The cost is that the estimate is no longer independent of the data: a systematically distorted triangle now corrupts the a priori as well as the development.
A distorted CDF corrupts both the used-up premium and the IBNR.

requirements.statement: The development (chain ladder) technique estimates ultimate claims by multiplying reported claims by the cumulative development factor (CDF) from historical patterns, and IBNR is ultimate minus reported claims.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Reported}$$

**Chain Ladder Method** (development or link-ratio method) projects each cohort to ultimate by multiplying its latest cumulative amount by a [[Cumulative Development Factor|cumulative development factor]] derived from the historical pattern.

requirements.statement: The development technique assumes the historical development pattern still applies; if reporting speeds up (operational change) and the factors are not adjusted, the CDFs are too high and ultimate claims and IBNR are overstated.

places.quote: Every development-based estimate of [[Unpaid Claims|unpaid claims]] assumes the past pattern will repeat; a changing condition is whatever breaks that assumption.
**The pattern is stable over calendar time.** Violated by a change in [[Case Adequacy|case adequacy]], [[Settlement Rate|settlement speed]] or [[Inflation|inflation]] — the diagonal effects.

requirements.statement: The development technique is sensitive to the level of reported claims, so a shift in mix producing higher reported claims in recent years leads stale factors to be applied to a larger base, magnifying the overstatement.

places.quote: In **reserving**, a mix shift breaks the [[Homogeneity|homogeneity]] assumption behind the [[Development Triangle|triangle]]. If the segments have different emergence patterns, the blended development factors drift as the weights drift
**Future development is proportional to what has emerged.** This is the strong one: the method takes whatever sits on the diagonal at face value and scales it.

requirements.statement: The expected claims technique estimates ultimate claims as premium times an a priori expected claims ratio, with IBNR equal to ultimate minus reported claims (or expected claims times the percent unreported), and does not use reported claims to develop ultimate.

places.quote: the [[Expected Loss Method|expected claims]] technique by subtracting reported from an a priori ultimate

**Expected Loss Method** (expected claims technique) estimates ultimate losses entirely from an a priori expectation — usually an expected loss ratio applied to earned premium — giving **no weight** to what has actually been reported.

requirements.statement: The expected claims technique is unaffected by changes in reporting pattern when the pattern is only used for percent unreported, and a mix shift to higher loss cost business that is priced adequately raises premium proportionally, leaving the expected claims ratio reasonable; if premium is inadequate for the shifted mix, the ratio is too low and IBNR is understated.

places.quote: Its virtue is **stability**: the estimate does not move with a thin diagonal, so a single early large claim or a slow month of reporting cannot swing it.
*Rising claim ratios*: development techniques still work; the [[Expected Loss Method|expected claims]] technique fails unless its ratio is updated;

requirements.statement: The Cape Cod technique computes the expected claims ratio as total reported claims divided by total used-up premium (premium divided by CDF), then applies it as in the expected claims technique to estimate IBNR.

places.quote: The ELR is estimated as total reported losses over total *used-up* (on-level, developed) premium across all years.

requirements.statement: With overstated CDFs, Cape Cod understates used-up premium (raising the expected claims ratio) and overstates the percent unreported, so IBNR is overstated, though by less than under the development technique because it is partly anchored on premium.

places.quote: The cost is that the estimate is no longer independent of the data: a systematically distorted triangle now corrupts the a priori as well as the development.
A distorted CDF corrupts both the used-up premium and the IBNR.

requirements.statement: Calendar year earned premium is the premium earned during the calendar year, found by earning each policy's premium pro rata over the portion of its term that falls within that calendar year.

places.quote: $$\text{EP for one policy} = \text{Full premium} \times \frac{\text{days elapsed}}{\text{policy term}}$$
premium is earned evenly, by either the **daily pro rata** method, which computes the unexpired portion of each policy

requirements.statement: A full-term premium for a mid-term endorsement is earned only over the period from the endorsement effective date to the policy expiration, so prorate it by the fraction of the full term that the endorsement is in effect.

places.quote: Additional premium for an endorsement is recorded on the endorsement's effective date and earned in the same way.

requirements.statement: A cancellation effective after the end of the calendar year does not affect that calendar year's earned premium, since the policy is still in force for the entire portion of the term that falls in that year.

places.quote: the portion of premium corresponding to coverage the insurer has actually provided — the premium it has earned the right to keep, recognized pro rata as the policy term elapses.
Cancellation returns the unearned portion.

requirements.statement: Policy year groups together all policies by their effective date within the year, so a policy year contains only policies written (effective) in that year, along with all of their premium and losses, including later endorsements.

places.quote: **Policy year** earned premium comes from one cohort only, and is fully earned $24$ months after the policy year begins (for annual policies).

**Policy Year** (PY), also called underwriting year or year of account, is a data aggregation method that groups every premium and loss transaction belonging to policies *incepting* in a given calendar year, and follows that cohort until the last claim closes.

requirements.statement: Policy year losses include all losses from accidents on policies effective in that year, regardless of when they occur or are paid, as long as they are within the evaluation date.

places.quote: **[[Policy Year]]** — every transaction on policies incepting in the year.

**Policy Year** (PY), also called underwriting year or year of account, is a data aggregation method that groups every premium and loss transaction belonging to policies *incepting* in a given calendar year, and follows that cohort until the last claim closes.

requirements.statement: For a canceled policy, policy year premium is the full-term premium prorated to the portion of the term the policy was in force before cancellation.

places.quote: Cancellation returns the unearned portion. **Pro rata** cancellation returns the full unearned premium

requirements.statement: Loss ratio equals losses divided by premium, where for a policy year evaluation, the premium is the fully earned premium of that policy year.

places.quote: Earned premium is the usual denominator of a [[Loss Ratio|loss ratio]]
**Loss Ratio** is losses (usually with LAE) divided by earned premium

requirements.statement: Average case outstanding per open claim is case outstanding divided by the number of open claims at the same evaluation date; the triangle of these averages is used to assess changes in case reserve adequacy.

places.quote: $$\text{Avg Case Outstanding} = \frac{\text{Case Reserves}}{\text{Open Claim Counts}}$$
**Open counts** — the inventory. Divided into case reserves it gives **average case outstanding**, the sharpest [[Case Adequacy|case adequacy]] diagnostic.

requirements.statement: If average case outstanding per open claim down a column (same maturity) rises faster than the selected severity trend, the excess indicates strengthened case reserve adequacy; a single evaluation point or increases in line with trend are not sufficient evidence.

places.quote: It should grow at roughly the severity trend. A jump concentrated on one **diagonal**, appearing at every maturity at once, is a change in reserving practice, not in claim cost.
**[[Case Adequacy|Case strengthening]]:** average case outstanding rises faster than trend on the latest diagonals, and paid-to-reported falls.

requirements.statement: To restate average case outstanding, take the latest diagonal as the current adequacy level and de-trend each value backward along its column (and across the diagonals) at the selected severity trend rate, dividing by (1+trend) for each year back.

places.quote: 3. **Trend the latest diagonal's** average case outstanding backwards at $t$ to restate each historical cell at today's adequacy level.

The remedy is the [[Berquist-Sherman Method|Berquist-Sherman]] case adjustment: restate historical average case outstanding to the current adequacy level using a selected severity trend, rebuild the reported triangle, and select factors from the restated history.

requirements.statement: Adjusted case outstanding equals adjusted average case outstanding times open claim count, and adjusted reported claims equal cumulative paid claims plus adjusted case outstanding.

places.quote: 4. Multiply the restated averages by the open claim counts to get adjusted case reserves, add paid, and rebuild the reported triangle.

requirements.statement: Compute age-to-age factors from the adjusted reported triangle, select factors (e.g., average or weighted average), multiply them with the given tail factor to get the cumulative development factor, and apply it to the latest adjusted reported claims to get ultimate claims.

places.quote: $$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \left(\prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1}\right) \times \text{Tail}$$

**The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.

requirements.statement: When case reserve adequacy has strengthened, unadjusted reported development factors are distorted upward (historical case reserves were weaker and developed further), so the unadjusted method overstates ultimate claims relative to the Berquist-Sherman adjusted result.

places.quote: Applying historical factors — built under weaker reserving — to a strengthened diagonal **over-states** ultimate, because the strengthening is developed a second time.
**Reported chain ladder** is now biased **high**: historical factors were built on weaker reserves and are being applied to a strengthened diagonal, developing the strengthening a second time.

requirements.statement: A limitation of the Berquist-Sherman case outstanding adjustment is that results are highly sensitive to the judgmentally selected severity trend, and it attributes all deviation from trend in average case outstanding to adequacy change even though changes in claim mix or settlement prioritization could cause it.

places.quote: The adjustments are **large and judgment-laden** — the severity trend and the target disposal pattern are both selections — so the restated result should be compared against methods that are insensitive to the distortion in question

requirements.statement: The S&S ratio at a given maturity is cumulative received salvage and subrogation divided by cumulative paid claims gross of S&S at that same maturity (not by ultimate claims).

places.quote: Auto physical damage. Historical ratios of cumulative received S&S to cumulative paid claims settle at $0.108$, having been $0.060$ at $12$ months and $0.095$ at $24$ months.

requirements.statement: Develop the S&S ratios by computing age-to-age factors of the ratios between successive maturities, selecting a factor for each interval (e.g., average), and setting the tail factor from the stated development (no development beyond the last age gives 1.000).

places.quote: A tail of exactly $1.000$ is itself an assumption — that development is complete — and it is the wrong one for any casualty line.
Ratio development to ultimate: $0.108 / 0.095 = 1.137$ from $24$ months; $0.108 / 0.060 = 1.800$ from $12$ months.

requirements.statement: The cumulative development factor to ultimate at a given age is the product of the selected age-to-age factors from that age through the final age (including the tail factor).

places.quote: $$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \left(\prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1}\right) \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: Estimate the ultimate S&S ratio for each accident year by multiplying its latest diagonal ratio by the CDF to ultimate for its age.

places.quote: \text{Ultimate ratio} &= 0.0950 \times 1.137 = 0.1080

requirements.statement: Select the ultimate S&S ratio for the immature year using judgment: an indication that is out of line with mature years because a highly leveraged early-age CDF is applied to an unusual ratio may be replaced by an average of prior years' ultimate ratios, unless a genuine trend is supported.

places.quote: Absent a reason, a selection near the historical level is typical

requirements.statement: Ultimate S&S for an accident year equals the selected ultimate S&S ratio times the accident year's selected ultimate claims gross of S&S.
IBNYR (pure IBNR) is the provision for claims that have occurred but have not yet been reported, as distinct from case outstanding and IBNER (development on reported claims).
requirements.concept: Unpaid Claim Components (Case Outstanding, IBNER, IBNYR)

places.quote: **Pure IBNR** (narrow IBNR) covers claims that have occurred but are unknown to the insurer.
Counts split broad IBNR into its two parts: **pure IBNR** (unreported claims, valued at an expected severity) and **IBNER** (development on known claims).

requirements.statement: IBNYR for an accident year equals ultimate claims times (1 minus reported claim counts divided by ultimate claim counts), i.e. unreported count share applied to ultimate claim dollars (equivalently unreported counts times ultimate severity).
requirements.concept: Unpaid Claim Components (Case Outstanding, IBNER, IBNYR)

places.quote: develop counts to ultimate, subtract reported counts to get unreported claims, and value them at an expected severity.

requirements.statement: Total unpaid claims for an accident year equal ultimate claims minus paid claims, and this total equals case outstanding plus IBNER plus IBNYR.
requirements.concept: Unpaid Claim Components (Case Outstanding, IBNER, IBNYR)

places.quote: $$\text{Unpaid} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Paid to date}$$
Total unpaid claim liability = Case Reserves + IBNR; case reserves cover known claims while IBNR covers unreported claims and development on known claims
$$\text{IBNR} = \underbrace{\text{Pure IBNR}}_{\text{unreported claims}} + \underbrace{\text{IBNER}}_{\text{development on known claims}}$$

requirements.statement: In the classical (Wendy Johnson) ULAE method, estimate the ULAE ratio as calendar-year paid ULAE divided by calendar-year paid claims, using a selected ratio across years.

places.quote: Compute the ratio $R$ of calendar-year paid ULAE to calendar-year paid loss, review it for trend, and apply it to unpaid claims.

requirements.statement: Under the classical ULAE method, the assumed split of ULAE work (opening vs closing) determines the weights: claims not yet reported (IBNYR) receive 100% of the ULAE, while reported open claims (case plus IBNER) receive only the closing percentage.

places.quote: If ULAE is assumed to be spent half at reporting and half at settlement, only $50\%$ remains on reported-but-unpaid claims while $100\%$ remains on [[IBNR]]

requirements.statement: Unpaid ULAE = ULAE ratio × [IBNYR + closing percentage × (case outstanding + IBNER)].

places.quote: $$\text{ULAE Reserve} = R \times \left(0.5 \times \text{Case} + 1.0 \times \text{IBNR}\right)$$

requirements.statement: Update a cumulative paid triangle's latest diagonal by adding each accident year's calendar-year payments to its prior cumulative value at the preceding age (the same accident year's previous diagonal entry).
In the additive ratio approach, build a triangle of cumulative paid ALAE divided by cumulative paid claims for each accident year and age.

places.quote: Friedland gives three approaches: develop a **combined** loss-and-ALAE triangle, develop **ALAE separately** in its own triangle, or develop a **ratio of ALAE to loss** and apply it to projected losses.

requirements.statement: Additive development factors are the differences between successive-age ALAE-to-claims ratios, and are cumulated by summing selected differences to give an age-to-ultimate additive factor.
The projected ultimate ALAE-to-claims ratio equals the current ratio plus the age-to-ultimate additive factor.
Estimate ultimate claims with the paid development (chain ladder) method: select age-to-age factors, multiply them into a cumulative development factor, and apply it to latest cumulative paid claims.

places.quote: **The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.
CDFs are built **backwards from the tail**: start with the tail factor, multiply in each successive age-to-age factor moving toward younger ages.

requirements.statement: Ultimate ALAE under the ratio approach is the projected ultimate ALAE-to-claims ratio multiplied by the estimated ultimate claims (not by paid claims to date).

places.quote: develop a **ratio of ALAE to loss** and apply it to projected losses.

requirements.statement: A disadvantage of ratio techniques for ALAE is that the ALAE estimate depends on the accuracy of the ultimate claims estimate, and the ratio can misstate ALAE when ALAE and claims do not move together (e.g., defense costs on claims closed without payment).

places.quote: Combining is simplest and is the usual choice, but it assumes ALAE develops like indemnity. It often does not: defence costs accrue steadily through litigation while indemnity lands at settlement, so an ALAE-only triangle can have a different shape and a different tail.

requirements.statement: The percent reported (or percent paid) at an age equals the reciprocal of the cumulative reported (or paid) development factor to ultimate at that age.

places.quote: $p_t = 1/\text{CDF}_t$ is the expected percentage reported (or paid) at age $t$.
The reciprocal is the **percentage reported** (or paid): $p_n = 1/\text{CDF}_n$, and $1 - p_n$ is the percentage unreported.

requirements.statement: To get the expected pattern at an age between evaluation points, assume linear emergence and linearly interpolate the percent reported/paid between the adjacent evaluation ages, not the development factors.

resolution.note: Data the question gives: it states loss emergence between evaluation points is linear, which is the interpolation of percent reported; the percent-reported mechanics are on Actual vs Expected Analysis (in reach).

requirements.statement: Expected incremental emergence over a period equals the unreported (or unpaid) amount at the start (selected ultimate minus actual reported/paid to date) times the change in percent reported/paid divided by one minus the starting percent.

places.quote: $$\text{Expected emergence} = U_{\text{prior}} \times \left(\frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n+1}} - \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n}}\right)$$
$$\text{Expected emergence} = \text{IBNR} \times \frac{p_{t+\Delta} - p_t}{1 - p_t}$$

requirements.statement: Expected cumulative reported/paid claims equal the latest actual cumulative amount plus the expected incremental emergence, and this is compared with the actual cumulative amount at the new evaluation date.

places.quote: $$\text{Expected emergence} = \text{IBNR} \times \frac{p_{t+\Delta} - p_t}{1 - p_t}$$
$$\text{Expected emergence} = U_{\text{prior}} \times \left(\frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n+1}} - \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n}}\right)$$

requirements.statement: The selected ultimate should be revised when actual-versus-expected variance reflects genuinely more claim dollars, such as a large loss or catastrophe claim occurring in the period, even if it is a one-off that is excluded from future accident-year expectations.

Reported claims exceeding expectation while paid claims track expectation can result from case reserve strengthening, which changes timing of emergence rather than the ultimate, so the ultimate need not be revised, though the pattern should be revisited.
requirements.concept: Changes in Case Reserve Adequacy and Settlement Rates

places.quote: **Strengthening** raises reported losses immediately, so recent age-to-age factors fall (more of the ultimate is already booked).
The wider consequence: paid A/E at $1.0$ means the ultimate cost of these claims may not have changed at all.

requirements.statement: The parallelogram method computes the average rate level for a calendar year by weighting each rate level by the portion of the year's earned premium written at that level, using the area of the parallelogram (or triangle) formed by a rate change's effective date and the policy term.

places.quote: each region's **area** is the share of the year's earned premium written at that rate level.
it uses geometry — and the assumption that policies are written evenly through time — to find what share of the period's premium was earned at each historical rate level.

requirements.statement: With policies of term length m (in years) and uniform writing, a rate change effective at time t within the year is fully earned after m years, and the portion of the calendar year earned at the new level is (1-t)^2/(2m) for a change occurring when the term exceeds the remaining time.

places.quote: For **annual** policies written uniformly, a rate change effective at time $p$ through year $Y$ earns over a triangle of area $\tfrac{1}{2}(1-p)^2$ in year $Y$ — so a $7/1$ change affects only $0.125$ of that year's earned premium, and a $1/1$ change affects $0.500$.
A rate change for policies written on or after a date is a **diagonal** line whose slope is set by the term (steeper for six-month policies).

requirements.statement: The on-level factor equals the current cumulative rate level divided by the average rate level for the period, where the cumulative rate level index is the product of (1 + overall average rate change) over successive changes.

places.quote: \text{On-Level Factor} = \frac{\text{Current cumulative rate level index}}{\text{Average rate level index for the period}}
\text{On-Level Factor} = \frac{\text{Current cumulative index}}{\text{Average index for the year}}
$I_k$ is the cumulative rate level index of rate level group $k$ (each index is the previous one times $1 +$ that change)

requirements.statement: The extension of exposures method computes the on-level factor for a policy or class by recalculating premium at current rates (base rate times class factors plus any per-exposure expense fee) and dividing by premium at the rates in effect on the policy's effective date.

places.quote: $\mathbf{x}_j$ is policy $j$'s set of rating characteristics (class, territory, limit, deductible, …), $e_j$ its exposure, and $P_{\text{current}}$ the premium the current [[Rating Algorithm|rating algorithm]] — rates, relativities, fees — produces for it.
\text{Premium} = \left[\text{Base Rate} \times \prod_i R_i + \sum_j A_j\right] \times (1 - D) + \text{Fees}

requirements.statement: The parallelogram method uses the overall average rate change at the aggregate level and cannot capture rate changes that differ across classes, so it is inappropriate for class-level on-leveling such as indicated class factors unless applied separately with each class's own rate impact; extension of exposures is appropriate instead.
requirements.concept: Parallelogram Method vs Extension of Exposures

places.quote: where the rate changes varied by class the on-level premium is unusable for classification ratemaking.

And it applies the *overall average* change, so if changes varied by class or territory the segment premiums are not on-level, which makes the result unacceptable for [[Classification Ratemaking|classification]] work

The premium is on-level *by segment* — which the [[Parallelogram Method|parallelogram method]]'s single average factor cannot deliver — so it is the method needed for [[Classification Ratemaking|classification]] and territorial analyses.

requirements.statement: A claims-made policy covers all claims reported during the policy period, regardless of when the loss occurred, so its report-year loss cost sums all lags for that report year.

places.quote: **Claims-Made Coverage** is a policy trigger under which the policy responds to claims *reported* during the policy period, provided the underlying loss occurred on or after the policy's **retroactive date**.
every claim reported during the policy period is covered by that policy, so the report year cohort and the coverage cohort coincide.

requirements.statement: An occurrence policy covers all claims occurring during the policy period regardless of when they are reported, so its accident-year loss cost sums losses across later report years and lags along the diagonal of the report-lag triangle.

places.quote: in Werner's report-year-by-lag table a claims-made policy is a row, where an occurrence policy is a diagonal.
**Occurrence Coverage** is a policy trigger under which the policy responds to losses that *occur* during the policy period, however long afterwards the claim is reported.

requirements.statement: An occurrence policy has a longer development period than a claims-made policy because it is exposed to both report lag and settlement lag, whereas claims-made is exposed to settlement lag only; hence an unexpected trend increase distorts occurrence pricing more.

places.quote: If there is a sudden, unpredictable change in the underlying trends, the claims-made policy priced on the prior trend will be closer to the correct price than an occurrence policy priced on the prior trend.

Pricing an occurrence policy means projecting claims that may not be reported, let alone settled, for many years, where a [[Claims Made Coverage|claims-made]] price needs only the claims reported in the coming policy period — so the pricing risk is greater.

requirements.statement: IBNR consists of pure IBNR (IBNYR: losses incurred but not yet reported) and IBNER (losses reported but not yet adequately valued).

places.quote: **Pure IBNR** (narrow IBNR) covers claims that have occurred but are unknown to the insurer.

**A claims-made book has no pure IBNR** by construction — every claim in a [[Report Year|report year]] is already reported — so its IBNR is entirely IBNER.

requirements.statement: Compute the projected pure premium by trending each accident year's ultimate loss per earned exposure (exposures not trended) at the pure premium trend, then averaging the years with selected weights (equal weights means a simple average of per-year pure premiums).

places.quote: Weighting across years in the experience period is a judgment: many companies sum projected losses and premium across all years, which weights each year's loss ratio by its premium; others select weights, often giving more to the most recent years.

historical losses developed to ultimate, trended to the forecast period, adjusted for [[Large Loss|large losses]] and [[Catastrophe Loss|catastrophes]], and divided by exposures that are themselves trended if the base inflates ([[Exposure Trend]]).

requirements.statement: Indicated average premium = [pure premium × (1 + ULAE ratio) + fixed expense per exposure + net reinsurance cost per exposure] / (1 − variable expense ratio − profit provision − contingency provision).

\text{Premium} = \frac{\text{Loss cost}\,(1 + \text{ULAE}) + \text{Fixed}}{1 - \text{Variable \%}}

places.quote: \text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Indicated Rate}}{\text{Current Rate}} - 1

requirements.statement: A large rate increase relative to competitors' prices lowers policyholder retention (renewal ratio) and new business close (hit) ratio, shrinking volume and market share, while improving the loss ratio and profit per risk on retained business.

places.quote: Past some price the business lost outweighs the higher price on what remains, and rate changes themselves prompt renewing customers to shop.
Mix shifts are frequently **endogenous to pricing**: a large [[Rate Change|rate increase]] drives away the risks with the most alternatives, which are usually the better ones.
At the competitor's $+4\%$, a $14\%$ increase would cost roughly $5.7$ points of retention and the shoppers who leave are disproportionately the better risks.

requirements.statement: An insured's propensity to renew depends on factors such as the size of the rate change at renewal, price relative to competitors, claim handling and service quality, tenure and loyalty, age of insured, product price level, and whether coverage is mandatory.

Customers' decisions to renew or switch depend on competitors' prices, the size of a rate change, how costly the product is, who the customer is, and their satisfaction with claims handling and service.

requirements.statement: A company can protect profitability without changing rates by reducing expenses such as commissions, marketing and overhead.

places.quote: reducing **expenses** — fixed or variable;
**Reduce expenses** — underwriting or LAE: a smaller marketing budget, lower staffing, lower acquisition cost.

Tightening usually **lowers** severity and may accelerate closing, so historical development factors — built on a riskier book — overstate ultimate for the post-change years.
*Change the portfolio* — tighten underwriting criteria, or non-renew policies whose premium is grossly inadequate.

requirements.statement: Improving claims handling, such as using more experienced adjusters and controlling claim leakage, reduces loss dollars paid and supports profitability without a rate change.

places.quote: to support the insurer's profit goal by paying no more than the policy owes and controlling the cost of adjusting.
The outcome of the process is a payment that keeps the insurer's promise and no more than the policy owes.

requirements.statement: Comparing average premiums across companies is distorted by differences in mix of business, such as risk profiles, coverage levels, limits, deductibles, and underwriting guidelines or target markets.

the drift caused by distributional shifts in the policies written (amounts of insurance, limits, deductibles, [[Mix of Business|mix of business]])

requirements.statement: To compare premiums fairly across companies, hold risk characteristics fixed by obtaining competitor quotes for representative risk profiles, re-rating the company's book with competitors' filed rates, or comparing by segment.

The statistical (chi-square/p-value) test judges a GLM variable's significance: if the p-value is above the significance threshold (commonly 5%), the variable is not statistically significant and fails.

places.quote: A 5% threshold admits roughly one useless variable in twenty when many are tried, and the monograph warns there is no "magic" p-value.
Reject $H_0$ at level $\alpha$ when $Q$ exceeds the upper-$\alpha$ [[Critical Value|critical value]] of the [[Chi-Squared Distribution|chi-squared distribution]] with $k - 1 - r$ degrees of freedom.

requirements.statement: The main effect test examines the GLM standard error bounds around each level's indicated relativity: if the bounds include 1.0 (the base) at most levels, the relativities are not distinguishable from unity and the variable fails.

places.quote: **Class C** has $p = 0.17$. Its relativity is $1.10$ with interval $[0.96, 1.26]$, which includes $1.00$. The data cannot tell Class C apart from the base.
The interval excludes $1.00$, so the effect is significant at $5\%$ — but it is wide enough that the indicated relativity is far from precisely known.

requirements.statement: The consistency test compares GLM-indicated relativities across time periods (e.g., years); a variable passes only if the indications move in a consistent pattern, and fails if years diverge or move in opposite directions.

Judgment is the final test of a variable; low exposure at levels with extreme indications explains wide error bounds and inconsistency, and a variable failing the quantitative tests should be excluded unless there is a judgmental reason to include it.

places.quote: Variable selection should combine statistical significance (from the [[Parameter Estimate Tables|parameter estimate table]]) with business and actuarial judgment, e.g., regulatory restrictions on certain rating variables

requirements.statement: Modeling loss ratios in a GLM requires premium to be on-leveled to current rate level, otherwise the model reflects past rate changes rather than risk.

places.quote: It works entirely in ratios, so it needs premium on level rather than exposure counts.
**On-Level Premium** is historical earned premium restated as though every policy had been written at the rate level currently in effect.

requirements.statement: Loss ratios have no natural error distribution or a priori expected shape (unlike Poisson-family for frequency and Gamma for severity), making distribution and link function choice difficult.
requirements.concept: GLM Challenges with Loss Ratio Data

requirements.statement: A GLM fitted to loss ratios is tied to the rate level during the experience period and becomes obsolete when rates change, unlike a pure premium model, which is independent of the rating structure.
requirements.concept: GLM Challenges with Loss Ratio Data

places.quote: The [[Pure Premium Method]] needs no on-levelling at all, because it never divides by premium. That is its principal practical advantage where rate history is messy or the book has been re-tiered.
Pure premium is the **premium-free** view of cost: because it never divides by premium, it needs no [[On-Leveling|on-levelling]] and is unaffected by rate history.

requirements.statement: Univariate analysis can be preferable to GLM because it is simpler and more transparent to explain to management, underwriters and regulators, and it suits thin data or limited software, computing power or expertise.

Written exposures are the exposures on policies recorded when the policy is written (or when a mid-term change takes effect), attributed to the calendar period in which that transaction is booked; a mid-term change adds or subtracts exposure in proportion to the remaining term.

places.quote: A $12$-month policy contributes **one** earned car-year in total, spread pro rata over its term: written the day it is issued, earned $1/12$ per month, in force from effective date to expiry.

requirements.statement: Earned exposures are the portion of exposure for which coverage has actually been provided during the period, equal to exposure multiplied by the fraction of the term elapsed within the period, and reflecting any mid-term changes.

places.quote: **Earned Exposure** is the portion of written exposure for which coverage has actually been provided during the period — the exposure analogue of [[Earned Premium|earned premium]], and the correct denominator for a pure premium.

requirements.statement: Policy year exposures include all transactions on policies effective in that policy year, but only those transactions that have occurred by the evaluation date, so later mid-term changes are excluded until they occur.

places.quote: With annual policies a PY cohort is not fully written until $12$ months after the year begins and not fully earned until $24$ months, so PY data is roughly a year less mature than the corresponding [[Accident Year]] at the same valuation date.

requirements.statement: A good exposure base should satisfy three criteria: it is proportional to expected loss, it is practical, and it has historical precedence.

places.quote: All else equal, a policy with two exposures should have twice the expected loss of a similar policy with one.

requirements.statement: An exposure base is practical if it is objectively defined, easy and inexpensive to obtain and verify, and not subject to manipulation by the insured.

places.quote: **Practical.** Objective, and relatively easy and inexpensive to obtain and verify — which also keeps policyholders and producers from manipulating it (declared annual mileage invites more dishonesty than car-years).

requirements.statement: Historical precedence means that changing the exposure base from the one currently used would cause system and rating algorithm costs, premium swings for policyholders, and loss of historical data and industry benchmarks.

places.quote: **Consistent with historical precedence.** A change of base can cause large premium swings for individual insureds, requires a change in the rating algorithm and systems, and may force significant adjustments to the several years of data a ratemaking analysis uses.

requirements.statement: Operational criteria for evaluating a rating variable are practical considerations for the insurer, including objective definition, verifiability/resistance to manipulation, and inexpensive administration.

places.quote: It should be objective and hard to manipulate, practical to collect and verify, and legal ([[Risk Classification Restrictions]], [[Unfair Discrimination]]) and socially acceptable.
**Operational** — objective, inexpensive to obtain and verify, not manipulable by the insured.

requirements.statement: Social criteria for evaluating a rating variable are considerations of public acceptability, including causality, controllability, affordability, and privacy.

places.quote: **Social** — privacy, causality, controllability and affordability; these are where public and regulatory objections arise.

**Standard criteria** for whether a classification variable is acceptable: actuarial (statistically significant, homogeneous, credible), operational (objective, cheap to verify, not manipulable), social (privacy, causality, affordability, controllability) and legal (permitted in the jurisdiction).

places.quote: The insured reports the figure, has every reason to under-report it, and the insurer cannot cheaply verify it.

requirements.statement: A rating variable is more acceptable to the public when it has an intuitive causal relationship to losses rather than only a statistical correlation.

places.quote: It must be statistically related to expected losses; a causal story strengthens the case, but ASOP No. 12 does not require one.
**Social** — privacy, causality, controllability and affordability; these are where public and regulatory objections arise.

requirements.statement: A variable is controllable if the insured can change it to reduce their risk and premium; a variable that is costly to change or does not affect risk gives the insured no real incentive to reduce losses.

Adverse selection in insurance pricing occurs when a company's rates are too low for high-risk insureds relative to competitors, so it attracts and retains underpriced high-risk insureds while losing overpriced low-risk insureds, producing losses.

places.quote: **Adverse Selection** is the tendency for those who know they are worse-than-average risks to buy more insurance, and better-than-average risks to buy less, when the insurer cannot distinguish between them.

In a competitive market an insurer that charges one average rate to a heterogeneous group loses the better risks to competitors that price them properly, and retains the worse ones — the **adverse selection spiral**.

requirements.statement: Price-shopping insureds in each risk class move to the company charging the lower rate for that class, so the shifted count is the shopping percentage times the losing company's insureds in that class, and each company's class counts are adjusted accordingly.

places.quote: Price at the population average; low risks find the price poor value and leave; the remaining pool is worse, so the price rises; more of the remaining low risks leave; repeat.
At each renewal, one driver in five in each group shops on price and moves to whichever insurer is cheaper.

requirements.statement: A company's underwriting profit equals the sum over risk classes of the number of insureds times (charged rate minus true expected cost), with no expenses or profit provision.

places.quote: $$\text{UW Profit} = \text{EP} - \text{Losses} - \text{LAE} - \text{UW Expenses}$$

requirements.statement: A company suffering adverse selection can reduce insolvency risk by refining its rate classification to charge each class a rate closer to its expected cost (raising rates on underpriced high-risk classes).

places.quote: [[Risk Classification Restrictions|risk classification]] (price to the risk, so nobody is overcharged)

requirements.statement: A company suffering adverse selection can tighten underwriting to decline or restrict high-risk applicants, or shift marketing toward low-risk insureds, to improve its mix of business and reduce losses.

places.quote: underwriting and medical or inspection requirements
freedom to underwrite (select, decline, set terms)

places.quote: A **univariate** (one-way) pure premium or loss ratio analysis attributes to a variable the effect of everything correlated with it.
A univariate analysis assigns the whole effect to territory and would double-count when the other variables are rated too — the problem multivariate methods exist to solve.

requirements.statement: The adjusted pure premium approach divides class losses by exposures adjusted by the exposure-weighted average relativity of the other rating variables, which removes much of the distributional bias.

places.quote: When other rating variables also apply, each class's exposures are first multiplied by their average relativity for those other variables, so that the factor measures only this variable's effect on the average premium.

requirements.statement: Assess GLM relativity credibility from diagnostic charts by comparing exposure volume at each level and the width of the standard-error bounds: many exposures and narrow bands indicate a credible estimate, while few exposures and wide bands indicate an unreliable one.

places.quote: the property **coinsurance clause**, which penalizes an insured who carries limits below a required percentage of value.
In the property insurance context, a **coinsurance clause** can instead refer to a penalty applied when the insured carries less coverage than a required percentage of replacement value

requirements.statement: When the insured amount is below the coinsurance requirement, the indemnity is the loss times (insured amount / required amount), capped at the insured amount (face value); if insured amount meets the requirement, the loss is paid up to the limit.

places.quote: $$\text{Recovery}_{\text{clause}} = \min\!\left(\frac{\text{Insurance Carried}}{\text{Coinsurance \% } \times \text{Value}},\, 1\right) \times \text{Loss}$$
$$\text{Property payment} = \min\left(\min\left(\frac{C}{p \times V},\ 1\right) \times L - D,\ C\right)$$
$$R = \min\left(\frac{C}{p \times V},\ 1\right)$$

requirements.statement: The coinsurance penalty is the amount the insured would have received without the coinsurance clause (loss capped at the face value) minus the indemnity actually paid.

places.quote: With at least \$450,000 of insurance the insurer would have paid \$79,000, so the penalty costs the insured \$16,000.
Without the penalty the insurer would pay \$295,000, so the insured bears \$39,130.43 more than the deductible.

places.quote: **Total losses:** The clause cannot raise the payment above the limit, and on a total loss the insurer pays the full limit whether or not the requirement is met. The penalty therefore matters only for partial losses.

requirements.statement: Rates per unit of insurance assume insurance to value, and since most losses are partial, an underinsured policy produces nearly the same expected loss as a fully insured one while paying less premium, making rates inadequate for the insurer.
