places.quote: Without the clause, under-insuring would be free money on partial losses, and the rate per $\$1{,}000$ of stated value would have to be set as though every policy were under-insured.
Without the clause, the rate would have to reflect the book's actual mix of insurance to value, and insureds who carry full value would subsidise the rest.

requirements.statement: Expected losses equal the expected loss rate per $100 of payroll times payroll divided by 100.

resolution.note: arithmetic: the question gives the expected loss rate per $100 of payroll and the payroll

requirements.statement: The D-ratio is the proportion of expected losses that are expected primary losses; expected excess losses equal expected losses minus expected primary losses.

resolution.quote: The expected primary losses are the expected losses multiplied by the D-ratio…which is the share of expected losses that is expected to be primary. The expected excess losses are the expected losses minus the expected primary losses
resolution.note: D-ratio; W&M Ch.15 pp.295-296 (PDF 307-308), Table 15.5

requirements.statement: The experience rating modification is M = (Ap + w*Ae + (1-w)*Ee + B) / (E + B), where Ap and Ae are actual primary and excess losses, Ee is expected excess losses, w is the weighting value, B is the ballast, and E is total expected losses.

places.quote: $$M = \frac{A_p + wA_e + (1-w)E_e + B}{E_p + (1-w)E_e + B + wE_e} = \frac{A_p + wA_e + (1-w)E_e + B}{E + B}$$

requirements.statement: The basic premium ratio in retrospective rating is the expense allowance minus (LCF - 1) times the expected loss ratio, plus LCF times (insurance charge - insurance savings) times the expected loss ratio; basic premium equals this ratio times standard premium.

places.quote: $B = e - (c - 1)E + c\,[\phi(r_G) - \psi(r_H)]\,E$

requirements.statement: Retrospective premium equals (basic premium + loss conversion factor times limited reported losses) times the tax multiplier.

places.quote: $$R = \left(\text{BP} + L \times \text{LCF}\right) \times \text{TM}$$
**Retro premium** is $R = (B + cL)\,T$, with loss conversion factor $c$ (loads LAE) and tax multiplier $T = 1/(1 - \text{tax rate})$.

requirements.statement: Minimum and maximum retrospective premiums equal the minimum and maximum premium ratios times standard premium, and the calculated retrospective premium is constrained to lie within them.
requirements.concept: Retrospective Rating Minimum and Maximum Premium

places.quote: $$\text{Retro Premium} = \min\!\left(\max(R,\, R_{\min}),\, R_{\max}\right)$$

requirements.statement: The experience rating modification factor is not used in the retrospective premium calculation, which is based on standard premium and limited reported losses.

places.quote: Order of application: schedule and experience modifications apply to the manual premium to give **standard premium**, which is then the base for a retro plan or a large-deductible programme.
Retrospective or large-deductible terms then act on standard premium ([[Commercial Lines Rating]]).

requirements.statement: Accident year (calendar-year accident period) groups claims by the year in which the accident occurred, so claims with accident dates in other years are excluded.

places.quote: **[[Accident Year]]** is the default reserving basis for direct business: claims grouped by occurrence date produce a [[Development Triangle]] whose rows share an exposure period and whose columns share a maturity.

**Accident Year** (AY) is a data aggregation method that groups losses by the calendar year in which the loss event *occurred*, and matches them against the [[Earned Premium|premium earned]] in that same year — regardless of when the policy was written, when the claim was reported, or when it was paid.

requirements.statement: Development ages for an accident year are measured from the start of the accident year on a common calendar basis, so 12 months is the end of the accident year (Dec 31), 24 months is the next Dec 31, etc., regardless of each claim's individual accident date.

places.quote: **Development Triangle** is the fundamental data structure of reserving: cumulative amounts arranged with **cohorts as rows** (usually [[Accident Year|accident years]]), **maturities as columns** (age in months since the start of the cohort), and **valuation dates as diagonals**.

resolution.quote: maturities as columns (age in months since the start of the cohort), and valuation dates as diagonals
resolution.note: stale re-quote: the page still says ages are measured from the start of the cohort (accident year), so 12 months is the year's end

requirements.statement: Paid claims as of an evaluation date are the cumulative sum of all payments made on or before that date.

places.quote: **Paid Losses** are the cumulative cash payments made on covered claims through a valuation date — the only loss figure that contains no estimate.

requirements.statement: Reported (incurred) claims as of an evaluation date equal cumulative paid claims plus the case outstanding reserve at that date.

places.quote: $$\text{Reported Losses} = \text{Paid Losses} + \text{Case Reserves}$$
**Incurred Losses** — more precisely **reported losses** — are cumulative [[Paid Losses|payments]] plus [[Case Reserves|case outstanding]] on known claims at a valuation date.

requirements.statement: The case outstanding at an evaluation date is the ending case outstanding from the claim's latest transaction on or before that date; if no later transaction occurs it carries forward, and a claim not yet reported by that date contributes zero.

resolution.note: reading the question's own transaction table (ending case outstanding carries until the next transaction); reported = paid + case is taught on Case Reserves

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson ultimate claims estimate equals reported claims plus expected claims times the percentage unreported (1 − 1/CDF).

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$
$$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$

requirements.statement: Expected claims for an accident year equal the a priori expected claims ratio times earned premium, with premium adjusted to a common rate level (no adjustment if there are no rate changes).

places.quote: $C$ is reported (or paid) losses to date, $U_0 = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}$ the a priori expectation, and $1 - 1/\text{CDF}$ the percentage unreported from the [[Development Triangle|development pattern]].
$$\text{On-Level Premium} = \text{Historical EP} \times \text{On-Level Factor}$$

requirements.statement: Estimate age-to-age development factors from a claims triangle as volume-weighted averages (sum of later-age cumulative claims over sum of earlier-age cumulative claims for the same accident years).

places.quote: **Volume-weighted average**: $\Sigma(\text{col }n{+}1) / \Sigma(\text{col }n)$ — gives more credibility to larger accident years; the standard default selection
$$f_{k \to k+1} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k}}$$

requirements.statement: Compute cumulative development factors to ultimate by multiplying age-to-age factors from the given age through the last age, including a tail factor (1.000 if no development beyond the final age).

places.quote: CDFs are built **backwards from the tail**: start with the tail factor, multiply in each successive age-to-age factor moving toward younger ages.
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: The ultimate claim ratio is the ultimate claims divided by earned premium for the accident year.

places.quote: $$\text{Loss Ratio} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Premium}}$$

The numerator's loss ratio must be **projected**: ultimate losses (developed), trended to the future policy period, over earned premium brought to **current rate level** ([[On-Leveling]]) and trended ([[Premium Trend]]).

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson technique relies on the a priori expected claims ratio for the unreported portion, so it is appropriate only if that expected ratio is reasonable; a trend in claim ratios that differs from the a priori shows it is understated or overstated, especially for immature years.

places.quote: The a priori is the weak point. A stale ELR that ignores [[Rate Level Change|rate changes]] and [[Loss Trend|trend]] produces a systematically biased reserve — and the bias persists year after year without ever showing up as instability.

The [[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method|BF]] and [[Expected Loss Method|expected claims]] techniques need an expected loss ratio per accident year, and a year written after a $+15\%$ rate change should carry a materially lower ELR than the year before it.

requirements.statement: In the frequency-severity technique, ultimate claims for an accident year equal projected ultimate claim counts multiplied by projected ultimate severity.

places.quote: $$U = N_{\text{ult}} \times S_{\text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: Develop reported claim counts to ultimate by computing age-to-age factors from the count triangle, selecting them (e.g., simple average), and multiplying the successive factors into an age-to-ultimate factor applied to the latest count.

places.quote: $$\text{Ultimate Counts} = N_n \times \text{CDF}^{\text{count}}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{AY}} = \frac{C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$

**The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.

requirements.statement: Average reported severity at a given age equals cumulative reported claims divided by cumulative reported claim counts at that age.

places.quote: **Severity** is the average cost per claim — total losses divided by claim count — as distinct from [[Frequency|how often claims occur]].
$$\text{Average Severity} = \frac{\text{Losses}}{\text{Claim Counts}}$$

requirements.statement: Build a severity triangle, compute and select severity age-to-age factors, and use age-to-ultimate severity factors to develop each accident year's latest severity to ultimate severity.

places.quote: Develop the count triangle to ultimate counts; develop an average severity triangle (dollars ÷ counts at each age) to ultimate severity; multiply.
Severity **develops**, and it develops in two directions at once: upward through IBNER on known claims, downward through the dilution of late-reported small claims.

requirements.statement: Trend each accident year's ultimate severity to the target accident year's level using the annual severity trend compounded over the number of years between them, then select (e.g., average) the trended severities.

places.quote: $$\text{Trend Factor} = (1 + t)^{n}$$
The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: Adjust the selected severity for a law change such as tort reform by multiplying by (1 minus the percentage reduction) when all claims in the projected accident year occur after the effective date; the adjustment applies to severity, not to claim counts or reporting.

The paid (or reported) development technique estimates ultimate claims by multiplying the latest diagonal of cumulative claims by a cumulative development factor derived from historical triangle patterns.

places.quote: **Chain Ladder Method** (development or link-ratio method) projects each cohort to ultimate by multiplying its latest cumulative amount by a [[Cumulative Development Factor|cumulative development factor]] derived from the historical pattern.

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson technique estimates ultimate claims as actual reported (or paid) claims to date plus expected claims times the percentage unreported (or unpaid), i.e. 1 − 1/CDF.

places.quote: **Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method** (BF) estimates ultimate losses by adding to what has actually been reported an estimate of what has *not* — computed from an a priori expectation and the percentage still unreported.

requirements.statement: The development technique leverages actual claims to date by the full development factor, so for immature years an unusually large shock loss or an unexpected speedup in payments in the latest diagonal is projected as if typical and overstates ultimate claims, whereas the BF technique includes it only once and is not distorted.

places.quote: the method takes whatever sits on the diagonal at face value and scales it. A [[Large Loss|shock loss]] reported early is multiplied by the full CDF.

The key structural property: **actual emergence is taken at face value and only the unemerged portion is estimated**. The chain ladder instead scales the whole diagonal, so a distorted diagonal is multiplied by the full CDF.

requirements.statement: The development technique assumes historical development patterns remain stable, so a change in claim settlement speed distorts paid development patterns but not reported development patterns, since a change moves amounts between case reserves and payments while reported claims stay unchanged (assuming adequate case reserves).

places.quote: **Faster settlement** pushes losses from open to paid, so the recent paid diagonal is high relative to history. Historical paid factors — built when claims closed more slowly — then **over-develop** it and overstate ultimate.
**Reported data is largely immune**, because reported losses include the case reserve whether or not the claim has closed.

requirements.statement: BF expected claims are usually computed as an expected claims ratio times on-level earned premium, so an inaccurate rate change history impairs the premium on-leveling and the BF estimate, unless expected claims are set another way, such as expected pure premium times exposures.

places.quote: The [[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method|BF]] and [[Expected Loss Method|expected claims]] techniques need an expected loss ratio per accident year, and a year written after a $+15\%$ rate change should carry a materially lower ELR than the year before it.

requirements.statement: The development technique uses actual claims to date and so reflects unexpectedly high severity trend, while BF expected claims rely on the assumed trend and respond only slowly, understating the unreported portion when trend is higher than expected.

places.quote: Development can be **downward**.

requirements.statement: The development technique relies only on the claim triangle and does not use premium or rate change information, so rate changes do not affect it.

places.quote: It is entirely **data-driven**: nothing external — premium, exposure, rate level or judgment about the year — enters the estimate.

requirements.statement: Bühlmann credibility parameter K equals the expected value of process variance divided by the variance of hypothetical means (K = EPV/VHM).

places.quote: | $k = v/a$ | Bühlmann credibility parameter | Ratio of process variance to structural variance |
$K = \text{EPV}/\text{VHM}$ — expected value of the process variance over the variance of the hypothetical means.

requirements.statement: Bühlmann credibility Z = N/(N+K), where N is the number of observations (exposures) and K is the Bühlmann credibility parameter.

places.quote: $$Z = \frac{n}{n + k}, \quad k = \frac{v}{a}$$
$$Z = \frac{n}{n + K} \qquad \text{(Bühlmann)}$$

requirements.statement: The credibility-weighted indicated value is Z times the indicated value plus (1 − Z) times the complement of credibility.

places.quote: $$\text{Estimate} = Z \cdot \bar{X} + (1-Z) \cdot \mu$$
$$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$

requirements.statement: When the complement of credibility is trended present rates, trend the current average premium at present rates from the target effective date of the prior (original) rate review to the target effective date of the new rates, using the annual trend over that number of years.
requirements.concept: Trended Present Rates Complement of Credibility

places.quote: the current rate adjusted to what was last *indicated* rather than implemented, and trended from the original target effective date of the current rates to that of the new rates.
$$\text{Trend Factor} = (1 + t)^{n}$$

requirements.statement: When a prior indicated rate change was only partly implemented, adjust the trended present-rate complement by the residual indication, computed as (1 + indicated change)/(1 + implemented change).
requirements.concept: Trended Present Rates Complement of Credibility

places.quote: the current rate adjusted to what was last *indicated* rather than implemented

requirements.statement: The trend period for the trended present rates complement is measured from the prior review's target effective date, not its actual effective date.
requirements.concept: Trended Present Rates Complement of Credibility

places.quote: trended from the original target effective date of the current rates to that of the new rates.

requirements.statement: The reported claim development technique projects ultimate claims by applying age-to-age factors from historical reported claims to the current diagonal of reported claims to get to ultimate.

places.quote: **Chain Ladder Method** (development or link-ratio method) projects each cohort to ultimate by multiplying its latest cumulative amount by a [[Cumulative Development Factor|cumulative development factor]] derived from the historical pattern.

requirements.statement: The case outstanding development technique applies historical ratios of future payments (or unpaid) to case outstanding at each age to the current case outstanding to project unpaid claims.

places.quote: $f_{\text{case}}$ converts the current case balance into *all* remaining payments — including payments on claims not yet reported. It is estimated from mature years: for each historical cohort, divide everything paid after a given valuation by the case outstanding at that valuation.

requirements.statement: Development techniques assume that case reserve adequacy (claims settlement and case reserving practices) is consistent over time, so historical factors remain applicable to the current diagonal.

places.quote: **The pattern is stable over calendar time.** Violated by a change in [[Case Adequacy|case adequacy]], [[Settlement Rate|settlement speed]] or [[Inflation|inflation]] — the diagonal effects.

Its weakness is the mirror image: it depends entirely on case adequacy being stable. A [[Case Adequacy|strengthening]] inflates the base to which $f_{\text{case}}$ is applied, and the historical factor was estimated under the old, weaker regime.

requirements.statement: If case reserve strength increases and no adjustment is made, reported claim development overstates ultimate claims, because historical factors include development that no longer occurs but are applied to a strengthened (higher) reported diagonal.

places.quote: **Strengthening** raises reported losses immediately, so recent age-to-age factors fall (more of the ultimate is already booked). Applying historical factors — built under weaker reserving — to a strengthened diagonal **over-states** ultimate, because the strengthening is developed a second time.

resolution.quote: Applying historical factors — built under weaker reserving — to a strengthened diagonal over-states ultimate, because the strengthening is developed a second time.
resolution.note: stale re-quote: same teaching, reworded

requirements.statement: If case reserve strength increases and no adjustment is made, the case outstanding development technique overstates unpaid claims, because historical payment-to-case ratios reflect weaker case reserves but are applied to a higher current case outstanding.

places.quote: Its weakness is the mirror image: it depends entirely on case adequacy being stable. A [[Case Adequacy|strengthening]] inflates the base to which $f_{\text{case}}$ is applied, and the historical factor was estimated under the old, weaker regime.

requirements.statement: Paid claim development techniques rely only on paid claim data and are therefore not affected by changes in case reserve adequacy.

places.quote: **Paid data is immune**, so a divergence between paid and reported chain ladder estimates is the corroborating evidence.

Paid data is **objective**. It carries no adjuster judgment, so a paid triangle is immune to changes in [[Case Adequacy|case reserve adequacy]] — the single most common distortion in reported triangles.

requirements.statement: In the Berquist-Sherman case outstanding adjustment, select the average case outstanding at each age from the basis diagonal (latest or chosen calendar year) and trend it back or forward at the annual severity trend rate to each accident year to get the adjusted average case outstanding triangle.

places.quote: 3. **Trend the latest diagonal's** average case outstanding backwards at $t$ to restate each historical cell at today's adequacy level.

requirements.statement: The disposal rate is cumulative closed claim counts divided by ultimate claim counts for an accident year at a given age, and it measures the speed of claim settlement.

places.quote: $$\text{Disposal Rate}_n = \frac{\text{Closed claims at age } n}{\text{Ultimate claim counts}}$$
$$\text{Disposal Rate}_n = \frac{\text{Closed claims at age } n}{\text{Ultimate claim counts}}$$

requirements.statement: To adjust for changes in settlement rate, apply the disposal rates from the selected basis diagonal at each age to every accident year's ultimate claim counts to get adjusted closed counts, then subtract them from reported counts to get adjusted open counts.
Adjusted reported (incurred) loss equals adjusted cumulative paid loss plus adjusted open claim counts times adjusted average case outstanding.

places.quote: $$\text{Adjusted Reported}_{\text{AY},n} = \text{Paid}_{\text{AY},n} + \text{Adjusted Case}_{\text{AY},n}$$

resolution.quote: Multiply the restated averages by the open claim counts to get adjusted case reserves, add paid, and rebuild the reported triangle.
resolution.note: stale re-quote: adjusted reported = paid + open counts x adjusted average case; with both adjustments the paid and open counts are the adjusted ones

requirements.statement: Compute volume-weighted age-to-age factors from the adjusted reported triangle, multiply them into a cumulative development factor (including a tail factor assumption), and apply it to the latest adjusted reported value to estimate ultimate loss; develop the Berquist-Sherman adjusted triangle, not the unadjusted data.

places.quote: **The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.
$$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{vol-wtd}} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$

requirements.statement: Berquist-Sherman adjustments are needed when case reserve adequacy or claim settlement rates have changed, since these distortions make the unadjusted paid and reported triangles unreliable for chain ladder development.

places.quote: **Berquist-Sherman Method** restates a historical [[Development Triangle|triangle]] so that every year reflects **current** claims practice, removing the distortion caused by a change in [[Case Adequacy|case reserve adequacy]] or in [[Settlement Rate|claim settlement rates]].
A *change* in adequacy over calendar time is one of the two distortions ([[Settlement Rate|settlement rate]] is the other) that make historical development factors misleading.

requirements.statement: Volume-weighted average age-to-age factor for a development age is the sum of cumulative claims at the later age divided by the sum of cumulative claims at the earlier age, over accident years that have both ages.

places.quote: $$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{vol-wtd}} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$

requirements.statement: Compute the age-to-ultimate (cumulative) development factor for each maturity by multiplying the selected age-to-age factors from that age onward, including the tail factor.

places.quote: CDFs are built **backwards from the tail**: start with the tail factor, multiply in each successive age-to-age factor moving toward younger ages.
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: Development technique ultimate claims equal the latest cumulative reported claims multiplied by the age-to-ultimate development factor.

places.quote: $$\text{Ultimate} = C_n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: To get net ultimate claims with a quota share followed by an aggregate stop loss, first multiply gross ultimate by the retained share (1 minus the ceded percentage), then cap the result at the stop loss attachment point because the stop loss covers all losses above it.
requirements.concept: Reinsurance Net Claims Estimation (Quota Share and Aggregate Stop Loss)

places.quote: Net loss is $(1-a)X$, so its coefficient of variation equals gross.
$I_d$ is the reinsurer's payment, and the insurer keeps $S \wedge d$, so the retention caps the insurer's total cost for the period.
Covers inure in a stated sequence. Typically per-occurrence excess comes off first, then the quota share applies to what remains, and the stop-loss applies last to protect the final net result.

requirements.statement: IBNR equals ultimate claims minus reported claims; net IBNR uses net ultimate and net reported claims, and ceded IBNR equals gross IBNR minus net IBNR.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Reported}$$
$$\text{Ceded IBNR} = \text{Ceded ultimate} - \text{Ceded reported}$$

requirements.statement: With aggregate stop loss reinsurance, the net tail factor is typically smaller than the gross tail factor (but not necessarily 1.0) because development above the attachment point is ceded, so net claims develop less than gross.
requirements.concept: Effect of Reinsurance on Loss Development Factors

places.quote: so net development patterns are frequently at or below gross ones, and a net tail factor larger than the gross one is generally not reasonable.

requirements.statement: With quota share reinsurance, the net tail factor equals the gross tail factor because the same proportion of every claim is ceded at every maturity, so net development mirrors gross development.
requirements.concept: Effect of Reinsurance on Loss Development Factors

places.quote: For reserving, ceded losses are a scalar multiple of gross and develop on the gross pattern
so the ceded triangle is a scalar multiple of the gross one and develops identically.
On a quota share the gross, ceded and net factors are identical.

requirements.statement: The classical paid-to-paid ratio is calendar-year paid ULAE divided by calendar-year paid claims.

places.quote: Compute the ratio $R$ of calendar-year paid ULAE to calendar-year paid loss, review it for trend, and apply it to unpaid claims.

requirements.statement: Select the ULAE ratio from the calendar-year ratios by judgment, using recent stable years and excluding outlier years (e.g., early years with very small claim volume) that would distort the ratio going forward, and justify the choice.

places.quote: Compute the ratio $R$ of calendar-year paid ULAE to calendar-year paid loss, review it for trend, and apply it to unpaid claims.

Selecting the three-year average of $6.6\%$ would understate the cost of running off the remaining claims. Selecting the latest $8.9\%$ is closer, but even that is a lagging figure if payments keep falling faster than expenses.

requirements.statement: The classical technique assumes half of a claim's ULAE is spent when the claim is opened and half when it is closed, so 50% of the ratio applies to case outstanding and IBNER (reported claims) and 100% applies to IBNYR.

places.quote: If ULAE is assumed to be spent half at reporting and half at settlement, only $50\%$ remains on reported-but-unpaid claims while $100\%$ remains on [[IBNR]] — the formula above.

requirements.statement: Total IBNR splits into IBNER (future development on known, reported claims) and IBNYR (claims incurred but not yet reported); IBNYR equals total IBNR minus IBNER.

places.quote: **Pure IBNR** (narrow IBNR) covers claims that have occurred but are unknown to the insurer.
Counts split broad IBNR into its two parts: **pure IBNR** (unreported claims, valued at an expected severity) and **IBNER** (development on known claims).

In the usual two-way split it covers claims from $2025$ that the insurer has not yet heard about (**pure IBNR**), and the amount by which case reserves on the claims it *has* heard about will prove insufficient (**IBNER**).

requirements.statement: Unpaid ULAE equals the selected ratio times [50% × (case outstanding + IBNER) + 100% × IBNYR].

places.quote: $$\text{ULAE Reserve} = R \times \left(0.5 \times \text{Case} + 1.0 \times \text{IBNR}\right)$$

requirements.statement: Kittel's refinement computes the ULAE ratio as calendar-year paid ULAE divided by the average of calendar-year paid claims and incurred claims, then applies it with the same 50/50 assumption.

places.quote: $$R_{\text{Kittel}} = \frac{\text{Paid ULAE}}{0.5(\text{Paid Loss}) + 0.5(\text{Incurred Loss})}$$

requirements.statement: The classical paid-to-paid ratio is distorted when claim volume is changing (e.g., a growing book), because ULAE spent on opening new claims runs ahead of claim payments, overstating the ratio; Kittel's refinement uses an average of paid and incurred claims as the base, which keeps pace with newly reported claims and removes the distortion.

places.quote: The classical ratio is distorted in a growing book, because paid ULAE reflects today's claim *activity* (much of it on newly reported claims) while paid loss reflects older claims. Kittel divides by the **average of paid and incurred** loss instead:

requirements.statement: An age-to-age (link ratio) factor is the ratio of cumulative reported claims at one age to cumulative reported claims at the previous age, and its period length equals the spacing between development ages (e.g., semi-annual factors span six months).

places.quote: **Age-to-Age Factor** (link ratio) is the ratio of a cohort's cumulative amount at one maturity to its amount at the previous maturity — the observed development between two ages.

requirements.statement: The age-to-ultimate factor at a given age equals the product of the age-to-age factors from that age through the tail factor.

places.quote: **Cumulative Development Factor** (CDF, or age-to-ultimate factor) is the product of all selected [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] from a given maturity through to ultimate, including the [[Tail Factor|tail]].
chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.

requirements.statement: The expected percentage of ultimate claims reported at a given age equals 1 divided by the age-to-ultimate factor at that age.

places.quote: The reciprocal is the **percentage reported** (or paid): $p_n = 1/\text{CDF}_n$, and $1 - p_n$ is the percentage unreported.

requirements.statement: Expected claim emergence over a period equals the selected ultimate claims times the change in expected percent reported from the start to the end of the period (incremental, not cumulative).

places.quote: $$\text{Expected emergence} = U_{\text{prior}} \times \left(\frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n+1}} - \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n}}\right)$$

resolution.quote: The expected figure comes from the prior ultimate and the emergence pattern: the share of ultimate the pattern says should report (or be paid) between the two valuations.
resolution.note: stale re-quote: expected emergence = prior ultimate x the share expected to report between the two valuations

requirements.statement: Actual emergence over a period equals the change in cumulative reported claims between the two evaluation dates, and is compared to expected emergence by taking the difference (actual minus expected).

places.quote: **Actual vs. Expected Analysis** (A/E) compares the emergence that actually occurred in a period against what the previous valuation's assumptions implied should occur.

requirements.statement: Reported claims (paid plus case reserves) emerge lower than expected when case reserve adequacy weakens, when reporting slows (e.g., a shift toward a longer-tailed line or processing backlog), or when frequency or severity is more favorable than expected.
requirements.concept: Reasons for Deviation of Actual from Expected Emergence

places.quote: **Weakening** does the reverse and understates ultimate, which is the more dangerous direction: the reserves are inadequate and the method that is supposed to catch it is biased in the same direction.
development is genuinely slower to emerge, or case reserving weakened, or the mix shifted toward longer-reporting claims.

requirements.statement: Reported claims emerge higher than expected when case reserve adequacy strengthens, when reporting speeds up (e.g., a shift toward a shorter-tailed line or faster claim recording), or when frequency, severity, or large/catastrophe losses are worse than expected.
requirements.concept: Reasons for Deviation of Actual from Expected Emergence

places.quote: A [[Large Loss|shock loss]] reported early is multiplied by the full CDF.
**Strengthening** raises reported losses immediately, so recent age-to-age factors fall (more of the ultimate is already booked).

requirements.statement: In the paid development technique applied to ALAE, compute age-to-age factors from the cumulative paid ALAE triangle itself (volume-weighted average = sum of later-age paid over sum of earlier-age paid for the same accident years), not from paid claims or paid-to-paid ratios.

places.quote: **Volume-weighted average**: $\Sigma(\text{col }n{+}1) / \Sigma(\text{col }n)$ — gives more credibility to larger accident years; the standard default selection

requirements.statement: Estimate ultimate ALAE by multiplying latest cumulative paid ALAE by the cumulative development factor (product of the age-to-age factors from the current age to ultimate, with a tail factor of 1.000 if no development beyond the last age).

places.quote: $$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \left(\prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1}\right) \times \text{Tail}$$
$$\text{Ultimate}_{\text{paid}} = \text{Paid}_n \times \text{CDF}^{\text{paid}}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: In the ratio of paid ALAE to paid claims technique with additive factors, the development factor from one age to the next is the average change (difference) in the paid ALAE-to-paid claims ratio, and the ultimate ratio equals the latest ratio plus the sum of the additive development through the final age.
requirements.concept: Ratio of Paid ALAE to Paid Claims Development Technique

requirements.statement: Ultimate ALAE under the ratio technique = projected ultimate ALAE-to-claims ratio × selected ultimate claims, done for every accident year.
requirements.concept: Ratio of Paid ALAE to Paid Claims Development Technique

places.quote: Friedland gives three approaches: develop a **combined** loss-and-ALAE triangle, develop **ALAE separately** in its own triangle, or develop a **ratio of ALAE to loss** and apply it to projected losses.

requirements.statement: The ratio technique depends on the selected ultimate claims and carries forward the latest observed ratio, so distortions in an accident year's paid claims (e.g., unusually low early paid claims inflating the ratio) or in the selected ultimate claims overstate ultimate ALAE; the paid ALAE technique relies only on ALAE data and is unaffected by claim data distortions.
Evaluate reasonableness of an ultimate ALAE estimate by comparing the implied ALAE per ultimate claim (or ALAE-to-claims ratio) with that of other accident years.

places.quote: Then test the *selected* ultimates by the ratios they imply: ultimate claim ratios, severities, frequencies and pure premiums by year

requirements.statement: An increase in case reserve adequacy inflates reported claims on the latest diagonal, so reported development and reported Bornhuetter-Ferguson methods, which use historical reported patterns built from weaker reserves, overstate ultimate claims.

places.quote: Applying historical factors — built under weaker reserving — to a strengthened diagonal **over-states** ultimate, because the strengthening is developed a second time.
**Reported chain ladder** is now biased **high**: historical factors were built on weaker reserves and are being applied to a strengthened diagonal, developing the strengthening a second time.

requirements.statement: Paid claim development and paid Bornhuetter-Ferguson methods are not affected by changes in case reserve adequacy, and agreement among paid methods indicates no change in payment patterns.

places.quote: **Paid data is immune**, so a divergence between paid and reported chain ladder estimates is the corroborating evidence.

Paid data is **objective**. It carries no adjuster judgment, so a paid triangle is immune to changes in [[Case Adequacy|case reserve adequacy]] — the single most common distortion in reported triangles.

requirements.statement: The reported Berquist-Sherman method restates case reserves (average case outstanding) to a consistent adequacy level, correcting the distortion from case reserve changes, so its estimate aligns with the paid and expected claims methods.

places.quote: The remedy is the [[Berquist-Sherman Method|Berquist-Sherman]] case adjustment: restate historical average case outstanding to the current adequacy level using a selected severity trend, rebuild the reported triangle, and select factors from the restated history.
4. Multiply the restated averages by the open claim counts to get adjusted case reserves, add paid, and rebuild the reported triangle.

requirements.statement: Diagnose a case reserve strengthening by examining average case outstanding (case outstanding divided by open claim counts) along the latest diagonals, which rises faster than the severity trend if case reserves were strengthened.

places.quote: The diagnostic is average case outstanding per open claim**, compared *down each column* of the triangle. It should grow at roughly the severity trend. A jump concentrated on one **diagonal**, appearing at every maturity at once, is a change in reserving practice, not in claim cost.
**[[Case Adequacy|Case strengthening]]:** average case outstanding rises faster than trend on the latest diagonals, and paid-to-reported falls.

requirements.statement: Diagnose a case reserve strengthening with the ratio of paid to reported claims, which declines along the latest diagonals relative to earlier years at the same maturity when reported claims rise while payments are unchanged.
requirements.concept: Ratio of Paid to Reported Claims

places.quote: **[[Case Adequacy|Case strengthening]]:** average case outstanding rises faster than trend on the latest diagonals, and paid-to-reported falls.
Paid ultimates above reported ultimates suggest case reserves are inadequate; the reverse suggests they are strengthening (or claims are closing slowly).

requirements.statement: The disposal rate is the ratio of closed claim counts to ultimate claim counts at each maturity, and measures the rate of claim settlement.

places.quote: $$\text{Disposal Rate}_n = \frac{\text{Closed claims at age } n}{\text{Ultimate claim counts}}$$
The [[Settlement Rate|disposal rate]] is closed counts over ultimate (or reported) counts.

requirements.statement: The paid Berquist-Sherman technique adjusts only for changes in settlement rate, so when disposal rates are stable across accident years its estimate is close to the paid development technique.

places.quote: Which adjustment applies is decided by the **diagnostic**, not by preference: a jump in average case outstanding across all years points to adequacy; a jump in closure rates points to settlement speed.

The remedy is the [[Berquist-Sherman Method|Berquist-Sherman]] paid adjustment: restate each historical year's paid losses to what they would have been at the *current* disposal pattern, by interpolating along each year's paid-versus-disposal-rate relationship, then select factors from the restated triangle.

requirements.statement: Data from competitor filings comes from a longer-established, larger and more credible body of experience than a new entrant's own limited data, which makes it useful for measuring loss trend in a new state.

places.quote: **external** ones — data calls and statistical plans, [[External Information in Reserving|aggregated industry data]], competitors' rate filings and third-party data — needed when pricing a new line and often helpful to supplement internal data.
A new product has no history of its own, and sparse or unstable internal data may need [[External Data|external data]] or [[Statistical Plan|industry statistical data]] as a benchmark.

requirements.statement: Competitor data reflects the competitor's own mix of business, underwriting, policy forms and claims handling, and may be dated or lack detail, so its trend may not apply to the company's book.

places.quote: A shift in the mix changes aggregate results even when nothing about any individual segment has changed
The loss costs of a larger related group may be biased.

requirements.statement: Internal company data reflects the company's own book, underwriting and claims practices, so it measures the trend the company will actually experience.

places.quote: It is the main source for pricing and modelling an existing product, because it describes the insurer's own book at the level of the individual policy and claim.

requirements.statement: Limited internal data, such as a single year in a new state, is immature, volatile and not credible for estimating a loss trend, which requires several periods of data.

places.quote: Partial credibility uses the **square root rule**, $Z = \sqrt{n / n_{\text{full}}}$, capped at $1$ — a class with a quarter of the required claims gets $Z = 0.50$.
A new product has no history of its own, and sparse or unstable internal data may need [[External Data|external data]] or [[Statistical Plan|industry statistical data]] as a benchmark.

requirements.statement: The loss development and trending overlap fallacy is the incorrect claim that applying both loss development and loss trend double-counts inflation, because development already includes inflation.

places.quote: Werner & Modlin call the belief that doing both double-counts inflation the **overlap fallacy**: development does include the inflation that raises payments on reported claims after reporting, but that does not prove an overlap.
Applying one without the other under-states the indication; applying both is not a double count — Werner & Modlin call that belief the *overlap fallacy*.

requirements.statement: Loss development moves an accident year's losses from their current immature value to ultimate at that accident year's cost level, while trend moves ultimate losses from the historical cost level to the future policy period's cost level, so the two adjustments do not overlap.

places.quote: Trend and [[Loss Development|development]] answer different questions and must both be applied: development brings immature losses to *their own* ultimate level; trend restates past losses to the level expected for similar losses in the *future* period.

In **ratemaking**, developing losses to ultimate is a distinct step from trending: development moves an immature year to its own ultimate value, while [[Loss Trend|trend]] restates it to the cost level of the future policy period.

requirements.statement: In classical credibility, the exposure standard for full credibility equals the claim-count standard for full credibility divided by the expected claim frequency (claims per exposure).

places.quote: A standard stated in claims converts to exposures by dividing by the expected claim frequency per exposure

requirements.statement: Select the expected claim frequency for each coverage separately by pooling the experience years (total claims divided by total exposures) rather than using a single year's frequency or combining coverages.

resolution.note: a step of this solution's plan: the examiners asked only that a frequency be selected; pooling the three years per coverage is one supportable selection

requirements.statement: An exposure-based full credibility standard is preferred because exposures are known or projectable in advance of the experience period, whereas claim counts are not known until the period has developed, so the needed volume of business is known up front and is simpler to apply.

resolution.note: Werner p.219 gives the exposure standard (claim standard / expected frequency) but no reason for preferring it; the reason in the requirement is in no Exam 5 reading.

requirements.statement: Advantages of classical credibility are that it is the most commonly used and accepted method and is easy to compute from readily available data.

places.quote: Bühlmann has the better theoretical footing; limited fluctuation persists because it needs only a claim count, and $1{,}082$ is embedded in decades of filings.

requirements.statement: Disadvantages of classical credibility are that it assumes Poisson claim frequency and constant severity, relies on an arbitrary choice of probability p and range k for the full credibility standard, and ignores the accuracy or quality of the complement of credibility.

resolution.quote: exposures are homogeneous, claim occurrence follows a Poisson distribution and there is no variation in the size of loss (constant severity).…It uses a selected complement but does not take into account the quality of that complement compared with the latest observation, so judgment is required.…Full credibility is defined by a probability p that the observed experience stays within a range k of its expected value, and Werner calls that range an arbitrary amount.
resolution.note: Classical credibility assumptions and disadvantages; W&M Ch.12 pp.217-220 (PDF 229-232)

requirements.statement: Criteria for a good complement of credibility include being unbiased, independent of the experience being weighted, readily available, easy to compute, and based on enough data to have low variance; candidates include the countrywide or larger-region indication and trended present rates.

places.quote: (2) **unbiased** — not routinely higher or lower than the observed experience; (3) **statistically independent** from the base statistic, or any error in the base statistic can be compounded; (4) **available** — the data needed to compute it readily obtainable

requirements.statement: The excess loss factor equals 1 plus the ratio of excess losses (losses above the threshold) to non-excess losses (losses limited to the threshold).

places.quote: The excess loss factor (ELF) is the long-run ratio of excess to non-excess losses, applied to each year's capped losses.

requirements.statement: To split ground-up losses at a threshold, losses below the threshold are entirely non-excess; for each loss above the threshold, the threshold amount counts as non-excess and the remainder counts as excess.

places.quote: $$\text{Capped Loss} = \min(X, M)$$
Each claim is capped at a threshold (the **non-excess** loss); the portion above it is **excess**.

requirements.statement: An event is a catastrophe if its industry-wide insured losses meet or exceed the catastrophe definition threshold, and a non-catastrophe excess loss factor is computed after removing catastrophe claims from the loss data.

places.quote: Werner cites the ISO Property Claim Services definition: at least $\$25$ million of direct insured property loss affecting a significant number of policyholders and insurers.
Catastrophe losses are **removed** from the experience period and replaced with a long-run expected load.

requirements.statement: Ground-up loss data are not censored: the excess loss factor must be computed by splitting large losses at the threshold, and it is a factor (1 + excess/non-excess), not an excess loss ratio, 1 minus the loss elimination ratio, or excess/total losses.

places.quote: $$\text{ELF} = 1 + \frac{\sum \text{Excess losses}}{\sum \text{Non-excess losses}}$$

requirements.statement: Large and catastrophe losses are rare and volatile, so capping losses at a threshold and adding a longer-term average excess loss provision (the excess loss factor) smooths rate indications from year to year.

places.quote: The rate then covers the full expected cost without being hostage to whether a shock loss happened to occur in the experience period.

In ratemaking they are removed from the historical data and replaced with a provision based on a long-term view, so that rates reflect their expected cost without jumping after a bad year and falling after a quiet one.

requirements.statement: A claims-made policy covers claims that are reported during the policy period and that occurred on or after the policy's retroactive date.

places.quote: **Claims-Made Coverage** is a policy trigger under which the policy responds to claims *reported* during the policy period, provided the underlying loss occurred on or after the policy's **retroactive date**.

requirements.statement: An occurrence policy covers claims that occur during the policy period, regardless of when they are reported.

places.quote: **Occurrence Coverage** is a policy trigger under which the policy responds to losses that *occur* during the policy period, however long afterwards the claim is reported.

requirements.statement: In a cumulative reported claim count triangle, each entry already includes all earlier reported claims for that accident year, so the count covered as of a given date is read directly from the entry at that age, and the latest diagonal value is the total reported to date, with no summing of cells.

resolution.quote: holds the cumulative amount for that accident year at age
resolution.note: a cumulative triangle cell already holds everything reported to that age; the count as of a date is read off its diagonal

requirements.statement: When switching from claims-made to occurrence coverage, a gap arises for claims that occurred during the claims-made period but are reported after the claims-made policies expire, because neither policy covers them.

places.quote: An **extended reporting endorsement** (ERP, or "tail coverage") covers claims that occurred during the claims-made coverage period but are reported after the last policy expires — what a retiring physician, or an insured switching to an occurrence policy, needs to avoid a gap.

requirements.statement: Claims-made step factors give the cumulative proportion of an accident year's ultimate claims that are reported by the end of each claims-made policy year (first year, second year, etc.), reaching 100% at maturity.

places.quote: With the retro date set at inception, year $1$ can only receive accident-year reports, year $2$ receives lag-$0$ and lag-$1$, and so on:

requirements.statement: Ultimate claim count is estimated as the latest cumulative reported count divided by the cumulative reporting percentage (step factor) at that age, equivalent to multiplying by the cumulative development factor.

places.quote: $$\text{Ultimate Counts} = N_n \times \text{CDF}^{\text{count}}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\hat{C}_m = \frac{P_m}{CF_{k(m)}}$$

requirements.statement: Estimate the number of claims in the coverage gap as the ultimate claims for the claims-made-period accident years minus the claims already reported and covered under the claims-made policies.

places.quote: covers claims that occurred during the claims-made coverage period but are reported after the last policy expires
leaving the programme without buying an ERP leaves the remaining $75\%$ of the exposure uninsured.

places.quote: If a claims-made CGL is cancelled or not renewed, replaced with an occurrence policy, or renewed with a later retroactive date, a basic extended reporting period applies automatically at no charge.

resolution.quote: covers claims that occurred during the claims-made coverage period but are reported after the last policy expires

requirements.statement: Split each expense category into a fixed portion and a variable portion using its percent-fixed assumption (fixed = expense × % fixed, variable = expense × (1 − % fixed)).

places.quote: Expense studies rarely split cleanly. Ideally detailed expense data or activity-based cost studies make the split; otherwise it is generally made judgmentally, with other professionals in the company, as a **fixed percentage** of each category (Werner's example: general expenses $75\%$ fixed).

requirements.statement: General expenses are incurred over the life of the policy so they are allocated using earned premium and earned exposures, while other acquisition expenses, taxes, licenses and fees, and commissions are incurred at policy writing so they use written premium and written exposures.

places.quote: Expenses incurred at the onset of the policy — commissions, other acquisition, and taxes, licenses and fees — are calculated on [[Written Premium]]; general expenses, incurred throughout the policy, on [[Earned Premium]].

those incurred at the onset of the policy (commissions, other acquisition, taxes, licenses and fees) are measured against written premium, those incurred throughout the policy (general expenses) against [[Earned Premium|earned premium]]

requirements.statement: Countrywide expenses (general, other acquisition) are spread over countrywide premium and exposures, while state-specific expenses (taxes, licenses and fees, commissions) are spread over that state's premium and exposures.
Average fixed expense per exposure for each expense type equals its fixed expense dollars divided by the appropriate exposures, and the total is the sum across expense types.

places.quote: $$F = \frac{\text{Total Fixed Expenses}}{\text{Exposures (or Policies)}}$$

requirements.statement: The variable expense provision is each variable expense divided by the appropriate premium (a ratio to premium, not exposures), summed across expense types.

places.quote: $$V = \frac{\text{Variable Expenses}}{\text{Premium}}$$

requirements.statement: Fixed expense fee = average fixed expense per exposure / (1 − variable expense provision − underwriting profit provision), grossing up so the fee also covers the variable expenses and profit it generates.

places.quote: $F$ enters the **numerator** of the rate; [[Variable Expenses|variable expenses]] $V$ and the profit provision $Q_T$ enter the **denominator**.
The denominator placement is not a convention but arithmetic: if commission is $15\%$ *of the rate being solved for*, the rate must be grossed up by dividing, not by adding $15\%$ of something else.

requirements.statement: Estimate age-to-age development factors as volume-weighted averages (sum of later-age cumulative losses over sum of corresponding earlier-age losses for years with both), and multiply them with the tail factor to get cumulative development factors to ultimate.

places.quote: $$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{vol-wtd}} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$
The chain ladder factors multiply to $14.4466$

requirements.statement: Compute on-level factors with the parallelogram method: for annual policies written evenly, determine the share of each calendar year's earned premium at old and new rate levels, then divide the current rate level by the year's average rate level.

places.quote: For **annual** policies written uniformly, a rate change effective at time $p$ through year $Y$ earns over a triangle of area $\tfrac{1}{2}(1-p)^2$ in year $Y$ — so a $7/1$ change affects only $0.125$ of that year's earned premium, and a $1/1$ change affects $0.500$.
$$\text{OLF}_Y = \frac{I_{\text{current}}}{\sum_k A_{Y,k}\, I_k}$$

requirements.statement: Cape Cod method: compute used-up premium as on-level, trended premium divided by the cumulative development factor, and set the expected claim ratio equal to total trended reported losses divided by total used-up premium.

places.quote: $$\text{ELR} = \frac{\sum_i C_i}{\sum_i \text{EP}_i \times \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}}$$
$P_i / \text{CDF}_i$ is the **used-up premium**, the share of the premium that the claims reported so far correspond to.

requirements.statement: Bring losses and premiums to a common cost level by trending losses from each accident year's average accident date and premium from each calendar year's average written date to the target date, using compound annual trend over the appropriate number of years.

places.quote: - $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.

The trend period $n$ runs from the average written date of the policies earning premium in the experience period to the **average written date of the policies in effect while the new rates are** — for calendar-year 2011 earned premium and annual policies written in 2013, $1/1/2011$ to $6/30/2013$, or $2.5$ years.
- The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: Convert the Cape Cod expected claim ratio back to each accident year's level by adjusting for on-level factor and net trend (premium trend over loss trend) so it applies to that year's actual earned premium.

places.quote: Premium **must be on level** and losses must be trended to a common cost level before the ELR is computed, or the derived ratio blends years written at different rate levels and different cost levels into one number.
$T_{i \to j}$ is the trend factor that restates year $i$'s claims at year $j$'s cost level, net of any change already in the on-level premium.
**Trend direction:** Claims of a year earlier than $j$ are trended up to year $j$'s level, and claims of a later year are trended down.

requirements.statement: Cape Cod ultimate loss = actual (untrended) reported loss + expected claims × (1 − 1/CDF), where expected claims are the year's expected loss ratio times its earned premium (Bornhuetter-Ferguson form).

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$
$$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$
$$\hat U_j = C_j + \text{IBNR}_j$$

requirements.statement: For annual policies, the average written date of a policy year is mid-year and the average accident date is one year after the average written date's start; a policy effective on a given date has average written date at the effective date plus half the rate-in-effect period and average accident date one half-year after (rates in effect one year).

places.quote: The trend period $n$ runs from the average written date of the policies earning premium in the experience period to the **average written date of the policies in effect while the new rates are** — for calendar-year 2011 earned premium and annual policies written in 2013, $1/1/2011$ to $6/30/2013$, or $2.5$ years.
Policies are written between $7/1/2025$ and $6/30/2026$; each provides coverage for a year after it is written.

requirements.statement: Indicated rate change = (projected loss ratio including ULAE + fixed expense ratio) / (1 − variable expense ratio − profit and contingencies provision) − 1, where ULAE is loaded as a percentage of loss and ALAE.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{\text{VPLR}} - 1$$

requirements.statement: Projected loss ratio = total trended ultimate losses divided by total trended on-level earned premium, summing across the experience years.

places.quote: many companies sum projected losses and premium across all years, which weights each year's loss ratio by its premium

The numerator's loss ratio must be **projected**: ultimate losses (developed), trended to the future policy period, over earned premium brought to **current rate level** ([[On-Leveling]]) and trended ([[Premium Trend]]).

requirements.statement: Weight each future policy year's premium, loss and expense by the cumulative probability the policy is still in force, which is the product of the renewal probabilities of all preceding renewals.

places.quote: The probabilities ${}_{t-1}p_{60}$ that a policy is still in force at the start of each year are $1$, $0.996602$, $0.992823$, $0.988619$ and $0.983943$.

**Survival in the denominator:** A premium is received only from a policy still in force. Using $P\,\ddot{a}_{\overline{n}|}$ without the survival factor overstates the premiums and understates the margin.

requirements.statement: Discount each year's cash flows to the policy inception date at the annual discount rate, using a factor of 1/(1+i)^t where t is the time from inception to when the cash flow occurs (no discounting for flows at inception).

places.quote: For $t > s$ the amount is accumulated ([[Accumulated Value]]); for $t < s$ it is discounted by $v^{s-t}$, where $v = 1/(1+i)$ is the [[Discount Factor]] ([[Present Value]]).
$$\text{EPV of premiums} = \sum_{t=0}^{n-1} P\,{}_tp_x\,(1+r)^{-t}$$

requirements.statement: Return on premium over a multi-year horizon equals (PV of premium minus PV of losses and expenses) divided by PV of premium, using persistency-weighted discounted amounts.

places.quote: $$\text{Profit margin} = \frac{\text{NPV}}{\text{EPV of premiums}}$$

requirements.statement: Both losses and expenses are costs deducted from premium when computing underwriting profit, and the profit percentage uses discounted premium (not undiscounted premium) as the denominator.

places.quote: **Underwriting Profit** is income from the insurance operation alone — earned premium less incurred losses, LAE and underwriting expenses — before any credit for investment income.
**The Profit Margin** of a policy is its [[Net Present Value|net present value]] divided by the expected present value of its premiums, both calculated at the risk discount rate.

requirements.statement: Higher persistency shifts more weight to later policy years, so a segment's multi-year return depends on both its per-year profitability and how likely it is to renew into the more profitable years.

places.quote: The acquisition swings from $+\$147$ to $-\$92$ on the retention assumption alone.
Fewer policies stay to earn about 90 a year, though, so the NPV falls from 93.00 to 80.07.

requirements.statement: In the univariate pure premium method, a level's pure premium is its losses divided by its exposures, and its relativity is that level's pure premium divided by the base level's pure premium.

places.quote: $$\text{Relativity}_i = \frac{\text{Pure Premium}_i}{\text{Pure Premium}_{\text{base}}}$$
$$\text{Pure Premium} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Exposures}} = \text{Frequency} \times \text{Severity}$$
$$\text{Pure Premium} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Exposures}}$$

requirements.statement: Exposure correlation between two rating variables exists when the distribution of exposures across levels of one variable differs across levels of the other, so univariate relativities can be distorted by overlap.

places.quote: A **univariate** (one-way) pure premium or loss ratio analysis attributes to a variable the effect of everything correlated with it. If young drivers also drive older cars, a one-way age relativity contains part of the vehicle-age effect, and rating both double-counts.
Urban territories carry different vehicle mixes, limit selections and driver populations, and a one-way territorial relativity absorbs all of it

requirements.statement: To test for exposure correlation, compare the percentage mix of one variable's levels (e.g., driver type) across each level of the other variable (e.g., territory); identical mixes mean no correlation and differing mixes mean correlation.
When two rating variables are not exposure correlated, no exposure adjustment is needed and the simple univariate relativities can be used for both.

To adjust for exposure correlation in sequential univariate analysis, first compute relativities for one variable, then compute adjusted exposures for the other variable's levels by weighting each exposure by the first variable's relativity, and compute pure premiums and relativities from losses divided by those adjusted exposures.
The exposure adjustment must use exposure tables (not loss tables) for the weights and pure premium relativities (not loss relativities) for the factors.
Under a large deductible policy, the insurer typically handles and pays claims ground-up (including those below the deductible) and then bills the insured to reimburse the deductible portion.

places.quote: usually the insurer handles every claim, so the premium must cover handling cost even on claims that never pierce the deductible
under a large deductible the insurer pays ground-up and collects afterwards.
the insurer pays every claim and bills the deductible back.

requirements.statement: Because the insurer administers claims below the deductible (claim handling, billing, processing), the rates for a large deductible policy appropriately include an expense provision for those below-deductible claims.

places.quote: usually the insurer handles every claim, so the premium must cover handling cost even on claims that never pierce the deductible
the premium carries the cost of processing the [[Deductible Recovery|deductible recoveries]] and a provision for credit risk, since collateral rarely covers it fully

requirements.statement: Credit (insolvency) risk in a large deductible policy is the risk that the insured becomes bankrupt or otherwise cannot reimburse the deductible amounts the insurer has already paid.
requirements.concept: Credit Risk in Large Deductible Policies

places.quote: a provision for the insured's inability to pay; collateral rarely covers that credit risk fully.
The insurer has already paid the claimant; if the insured becomes insolvent before reimbursing, the shortfall is a retained loss.

requirements.statement: Credit risk from unrecoverable deductible payments is a legitimate cost of writing a large deductible policy, so the rates may include a provision for it, and it is much smaller or absent under a small deductible policy.
requirements.concept: Credit Risk in Large Deductible Policies

places.quote: a provision for the insured's inability to pay; collateral rarely covers that credit risk fully.
the premium carries the cost of processing the [[Deductible Recovery|deductible recoveries]] and a provision for credit risk, since collateral rarely covers it fully

requirements.statement: Losses retained by the insurer above a large deductible are higher severity, sparser, and more volatile and harder to predict, so greater risk justifies a higher profit margin (required return) than for a small deductible policy.
requirements.concept: Profit Margin and Risk in Ratemaking

places.quote: losses above a large deductible are more uncertain than those below, so the profit margin may need to rise.
Few claims reach the upper layers, so pricing leans on fitted curves and industry data, and the tail fit drives the answer.

requirements.statement: The loss ratio method indicated rate change equals the ultimate (expected) loss ratio divided by the permissible loss ratio, minus 1.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio}}{\text{PLR}} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss Ratio}}{\text{PLR}} - 1 \quad \text{(all-variable form)}

requirements.statement: Retention ratio is the number of policies renewed divided by the number of policies currently in force (up for renewal); a minimum retention ratio target caps the rate increase that can be taken.

resolution.quote: the retention ratio is policies renewed
resolution.note: retention ratio definition (syllabus page); the minimum-retention target itself is the question's management constraint

requirements.statement: Apply a retention constraint by computing the minimum retained policy count (current count times minimum retention ratio), finding the largest rate change in the retention model output that still meets it, and capping the indicated rate change at that level.

resolution.note: a step of this solution's plan: reading the question's retention-model table against its own minimum-retention target

requirements.statement: When a capped territory's rate change falls short of its indication, compute the premium shortfall (indicated factor minus capped factor, times current premium) and offset it with an additional rate increase in another territory (shortfall divided by that territory's premium) so the total book still meets the permissible loss ratio, then verify the retention constraint in that territory.

places.quote: a cap on the change for any level of a rating variable is made up by adjusting the base rate and the other relativities
The base rate has to be adjusted to make up the capped premium, and the actuary must decide whether the overall target is met over the whole transition or only by its end.

requirements.statement: Adverse selection arises when rates deviate from indicated: overcharged (overpriced) segments leave for cheaper competitors while undercharged segments stay or grow, shifting the mix toward less profitable business and worsening the loss ratio.

places.quote: A rate change also changes the **mix**: price-sensitive risks shop, so a large increase can worsen the remaining experience through adverse selection — an effect the indication itself does not capture.
**The death spiral.** Price at the population average; low risks find the price poor value and leave; the remaining pool is worse, so the price rises; more of the remaining low risks leave; repeat.

requirements.statement: When rate increases are constrained, the fundamental insurance equation can be rebalanced by non-pricing actions such as reducing expenses (lower expense ratio) or reducing losses through underwriting tightening or loss control/claims management.

places.quote: **Reduce expenses** — underwriting or LAE: a smaller marketing budget, lower staffing, lower acquisition cost. This lowers $\bar{E}_F$ or $V$.
tightening **underwriting** criteria or non-renewing policies whose premium is grossly inadequate;

requirements.statement: Data with low claim counts is not fully credible on its own; combining it with a related, higher-volume coverage gives more credible and stable unpaid claim estimates.

places.quote: Where a level is too thin, combine similar levels or find more data.

requirements.statement: Data combined for an unpaid claim analysis should be homogeneous; segments with different development patterns (e.g., differing age-to-ultimate factors) should not be combined.
requirements.concept: Homogeneity and Segmentation of Claims Data

places.quote: **Reserving practice (Friedland):** group claims that share coverage (the same laws, policy terms and claims handling), with enough claim counts, and similar reporting patterns, ability to set case reserves, settlement patterns, reopening likelihood and severity
If the segments have different emergence patterns, the blended development factors drift as the weights drift — and the triangle gives no signal that this is what is happening.
Combining them would average a multi-year liability pattern with an essentially immediate property pattern, producing development factors that fit neither.

requirements.statement: Segments whose exposure and claim counts grow at different rates are unlike populations, and combining them can distort the projected results.
requirements.concept: Homogeneity and Segmentation of Claims Data

places.quote: Do not combine segments whose relative volume is changing — see [[Mix of Business]] and [[Reserving Data Organization]].
A shift in the mix changes aggregate results even when nothing about any individual segment has changed

requirements.statement: Pure premium (loss cost) = frequency × severity = (ultimate claim count × ultimate severity) / earned exposure.

places.quote: $$\text{Pure Premium} = \text{Frequency} \times \text{Severity}$$
$$\text{Frequency} = \frac{\text{Number of Claims}}{\text{Earned Exposures}}$$
$$\text{Severity} = \frac{\text{Total Losses}}{\text{Number of Claims}}$$

requirements.statement: Premium and pricing decisions should be based on loss cost (pure premium), which reflects both frequency and severity, not on severity alone.

places.quote: Pure premium is the building block of the [[Pure Premium Method]] indication, where the indicated rate is the projected pure premium plus fixed expenses, grossed up for variable expenses and profit.
Pure premium is the **premium-free** view of cost: because it never divides by premium, it needs no [[On-Leveling|on-levelling]] and is unaffected by rate history.

requirements.statement: Ultimate claim counts are already developed to ultimate, so paid age-to-ultimate loss development factors should not be applied to them.

places.quote: Develop the count triangle to ultimate counts; develop an average severity triangle (dollars ÷ counts at each age) to ultimate severity; multiply.

**Claims-only frequency understates true development.** Frequency computed on reported counts at an immature age is biased low, since claims are still being reported — the counts must be developed to ultimate with their own [[Claim Count Triangle|count triangle]].

requirements.statement: Reported claims equal paid claims plus case outstanding reserves, so changes in reported and case outstanding amounts imply changes in paid amounts (paid = reported minus case outstanding).
requirements.concept: Claim Development Relationships (Paid, Reported, Case Outstanding)

places.quote: $$\text{Reported Losses} = \text{Paid Losses} + \text{Case Reserves}$$
$$\text{Reported (Incurred)} = \text{Paid} + \text{Case Reserves}$$

requirements.statement: Evaluate a development technique's reasonableness by computing age-to-age factors of the relevant (average) triangles and comparing them across accident years, looking for shifts in the latest diagonal.

places.quote: **Along a diagonal** — everything that happened in one calendar period. A diagonal effect is [[Inflation|inflation]], a reserve strengthening, or a settlement push, and it hits every cohort at once.

A factor that moves along the **diagonal** rather than down the column is a calendar-year effect ([[Development Triangle]]) and should be addressed by restating the triangle, not by averaging it away.

requirements.statement: Compute diagonal (calendar/accident-year) growth rates in average values at a fixed age and compare them to the industry claim cost trend to detect abnormal changes.

places.quote: average case outstanding rises faster than trend on the latest diagonals, and paid-to-reported falls.
It should grow at roughly the severity trend.

requirements.statement: A spike in average case outstanding without a matching rise in average reported claims indicates slower claim settlement (decreased paid), not merely higher case reserve adequacy, which would also raise average reported claims.
requirements.concept: Changes in Settlement Rates and Case Reserve Adequacy

places.quote: **Strengthening** raises reported losses immediately, so recent age-to-age factors fall (more of the ultimate is already booked).
Paid ultimates above reported ultimates suggest case reserves are inadequate; the reverse suggests they are strengthening (or claims are closing slowly).

requirements.statement: The paid development technique assumes historical payment patterns persist; a slowdown in settlement makes historical paid factors too high-speed and leads to understated ultimate claims, so the technique is unreasonable.

places.quote: - **Slower settlement** does the reverse and understates ultimate from paid data.

requirements.statement: The reported claim development technique is not distorted by changes in settlement rates and is more appropriate when paid patterns shift but reported development is stable.

places.quote: - **Reported data is largely immune**, because reported losses include the case reserve whether or not the claim has closed.
- **Reported development is largely unaffected**, since reported losses include case reserves whether or not the claim has closed.

requirements.statement: Average case outstanding can exceed average reported values because small claims close early, leaving larger claims open; also an average paid triangle cannot be derived without claim count information on a consistent basis.
In the frequency-severity technique, project ultimate claims as ultimate claim count times ultimate average severity, where each is developed separately from its own triangle.

places.quote: Develop the count triangle to ultimate counts; develop an average severity triangle (dollars ÷ counts at each age) to ultimate severity; multiply.
Severity analysis is what the [[Frequency-Severity Method]] rests on: project counts and severities separately, then multiply.

requirements.statement: An age-to-age development factor is the cumulative value at a later age divided by the cumulative value at the prior age for the same accident year.

places.quote: $$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{AY}} = \frac{C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$

requirements.statement: Select age-to-age factors by averaging the available observed factors at each age (e.g. a simple average), then multiply the selected factors from the current age through the last age, with a tail of 1.000 when there is no further development, to get the age-to-ultimate factor.

places.quote: **The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.
**Simple average** — equal weight to each year, so a small, volatile year counts as much as a large one.
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \left(\prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1}\right) \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: Develop reported claim counts to ultimate by multiplying the latest reported count by the cumulative count age-to-ultimate factor.

places.quote: $$\text{Ultimate Counts} = N_n \times \text{CDF}^{\text{count}}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: Average severity (average claim size) at each age equals cumulative reported claims divided by cumulative reported claim count at that age; a severity triangle is built from this and developed with age-to-age severity factors.
