places.quote: develop an average severity triangle (dollars ÷ counts at each age) to ultimate severity
$$\text{Severity} = \frac{\text{Total Losses}}{\text{Number of Claims}}$$
$$\text{Average Severity} = \frac{\text{Losses}}{\text{Claim Counts}}$$

requirements.statement: Unpaid claims estimate equals ultimate claims minus claims paid to date (not minus reported claims).

places.quote: $$\text{Unpaid} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Paid to date}$$

requirements.statement: Cumulative reported claim counts can decrease over time when claims that were reported are later closed without payment (e.g. found fraudulent, outside coverage, or otherwise not payable) and removed from the count.
An age-to-age (link ratio) development factor is the ratio of cumulative reported claims at one maturity to cumulative reported claims at the previous maturity for the same accident year.

places.quote: **Age-to-Age Factor** (link ratio) is the ratio of a cohort's cumulative amount at one maturity to its amount at the previous maturity — the observed development between two ages.

requirements.statement: Select each age-to-age factor from the observed factors using an average (e.g., simple or volume-weighted average) across accident years.

places.quote: **Volume-weighted (all-year)** — the ratio of column sums. Weights each year by its size, so it is stable and dominated by the large years. The default choice.
$$f_{k \to k+1} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k}}$$

requirements.statement: The cumulative development factor to ultimate at a given maturity is the product of the selected age-to-age factors from that maturity onward, including the tail factor.

places.quote: **Cumulative Development Factor** (CDF, or age-to-ultimate factor) is the product of all selected [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] from a given maturity through to ultimate, including the [[Tail Factor|tail]].
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: In the reported development technique, ultimate claims equal current cumulative reported claims multiplied by the cumulative development factor to ultimate for that maturity.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate} = C_n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: Before supplementing company data with industry development data, one should check comparability of the industry data, such as differences in mix of business, gross vs. net of reinsurance basis, claims handling practices, large claim distortions, aggregation basis (policy/accident/calendar year), and claim definitions; also the credibility of own data, cost of the data, and independence of industry data.
requirements.concept: Use of Industry Benchmark Data in Loss Development

places.quote: **Never use external data unadjusted.** It must be reconciled to the subject book on the dimensions that actually drive development: coverage and [[Line of Business|line of business]] definitions, policy limits and attachment points, [[Mix of Business|mix of business]],
**Gross, ceded or net.** Data may be organized before reinsurance, as the reinsurer's share alone, or [[Net of Reinsurance|net]] of cessions.

requirements.statement: The reported development technique assumes historical development patterns remain stable; changes in claims handling (e.g., more adjusters changing settlement speed, case reserve timing or adequacy) alter reported development and can distort the projection, causing over- or underestimation of ultimate claims.
requirements.concept: Reported Development Technique Assumptions and Limitations

places.quote: **The pattern is stable over calendar time.** Violated by a change in [[Case Adequacy|case adequacy]], [[Settlement Rate|settlement speed]] or [[Inflation|inflation]] — the diagonal effects.
Faster closing inflates the recent paid diagonal, so historical paid factors **over-develop** it.
Applying historical factors — built under weaker reserving — to a strengthened diagonal **over-states** ultimate, because the strengthening is developed a second time.

requirements.statement: Bornhuetter-Ferguson ultimate claims = reported claims + expected claims ratio × earned premium × (1 − 1/age-to-ultimate factor), where the bracketed term is the percent unreported.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$
$$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$

requirements.statement: The percent unreported at a given maturity equals 1 minus the reciprocal of the reported age-to-ultimate factor (1 − 1/CDF).

places.quote: $1 - 1/\text{CDF}$ the percentage unreported from the [[Development Triangle|development pattern]].
the [[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method]] uses the *complement* $(1 - 1/\text{CDF})$ to weight an a priori expectation.

requirements.statement: A combined expected claims ratio is the premium-weighted average of the regional expected claims ratios, so one region's ELR can be backed out from the combined ELR and the other region's ELR using the business mix weights.

places.quote: $$\overline{\text{LR}} = \sum_i w_i \times \text{LR}_i$$

requirements.statement: To trend an expected claims ratio from one accident year to another, multiply by (1 + frequency trend) × (1 + severity trend) for each year of difference; with no premium trend or rate changes, the loss ratio trends by the claims trend alone.

places.quote: $$1 + t_{PP} = (1 + t_{\text{freq}})(1 + t_{\text{sev}})$$
Separately selected frequency and severity trends combine multiplicatively: $1 + T_{PP} = (1 + T_F)(1 + T_S)$.

requirements.statement: Each age-to-ultimate factor applies to the accident year at its corresponding maturity at the evaluation date (e.g., latest accident year at 12 months, prior year at 24 months), and BF is applied to each region separately with its own factors, ELR, and premium.

places.quote: - Cell $C_{\text{AY},k}$ holds the cumulative amount for that accident year at age $k$.
The overall indication is normally produced for each jurisdiction and line whose rates are filed separately.

requirements.statement: Data from segments should not be combined when they have different development patterns, different trends, or a shifting mix of business; in such cases use segment-specific assumptions, because combined factors or ELRs based on past mix would be distorted.
requirements.concept: Data Segmentation and Credibility of Combined Data

places.quote: Assumptions being made implicitly by using one at all: each cohort develops in a similar pattern, the pattern is stable over time, and the mix inside each cohort is comparable.
Do not combine segments whose relative volume is changing — see [[Mix of Business]] and [[Reserving Data Organization]].
If the segments have different emergence patterns, the blended development factors drift as the weights drift — and the triangle gives no signal that this is what is happening.

requirements.statement: Cape Cod ultimate claims for an accident year equal reported claims plus the expected claims ratio times earned premium times the percent unreported (1 − 1/age-to-ultimate factor).

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$
$$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$

requirements.statement: Used-up premium (premium exposed to date) for an accident year is its on-level earned premium divided by its age-to-ultimate development factor (earned premium times the percent reported).

places.quote: **Used-up premium** $\text{EP}_i / \text{CDF}_i$ is the share of each year's premium "exposed" to the losses reported so far.
$P_i / \text{CDF}_i$ is the **used-up premium**, the share of the premium that the claims reported so far correspond to.

requirements.statement: The Cape Cod expected claims ratio is the sum of trended reported claims across accident years divided by the sum of used-up premiums across accident years.

places.quote: $$\text{ELR} = \frac{\sum_i C_i}{\sum_i \text{EP}_i \times \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}}$$
$$\text{ELR}_j = \frac{\sum_i D^{|i-j|}\, C_i\, T_{i \to j}}{\sum_i D^{|i-j|}\, P_i / \text{CDF}_i}$$

requirements.statement: To put each accident year's claims on the cost level of the target year, apply pure premium trend factors (to a common cost level, e.g., dividing by the target year's factor if factors are relative to a later year); the trend applies to losses, not premium.

places.quote: applied to bring historical losses from the cost level of the experience period to the cost level of the **future policy period**.
$T_{i \to j}$ is the trend factor that restates year $i$'s claims at year $j$'s cost level, net of any change already in the on-level premium.

requirements.statement: Premium is brought to current rate level (on-leveled) and adjusted for premium trend before use in Cape Cod; with no rate changes and no premium trend, earned premium is used as is.

places.quote: Premium **must be on level** and losses must be trended to a common cost level before the ELR is computed, or the derived ratio blends years written at different rate levels and different cost levels into one number.
$$\text{Premium Trend Factor} = (1 + t_P)^{n}$$
**On-Level Premium** is historical earned premium restated as though every policy had been written at the rate level currently in effect.

requirements.statement: A change in case reserve adequacy distorts reported claims and reported development factors, so reported Cape Cod gives distorted ultimates (overstated if case reserves are strengthened) while paid Cape Cod, which uses only paid claims, is unaffected; paid is therefore preferred when case reserve adequacy has changed.

places.quote: **Paid data is immune**, so a divergence between paid and reported chain ladder estimates is the corroborating evidence.

requirements.statement: The reported development technique estimates ultimate claims as reported claims times the reported age-to-ultimate (cumulative development) factor.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate} = C_n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson technique estimates ultimate claims as reported claims plus expected claims (expected claims ratio times premium) times the percent unreported (1 − 1/age-to-ultimate factor).

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$
$$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$

requirements.statement: Unpaid claims equal ultimate claims minus paid claims, and consist of case reserves (reported minus paid claims) plus pure IBNR (ultimate minus reported claims).

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Reported}$$
$$\text{Unpaid} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Paid to date}$$
$$\text{Reported Losses} = \text{Paid Losses} + \text{Case Reserves}$$

requirements.statement: A change in the legal environment such as tort reform affects only future claim payments: already-paid claims are unchanged, while both case reserves and IBNR (all unpaid claims) are scaled by the expected reduction.
requirements.concept: Adjusting Claims Development Methods for Changes in Legal Environment

resolution.note: the question states the reform reduces future claim payments by 20%; that paid claims are past and case + IBNR are the future payments is the definition of unpaid claims (Unpaid Claims page)

requirements.statement: To incorporate a change affecting future payments, compute the unadjusted unpaid estimate under the technique, multiply it by (1 − reduction), and add back paid claims to obtain adjusted ultimate claims.
requirements.concept: Adjusting Claims Development Methods for Changes in Legal Environment

resolution.note: a step of this solution's plan: unadjusted unpaid x (1 - reduction) + paid, arithmetic on the question's stated reduction

requirements.statement: The parallelogram method on-levels earned premium by splitting the calendar-year earned premium into regions of each rate level, based on rate change effective dates and the policy term, with policies written uniformly.

places.quote: A calendar year is a unit square: time across, fraction of the policy term earned up. A rate change for policies written on or after a date is a **diagonal** line whose slope is set by the term (steeper for six-month policies).

Picture a unit square whose horizontal axis is calendar time and whose vertical axis is the fraction of the policy term elapsed. A rate change effective on date $d$ enters as a diagonal line; each region's **area** is the share of the year's earned premium written at that rate level.

requirements.statement: The on-level factor equals the current rate level divided by the average rate level in the period; on-level premium equals earned premium times the on-level factor.

places.quote: $$\text{On-Level Factor} = \frac{\text{Current cumulative rate level index}}{\text{Average rate level index for the period}}$$
$$\text{On-Level Factor} = \frac{\text{Current cumulative index}}{\text{Average index for the year}}$$
applies an [[On Level Premium|on-level factor]] to aggregate premium: $\text{OLF}$ is the current rate level divided by the average historical rate level.

requirements.statement: Cumulative rate level indices are found by multiplying successive (1 + rate change) factors.

places.quote: Rate level indices **compound**: successive changes of $+8\%$ and $+5\%$ give a cumulative index of $1.08 \times 1.05 = 1.134$, not $1.13$.
$I_k$ is the cumulative rate level index of rate level group $k$ (each index is the previous one times $1 +$ that change)

requirements.statement: Estimate the premium trend from the year-over-year change in average written premium at current rate level (comparing like quarters) and select an annual trend rate.

places.quote: The trend is measured on the **average premium per exposure at current rate level**, usually from written data — a leading indicator, reflecting distributional shifts sooner than earned premium — often quarterly.

requirements.statement: The trend period runs from the average written date of the historical earned premium (average earned date less half the policy term) to the average written date of the future policies under the new rates (midpoint of the period the rates are in effect).

places.quote: The trend period $n$ runs from the average written date of the policies earning premium in the experience period to the **average written date of the policies in effect while the new rates are**

requirements.statement: Trended premium equals on-level premium times (1 + annual trend) raised to the trend period in years.

places.quote: $$\text{Premium Trend Factor} = (1 + t_P)^{n}$$
$$\text{Projected EP} = \text{EP} \times \text{OLF} \times \text{Trend}$$

requirements.statement: Longer policy terms (annual vs semi-annual) give an earlier average written date for the earned premium, lengthening the trend period and raising trended premium when the trend is positive.

places.quote: with six-month policies the trend-from date moves to $4/1/2011$ and the period is $2.25$ years.

requirements.statement: Longer policy terms spread rate changes over a longer earning period, so more of the calendar-year earned premium is at older, lower rate levels, giving a lower average rate level and a larger on-level factor when rates have increased.

places.quote: Six-month policies take on a change faster, so they need a smaller adjustment

requirements.statement: A frequency-severity tail severity is computed by pooling all incremental paid claims and closed claim counts at the maturity age and older, then dividing total adjusted paid by total claim count (a count-weighted pooled severity).

Adjust historical claim costs for a legislative change by applying the cost-change factor (1 minus the reduction) only to accident years whose claims occurred before the effective date, since later accident years already reflect the new cost level.

places.quote: A benefit-level change is restated in the data, or allowed for in the selection, so that it is not double counted.
A deductible increase in the middle of the experience lowers paid claims and looks like a low trend. Normalize the history to one benefit design before measuring trend.

requirements.statement: Trend severities to a target cost level by compounding the annual severity trend over the period from each accident year's average accident date (midpoint, July 1) to the target date.

places.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.
$m$ is the number of months from the midpoint of the experience period to the midpoint of the rating period.

requirements.statement: The maturity age for the tail should be set where data becomes erratic or sparse, so pooling older data gives a more stable and credible estimate than separate age-to-age factors.

Choosing the tail maturity age involves a trade-off: too late leaves too little data in the tail for credibility, too early discards reliable individual age-to-age factors; also consider the share of claims expected to close after that age, the impact on total projections, and alignment with industry data maturity age for supplementing data.

Elevated reported claims at constant frequency, with no catastrophe/large claims and no change in case reserve adequacy or claims handling, can be explained by higher severity (e.g., mix of business shift, tort reform), higher exposure volume (more business written or acquisition), reduced deductibles, or retained reinsurance changes (higher stop loss threshold, lower quota share percentage).
requirements.concept: Claims Development Method Assumptions and Diagnostics

places.quote: **External environment:** [[Inflation|inflation]] (a calendar-year effect on every open claim) and the legal environment ([[Tort Reform|tort reform]], court decisions, [[Tort Litigation|litigation]]).
A change in the attachment point changes both the **ceded** and the **net** triangle: every prior year then reflects different terms.
Premium grew $74\%$ in two years while **average premium per unit fell $19\%$** — so the growth is in unit count, and the new units are cheaper ones.

requirements.statement: The reported (chain ladder) development method is responsive to changes in the claims ratio and is appropriate when claims handling and case reserve adequacy are unchanged; if new business differs from existing business, claims should be split into homogeneous groups and developed separately.

places.quote: With reported claims the [[Chain Ladder Method|development technique]] assumes [[Case Adequacy|case adequacy]] has not changed; with paid claims, that settlement speed has not.
The response is to give **less weight to pre-change accident years** when selecting factors, and to segment the data by hazard grade so the two populations can be seen separately.

requirements.statement: The frequency/severity method projects ultimate claim counts (frequency times exposure) and ultimate severity separately, so it can isolate and account for a severity change while frequency is stable; ultimate claims equal ultimate counts times ultimate severity.

places.quote: **Frequency-Severity Method** projects [[Claim Count Triangle|claim counts]] and average [[Severity|severity]] separately and multiplies them, instead of developing loss dollars directly.
$$\widehat{PP}_i = \hat{f}_i \times \hat{s}_i$$

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson method blends reported claims with an a priori expected claims ratio applied to the unreported portion, so it is not driven solely by elevated reported claims and reflects exposure growth in the unreported portion.

places.quote: the [[Bornhuetter-Ferguson Method|BF]] method by applying the unreported percentage to an a priori
The key structural property: **actual emergence is taken at face value and only the unemerged portion is estimated**.

requirements.statement: The expected claims method applies an expected claims ratio to premium (exposure), so it accounts for changes in premium or volume independent of reported claims.

places.quote: **Expected Loss Method** (expected claims technique) estimates ultimate losses entirely from an a priori expectation — usually an expected loss ratio applied to earned premium — giving **no weight** to what has actually been reported.
**Expected.** The usual estimate is an expected loss ratio times earned premium.

requirements.statement: When reinsurance terms change, estimate ultimate claims on gross (direct) data, then adjust for the new contract; alternatively, restate prior years' net data to the new reinsurance terms so all years are consistent before applying development methods.

places.quote: restate history to current retentions or benefit levels.
A change in attachment point makes prior net years non-comparable, while gross years remain usable.

requirements.statement: Reported (case-incurred) claims equal cumulative paid claims plus case outstanding reserves, where case outstanding equals average case outstanding times open claim count.

places.quote: $$\text{Avg Case Outstanding} = \frac{\text{Case Reserves}}{\text{Open Claim Counts}}$$
$$\text{Reported (Incurred)} = \text{Paid} + \text{Case Reserves}$$

requirements.statement: To adjust for a change in case reserve adequacy, restate historical average case outstanding at the latest (current) adequacy level by detrending the latest level back to earlier accident years and deflating by the severity trend, then recompute adjusted reported claims.
requirements.concept: Adjusting for Changes in Case Reserve Adequacy

places.quote: $$\text{Adjusted Case}_{\text{AY},n} = \text{Case}_{\text{latest},n} \times \left(1 + t\right)^{-(\text{years before latest})}$$
**Trend the latest diagonal's** average case outstanding backwards at $t$ to restate each historical cell at today's adequacy level.

The remedy is the [[Berquist-Sherman Method|Berquist-Sherman]] case adjustment: restate historical average case outstanding to the current adequacy level using a selected severity trend, rebuild the reported triangle, and select factors from the restated history.

requirements.statement: Apply the adjustment only to the claim segment affected by the change in case reserve adequacy (e.g., large claims) and leave unaffected segments (e.g., small claims) unadjusted, using their unadjusted reported data.
requirements.concept: Adjusting for Changes in Case Reserve Adequacy

resolution.note: a step of this solution's plan: the question's own data show only large-claim average case outstanding changed; the case-adequacy diagnostic itself is taught (Case Adequacy, Data Diagnostic Analysis)

requirements.statement: Age-to-age development factors are computed as ratios of successive cumulative reported claims for each accident year, and the selected factor (e.g., volume-weighted or average) is chosen for each age.

places.quote: $$f_{k \to k+1} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k}}$$
$$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{AY}} = \frac{C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$

requirements.statement: Age-to-ultimate factors are the cumulative product of selected age-to-age factors from a given age through the tail factor (including the tail/48-to-ultimate factor).

places.quote: **The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \left(\prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1}\right) \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: Ultimate claims under the reported development technique equal reported claims at the current age times the age-to-ultimate reported development factor.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate} = C_n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: Total ultimate claims are obtained by estimating ultimates separately for large and small claim segments and summing them.

places.quote: Corrected — remove the shock loss, develop the rest, add it back:
so severities are usually capped and the excess layer added back separately.

requirements.statement: Under the reported development technique, ultimate claims equal reported claims divided by the percent reported (the reciprocal of the reported loss development factor).

places.quote: $$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Reported \%} = \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}}$$

requirements.statement: A per occurrence retention limits the retained amount of each claim to the retention, so a large claim's retained amount is the lesser of the gross claim and the retention, using the retention applicable to its accident year.

places.quote: $$\text{Capped Loss} = \min(X, M)$$
$$\text{Retained Loss} = \sum_i \min(X_i, R)$$

requirements.statement: Large claims known to have no further development are handled separately from the development of the remaining claims: they are held at their capped retained amounts, not given development factors, and added to the developed ultimate of other claims by accident year.
requirements.concept: Large Claim Treatment in Self-Insured Reserving

places.quote: **Corrected — remove the shock loss, develop the rest, add it back:**
the actuary may exclude large claims from the initial projection, then add back a case-specific projection for the reported large claims

requirements.statement: A stop-loss (aggregate) limit caps total retained ultimate claims at the limit; when one limit applies to several accident years combined, the years' retained claims are summed before applying the cap.

places.quote: The reinsurer pays the aggregate in excess of an aggregate retention $A$, up to an aggregate limit $L_A$.
A stop-loss retention applies to the total for the period.

resolution.quote: Only an aggregate cover limits the total.
resolution.note: tagged page: an aggregate (stop-loss) cover caps the total; that the 2015-16 limit is shared is stated in the question

requirements.statement: Retained IBNR equals total retained ultimate claims (net of per occurrence retention and stop-loss limits) minus total retained reported claims, including reported large claims at their retained amounts.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Reported}$$
$$\text{IBNR} = U_{\text{AY}} - C_{\text{AY},\,n}$$

requirements.statement: The ALAE ratio at a given maturity is cumulative paid ALAE divided by cumulative paid claims (loss) only at that same maturity.

places.quote: $$\text{ALAE Ratio} = \frac{\text{ALAE}}{\text{Indemnity}}$$

requirements.statement: In the multiplicative ratio development approach, compute age-to-age link ratios as the ratio of successive ALAE ratios (ALAE ratio at later age divided by ALAE ratio at earlier age) for each accident year, then select a factor per age by averaging.

places.quote: $$f_{n \to n+1}^{\text{AY}} = \frac{C_{\text{AY},\,n+1}}{C_{\text{AY},\,n}}$$
**Simple average** — equal weight to each year, so a small, volatile year counts as much as a large one.

requirements.statement: Multiply the selected age-to-age ratio factors (with a tail factor of 1.000 when there is no development beyond the last age) to get the cumulative factor to ultimate, then apply it to the latest ALAE ratio to get the ultimate ALAE ratio.

places.quote: **The procedure:** build the cumulative [[Development Triangle|triangle]] → compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.

requirements.statement: Ultimate ALAE equals the projected ultimate ALAE ratio multiplied by the selected ultimate claims (loss) estimate for the accident year.

places.quote: Friedland gives three approaches: develop a **combined** loss-and-ALAE triangle, develop **ALAE separately** in its own triangle, or develop a **ratio of ALAE to loss** and apply it to projected losses.

requirements.statement: The additive ratio approach is preferred over the multiplicative approach when ALAE ratios are very small (especially at early maturities), because multiplicative link ratios then become highly leveraged while additive differences are less leveraged and more stable.

Advantages of ratio techniques: they recognize the relationship between losses and ALAE, provide diagnostics (unreasonable year ratios can be excluded), and give less leveraged, more stable factors than developing paid ALAE dollars directly.

Disadvantages of ratio techniques: errors in ultimate claims estimates carry into ultimate ALAE, early-maturity ratios are distorted when ALAE is paid without accompanying paid claims, and the method is inaccurate if ALAE trends differently from claims.

places.quote: If instead ALAE were $85\%$ paid against $63\%$ on indemnity, the ratio method would be projecting ALAE that has largely already been spent, and a **separate ALAE triangle** would be the better estimator.

requirements.statement: Calendar year aggregation groups premium/exposure and losses by the calendar period in which they are earned/recorded (transactions occur), regardless of the accident or policy date.

places.quote: **[[Calendar Year]]** — everything booked in the year.

**Calendar Year** (CY) is a data aggregation method that groups every transaction by the calendar year in which it is *booked* — premium as it is earned, losses as they are paid or as case reserves change — without regard to the policy's effective date or the claim's accident date.

requirements.statement: An advantage of calendar year data is that it is fixed at the end of the period, so it is immediately available, easy and inexpensive to compile, and needs no further development.

places.quote: Available quickly and already collected for financial reporting
CY is the **financial reporting** basis: most insurers report financially by calendar year, so the data is available quickly once the year ends and costs nothing extra to aggregate for ratemaking.

requirements.statement: A disadvantage of calendar year data is a poor match of losses to premium/exposure, since it mixes losses and exposures from different accident or policy periods, making it vulnerable to distortion from rate changes, mix shifts, or claims handling changes.

places.quote: Available quickly and already collected for financial reporting, but its losses include payments and reserve changes on claims from policies issued years ago, a mismatch with the premium earned in the year.
CY incurred losses **mix accident years**: a CY 2024 figure contains payments and reserve changes on claims from $2024$ and from every prior year.

requirements.statement: Accident year aggregation groups losses by the date of occurrence and policy year aggregation groups losses by the effective date of the policy that covers them, while report year aggregation groups claims by the date they are reported.

places.quote: **[[Accident Year]]** — losses by occurrence date against premium earned in the same year.
**Report Year** (RY) is a data aggregation method that groups claims by the calendar year in which the claim was first *reported* to the insurer, regardless of when the loss occurred.

**Policy Year** (PY), also called underwriting year or year of account, is a data aggregation method that groups every premium and loss transaction belonging to policies *incepting* in a given calendar year, and follows that cohort until the last claim closes.

requirements.statement: Accident year and policy year aggregation match losses to premium/exposure much better than calendar year data (policy year most closely), at the cost of needing loss development; policy year has a longer development tail than accident year.

places.quote: [[Accident Year]] aggregation matches premium and losses better, and [[Policy Year]] best — see [[Ratemaking Data Organization]].
AY matches premium and losses better than [[Calendar Year]], and its claims occur over a shorter time frame than a [[Policy Year]]'s, so its ultimate can be reliably estimated sooner.

The price of that match is **time**. With annual policies a PY cohort is not fully written until $12$ months after the year begins and not fully earned until $24$ months, so PY data is roughly a year less mature than the corresponding [[Accident Year]] at the same valuation date.

requirements.statement: Risk classification analysis requires losses to be well matched to the exposures that generated them, so accident year or policy year aggregation (with development to ultimate) is appropriate for long-tailed lines, rather than calendar year or report year (non-claims-made).

places.quote: Werner & Modlin set three objectives for it: **accurately match losses and premium** for the policy, **use the most recent data** available, and **minimize the cost** of data collection and retrieval.

Because of that mismatch, Werner & Modlin say calendar-year aggregation for ratemaking may be most appropriate for lines or coverages whose losses are reported and settled relatively quickly, such as homeowners.
AY matches premium and losses better than [[Calendar Year]], and its claims occur over a shorter time frame than a [[Policy Year]]'s, so its ultimate can be reliably estimated sooner.

requirements.statement: Under claims-made coverage, the trigger is the report date of the claim, so report year aggregation matches losses to the premium/exposure of the policy providing coverage.

places.quote: RY is the correct basis for [[Claims Made Coverage|claims-made]] coverage, because a claims-made policy's trigger *is* the report date: every claim reported during the policy period is covered by that policy, so the report year cohort and the coverage cohort coincide.
Claims-made business is organized on a [[Report Year]] basis: in Werner's report-year-by-lag table a claims-made policy is a row, where an occurrence policy is a diagonal.

requirements.statement: Claims-made policies and report year data have no pure IBNR once the period ends, only IBNER on reported claims, so report year data develops quickly toward ultimate.

places.quote: A report year **closes to new claims** at year end — pure [[IBNR]] is zero by construction, since every claim in the cohort is already known. All remaining development is **IBNER**: re-estimation of claims already reported.

Because the trigger is the report date, a claims-made policy has **no pure IBNR** — only IBNER on claims already reported — so the risk of reserve inadequacy is greatly reduced relative to the [[Occurrence Coverage|occurrence]] form.

requirements.statement: To measure the basic limits loss trend, apply the severity trend factor to each ground-up (total limits) loss, cap both the original and the trended losses at the basic limit, sum each set, and take the ratio of trended to original capped totals minus 1.
requirements.concept: Increased Limits Factors and Loss Trend by Layer

places.quote: **Leverage:** untrended layer losses are $150 + 0 + 650 + 50 = 850$, so trend raised them by $1{,}107/850 - 1 = 30.2\%$.

requirements.statement: A claim's excess loss is the portion of its total limits loss above the basic limit, equal to total limits loss minus basic limits (capped) loss.

places.quote: reflecting the additional expected loss in the layer above the basic limit
the reinsurer pays the part of each loss — per risk or per occurrence — above the cedant's retention $R$ (the attachment point), up to a limit $L$.

requirements.statement: To measure the excess loss trend, compute trended excess loss as trended total (uncapped) loss minus trended basic limits loss, and compare it with the original excess loss; trend must be applied to the full loss before splitting into layers, not only to the excess portion.
requirements.concept: Increased Limits Factors and Loss Trend by Layer

places.quote: Trend each historical loss individually *before* applying the layer. Excess losses grow faster than trend because a loss just below $R$ trends into the layer.

requirements.statement: When a uniform severity trend applies to total limits losses, the basic limits layer trends slower than the total trend and the excess layer trends faster, because trend on losses that reach the limit flows entirely into the excess layer and losses near the limit migrate into the excess layer.
requirements.concept: Increased Limits Factors and Loss Trend by Layer

places.quote: for a positive trend, basic-limits losses trend more slowly than total-limits losses and the excess layer faster
As losses grow, more of them pierce the basic limit and the excess layers grow faster than the ground-up trend

requirements.statement: Applying the total limits trend to basic limits losses is inappropriate because it overstates basic limits trend; basic limits and excess layers should be trended separately with layer-appropriate rates, and total limits trend is valid only if trends are equal across layers.
requirements.concept: Increased Limits Factors and Loss Trend by Layer

places.quote: so a severity trend measured on total-limits data must be adjusted before it is applied to basic-limits losses
A rate for the excess layer that is trended at the ground-up $10\%$ is inadequate.

requirements.statement: Select frequency and severity trends from exponential-trend fits over different numbers of points, choosing longer-term fits when the trend is stable (for credibility) and justifying the choice from how the trend behaves over time.

places.quote: Werner's example fits windows of 20, 16, 12, 8, 6 and 4 points, and $R^2$ is the usual diagnostic; the recent windows show whether the trend has shifted.

exponential models may be fit to the whole of the data and to more recent periods, supplemented with multi-state, countrywide or industry data and non-insurance indices, and the trend selected with judgment.

requirements.statement: When severity trend has changed recently, use two-step trending: the longer-term trend for the historical experience period to the current level, and the most recent (shorter-period) trend for the projection period into the future.

places.quote: losses are first trended at a *current* trend from the experience period's average accident date to that of the latest data point in the trend data, then projected at a separately selected trend to the forecast period's average accident date.
Step one brings historical average earned premium up to the **current** average written premium level (a known, observed figure); step two projects forward from there at a selected prospective trend:

requirements.statement: Determine the number of trend years for each accident year as the time from the average accident date of that year (for annual policies, July 1 of the year in the experience period) to the average accident date of the future period (policy effective date plus half the policy term plus half the rate-in-effect period), and apply compounded frequency and severity trends over those periods.

places.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.
The trend period runs from the average date of historical losses (midpoint of the accident year) to the average date of future losses (midpoint of the prospective rating period)
The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: Trend historical cumulative losses and shock (ground-up) losses to the future level, removing trended shock losses from trended total losses but retaining the threshold amount for each shock claim, to get the basic (primary) losses.

places.quote: Ideally the procedure is run on losses trended to future levels, since higher layers are subject to greater inflation.
Each claim is capped at a threshold (the **non-excess** loss); the portion above it is **excess**.

requirements.statement: Excess loss load (ratio) equals trended excess losses (shock losses minus threshold per claim) divided by trended losses with excess removed (threshold retained), computed from selected years and applied as a multiplier (1 + load) to capped losses.

places.quote: $$\text{Excess Load} = \frac{\text{Expected losses above } M}{\text{Expected losses below } M}$$
$$\text{ELF} = 1 + \frac{\sum \text{Excess losses}}{\sum \text{Non-excess losses}}$$

requirements.statement: Develop the latest-year losses (after removing excess over the threshold) to ultimate by multiplying by the cumulative product of selected age-to-age factors from the current age to ultimate, with the same development applied to basic and excess losses.

places.quote: $$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
**1. Remove the shock loss** before developing — a [[Large Loss|large loss]] does not develop like ordinary claims and would be multiplied by the CDF:

requirements.statement: Approaches to selecting an excess (shock) loss threshold include choosing a quantile/percentile of the loss distribution where large losses become volatile and sparse, using a percentage of the amount of insurance, using a reinsurance attachment point, basic limit or policy limit, and balancing stability against responsiveness of the indication.

places.quote: Otherwise Werner sets it to balance including as many losses as possible against minimizing volatility: for example at the $99$th percentile of claim sizes, or at a percentage of losses;
a percentile of the size-of-loss distribution such as the 99th, or for property a percentage of the amount of insurance.

requirements.statement: Compute each expense ratio using the appropriate premium base: commissions, other acquisition and taxes/licenses/fees are divided by direct written premium, while general expenses are divided by direct earned premium.

places.quote: Werner splits the categories by when they are incurred: those incurred at the onset of the policy (commissions, other acquisition, taxes, licenses and fees) are measured against written premium, those incurred throughout the policy (general expenses) against [[Earned Premium|earned premium]], and the category ratios are added.

Expenses incurred at the onset of the policy — commissions, other acquisition, and taxes, licenses and fees — are calculated on [[Written Premium]]; general expenses, incurred throughout the policy, on [[Earned Premium]].

requirements.statement: Select a ratemaking expense ratio for each expense category by comparing the latest year's ratio with prior years and averaging stable years while excluding anomalous years or relying on the latest data.
Variable permissible loss ratio = 1 - variable expense ratio - profit provision.

places.quote: The **variable permissible loss ratio** is what is left after the variable expense and profit provisions, $\text{VPLR} = 1 - V - Q_T$, and pays for loss, LAE and fixed expenses;

requirements.statement: Expenses that do not vary with premium are removed from the variable expense ratio and recovered as a flat fixed dollar amount per policy (or exposure), so only the variable portion of each expense category enters the variable permissible loss ratio.

places.quote: They cost roughly the same on a $\$500$ policy as on a $\$5{,}000$ one, so they are recovered as a **dollar amount per exposure**, not as a percentage of premium.
They are converted to a **dollar amount per exposure** and added to the pure premium in the numerator.

requirements.statement: Treating fixed expenses as variable with premium understates the premium for small-premium policies and overstates it for large-premium policies.

places.quote: Loading fixed expenses as a percentage of premium instead — the **all-variable expense method** — undercharges risks with below-average premium and overcharges those above it, so large policies subsidize small ones.
Treating a fixed cost as variable over-charges large policies and under-charges small ones.

requirements.statement: Countrywide or benchmark expense ratios may be inappropriate for a new state because expenses (e.g., taxes, commissions) vary by state and start-up costs make initial expenses higher than historical benchmarks.
requirements.concept: Expense Provisions for a New State

requirements.statement: Bornhuetter-Ferguson ultimate loss = reported loss + (1 - 1/CDF to ultimate) × earned premium × expected loss ratio, where the unreported percentage is 1 - 1/CDF.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$
$$\text{IBNR}_j = \text{ELR}_j \times P_j \times \left(1 - \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_j}\right)$$

requirements.statement: On-level earned premium is calculated by multiplying earned premium by an on-level factor equal to the current rate level divided by the average rate level in effect during the period, with average rate levels found using the parallelogram method for annual policies written evenly.

places.quote: $$\text{On-Level Premium} = \text{Historical EP} \times \text{On-Level Factor}$$
$$\text{OLF}_Y = \frac{I_{\text{current}}}{\sum_k A_{Y,k}\, I_k}$$

For **annual** policies written uniformly, a rate change effective at time $p$ through year $Y$ earns over a triangle of area $\tfrac{1}{2}(1-p)^2$ in year $Y$ — so a $7/1$ change affects only $0.125$ of that year's earned premium, and a $1/1$ change affects $0.500$.

requirements.statement: Premium and loss are trended from the average written/accident date of the historical period to the average written/earned or loss date of the future policy period, using the annual trend rate compounded over the trend period; for annual policies with rates in effect for one year, the average accident date is one year after the rate effective date plus half a year of written-to-accident lag.

places.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.

The trend period $n$ runs from the average written date of the policies earning premium in the experience period to the **average written date of the policies in effect while the new rates are** — for calendar-year 2011 earned premium and annual policies written in 2013, $1/1/2011$ to $6/30/2013$, or $2.5$ years.
The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: ULAE is incorporated by loading loss and ALAE with the ULAE provision percentage (multiplying by 1 + ULAE ratio) before computing the loss ratio.

places.quote: In **ratemaking**, ULAE may be handled as a load on losses or as a [[Fixed Expenses|fixed expense]] provision.
$$\text{Loss \& LAE} = \text{Loss} + \text{ALAE} + \text{ULAE}$$

requirements.statement: Loss ratio method indicated rate change = (projected loss ratio + fixed expense ratio) / (1 - variable expense ratio - profit provision) - 1.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + \text{Fixed Expense Ratio}}{1 - V - Q} - 1$$

requirements.statement: The credibility-weighted indicated change equals Z × the company's indicated change plus (1 - Z) × the complement of credibility.

places.quote: $$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$
$$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$
$Z$ multiplies the observed experience; $1 - Z$ goes to the [[Complement of Credibility]]

requirements.statement: A competitor's rate change is a poor complement of credibility because the competitor's book (mix of business, limits, underwriting, and goals) differs and its filing may not reflect the company's needed change; better complements are the trended present rates or a related-experience complement such as the Harwayne method or the larger group's indication, since they reflect similar exposure and are unbiased.

places.quote: 5. **Trended present rates** — the current rate adjusted to what was last *indicated* rather than implemented, and trended from the original target effective date of the current rates to that of the new rates.

requirements.statement: Expected total profit equals total revenue (sum over classes of number of risks times rate per risk) minus total losses and expenses minus any one-time implementation expense.

places.quote: $$\text{LTV} = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{\left(P_t - L_t - E_t\right) \times {}_{t}p}{(1 + r)^{t}}$$
[[Underwriting Profit|underwriting profit]], what the policies earn as premium less losses and expenses

requirements.statement: Insureds are price sensitive: when an insurer raises rates relative to competitors, insureds may shop elsewhere and the number of risks falls, and when it lowers rates, it retains or attracts more risks (price elasticity of demand).

places.quote: price-sensitive risks shop, so a large increase can worsen the remaining experience through adverse selection

Modelling renewal probability as a function of the rate change offered lets an insurer see the trade-off directly: a larger increase raises premium per policy and lowers the number of policies, and the optimum is rarely at either extreme.
Profit is earned only on policies that are sold, and demand falls as price rises.

requirements.statement: Introducing a rating variable that better matches rates to risk lets the insurer attract lower-risk classes with lower rates and shed higher-cost classes with higher rates, which improves long-run profitability and avoids adverse selection.

places.quote: In a competitive market an insurer that charges one average rate to a heterogeneous group loses the better risks to competitors that price them properly, and retains the worse ones — the **adverse selection spiral**.
**Defences:** [[Risk Classification Restrictions|risk classification]] (price to the risk, so nobody is overcharged)

In **ratemaking**, a non-homogeneous class means systematic cross-subsidy: the better risks in the class are overcharged and leave (see [[Classification Ratemaking]]), while the worse risks stay — the adverse selection spiral that risk classification exists to prevent.

requirements.statement: An across-the-board rate increase may cause the best risks, who can find cheaper rates elsewhere, to leave while higher-risk insureds with fewer alternatives stay, worsening the risk mix and making a static profit calculation overstate expected profit.

places.quote: price-sensitive risks shop, so a large increase can worsen the remaining experience through adverse selection
rate changes themselves prompt renewing customers to shop

insureds receiving large increases non-renew — the realized average premium change may differ from $+6.0\%$, and if the risks that leave are not equally profitable, the shift affects the adequacy of the overall rates.

requirements.statement: Holding the number of risks fixed when rates change ignores customer response, so calculated profit may over- or understate true profit; the net effect depends on whether the profit lost from departing risks outweighs the gain from added risks.

places.quote: The traditional indication sets a rate without regard to whether the product will be bought. Past some price the business lost outweighs the higher price on what remains, and rate changes themselves prompt renewing customers to shop.
Total profit therefore rises with price only up to a point, after which the business lost outweighs the higher price on the business kept.

requirements.statement: Validate a GLM by comparing predicted versus actual values (e.g., pure premium by equal-volume decile sorted by actual loss) on both the training data and a hold-out sample.

places.quote: A [[Quantile Plot|quantile plot]] sorts records by predicted loss cost into equal-exposure buckets and compares actual with predicted in each, judged on accuracy, monotonicity and the spread between the first and last buckets.
Sort the holdout records by predicted value, group them into buckets of equal weight (quintiles, deciles), and compare the average actual with the average predicted in each.

requirements.statement: An overfit model captures noise in the training data rather than the underlying signal, so it fits training data very well but fails to generalize to new data.

places.quote: A model with small training error and large test error is [[Overfitting|overfitting]]: it has learned patterns in the training data that arose by chance (*ISLR*, §2.2).

**Overfitting** is fitting a model so closely to its training data that it follows the noise in that sample as well as the signal, so that it predicts new observations worse than a simpler model would.

resolution.quote: holdout error falls, then rises once the model starts fitting noise
resolution.note: linked page teaches overfitting as fitting noise that fails on new data (with ASOP 56's definition beside it)

requirements.statement: A model that fits the training data nearly perfectly but gives erratic, volatile predictions that diverge from actuals on the hold-out sample is overfit and performs poorly.

places.quote: Training error always falls as flexibility rises, while validation error turns up once the model starts fitting noise: the U-shape of the [[Bias-Variance Tradeoff|bias-variance tradeoff]] that validation is used to locate, for instance to choose a [[Hyperparameter|hyperparameter]]
The signature is a validation or CV error that turns upward as flexibility keeps rising while the training error keeps falling.

resolution.quote: training error is tiny and test error is much larger
resolution.note: linked page: the overfitting signature is near-perfect training fit with much worse holdout performance

requirements.statement: A model whose predictions are stable and consistent across training and hold-out samples, following the trend of actuals, is more likely to generalize well and focuses on signal rather than noise.

places.quote: Model stability is the sensitivity of the model to changes in the modelling data.
**How to split:** a random split (commonly $60$–$80\%$ training) or an **out-of-time** split (fit on earlier years, test on the latest), which also tests stability over time.

requirements.statement: Predictions that are flat and fail to match the amplitude of actual differences across deciles (underestimating high deciles, overestimating low ones) may indicate the model is missing predictive variables.

Written exposures are exposures on policies written (incepted) in a period; earned exposures are the portion of written exposures whose coverage has elapsed by a date; unearned exposures are the portion not yet elapsed; in-force exposures are those on policies incepted and not yet expired at a date.
requirements.concept: Written, Earned, Unearned, and In-Force Exposures

places.quote: **Earned Exposure** is the portion of written exposure for which coverage has actually been provided during the period
In-force exposures count the insured units exposed to loss at the date — a snapshot with no regard to the duration of the exposure.
**Unearned Premium** is the portion of written premium corresponding to coverage not yet provided

requirements.statement: To derive a non-uniform quarterly earning pattern from exposure data, divide each calendar quarter's earned exposures by the exposures in force during that quarter (starting with the first quarter, where only the first cohort is in force); the resulting fractions sum to 1 over a policy's term.

resolution.note: the question's own non-uniform seasonal pattern, recovered from its own written and earned exposures; Werner & Modlin teach only uniform earning (Ch.4)

requirements.statement: Earned exposures for a cohort of annual policies as of a date equal the written exposures times the sum of the earning pattern fractions for the calendar quarters the cohort has been in force; policies past their expiration are fully earned.

places.quote: written the day it is issued, earned $1/12$ per month, in force from effective date to expiry.
\text{EP for one policy} = \text{Full premium} \times \frac{\text{days elapsed}}{\text{policy term}}

requirements.statement: In-force exposures at a date are found by summing written exposures of policies already incepted whose term (e.g., twelve months from the first day of the quarter written) has not yet ended; no earning pattern is needed.

places.quote: \text{In-force at date } t = \sum_{\text{policies}} \mathbf{1}\{\text{effective} \le t < \text{expiration}\}

requirements.statement: Unearned exposures at a date equal the sum over unexpired cohorts of written exposures times the unearned fraction (one minus the cumulative earned fraction); equivalently cumulative written minus cumulative earned exposures.

places.quote: \text{Earned Exposure} = \text{Written Exposure} - \Delta\text{Unearned Exposure}
\text{UEP for one policy} = \text{Full premium} \times \frac{\text{days remaining}}{\text{policy term}}

requirements.statement: Calendar period earned exposures equal the in-force exposures during the period (by cohort) times that calendar quarter's earning pattern fraction, so future earned exposures after writing stops are based on in-force (not unearned) exposures.

resolution.note: a step of this solution's plan using the pattern recovered from the question's data (earned = in-force x the quarter's share)

requirements.statement: Calendar year earned exposures differ from policy year earned exposures: calendar-year figures include earning from all policy years during the calendar period, while policy year figures group exposures by the year the policy was written.
requirements.concept: Calendar Year vs Policy Year Aggregation

places.quote: groups every premium and loss transaction belonging to policies *incepting* in a given calendar year, and follows that cohort until the last claim closes.

groups every transaction by the calendar year in which it is *booked* — premium as it is earned, losses as they are paid or as case reserves change — without regard to the policy's effective date or the claim's accident date.

requirements.statement: The consistency test fits the same GLM separately to each year of experience and plots the resulting relativities for a variable side by side to check whether the variable's signal is stable over time.

A variable whose fitted relativities keep the same direction, shape and slope across years passes the consistency test and is a stable predictor to retain; relativities that jump around or reverse direction indicate noise.
Exposure volume bars shown on a relativity plot indicate how much data supports each level, helping distinguish genuinely unstable relativities from those of thinly populated levels.

places.quote: risk classes should be large enough to allow credible statistical inferences about expected outcomes; where the data are not sufficient, the actuary balances predictability against homogeneity.
A small class with one unusually large loss can look very risky with the loss in the data and very safe without it, with the same confidence both times.

requirements.statement: Statistical significance test: test the null hypothesis that a variable's parameters are zero using a chi-square test on the deviance with and without the variable, an F-test, or a t-test on the parameter; a p-value below the threshold (e.g., 5%) means the variable is predictive and should be retained.
requirements.concept: Statistical Significance Testing of GLM Variables

places.quote: Reject $H_0$ when p-value $< \alpha$

With a log link, a class coefficient $\hat{\beta}$ is a relativity of $e^{\hat{\beta}}$, and the [[p-Value|p-value]] behind $z$ is the chance of an estimate that far from zero if the class truly had no effect.

requirements.statement: Standard error test: examine the standard errors or confidence intervals around fitted parameters; wide intervals, especially those spanning the base level's relativity of 1.00, mean the level is not reliably distinguishable from base, while tight intervals support inclusion.
requirements.concept: Standard Error and Confidence Intervals of GLM Parameters

places.quote: The 95% [[Confidence Interval|confidence interval]] is $\hat{\beta} \pm 1.96\,\mathrm{SE}$, and exponentiating it gives an interval for the class's relativity, and so for its [[Loss Cost|loss cost]].
for a GLM coefficient it is $\hat\beta_j \pm z_{\alpha/2}\text{SE}(\hat\beta_j)$, and exponentiating both endpoints gives an interval for the multiplicative rating factor

requirements.statement: Judgment (common-sense) test: fitted relativities should be intuitive and explainable in direction and magnitude, and the variable must be practical to collect and acceptable from regulatory and social standpoints.

places.quote: Variable selection should combine statistical significance (from the [[Parameter Estimate Tables|parameter estimate table]]) with business and actuarial judgment, e.g., regulatory restrictions on certain rating variables
It should be objective and hard to manipulate, practical to collect and verify, and legal ([[Risk Classification Restrictions]], [[Unfair Discrimination]]) and socially acceptable.

requirements.statement: Tests for deciding whether to include a specific variable (significance, standard error, consistency, judgment) are distinct from measures of overall model fit or lift, which assess the model as a whole.
requirements.concept: GLM Variable Selection and Model Validation

places.quote: Lower [[AIC]] or [[BIC]] indicates a better trade-off between fit and complexity
The $F$-statistic compares nested GLMs using the unscaled [[Deviance|deviances]] $D$ of the small ($S$) and big ($B$) models and the big model's dispersion estimate $\hat{\phi}_B$.

requirements.statement: The base level of a rating variable is the reference level whose relativity is set to 1.00, and all other levels' relativities are expressed relative to it.

places.quote: the factors by which each class's rate differs from the base class
Coefficients for the territory variable, relative to the base territory:

requirements.statement: In both one-way analyses and GLMs the base level of a variable is conventionally chosen as the level with the most exposures, since it is the most stable and credible reference, so the two methods' relativities necessarily agree there.
A one-way analysis estimates each level of a rating variable using only the raw experience of that level, ignoring all other rating variables.

places.quote: A univariate** (one-way) pure premium or loss ratio analysis attributes to a variable the effect of everything correlated with it.
because a univariate pure premium picks up the effect of every correlated variable

requirements.statement: Exposure correlation (distributional bias) occurs when the distribution of one rating variable differs across levels of another, so that a one-way analysis attributes effects of other variables to the variable being analyzed.

places.quote: If young drivers also drive older cars, a one-way age relativity contains part of the vehicle-age effect, and rating both double-counts.
If urban policyholders also skew toward younger drivers or higher limits, part of the $2.00$ belongs to those variables rather than to geography.

requirements.statement: A GLM estimates all rating variables simultaneously, holding the others constant, so each variable's relativity reflects only its own effect, and it can also model interactions between variables, which one-way analysis cannot.

places.quote: it estimates every rating variable *simultaneously* and so reports each one net of the others
Both classes can include [[Interaction|interactions]], transformations such as polynomial terms, and banded variables

requirements.statement: Using less accurate one-way relativities overcharges some segments and undercharges others, causing adverse selection: the insurer loses overpriced business to competitors with more accurate pricing and attracts underpriced business, worsening loss ratios and profitability.

places.quote: **Adverse Selection** is the tendency for those who know they are worse-than-average risks to buy more insurance, and better-than-average risks to buy less, when the insurer cannot distinguish between them.
The univariate structure over-charges that cell by $51\%$ — and, because the relativities are balanced back to the overall level, correspondingly under-charges adult drivers in new vehicles.

requirements.statement: Harwayne's Method builds a complement of credibility from another group's (e.g., other states') experience by adjusting for differences in exposure mix between the subject state and the comparison group, using a class-level pure premium re-weighting and an adjustment factor.

places.quote: **Harwayne's method** — other states' data adjusted to remove the overall differences between states before it is used, so that a state with a higher cost level does not import that level into the class complement.

requirements.statement: When the complement is built from all other states, remove the subject state's exposures and losses from the countrywide totals for each class before computing the other states' class pure premiums.

resolution.note: the question says the complement is all other states; removing State A from the countrywide totals is subtraction on the given data

requirements.statement: Pure premium for a class equals losses divided by exposures.

places.quote: $$\text{Pure Premium} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Exposures}}$$
$$\text{Pure Premium} = \frac{\text{Losses} + \text{LAE}}{\text{Earned Exposures}} = \text{Frequency} \times \text{Severity}$$

requirements.statement: In Harwayne's Method, compute the other states' overall average pure premium using the subject state's exposure distribution as weights across all classes (weighted average of class pure premiums), and compute the subject state's overall pure premium on its own exposures.

places.quote: **Step 2 — Y's and Z's average pure premiums on State X's class mix** (X's exposures, each state's own class pure premiums):

requirements.statement: Harwayne's adjustment factor equals the subject state's overall pure premium divided by the other states' overall pure premium re-weighted to the subject state's exposure distribution.
The Harwayne complement for a class equals the adjustment factor times the other states' pure premium for that class.

Advantages of using the current rate as the complement of credibility over Harwayne's method are that it is simpler and quicker to compute with fewer opportunities for error, and that it has a clear, direct relationship to the subject experience so it is easy to explain to management and regulators.

places.quote: **easy to compute** — easy to perform and understand, which matters most when the actuary must justify it to a third party such as a regulator

requirements.statement: The increased limit factor (ILF) for a limit is the ratio of the limited average severity at that limit to the limited average severity at the basic limit.

places.quote: $$\text{ILF}(L) = \frac{E[X \wedge L]}{E[X \wedge B]}$$

requirements.statement: Limited average severity at a limit equals the sum of the limited average severities of successive layers from zero up to that limit (e.g., LAS(0 to a) plus LAS of the layer between a and the limit).

places.quote: Layers stack: the layers of a tower add up to the ground-up loss.

resolution.quote: The limited average severity at a higher limit is the limited average severity at the lower limit plus that weighted layer severity, and each further layer is added the same way.
resolution.note: LAS stacked layer by layer, plus link to Layer of Insurance; W&M Ch.11 pp.195-197 (PDF 207-209)

requirements.statement: Policy limits censor the loss data: a policy cannot show losses above its limit, so for each layer only policies with limits at or above the top of that layer are used, and policies with lower limits are excluded.
requirements.concept: Censored Data in Increased Limit Factors

places.quote: building the limited average severity layer by layer so that losses censored at policy limits introduce no bias

**Censoring:** A limit right-censors the loss. The variable $X \wedge u$ has a point mass of $S(u)$ at $u$, and a claim recorded at the limit says only that the loss was at least $u$, which is why such a claim enters a likelihood as $S(u)$ (see [[Censoring]]).

requirements.statement: Compute a layer's average severity by pooling all eligible policies' claims, taking each claim's contribution as min(loss, layer top) minus layer bottom (floored at zero), and dividing the total by the number of claims from all eligible policies.

places.quote: Cap each claim at $750$ and at $250$, then difference the totals:

resolution.quote: A layer's losses are what each claim puts into it: the claim capped at the top of the layer minus the bottom of the layer, or zero for a claim below the bottom, so a claim above the top contributes the full width of the layer.…That is the same as dividing the layer's losses by the total claim count of those policies.
resolution.note: A layer's losses per claim and division by all eligible policies' claims; W&M Ch.11 pp.196-197 (PDF 208-209)

requirements.statement: Using the stated assumption about payment amounts (e.g., claims are paid at either a fixed fraction of the limit or the full limit), split each policy limit's claim count by the percentage at the limit to get the number of claims at each claim size.

resolution.note: the question's own stated assumption (payments are 50% or 100% of the limit) applied to its own table

requirements.statement: A coinsurance clause requires the insured to carry insurance of at least a specified coinsurance percentage times the property's value, and penalizes the loss payment if the insured carries less.

places.quote: the insured agrees to carry limits of at least, say, $80\%$ of the property's value. Fall short and every partial loss is settled at the ratio of insurance carried to insurance required.
In the property insurance context, a **coinsurance clause** can instead refer to a penalty applied when the insured carries less coverage than a required percentage of replacement value

requirements.statement: The coinsurance apportionment factor is the lesser of 1 and (insurance carried) divided by (coinsurance percentage times property value).

places.quote: $$\text{Recovery}_{\text{clause}} = \min\!\left(\frac{\text{Insurance Carried}}{\text{Coinsurance \% } \times \text{Value}},\, 1\right) \times \text{Loss}$$
$$a = \min\!\left(\frac{F}{cV},\ 1.0\right)$$
$$R = \min\left(\frac{C}{p \times V},\ 1\right)$$

requirements.statement: The insurer's payment equals the lesser of the apportionment factor times the loss and the insured amount (policy limit); the policyholder bears the loss minus this payment.

places.quote: $$\text{Property payment} = \min\left(\min\left(\frac{C}{p \times V},\ 1\right) \times L - D,\ C\right)$$
$$I = L \times \frac{F}{cV}, \quad \text{where } I \le F \text{ and } I \le L$$
$$\text{Payment} = \min\big(R \times L - D,\ C\big)$$

requirements.statement: Coinsurance is a penalty on underinsurance applied to the loss payment, distinct from a copayment in which the insured shares a fixed percentage of every loss.

places.quote: **Coinsurance Rating** prices the two distinct provisions that go by the name *coinsurance*: the **percentage participation** under which the insured shares each covered loss, and the property **coinsurance clause**, which penalizes an insured who carries limits below a required percentage of value.

The insured must carry insurance of at least $cV$, e.g. $80\%$ of the property's value $V$, or the payment on a covered loss is reduced in proportion to the underinsurance. It is not the insurer's share of each loss
In health insurance, coinsurance is the insured's share of every loss. In property insurance, it is a condition on the limit carried, and an insured who meets it pays no share beyond the deductible.

requirements.statement: Coinsurance promotes equitable rates because property rates assume insurance to value, and reducing loss payments at the time of loss only for underinsured risks prevents them from being subsidized by fully insured risks, so loss cost per dollar of insurance is equal across insureds.

places.quote: Because most property losses are partial, an insured carrying $50\%$ of value would otherwise pay half the premium for nearly the same expected recovery, and the rate per $\$1{,}000$ would have to rise for everyone.
Without the clause, the rate would have to reflect the book's actual mix of insurance to value, and insureds who carry full value would subsidise the rest.

requirements.statement: Coinsurance promotes adequate rates by reducing losses paid on underinsured risks and by encouraging (not requiring or guaranteeing) insureds to insure to value, so premium base matches exposure and the overall rate level is adequate.

places.quote: Because most property losses are partial, an insured carrying $50\%$ of value would otherwise pay half the premium for nearly the same expected recovery, and the rate per $\$1{,}000$ would have to rise for everyone.

A book insured below value therefore collects too little premium at the filed rate. The coinsurance clause lets the insurer charge one rate per \$100 by making under-insurance cost the insured on every partial loss.

requirements.statement: Schedule rating is a subjective debit or credit applied by the underwriter to reflect risk characteristics not otherwise captured in the manual rate or experience rating.

places.quote: **Schedule Rating** applies underwriter-assigned debits and credits to the manual premium for characteristics of the individual risk that the classification system does not capture — the physical condition of premises, management quality, safety programmes, employee selection and training, loss-control practices.

requirements.statement: Experience rating looks backward at the insured's historical losses, so a recent change such as a new loss-control program has no emerged experience and cannot be reflected by it; schedule rating is used as a stop-gap until the experience emerges.

places.quote: If a risk has made a recent change that will likely impact its loss experience, then it is appropriate to use a schedule credit or debit, because the change is not yet reflected in the experience period.

requirements.statement: Once a change's effect has emerged in the insured's loss experience and is reflected in the experience modification, the schedule credit granted for it should be removed to avoid double-counting the same benefit.

places.quote: A risk that has always had the characteristic — a full-time safety manager throughout the experience period — gets no schedule credit for it, because its effect is already reflected in the loss experience, and crediting it again would double-count it: first by the schedule credit and second by the experience mod.

requirements.statement: Manual premium equals the manual rate times the exposure base, so a change in exposure (e.g., workers compensation payroll) flows directly into premium without a special adjustment.

places.quote: $$\text{Manual Premium} = \text{Exposure} \times \text{Base Rate} \times \prod_k f_k$$

resolution.quote: base rates are expressed per exposure
resolution.note: syllabus page (also gives Premium = Rate x Exposures): premium moves with the exposure base, e.g. payroll

requirements.statement: Workers compensation is rated using payroll as the exposure base, so a larger workforce increases exposure and premium roughly proportionally.

places.quote: Payroll is the workers compensation base because it is responsive to changes in exposure: as the number of workers or the hours they work rise or fall, both payroll and the risk of loss move with them. Headcount would miss the hours.
**Payroll and its audit:** Remuneration is the usual [[Exposure Base|premium base]].

requirements.statement: A premium discount reduces the premium for larger policies because fixed expenses are a smaller percentage of premium as policy size grows.

places.quote: premium discount (for size)

requirements.statement: Retrospective rating determines the final premium after the policy period from the insured's own losses during that period, subject to a minimum and maximum premium, giving the insured an incentive to control losses.

places.quote: **Retrospective Rating** adjusts a policy's premium *after* the period, based on the insured's own losses during that period, within a guaranteed minimum and maximum.
Retro plans suit **large accounts** with credible volume, and they align incentives directly: every dollar of loss inside the band costs the insured $\text{LCF} \times \text{TM}$ dollars of premium.

requirements.statement: A large deductible policy has the insured retain losses below a substantial deductible, lowering premium while the insurer covers losses above the deductible.

places.quote: *Large deductible:* the insurer pays every claim and bills the deductible back. It must have a per-occurrence limit, may have an aggregate, and has no minimum. Reimbursements are not premium, so they escape premium tax.

resolution.quote: a deductible set high enough that the insured bears significant risk
resolution.note: linked page defines a large deductible program (Werner's WC and CGL examples)

requirements.statement: Case outstanding is the unpaid amount held on claims that have been reported to and recorded by the insurer, as set by claims adjusters.

places.quote: **Case reserves** (also called case outstanding) are claim-specific estimates of the expected future payments on individual reported claims, established by claims adjusters based on the known facts of each loss.

requirements.statement: IBNER (incurred but not enough reported) is the expected future development on reported claims, i.e. the amount by which case reserves on known claims prove inadequate or redundant as the claims mature.

places.quote: **IBNER** — incurred but not enough reported — is expected development on claims already in the case reserves. It is a function of **case reserving practice** and can be negative where reserves are set conservatively.

requirements.statement: IBNYR (pure IBNR, incurred but not yet reported) is the estimate for claims that have occurred but have not yet been reported to the insurer.

places.quote: **Pure IBNR** (narrow IBNR) covers claims that have occurred but are unknown to the insurer.
**Pure IBNR**: claims that occurred in $2022$ and are still unknown to the insurer at $24$ months.
