requirements.statement: Unpaid claims estimate = case outstanding + IBNER + IBNYR; reopened claims and claims in transit (reported but not yet recorded) are additional possible components.

places.quote: $$\text{Unpaid} = \text{Case Reserves} + \text{IBNR}$$
$$\text{IBNR} = \underbrace{\text{Pure IBNR}}_{\text{unreported claims}} + \underbrace{\text{IBNER}}_{\text{development on known claims}}$$

Friedland's broad definition of IBNR, the one she uses throughout, has four components: future development on known claims, reopened claims, pure IBNR, and claims in transit (reported but not recorded).

requirements.statement: An inadequate (understated) unpaid claims estimate makes recent results look more profitable than they are, so internal management may set rates too low, loosen underwriting, expand into unprofitable segments, or commit capital it lacks through dividends or projects based on overstated surplus.
requirements.concept: Users and Uses of Unpaid Claim Estimates

places.quote: Under-reserving can put **solvency** at risk: it presents the insurer as stronger than it is, and an inadequate estimate can lead it to cut rates on business already underpriced — worse still if the lower rates win market share (Friedland Ch. 1).

Redundancy is a profit deferral; deficiency understates the loss ratio, overstates surplus, and feeds an inadequate rate indication back into pricing, so the same error appears again in next year's business.

requirements.statement: An understated unpaid claims liability overstates earnings and surplus, so investors overvalue the company and invest capital they otherwise would not, and suffer losses in earnings and share value when reserves are later strengthened.
requirements.concept: Users and Uses of Unpaid Claim Estimates

places.quote: **Investors and rating agencies** — reserve development history, volatility, and the earnings effect. Adverse development is a disclosure item; a pattern of it affects the rating and the cost of capital.

requirements.statement: Regulators rely on reported liabilities to monitor solvency, so an inadequate estimate makes capital appear adequate and delays regulatory intervention in a company heading toward insolvency; it can also lead them to deny needed rate increases because filed indications rest on understated losses.
requirements.concept: Users and Uses of Unpaid Claim Estimates

places.quote: It is how regulators monitor reserve adequacy across the industry and identify deteriorating companies.

**Its limits.** Every tool reads statutory statements, so an insurer that understates reserves looks healthy until development reveals it — which is why reserve-development ratios, the actuarial opinion and exam actuaries carry so much weight.

requirements.statement: Internal company changes (within management's control), such as changes in case reserve adequacy, claim settlement rate, business mix or underwriting rules, claim reporting, reinsurance, subrogation, litigation stance, or fraud units, can distort paid and reported development patterns, whereas external events like tort reform, inflation or catastrophes are not internal changes.

places.quote: **Changing Conditions** are changes in an insurer's internal operations or in its external environment during the experience period that make historical claims data a biased guide to future development.
**Claims Processing Changes** are changes in how claims are handled … that alter the **timing** of payments and case reserve changes, and therefore the shape of the development pattern.

requirements.statement: Average case outstanding per open claim is a diagnostic triangle computed as case outstanding divided by open claim counts at each accident year and maturity.

places.quote: $$\text{Avg Case Outstanding} = \frac{\text{Case Reserves}}{\text{Open Claim Counts}}$$
**Open counts** — the inventory. Divided into case reserves it gives **average case outstanding**, the sharpest [[Case Adequacy|case adequacy]] diagnostic.
$$\text{Avg Case O/S} = \frac{\text{Case Reserves}}{\text{Open Claims}}$$

requirements.statement: Strengthened case reserve adequacy appears as average case outstanding per open claim increasing down the column (same maturity, more recent accident years) and as the paid-to-reported claims ratio decreasing down the column.

places.quote: a rising ratio is consistent with faster settlement or weaker case reserves, a falling one with slower settlement or stronger case reserves
**The diagnostic is average case outstanding per open claim**, compared *down each column* of the triangle. It should grow at roughly the severity trend.
**[[Case Adequacy|Case strengthening]]:** average case outstanding rises faster than trend on the latest diagonals, and paid-to-reported falls.

requirements.statement: The disposal rate is closed claim counts divided by ultimate (or reported) claim counts, shown in a triangle by accident year and maturity.

places.quote: $$\text{Disposal Rate}_n = \frac{\text{Closed claims at age } n}{\text{Ultimate claim counts}}$$
The [[Settlement Rate|disposal rate]] is closed counts over ultimate (or reported) counts.

requirements.statement: A speed-up in claim settlement appears as the disposal rate and the paid-to-reported claims ratio increasing down the column, since recent accident years have more claims closed or paid at the same maturity.

places.quote: a rising ratio is consistent with faster settlement or weaker case reserves, a falling one with slower settlement or stronger case reserves
**Faster settlement** pushes losses from open to paid, so the recent paid diagonal is high relative to history.
**Faster [[Settlement Rate|settlement]]:** closure rates and paid-to-reported rise together.

requirements.statement: Average severity triangles are reported (or paid) claims divided by reported (or closed) claim counts at each accident year and maturity.

places.quote: develop an average severity triangle (dollars ÷ counts at each age) to ultimate severity
$$\text{Average Severity} = \frac{\text{Losses}}{\text{Claim Counts}}$$
Reported losses over reported counts, paid over closed, ultimate over ultimate

requirements.statement: A shift in business mix toward larger risks or higher policy limits appears as average severity increasing down the column at each maturity, and splitting triangles by segment shows whether one part of the book is driving the shift rather than a true change in development.

places.quote: The only fix is structural: **split the triangle** by coverage ([[Reserving Data Organization]]).
**Mix and dilution** — late-reported small claims pulling averages down, or a shift in the [[Mix of Business|mix]] of coverages and limits.

requirements.statement: The case outstanding development technique projects future payments from the latest case outstanding using two sets of factors: the ratio of case outstanding at one maturity to case outstanding at the prior maturity, and the ratio of incremental paid in a period to case outstanding at the start (prior maturity) of that period.

places.quote: Friedland's fuller version works period by period, using two ratios estimated from history: **paid in the next period ÷ case outstanding at the start**, and **case outstanding at the end ÷ case outstanding at the start**. Rolling these forward generates a payment stream and runs the case balance down to zero.

requirements.statement: Incremental paid claims are obtained by differencing the cumulative paid triangle, and the case outstanding method uses incremental (not cumulative) paid claims in its paid-to-prior-case-outstanding ratios.

places.quote: Friedland's fuller version works period by period, using two ratios estimated from history: **paid in the next period ÷ case outstanding at the start**, and **case outstanding at the end ÷ case outstanding at the start**.

requirements.statement: The incremental paid to prior case outstanding factor for a period equals the incremental paid during the period divided by the case outstanding at the start of the period (previous maturity), not the current one.

places.quote: Friedland's fuller version works period by period, using two ratios estimated from history: **paid in the next period ÷ case outstanding at the start**, and **case outstanding at the end ÷ case outstanding at the start**. Rolling these forward generates a payment stream and runs the case balance down to zero.

requirements.statement: Factors are selected by averaging the observed age-to-age ratios across accident years (e.g., a weighted or simple average), and a tail factor from the 48-to-ultimate maturity is applied to the final case outstanding to reach ultimate payments.

places.quote: **Volume-weighted (all-year)** — the ratio of column sums. Weights each year by its size, so it is stable and dominated by the large years. The default choice.
**Tail Factor** is the development factor applied beyond the last maturity observable in the triangle — the estimate of all emergence that will occur after the data runs out.

requirements.statement: Unpaid claims under the case outstanding method equal the sum of projected future incremental payments only; amounts already paid are excluded, and the result is not ultimate claims.

places.quote: $$\text{Unpaid} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Paid to date}$$
**An unpaid claim distribution** is the probability distribution of the total amount $R$ that will be paid after the valuation date on claims that have already occurred.

requirements.statement: In the alternative case outstanding method, the case outstanding development factor equals (CDF_reported − 1) × CDF_paid / (CDF_paid − CDF_reported) + 1, and unpaid claims equal case outstanding times this factor.

The case outstanding development technique is appropriate when there is little or no pure IBNR, such as for short-tailed lines, claims-made coverage, or a self-insured entity with only case reserve data, because it projects only from already reported claims.

places.quote: **A claims-made book has no pure IBNR** by construction — every claim in a [[Report Year|report year]] is already reported — so its IBNR is entirely IBNER.

**Short Tail Insurance** covers lines whose claims are reported and settled quickly — typically within a year — so that reported losses are close to ultimate almost immediately and [[IBNR]] is small relative to case reserves.

Because the trigger is the report date, a claims-made policy has **no pure IBNR** — only IBNER on claims already reported — so the risk of reserve inadequacy is greatly reduced relative to the [[Occurrence Coverage|occurrence]] form.

requirements.statement: The Cape Cod method computes a single expected claims ratio for all years combined as total trended reported claims divided by total used-up (on-level, trended) premium, rather than averaging yearly ratios.

places.quote: The ELR is estimated as total reported losses over total *used-up* (on-level, developed) premium across all years.

requirements.statement: Used-up premium is on-level, trended earned premium multiplied by the percentage of claims reported (1/CDF), serving as the exposure base in Cape Cod.

places.quote: **Used-up premium** $\text{EP}_i / \text{CDF}_i$ is the share of each year's premium "exposed" to the losses reported so far.
$P_i / \text{CDF}_i$ is the **used-up premium**, the share of the premium that the claims reported so far correspond to.

requirements.statement: Cape Cod ultimate claims = reported claims + ECR × premium (at the matching level) × (1 − 1/CDF), i.e., reported plus expected unreported claims.

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR}_i = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}_i \times \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}_i}\right)$$
$$U = \text{Reported} + \text{IBNR}$$

requirements.statement: Use the parallelogram method to compute on-level factors: for annual policies written evenly, a mid-year rate change affects a fraction of each calendar year's earned premium (area of the triangle, e.g. 1/2·(0.5)^2 = 12.5%), giving average rate level per year; the on-level factor is current rate level divided by the average rate level.

places.quote: $$\text{On-Level Factor} = \frac{\text{Current cumulative rate level index}}{\text{Average rate level index for the period}}$$
The second formula is the area earned in the same calendar year at a new level effective a fraction $p$ of the way through it, for annual policies.

For **annual** policies written uniformly, a rate change effective at time $p$ through year $Y$ earns over a triangle of area $\tfrac{1}{2}(1-p)^2$ in year $Y$ — so a $7/1$ change affects only $0.125$ of that year's earned premium, and a $1/1$ change affects $0.500$.

requirements.statement: Trend claims and premium to a common cost level by applying annual trend over the number of years between each accident year and the target year (trend forward for earlier years, de-trend for later years); the expected claims ratio must then be adjusted (de-trended and de-leveled) to the level of the accident year being estimated.

places.quote: Premium **must be on level** and losses must be trended to a common cost level before the ELR is computed, or the derived ratio blends years written at different rate levels and different cost levels into one number.
$t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.
Claims of a year earlier than $j$ are trended up to year $j$'s level, and claims of a later year are trended down.

requirements.statement: In the Cape Cod method, claims used in the ECR are reported (not developed to ultimate) claims, and the result is independent of the chosen common level as long as the ECR and premium are at the same level.

places.quote: The ELR is estimated as total reported losses over total *used-up* (on-level, developed) premium across all years.
$C_i$ is the reported (or paid) claims of accident year $i$ to date

requirements.statement: Written premium for an aggregation period (calendar, fiscal, or policy year) is the full premium of policies whose effective date falls within that period, plus mid-term premium adjustments recorded in the period.

places.quote: $$\text{Written Premium} = \sum_{\text{policies issued in period}} \text{full-term premium}$$
Additional premium for an endorsement is recorded on the endorsement's effective date and earned in the same way.

requirements.statement: In-force premium at a valuation date is the full written premium of policies that have incepted and not yet expired or been cancelled as of that date.

places.quote: In-force premium is the **full-term** premium of each policy in effect at the date — the policy's own term, not an annualized one

requirements.statement: A mid-term cancellation produces a return premium equal to the unexpired fraction of the term times the premium, recorded as negative written premium in the period in which the cancellation occurs, regardless of when the policy was written.

places.quote: Cancellation returns the unearned portion. **Pro rata** cancellation returns the full unearned premium; **short-rate** cancellation, used when the insured cancels, returns less than pro rata to recover acquisition costs that were incurred up front.
Written premium may still change after issuance — endorsements, cancellations and [[Premium Audit|audits]] all book additional or return premium into a later period

requirements.statement: Written premium equals earned premium plus the change in unearned premium (WP = EP + ΔUEP).
requirements.concept: Written, Earned, and Unearned Premium Relationship

places.quote: $$\text{Earned Premium} = \text{Written Premium} - \Delta\text{UEP}$$
$$\text{Earned Premium} = \text{Written Premium} - \Delta\text{UEP}$$
The change in the UEP is the entire bridge between written and [[Earned Premium|earned]] premium.

requirements.statement: Averaging beginning and ending in-force premium approximates calendar year earned premium only if policies have the same term (e.g., all annual) and are written uniformly throughout the year; shorter-term policies can incept and expire between valuations and be missed, and irregular writing or a small, changing book makes the estimate unreliable.

In-force premium has practical uses besides estimating earned premium, such as measuring the premium impact of a proposed rate change, determining reinsurance needs, tracking growth or contraction of the book, and assessing current potential for loss.

places.quote: the latest in-force premium is used to measure the impact of a rate change on the existing portfolio

**[[In-Force]]** premium is the full-term premium of every policy in effect on a date — the best estimate of the current mix of business, and often used to measure the impact of a rate change on existing customers.

requirements.statement: The disposal rate is the cumulative closed claim count at a given age divided by the ultimate claim count for the accident year.

places.quote: $$\text{Disposal Rate}_n = \frac{\text{Closed claims at age } n}{\text{Ultimate claim counts}}$$
The [[Settlement Rate|disposal rate]] is closed counts over ultimate (or reported) counts.

requirements.statement: To project future closed counts for an immature accident year, take the remaining open claims (ultimate minus closed to date) and allocate them across future ages in proportion to the incremental selected disposal rates divided by one minus the current disposal rate.

Incremental severity is computed as incremental paid claims divided by incremental closed claim counts for each accident year and age, and a severity is selected for each future age (e.g., by averaging the column).

places.quote: develop an average severity triangle (dollars ÷ counts at each age) to ultimate severity

requirements.statement: Unpaid claims equal the sum over future ages of projected incremental closed counts multiplied by selected incremental severity.

places.quote: Project the number of claims closing in each future period from historical **disposal rates**, value them at a trended severity for that maturity, and sum the future payments.

requirements.statement: With no severity trend, historical severities need no trend adjustment and the selected severities can be used as observed.

resolution.note: the question states there is no severity trend

requirements.statement: A law or court change that increases future payments is reflected by multiplying the projected future severities (all unpaid amounts for periods after the effective date) by the increase factor.

places.quote: and are handled by a law-level adjustment factor applied to historical losses before trend

requirements.statement: The frequency-severity technique separates claim counts from severity, so assumptions such as a sudden severity change from a legal change or changes in settlement speed can be explicitly and independently reflected, whereas paid development link ratios rely on historical patterns and cannot isolate such changes.

places.quote: A dollar triangle tells you losses grew; frequency and severity tell you *why*, and the two causes call for different responses and carry different persistence.
A change in it distorts **paid** development in the same way a change in [[Case Adequacy|case adequacy]] distorts reported development.

requirements.statement: The reported Berquist-Sherman technique adjusts a reported claims triangle for a change in case reserve adequacy, which shows up as a shift in average case outstanding along the latest diagonal.

places.quote: a jump in average case outstanding across all years points to adequacy; a jump in closure rates points to settlement speed.
appearing at every maturity at once, is a change in reserving practice, not in claim cost.

requirements.statement: Case outstanding is derived as reported claims minus paid claims, and open claim counts as reported counts minus closed counts, each cell by cell.

places.quote: $$\text{Reported Losses} = \text{Paid Losses} + \text{Case Reserves}$$

requirements.statement: Average case outstanding is case outstanding divided by the number of open claims at each age and accident year.

places.quote: $$\text{Avg Case Outstanding} = \frac{\text{Case Reserves}}{\text{Open Claim Counts}}$$
$$\text{Avg Case O/S} = \frac{\text{Case Reserves}}{\text{Open Claims}}$$

requirements.statement: To de-trend average case outstanding, keep the latest diagonal value in each column as current adequacy and divide it by one plus the severity trend rate, raised to the number of years between that accident year and the latest diagonal year, to get the value for each earlier accident year.

places.quote: $$\text{Adjusted Case}_{\text{AY},n} = \text{Case}_{\text{latest},n} \times \left(1 + t\right)^{-(\text{years before latest})}$$
restate historical average case outstanding to the current adequacy level using a selected severity trend, rebuild the reported triangle, and select factors from the restated history.

requirements.statement: The adjusted reported claims triangle is the de-trended average case outstanding multiplied by open claim counts, plus unadjusted paid claims; the latest diagonal is unchanged by the adjustment.

places.quote: Multiply the restated averages by the open claim counts to get adjusted case reserves, add paid, and rebuild the reported triangle.

requirements.statement: Develop the adjusted reported triangle with the chain ladder: compute age-to-age factors, select them by an average (straight or volume-weighted), and multiply them into a cumulative development factor to age-to-ultimate.

places.quote: $$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$
compute [[Age to Age Factor|age-to-age factors]] → select a factor for each interval → chain them into CDFs with a [[Tail Factor|tail]] → apply to the latest diagonal.
equal weight to each year, so a small, volatile year counts as much as a large one.

requirements.statement: Unpaid claims for an accident year equal the ultimate claims (latest adjusted reported claims times the CDF) minus the paid claims to date, with paid claims left unadjusted.

places.quote: $$\text{Unpaid} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Paid to date}$$
$$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: In the ratio approach to salvage and subrogation, form a triangle of cumulative received S&S divided by cumulative paid claims gross of S&S at each age, develop these ratios with age-to-age factors to an ultimate ratio, and apply the selected ultimate ratio to ultimate gross paid claims.

places.quote: **Salvage and subrogation** (Friedland Ch. 14) are projected either by the development technique on reported or received S&S, or by the **ratio approach**: develop the ratio of received S&S to paid claims to an ultimate ratio, and multiply by selected ultimate claims gross of S&S.

requirements.statement: Ultimate gross paid claims for an accident year equal its latest cumulative paid claims times the age-to-ultimate development factor for paid claims.

places.quote: $$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: When there is no development beyond the last triangle age, the tail factor is 1.000, so an accident year at that age is fully developed and its observed ratio equals its ultimate ratio.

places.quote: A tail of exactly $1.000$ is itself an assumption — that development is complete — and it is the wrong one for any casualty line.

requirements.statement: Select the ultimate S&S ratio using judgment: if an immature year's projected ratio is out of line with consistent mature years, treat it as random fluctuation or a timing lag because the large development factor leverages it, and select a ratio consistent with the mature years (or justify a real shift).

places.quote: Before accepting it, ask whether recording or recovery practice changed or one large claim is distorting the ratio. Absent a reason, a selection near the historical level is typical
Because the [[Cumulative Development Factor|CDF]] at early maturities is large, estimates are highly **leveraged**: a small proportional change in a factor moves ultimate by a large dollar amount.

requirements.statement: The S&S recoverable (still to be collected) equals the estimated ultimate S&S minus S&S already received to date.

places.quote: \begin{aligned} \text{Recoverable} &= \text{Ultimate Recoveries} \\ &\quad - \text{Recoveries Received} \end{aligned}

requirements.statement: Advantages of the ratio approach over developing S&S dollars: ratios to paid claims act as a diagnostic benchmark that exposes unreasonable values and support judgment, and ratio development factors are less leveraged and less volatile than dollar factors, reflecting that recoveries arise from paid claims.

places.quote: The ratio's development factors are less leveraged than those of S&S dollars, and the ultimate ratio is easier to select for immature years.

requirements.statement: The reported development (chain-ladder) method estimates ultimate claims as reported claims times a cumulative development factor built from historical age-to-age factors.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{AY}} = C_{\text{AY},\,n} \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$
$$\text{Ultimate Losses} = \text{Losses at age } n \times \text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}}$$

requirements.statement: The development method relies entirely on historical development patterns and does not adjust for a change such as a law change, so factors from pre-change years understate ultimate claims when severity rises, and the change is recognized only as it emerges in reported claims.

places.quote: Every development-based estimate of [[Unpaid Claims|unpaid claims]] assumes the past pattern will repeat; a changing condition is whatever breaks that assumption.
**The pattern is stable over calendar time.** Violated by a change in [[Case Adequacy|case adequacy]], [[Settlement Rate|settlement speed]] or [[Inflation|inflation]] — the diagonal effects.

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson method estimates ultimate claims as actual reported claims plus the a priori expected claims times the percentage unreported (1 minus 1/CDF).

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$

requirements.statement: The BF a priori expected claims ratio is selected with judgment, so an anticipated change like higher severity can be built into it immediately, and as the year matures weight shifts from the a priori to actual reported claims; BF thus acts as a credibility weighting between the development and expected claims estimates.

places.quote: BF is a **credibility weighting** in disguise: it equals $Z \, U_{\text{CL}} + (1-Z)\,U_0$ with $Z = 1/\text{CDF}$. The more of the year that has emerged, the more the answer relies on the data — automatically, without a separate credibility judgment.
That makes Cape Cod the right choice when **no credible external ELR exists** — a book whose pricing history is unreliable — and it removes BF's dependence on a judgmentally selected loss ratio.

requirements.statement: The Cape Cod method derives the expected claims ratio from the experience of the data itself (reported claims relative to used-up exposure/premium across years) rather than from judgment, then applies it like BF.

places.quote: The ELR is estimated as total reported losses over total *used-up* (on-level, developed) premium across all years.

requirements.statement: Because the Cape Cod expected claims ratio is based on mostly historical experience, a sudden severity increase is understated in both the reported claims and the expected claims ratio, making Cape Cod slow to respond and its estimates move substantially as post-change experience emerges.

places.quote: The cost is that the estimate is no longer independent of the data: a systematically distorted triangle now corrupts the a priori as well as the development.

requirements.statement: The frequency/severity technique projects claim counts and average severity separately, so an actuary can directly adjust the severity assumption for a known change (e.g., tort reform) without waiting for the data to emerge, making it highly responsive.

places.quote: **Counts and trended severity.** Develop counts, but estimate severity by **trending** a mature year's severity forward rather than developing an immature one — useful where severity development is unstable but severity trend is well understood.

requirements.statement: The Kittel refinement ULAE ratio equals calendar-year paid ULAE divided by the average of calendar-year paid claims and incurred claims (0.5 × paid + 0.5 × incurred), which corrects the classical paid-to-paid method for a growing or changing book.

places.quote: $$R_{\text{Kittel}} = \frac{\text{Paid ULAE}}{0.5(\text{Paid Loss}) + 0.5(\text{Incurred Loss})}$$

requirements.statement: Select the ULAE ratio from the yearly ratios: if they show no trend, treat variation as random and use the simple average; if there is a trend, a selection reflecting it is warranted.

places.quote: Selecting the three-year average of $6.6\%$ would understate the cost of running off the remaining claims. Selecting the latest $8.9\%$ is closer, but even that is a lagging figure if payments keep falling faster than expenses.

requirements.statement: Reported Bornhuetter-Ferguson ultimate claims equal reported claims plus earned premium × expected claims ratio × percent unreported.

places.quote: $C$ is reported (or paid) losses to date, $U_0 = \text{ELR} \times \text{EP}$ the a priori expectation, and $1 - 1/\text{CDF}$ the percentage unreported from the [[Development Triangle|development pattern]].

requirements.statement: Case reserves equal reported claims minus paid claims, and total IBNR equals ultimate claims minus reported claims; IBNR consists of pure IBNR (IBNYR, claims not yet reported) plus IBNER (development on reported claims).

places.quote: $$\text{IBNR} = \text{Ultimate} - \text{Reported}$$
$$\text{Reported Losses} = \text{Paid Losses} + \text{Case Reserves}$$

requirements.statement: Under claims-made policies coverage is triggered by the report date, so there are no unreported covered claims for report years already closed to reporting; pure IBNR is zero and all IBNR is IBNER. Under occurrence policies, coverage is triggered by the date of loss, so IBNR includes both pure IBNR and IBNER and the two must be split.

places.quote: Because the trigger is the report date, a claims-made policy has **no pure IBNR** — only IBNER on claims already reported — so the risk of reserve inadequacy is greatly reduced relative to the [[Occurrence Coverage|occurrence]] form.
It must reserve for **pure [[IBNR]]** — claims it has no knowledge of — for as long as claims from expired policies can still emerge, which for a product like medical malpractice can be many years.

requirements.statement: Under the Kittel refinement, unpaid ULAE equals the ULAE ratio × [pure IBNR + 0.5 × (case reserves + IBNER)], since unreported claims have had none of their ULAE incurred while reported claims have already incurred the opening half.

places.quote: If ULAE is assumed to be spent half at reporting and half at settlement, only $50\%$ remains on reported-but-unpaid claims while $100\%$ remains on [[IBNR]] — the formula above.

requirements.statement: Expected paid claims between two evaluation ages equals current paid claims times (CDF at earlier age / CDF at later age − 1), because ultimate = paid × CDF and expected paid at the later age = ultimate / later-age CDF.

places.quote: $$\text{Expected emergence} = U_{\text{prior}} \times \left(\frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n+1}} - \frac{1}{\text{CDF}_{n}}\right)$$
$$\text{Expected emergence} = \text{IBNR} \times \frac{p_{t+\Delta} - p_t}{1 - p_t}$$
The reciprocal is the **percentage reported** (or paid): $p_n = 1/\text{CDF}_n$, and $1 - p_n$ is the percentage unreported.

requirements.statement: Under a quota share reinsurance agreement the reinsurer takes a fixed proportion of premium and losses, so net claims equal gross claims times (1 − ceded percentage).

places.quote: Because every policy is shared alike, a quota share reduces the cedant's net premium and net losses in proportion without changing the shape of its results.
Net loss is $(1-a)X$, so its coefficient of variation equals gross.

resolution.quote: Under quota share, ceded is a fixed share
resolution.note: linked page: quota share cedes a fixed share of gross, so net = gross x (1 - ceded share)

requirements.statement: Under a uniform emergence assumption, the expected payments in an interval are spread equally across its sub-periods, so each quarter of a four-quarter interval receives 25%.

resolution.note: the question states claims emerge uniformly between evaluation points; 25% per quarter is arithmetic

requirements.statement: Using an industry incremental payment pattern, allocate the interval's expected payments to a sub-period by multiplying by that sub-period's percent paid.

places.quote: The **expected** figure comes from the prior ultimate and the emergence pattern: the share of ultimate the pattern says should report (or be paid) between the two valuations.

requirements.statement: To decide whether to revise the unpaid estimate, compare actual emergence to expected emergence under the more realistic benchmark and revise only if the difference is significant or traceable to an identifiable change (e.g., large loss or recovery).

places.quote: One period's deviation is noise; a run of them is a signal.

requirements.statement: Paid development estimates at immature ages with large development factors are highly leveraged, so small timing differences cause large swings in projected ultimate and reacting to them makes estimates unstable.

places.quote: A CDF of $2.27$ means more than half the ultimate estimate is unreported. A $5\%$ error in the $12\text{–}24$ factor moves ultimate by roughly $\$480{,}000$
The CDF measures **leverage**. At a CDF of $4$, a dollar of distortion on the diagonal becomes four dollars of ultimate

requirements.statement: An industry payment pattern will not exactly match a company's own experience because of differences in policy types, claim settlement practices and mix, so small deviations from it are not strong evidence the estimate is wrong.

resolution.quote: It must be reconciled to the subject book on the dimensions that actually drive development
resolution.note: syllabus page: an industry pattern differs from the company's book (coverage, limits, mix, practices), so small deviations from it are expected

requirements.statement: Under classical (limited fluctuation) credibility, the full credibility standard in claims is (z/k)^2, where k is the allowed tolerance around the expected value and z is the standard normal percentile for the stated probability.

places.quote: - **Frequency**, Poisson: $\sigma_N^2/\mu_N = 1$ and there is no severity term, so the standard reduces to $n_F = (z/k)^2$ expected claims
$$n_{\text{full}} = \left(\frac{z_{(1+p)/2}}{k}\right)^{2}$$

requirements.statement: A probability P of being within k of the expected value is a two-sided interval, so the z-value is the percentile (1+P)/2 of the standard normal (e.g., 90% uses z(0.95)).

places.quote: **Limited fluctuation (classical) credibility** asks how much data is needed for the observation to be stable within tolerance $k$ with probability $p$:

requirements.statement: Convert exposures to expected claims by multiplying by the projected claim frequency, so experience can be compared with a claims-based full credibility standard (or convert the standard to exposures by dividing by frequency).

places.quote: A standard stated in claims converts to exposures by dividing by the expected claim frequency per exposure

requirements.statement: Partial credibility under the square-root rule is Z = sqrt(n / n_full), capped at 1, where n is expected claims (or exposures) and n_full is the full credibility standard.

places.quote: $$Z = \min\!\left(1,\, \sqrt{\frac{n}{n_{\text{full}}}}\right)$$
$$Z = \min\left(\sqrt{\frac{n}{n_F}},\; 1\right)$$

requirements.statement: The trended present rates complement of credibility equals the unimplemented residual of the prior indication, (1 + prior indicated change)/(1 + prior implemented change), multiplied by net trend (loss trend over premium trend) compounded over the period from the prior rates' effective date to the target effective date.

places.quote: **Trended present rates** — the current rate adjusted to what was last *indicated* rather than implemented, and trended from the original target effective date of the current rates to that of the new rates.

requirements.statement: The credibility-weighted indicated rate change is Z × (indicated change factor) + (1 − Z) × (complement factor), expressed as a factor and then converted to a percent change by subtracting 1.

places.quote: $$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$
$$\text{Estimate} = Z \times \text{Experience} + (1 - Z) \times \text{Complement}$$

requirements.statement: Complements of credibility appropriate for first dollar ratemaking include loss costs of a larger related group, rate change of a larger related group, Harwayne's method, competitors' rates, and industry benchmarks.

places.quote: 2. **Loss costs of a larger related group** — a *separate* but similar group, e.g. owners-form contents experience for the condo form.

requirements.statement: A claims-made policy is triggered by the date the claim is reported during the policy term (subject to any retroactive date), regardless of when the event occurred.

places.quote: **Claims-Made Coverage** is a policy trigger under which the policy responds to claims *reported* during the policy period, provided the underlying loss occurred on or after the policy's **retroactive date**.

requirements.statement: An occurrence policy is triggered by the date of loss: coverage applies if the event occurs during the policy term, regardless of when the claim is reported.

places.quote: **Occurrence Coverage** is a policy trigger under which the policy responds to losses that *occur* during the policy period, however long afterwards the claim is reported.

requirements.statement: To cost a claims-made policy from a report-year-by-report-lag triangle, sum the entire row for the policy's report year (all lags, same report-year cost level); to cost an occurrence policy, sum the diagonal of cells whose occurrence year (report year minus lag) equals the policy year.

places.quote: Claims-made business is organized on a [[Report Year]] basis: in Werner's report-year-by-lag table a claims-made policy is a row, where an occurrence policy is a diagonal.
Occurrence business is aggregated on an [[Accident Year]] basis, because the accident date is the trigger: in Werner's report-year-by-lag table an occurrence policy is a diagonal.

requirements.statement: With positive loss cost trend, an occurrence policy costs more than a claims-made policy because its later-reported claims are trended through additional report years, whereas all claims-made claims are at the policy's report-year cost level.

places.quote: A claims-made policy should always cost less than an occurrence policy **as long as claim costs are increasing**.
And as long as claim costs are increasing, the occurrence policy costs more than the claims-made one (Principle 1 of claims-made policies).

requirements.statement: A claims-made policy's price is set by the report-year cost level, so misestimating report-year trend affects it little, while an occurrence policy is exposed to trend compounding over multiple report years and is more underpriced when actual trend exceeds the assumed trend.

places.quote: If there is a sudden, unpredictable change in the underlying trends, the claims-made policy priced on the prior trend will be closer to the correct price than an occurrence policy priced on the prior trend.

requirements.statement: An occurrence policy has both pure IBNR (report lag) and IBNER (settlement development), while a claims-made policy has essentially no pure IBNR because all covered claims are reported by the end of the term, leaving only IBNER.

places.quote: Because the trigger is the report date, a claims-made policy has **no pure IBNR** — only IBNER on claims already reported — so the risk of reserve inadequacy is greatly reduced relative to the [[Occurrence Coverage|occurrence]] form.
It must reserve for **pure [[IBNR]]** — claims it has no knowledge of — for as long as claims from expired policies can still emerge, which for a product like medical malpractice can be many years.

requirements.statement: An occurrence policy earns more investment income than a claims-made policy because the time from premium collection to claim payment includes report lag in addition to settlement lag.

places.quote: The investment income earned from claims-made policies is substantially less than under occurrence policies — which the target underwriting profit provision must reflect, along with the reduced pricing risk.

requirements.statement: A loss trend factor is computed from the average loss date of the experience period to the average loss date of the future period being priced, and equals (1 + annual trend) raised to the length of that period in years.

places.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.
The selected trend is applied as a factor $(1 + \hat{T})^{n}$, where $n$ is the trend period from the average date of the experience period to the average date of the forecast period.

requirements.statement: The future period's average loss date is found by taking the rate-effective period (policies written for the length of time rates are in effect), finding the average written date, and adding half a policy term, since losses occur on average midway through the policy term after writing.

places.quote: The first policy is exposed $7/1/2025$–$6/30/2026$ and the last $7/1/2026$–$6/30/2027$, so the exposure period runs $7/1/2025$ to $6/30/2027$ and its midpoint — the average loss date — is $7/1/2026$.

requirements.statement: For an accident year with losses occurring uniformly, the average loss date is the midpoint of the year (July 1).

places.quote: Accident year $2023$ runs $1/1$–$12/31/2023$; with losses occurring uniformly, its average loss date is $7/1/2023$.
The trend runs from the AY $2024$ average accident date, $7/1/2024$, to the average accident date of policies written in $2026$, $12/31/2026$: $n = 2.5$ years.

requirements.statement: A policy year of annual policies spans two years of exposure with an average written date at mid-year, so its average loss date is half a policy term later than the average written date, i.e. six months later than the same-numbered accident year's average loss date.

places.quote: This is why PY 2024 at $24$ months of maturity is comparable to AY 2024 at about $18$ months: the exposure period is twice as long, so the cohort's average loss date is six months later.

requirements.statement: Loss development projects losses for a fixed accident or policy year from their current valuation to ultimate, accounting for claims yet to be reported and closed.

places.quote: **Loss Development** is the change in the reported or paid value of a cohort of claims as it matures — the difference between losses valued at an early age and their eventual [[Ultimate Loss|ultimate]] settled value.

An AY cohort is **not final** at year end: losses still develop as claims are reported and case reserves are re-estimated, so an AY must be brought to ultimate with a [[Cumulative Development Factor|CDF]] before it can be compared with a mature year.

requirements.statement: Trending restates ultimate losses of a past period to the cost level of the future period being priced, reflecting changes in frequency and severity; because development changes valuation and trend changes cost level, the two adjustments do not overlap.

places.quote: Trend and [[Loss Development|development]] answer different questions and must both be applied: development brings immature losses to *their own* ultimate level; trend restates past losses to the level expected for similar losses in the *future* period.

In **ratemaking**, developing losses to ultimate is a distinct step from trending: development moves an immature year to its own ultimate value, while [[Loss Trend|trend]] restates it to the cost level of the future policy period.

requirements.statement: Under proportional reinsurance (quota share or surplus share) the same percentage of premium and losses is ceded, so the net loss ratio equals the direct loss ratio and no explicit reinsurance adjustment is needed in a primary rate indication.

places.quote: Proportional reinsurance may need no explicit treatment; for non-proportional reinsurance the projected losses are reduced for expected recoveries and the premium reduced by the amount ceded — or the net cost (cost of the reinsurance less expected recoveries) is included as an expense item.
Proportional reinsurance may need no explicit treatment.
Proportional reinsurance cedes premium and losses in the same proportion and may need no explicit treatment.

requirements.statement: Under non-proportional reinsurance (excess of loss, stop loss, catastrophe) premium and losses are ceded disproportionately, which distorts the loss ratio and loss development, so the reinsurance cost must be accounted for explicitly in primary ratemaking.

places.quote: Proportional reinsurance may need no explicit treatment; for non-proportional reinsurance the projected losses are reduced for expected recoveries and the premium reduced by the amount ceded — or the net cost (cost of the reinsurance less expected recoveries) is included as an expense item.

In **ratemaking**, Werner reduces projected losses by the expected non-proportional recoveries and premium by the amount ceded — or, alternatively, includes the **net cost of reinsurance** (the cost of the reinsurance minus the expected recoveries) as an expense item in the indication.

requirements.statement: Sources of investment income in the total profit provision include policyholder-supplied funds (unearned premium reserve), loss reserves (case and IBNR), and investor-supplied funds (capital and surplus); collected premium alone and underwriting income are not sources.

places.quote: Total return also includes investment income on policyholder-supplied funds (the loss and unearned premium reserves) and on capital (whether to include the latter is disputed)
**In P&C pricing:** Investment income on the [[Unearned Premium|unearned premium]] and loss reserves lets a line accept a lower underwriting profit and still earn its target return.

requirements.statement: Variable expenses are defined as a fixed percentage of premium, so they change automatically with premium and need no separate trend.

places.quote: Expense **trend**: a variable expense ratio needs none, since it changes with premium automatically.

**Variable Expenses** are underwriting expenses that vary directly with premium — premium taxes and commissions are the standard examples — and are therefore expressed as a percentage $V$ of premium and carried in the **denominator** of the rate formula.

requirements.statement: In the exposure-based projection method, fixed expenses per exposure may need trending because fixed expenses can trend at a different rate than the exposure base, whether or not the exposure base is inflation sensitive.

places.quote: A fixed expense *per exposure* on a base that does not inflate (car-years, house-years) or per policy is expected to change and is trended (see [[Loss Trend]], [[Premium Trend]]).
Because $F$ is a dollar amount, it is expected to rise with inflation.

requirements.statement: In the premium-based projection method, fixed expenses must be trended independently unless one explicitly assumes they trend at the same rate as premium, since a fixed-expense-to-premium ratio is not constant by definition.

places.quote: A fixed expense *ratio* (premium-based method) needs none if average fixed expense and average premium change at the same rate
In the premium-based method no trend is needed if average fixed expense and average premium change at the same rate

requirements.statement: Compute age-to-age development factors from a cumulative loss triangle as ratios of successive evaluations and select an average across accident years for each age interval.

places.quote: $$f_{k \to k+1} = \frac{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k+1}}{\sum_{\text{AY}} C_{\text{AY},\,k}}$$

requirements.statement: The cumulative development factor to ultimate at a given age is the product (not the sum) of the selected age-to-age factors from that age onward, including the tail factor.

places.quote: $$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1} \times \text{Tail}$$
$$\text{CDF}_{n \to \text{ult}} = \left(\prod_{k \ge n} f_{k \to k+1}\right) \times \text{Tail}$$

requirements.statement: The Bornhuetter-Ferguson ultimate equals reported loss plus expected loss (premium times expected loss ratio) times the percent unreported, 1 − 1/CDF; expected loss uses unadjusted earned premium, and trend is applied to the resulting ultimate, not to reported loss within the formula.

places.quote: $$U_{\text{BF}} = C + \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\text{CDF}}\right) \times U_{0}$$
$$U = \text{ELR} \times \text{Earned Premium}$$

requirements.statement: Trend ultimate losses and premium from each accident year's average accident date to the average accident date of the future policy period, which for annual policies written evenly is one year after the effective date of the rates.

places.quote: $t$ is the selected annual trend and $n$ the **trend period**, measured from the average date of loss in the experience period to the average date of loss in the forecast period.

The trend period $n$ runs from the average written date of the policies earning premium in the experience period to the **average written date of the policies in effect while the new rates are** — for calendar-year 2011 earned premium and annual policies written in 2013, $1/1/2011$ to $6/30/2013$, or $2.5$ years.

requirements.statement: ULAE is loaded onto loss and ALAE by multiplying by one plus the ULAE provision percentage.

places.quote: ULAE loaded at $4\%$ of loss and ALAE

requirements.statement: Use the parallelogram method to compute on-level factors: determine the portion of each year's earned premium written at each rate level, compute the average rate level, and divide the current rate level by it.

places.quote: **Werner's six steps:** date the changes and form rate level groups; find each group's area in each year; build cumulative indices; take the area-weighted average index; divide it into the current index; apply the factor to the year's earned premium.

For **annual** policies written uniformly, a rate change effective at time $p$ through year $Y$ earns over a triangle of area $\tfrac{1}{2}(1-p)^2$ in year $Y$ — so a $7/1$ change affects only $0.125$ of that year's earned premium, and a $1/1$ change affects $0.500$.

requirements.statement: For annual policies written evenly, a mid-year (July 1) rate change affects a triangle equal to 12.5% of that calendar year's earned premium.

places.quote: so a $7/1$ change affects only $0.125$ of that year's earned premium, and a $1/1$ change affects $0.500$.

requirements.statement: Fixed expense ratio is computed as fixed expenses divided by (unadjusted) earned premium; a non-recurring outlier year is excluded and the remaining years averaged to select the ratio.

places.quote: The fixed dollars are then put per exposure either by multiplying the fixed expense ratio by the projected average premium, or by dividing fixed expenses directly by exposures or policy count.
those incurred throughout the policy (general expenses) against [[Earned Premium|earned premium]], and the category ratios are added.

requirements.statement: With fixed expenses, the loss ratio method indicated rate change is (loss & LAE ratio + fixed expense ratio) / (1 − variable expense ratio − profit provision) − 1, where the loss ratio is trended ultimate loss & LAE divided by trended on-level premium, averaged across accident years.

places.quote: $$\text{Indicated Change} = \frac{\text{Projected Loss \& LAE Ratio} + F\%}{1 - V - Q_T} - 1$$
$$\text{Rate} = \frac{\text{Pure Premium} + F}{1 - V - Q_T}$$

requirements.statement: Customer lifetime value is the profit expected from a customer over their entire expected life with the insurer, summing expected profit across current and future renewal terms (discounted at the discount rate).

places.quote: **Lifetime Value** (LTV) is the present value of the expected profit from a customer relationship over its whole life, rather than over a single policy period.

requirements.statement: The retention ratio is the proportion of policies that renew at a given renewal and is predicted by a retention model as a function of the percentage rate change.

places.quote: Modelling renewal probability as a function of the rate change offered lets an insurer see the trade-off directly
$\rho(P)$ is the probability that the customer buys or renews at price $P$ (a conversion or retention model)

requirements.statement: To compute expected lifetime profit per policy, multiply each renewal term's net profit (premium minus loss & LAE, expenses) by the cumulative probability the policy is retained to that term, then sum across terms.

places.quote: \text{LTV} = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{\left(P_t - L_t - E_t\right) \times {}_{t}p}{(1 + r)^{t}}
\Pi_t = {}_{t-1}p_x\,\mathrm{Pr}_t

requirements.statement: In optimized pricing, evaluate each candidate rate change by its resulting premium and retention, compute profit for each, and select the rate change giving the highest profit (or profit as a percentage of premium).

places.quote: a larger increase raises premium per policy and lowers the number of policies, and the optimum is rarely at either extreme
P^{*} = \arg\max_{P} \; (P - C)\,\rho(P)

requirements.statement: With a 0% discount rate no present-valuing is needed, and a 0% retention at a later renewal ends the customer's life so later terms contribute no profit.

places.quote: ${}_{t}p$ is the probability the customer is still on the books at time $t$ and $r$ the discount rate.

requirements.statement: The CAS Statement of Principles Regarding Property Casualty Insurance Ratemaking has four principles, including that a rate provides for all costs associated with the transfer of risk and that a rate is reasonable, not excessive, inadequate, or unfairly discriminatory if it is an actuarially sound estimate of expected future costs of an individual risk transfer.
requirements.concept: Statement of Principles Regarding Property Casualty Insurance Ratemaking

places.quote: A rate is reasonable and not excessive, inadequate, or unfairly discriminatory if it is an actuarially sound estimate of the expected value of all future costs associated with an individual risk transfer.
**Ratemaking** (May 1988): a rate is an estimate of the expected value of future costs and provides for all of them

requirements.statement: Affordability is not part of the CAS ratemaking principles, and a rate chosen to maximize profit via a retention model, rather than from estimated future costs, does not by itself demonstrate compliance with the cost-based principles.
requirements.concept: Statement of Principles Regarding Property Casualty Insurance Ratemaking

places.quote: involving considerations such as marketing goals, competition and legal restrictions *to the extent they affect the estimation of future costs* — and the Statement confines itself to that estimation.

The indication is the actuary's best cost-based estimate; the company may still elect to implement something else, and the Statement asks that material assumptions be documented and available for disclosure.

adjustments based on **price elasticity of demand**, **propensity to shop**, **retention at an individual level** or a **propensity to ask questions or complain** are, at a minimum, inconsistent with "not unfairly discriminatory"

requirements.statement: Risk classification groups insureds with similar characteristics into classes and uses relativities to differentiate the rates of the classes, whereas individual risk rating prices a single risk using its own loss experience and characteristics.

places.quote: **Classification Ratemaking** is the segmentation of a book into rating classes and the derivation of **relativities** — the factors by which each class's rate differs from the base class — so that each risk pays according to its own expected cost.
**Individual Risk Rating** is the adjustment of one insured's premium away from the manual (class) rate, to reflect that risk's own characteristics or its own loss experience.

requirements.statement: Risk classification and individual risk rating share the purpose of matching the premium to each insured's expected losses more closely than a single average rate would, which reduces adverse selection.

places.quote: In a competitive market an insurer that charges one average rate to a heterogeneous group loses the better risks to competitors that price them properly, and retains the worse ones — the **adverse selection spiral**.
**Defences:** [[Risk Classification Restrictions|risk classification]] (price to the risk, so nobody is overcharged)
No class is perfectly [[Homogeneity|homogeneous]]: experience rating picks up the variance of the hypothetical means *within* a class.

requirements.statement: Classification rating is more appropriate than individual risk rating when there are many small, homogeneous risks, because no single risk's experience is credible but groups of similar risks yield credible relativities.

places.quote: - **Credibility** — risk classes should be large enough to allow credible statistical inferences about expected outcomes; where the data are not sufficient, the actuary balances predictability against homogeneity.
Credibility rises with size. A small risk's mod stays near $1.0$ however good or bad its recent record, because a few claims say little; a large risk approaches $Z = 1$ and effectively self-rates.
Credibility governs the **homogeneity trade-off**: splitting a book finer improves [[Homogeneity|homogeneity]] but shrinks $n$ in each cell, lowering $Z$ and handing the answer to the complement.

requirements.statement: Neither classification rating nor individual risk rating is necessary when all risks have the same expected loss cost (nothing to differentiate) or when rates are set by the regulator rather than the insurer.

resolution.quote: an insurer that charges one average rate to a heterogeneous group loses the better risks to competitors that price them properly
resolution.note: classification exists because risks are heterogeneous; where every risk has the same expected cost there is nothing to differentiate. The regulator-set-rates case is an example, not a fact to learn

requirements.statement: A rating characteristic should be excluded from a classification plan if it is not statistically significant or is highly correlated with another rating variable already in the plan, since it adds complexity or double-counts information.

places.quote: If young drivers also drive older cars, a one-way age relativity contains part of the vehicle-age effect, and rating both double-counts.
It must be statistically related to expected losses; a causal story strengthens the case, but ASOP No. 12 does not require one.

requirements.statement: A rating characteristic may be excluded if it is not objectively verifiable, because self-reported or judgment-based values are open to manipulation and inconsistent application.

places.quote: **Operational** — objective, inexpensive to obtain and verify, not manipulable by the insured.
It should be objective and hard to manipulate, practical to collect and verify, and legal ([[Risk Classification Restrictions]], [[Unfair Discrimination]]) and socially acceptable.

requirements.statement: A rating characteristic may be excluded for legal, social or cost reasons: it is prohibited by law, raises privacy or social acceptability concerns, or is too costly to collect and administer relative to its benefit.

places.quote: **Social** — privacy, causality, controllability and affordability; these are where public and regulatory objections arise.

In Canadian auto insurance the restricted list typically includes age, sex, marital status (in some provinces), credit score, and limits on [[Territorial Rating|territory]] — restrictions imposed on **social** grounds even where the variable is statistically valid.
It should be objective and hard to manipulate, practical to collect and verify, and legal ([[Risk Classification Restrictions]], [[Unfair Discrimination]]) and socially acceptable.

requirements.statement: A rating characteristic may be excluded if there is too little data at its level to estimate a stable, credible relativity.

places.quote: - **Credibility** — risk classes should be large enough to allow credible statistical inferences about expected outcomes; where the data are not sufficient, the actuary balances predictability against homogeneity.
Credibility governs the **homogeneity trade-off**: splitting a book finer improves [[Homogeneity|homogeneity]] but shrinks $n$ in each cell, lowering $Z$ and handing the answer to the complement.

**Why it is hard to estimate:** location is heavily correlated with other rating variables, so a univariate analysis of territory is distorted, and the data in each small geographic unit is sparse (Werner & Modlin Ch.11).

requirements.statement: Written exposures for a period are the exposures of all policies written (effective) during that period, counted in full over the policy term (each policy's exposure units times its term length in years).

places.quote: A $12$-month policy contributes **one** earned car-year in total, spread pro rata over its term: written the day it is issued, earned $1/12$ per month, in force from effective date to expiry.

requirements.statement: Earned exposures for a period equal the exposure units times the portion of the policy term (in years) that has expired within that period.

places.quote: **Earned Exposure** is the portion of written exposure for which coverage has actually been provided during the period — the exposure analogue of [[Earned Premium|earned premium]], and the correct denominator for a pure premium.

requirements.statement: In-force exposures at a point in time are the exposure units of policies whose effective date is on or before that date and whose expiration date is after it, counted in full without scaling by term length.

places.quote: In-force exposures count the insured units exposed to loss at the date — a snapshot with no regard to the duration of the exposure.

requirements.statement: Calendar year earned exposures count only the exposure earned within the calendar year, whereas policy year earned exposures count all exposure earned on policies written in that year, including portions earned after year-end up to the evaluation date.

places.quote: With policies written **uniformly** through the year, a calendar year earns roughly half of that year's written exposure plus half of the prior year's.

With annual policies a PY cohort is not fully written until $12$ months after the year begins and not fully earned until $24$ months, so PY data is roughly a year less mature than the corresponding [[Accident Year]] at the same valuation date.

requirements.statement: An exposure base is a measurable unit that is proportional to expected losses, practical (easy to obtain, inexpensive to verify, objective), and considerate of historical precedence.

places.quote: **Proportional to expected loss.** All else equal, a policy with two exposures should have twice the expected loss of a similar policy with one.

requirements.statement: To evaluate a proposed exposure base such as miles driven, assess it against each criterion with reasoning: more miles raises accident likelihood (proportional to losses, though less so for comprehensive), verification requires telematics or is subject to self-report manipulation (practicality), and changing from car-years brings IT cost, adjustment of historical data, and premium swings (historical precedence).

places.quote: **Practical.** Objective, and relatively easy and inexpensive to obtain and verify — which also keeps policyholders and producers from manipulating it (declared annual mileage invites more dishonesty than car-years).

requirements.statement: Close-year (closed-claim) average severity equals paid losses on claims closed during a period divided by the number of claims closed during that period.

places.quote: **Close Year** is a data aggregation method that groups claims by the calendar year in which they were finally *settled and closed*, regardless of when the loss occurred, when it was reported, or when partial payments were made.
Reported losses over reported counts, paid over closed, ultimate over ultimate — mixing them (reported losses over closed counts is the classic) produces a series that measures nothing.

requirements.statement: Changes in claims handling procedures or settlement speed (e.g., adding adjusters, clearing a backlog) change which claims close in a period, so they can shift the closed-claim severity without any change in the underlying cost of claims.
requirements.concept: Claim Settlement Patterns and Severity Distortion

places.quote: Processing changes hit the **diagonal**: they affect every open accident year in the calendar period when the change happens, which is what distinguishes them from a change in one cohort's experience.

Drivers to ask about (Friedland Ch. 4): staffing levels and adjuster caseloads, changes in settlement authority, a "close the old inventory" initiative, litigation strategy, outsourcing, and the economic or legal environment.

requirements.statement: Closing a disproportionate number of small claims lowers average closed-claim severity because the claim count rises by more than the paid losses; this is a change in mix, not a true change in claim cost.

places.quote: The trade-off is severe selection bias: within any recent accident year the claims that close first are the small, simple ones.
**Mix and dilution** — late-reported small claims pulling averages down, or a shift in the [[Mix of Business|mix]] of coverages and limits.

requirements.statement: A severity change caused by claims-processing or mix shifts should not be read as a real loss cost trend, so it should not be reflected in the selected severity trend without adjustment.

places.quote: Three distinct forces move a severity series and the analysis must separate them:

requirements.statement: A data review (verification of the data) checks several components: consistency with financial statement data, consistency with prior data, reasonableness of the data, and data definitions.

places.quote: *consistency with financial statement data*; *consistency with the prior analysis's data*, with any difference explained; … *definitions* — know what each field means (incurred, reserves and paid all mean different things to different departments)
Check that the data are internally consistent, and compare them with the data used in the prior analysis where that consistency can be expected.

requirements.statement: Reconciling data totals to financial statements is only one component of data review; totals can tie out while individual values are unreasonable or offsetting, so reconciliation alone does not make the data adequate.

places.quote: Premium can reconcile in total while records are coded to the wrong territory or class. Record-level checks are needed as well as control totals.

requirements.statement: Questionable data values, such as large negative paid claims, are not always incorrect values (e.g., they may be recoveries such as salvage and subrogation or correcting entries), so they should not be deleted or discarded without examination.

places.quote: *reasonableness* — questionable values such as large negative paid claims or fields that contradict each other are investigated, though not presumed wrong
A strange value is investigated and its definition learned before it is changed or excluded.
others combine them, record payments only, or book recoveries as negative claim payments.

requirements.statement: When questionable values are found, especially material ones, the actuary should investigate what they represent before using the data, rather than replacing the data with benchmarks or ignoring the issue.

places.quote: First, **find the definition**: ask the data owner what the field means and why these values occur.
An extreme value that is genuine carries information. Dropping it without a cause, or without disclosing it, biases the data.

requirements.statement: Actuarial standards of practice require the actuary to take steps to verify that data are reliable and sufficient, and to document the review, but do not require a formal audit of the data.
requirements.concept: Actuarial Standard of Practice on Data Quality

places.quote: A review is not an **audit**, and the actuary is not required to perform one
The analyst tests the data for reasonableness and consistency but is not required to audit the source transactions.

requirements.statement: A linear trend assumes the statistic changes by a constant dollar amount each period, so projected change equals the annual slope times the trend period length.

places.quote: Werner & Modlin: with a linear selection the trend is a constant amount, so the projected change is the selected annual amount multiplied by the length of the trend period.

requirements.statement: The least-squares slope is b = Σ(t − t̄)(y − ȳ) / Σ(t − t̄)², fitted to the observed values against time.

places.quote: $$b = \frac{\sum (t - \bar{t})(y_t - \bar{y})}{\sum (t - \bar{t})^2}$$
$\hat\beta_1 = S_{xy}/S_{xx}$ and $\hat\beta_0 = \bar{y} - \hat\beta_1\bar{x}$, where $S_{xy} = \sum(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})$ and $S_{xx} = \sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2$

requirements.statement: To project a trended value, add the slope times the trend period length to the most recent observed value (the base to be trended), not to the average of the data.
requirements.concept: Trending Historical Data to Future Period

places.quote: It is fitted by least-squares regression of the statistic itself on time, and projected by adding the slope times the length of the trend period.

requirements.statement: Underwriting-year (policy-year) data group claims by the year in which the reinsurance policy or contract became effective, so each cohort contains all contracts incepting in that year.

places.quote: **Underwriting Year** (UY), also called treaty year or contract year, groups all premium and losses by the year in which the reinsurance *contract became effective* (incepted).

**Policy Year** (PY), also called underwriting year or year of account, is a data aggregation method that groups every premium and loss transaction belonging to policies *incepting* in a given calendar year, and follows that cohort until the last claim closes.

requirements.statement: The main advantage of policy-year (underwriting-year) aggregation is a close match of claims with the premium and exposures from the same contracts.

places.quote: The offsetting advantage is an exact match of premium to exposure: … all belong to one set of contract terms — attachment point, limit, and treaty conditions

PY gives the **cleanest match** of premium to loss: every dollar of premium and every claim in the cohort arises from the same set of policies, written under the same rates, forms and underwriting rules.

requirements.statement: Policy-year (underwriting-year) claims for 12-month contracts occur over about a 24-month period, so claims take longer to be reported and ultimate claims take longer to estimate reliably than for accident-year data.
requirements.concept: Policy Year vs Accident Year Aggregation

places.quote: The price of that match is **time**. With annual policies a PY cohort is not fully written until $12$ months after the year begins and not fully earned until $24$ months, so PY data is roughly a year less mature than the corresponding [[Accident Year]] at the same valuation date.
**Accident dates** run $1/1/2024$ through $12/30/2025$ — a $24$-month exposure window.

requirements.statement: Accident-year data occur within a shorter time frame and are useful for isolating and tracking the effect of a single event such as a catastrophe or a court ruling, whereas policy-year data make such effects difficult to isolate because the claims are spread across many cohorts.

Short-tail lines (e.g., automobile physical damage, property) have short reporting and settlement periods, so paid claims and case outstanding make up a high proportion of ultimate claims at early maturities and IBNR is a small share of unpaid claims.
requirements.concept: Short-Tail and Long-Tail Lines of Business

places.quote: [[Short Tail Insurance|Short-tail]] lines — auto physical damage, homeowners property, inland marine — are near ultimate within a year or two; the estimate is mostly known, and the risk is a catastrophe rather than development.

covers lines whose claims are reported and settled quickly — typically within a year — so that reported losses are close to ultimate almost immediately and [[IBNR]] is small relative to case reserves.

requirements.statement: Long-tail lines (e.g., medical malpractice occurrence) have lengthy reporting and settlement periods, so IBNR is a large share of unpaid claims at early maturities.
requirements.concept: Short-Tail and Long-Tail Lines of Business

places.quote: [[Long Tail Lines|Long-tail]] lines — medical malpractice, workers compensation, general liability, products, excess casualty — report and settle over many years, carry large [[IBNR]], and are dominated by development uncertainty.

**Long Tail Lines** are lines of insurance whose claims take many years to be reported, litigated and paid — so that at any valuation date most of the ultimate cost is still an estimate rather than a fact.

requirements.statement: For long-tail lines, cumulative development factors for the most recent accident years can be very large, so projections based on them are highly leveraged.

places.quote: Because the [[Cumulative Development Factor|CDF]] at early maturities is large, estimates are highly **leveraged**: a small proportional change in a factor moves ultimate by a large dollar amount.
The CDF measures **leverage**. At a CDF of $4$, a dollar of distortion on the diagonal becomes four dollars of ultimate

requirements.statement: A claims-made policy covers claims reported during the policy period, whereas an occurrence policy covers claims arising from events occurring during the policy period.

places.quote: **Claims-Made Coverage** is a policy trigger under which the policy responds to claims *reported* during the policy period, provided the underlying loss occurred on or after the policy's **retroactive date**.
**Occurrence Coverage** is a policy trigger under which the policy responds to losses that *occur* during the policy period, however long afterwards the claim is reported.

requirements.statement: Claims-made experience should be segregated from occurrence experience, and actuaries often prefer report-year aggregation for claims-made data.

places.quote: Claims-made business is organized on a [[Report Year]] basis: in Werner's report-year-by-lag table a claims-made policy is a row, where an occurrence policy is a diagonal.
RY is the correct basis for [[Claims Made Coverage|claims-made]] coverage, because a claims-made policy's trigger *is* the report date

requirements.statement: Reserve estimates tend to be more accurate for high-frequency, low-severity groups of claims than for low-frequency, high-severity groups, which ordinarily require more extensive analysis.
requirements.concept: Statement of Principles Regarding Property and Casualty Loss and LAE Reserves

places.quote: **Low frequency, high severity** (excess liability, medical malpractice, property catastrophe): a handful of claims drives the result, so a single [[Large Loss|large loss]] can move a whole accident year and raw experience is rarely [[Credibility|credible]] on its own.

Frequency is usually the **more stable and more credible** of the two components: claim counts are less skewed than claim dollars, so a modest volume of exposure supports a credible frequency estimate long before it supports a credible severity estimate.

requirements.statement: The development technique assumes that historical claim development patterns are predictive of future development, so the factors from past periods apply to the latest year.

places.quote: projects each cohort to ultimate by multiplying its latest cumulative amount by a [[Cumulative Development Factor|cumulative development factor]] derived from the historical pattern.
Assumptions being made implicitly by using one at all: each cohort develops in a similar pattern, the pattern is stable over time, and the mix inside each cohort is comparable.

Development techniques assume that past development patterns will account for inflationary forces; frequency-severity techniques reflect inflation explicitly instead, at the price of being highly sensitive to the inflation assumption.

requirements.statement: Changes in the external environment, such as legal or judicial changes, can invalidate the development technique's assumption even when internal case reserving practices and settlement speed are unchanged; the actuary should then consider alternative techniques or adjust the selected development factors.

places.quote: Development patterns depend on court backlogs, limitation periods and settlement practice as much as on injury severity.
Every development-based estimate of [[Unpaid Claims|unpaid claims]] assumes the past pattern will repeat; a changing condition is whatever breaks that assumption.

requirements.statement: The expected claims technique is appropriate for the latest accident year after major changes in the legal environment (e.g., longer statute of limitations, expanded coverage from court decisions), provided a reliable expected claim ratio reflecting the changed environment can be estimated.

places.quote: The **ELR** is the whole method, and it must be derived, not assumed: from the pricing indication for that year, from mature years' ultimate loss ratios adjusted for [[Rate Level Change|rate level]] and [[Loss Trend|trend]], or from [[External Information in Reserving|industry benchmarks]].

Accidents after the reform should settle lower and possibly faster; the old pattern and claim ratios overstate them. Split accident years at the effective date and adjust expected claim ratios with a law-change estimate.

requirements.statement: A case outstanding adequacy adjustment (such as Berquist-Sherman) addresses changes in case reserve strength, not changes in the legal environment.

places.quote: restates a historical [[Development Triangle|triangle]] so that every year reflects **current** claims practice, removing the distortion caused by a change in [[Case Adequacy|case reserve adequacy]] or in [[Settlement Rate|claim settlement rates]].
A *change* in adequacy over calendar time is one of the two distortions ([[Settlement Rate|settlement rate]] is the other) that make historical development factors misleading.

requirements.statement: Both paid and reported development techniques rest on the same assumption that past development predicts future development, so a change in the legal environment affects both and unchanged settlement speed does not fix it.

places.quote: With reported claims the [[Chain Ladder Method|development technique]] assumes [[Case Adequacy|case adequacy]] has not changed; with paid claims, that settlement speed has not.
Assumptions being made implicitly by using one at all: each cohort develops in a similar pattern, the pattern is stable over time, and the mix inside each cohort is comparable.

requirements.statement: To adjust historical claims for a tort reform (legal environment change), restate each period's claims to the legal environment of the projection period, so periods in a different environment from the projection period are adjusted and periods already in that environment are left unchanged.

places.quote: A benefit-level change is restated in the data, or allowed for in the selection, so that it is not double counted.
So historical loss costs are multiplied by $1 - 0.11 = 0.89$ to restate them at the post-reform benefit level, **before** trending forward.

requirements.statement: The reform adjustment factor applied to pre-reform claims is one minus the reform's percentage reduction in claim cost (e.g., a 20% reduction gives a factor of 0.80), multiplied against the pre-reform claim ratios.

places.quote: So historical loss costs are multiplied by $1 - 0.11 = 0.89$ to restate them at the post-reform benefit level, **before** trending forward.

requirements.statement: Claims are affected by a law or tort reform based on the accident date: only claims occurring on or after the effective date are subject to the reform, so accident years before it are pre-reform.

places.quote: The insurer's data covers accident years before the reform.

resolution.note: the question states the reform reduces claims occurring on or after its effective date

requirements.statement: The expected claim ratio is selected by averaging the trended, on-level, reform-adjusted historical claim ratios across accident years (a straight average when equal weighting is chosen).

places.quote: The **ELR** is the whole method, and it must be derived, not assumed: from the pricing indication for that year, from mature years' ultimate loss ratios adjusted for [[Rate Level Change|rate level]] and [[Loss Trend|trend]], or from [[External Information in Reserving|industry benchmarks]].
as a weighted average of the trended, on-level loss ratios of all the years, with weights that decay as the years move further apart.
